News.title: Distressing audio reveals chaotic scene after Amazon plane crash in Miami that left 5 dead & victims trapped in cars
News.content:
'THE PLANE IS ON FIRE'

'THE PLANE IS ON FIRE' Distressing audio reveals chaotic scene after Amazon plane crash in Miami that left 5 dead & victims trapped in cars

HARROWING emergency audio has revealed firefighters scrambling to tackle a raging blaze after an Amazon cargo plane crashed off a runway in Miami, leaving five people dead.

Crews were heard desperately trying to reach the burning Boeing 767 after it ploughed into vehicles on a busy road, trapping victims and injuring five others.



“The plane is on fire. The plane is on fire,” one firefighter warned colleagues in chilling radio traffic obtained by the Miami Herald.

“Put your game faces on guys.”



The dramatic dispatches reveal the chaos facing emergency crews after Flight 7598 overshot a runway at Miami International Airport at around 2pm on Sunday.

Firefighters raced to get hoses close enough to the aircraft to douse the heavy flames and smoke pouring from the wreckage.

But the operation was made even more dangerous because the plane’s left engine was reportedly still running.

The live engine prevented firefighters from safely entering the aircraft to search for anyone trapped inside.

Radio traffic reportedly captured crews saying the pilots had told them they could not shut it down because they would need to “energize” the aircraft.

Firefighters were then forced to flood the engine with water in an attempt to disable it.



At the same time, other rescuers were battling to free seriously injured people from vehicles struck by the cargo jet.

One victim was trapped underneath a vehicle and had to be freed by specialist rescue crews.

Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Raied “Ray” Jadallah described the operation as a “very complex situation,” with crews also battling an active fuel leak.

Around 200 firefighters and 60 units were involved in the mammoth emergency response, with crews arriving within just 30 seconds of receiving the call.

Five people were killed in the horror crash, Miami-Dade Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz confirmed.



Another five were rushed to hospital, including three who remained in critical condition.

Officials have not yet publicly identified those killed or injured.

The pilot and co-pilot were also trapped inside the plane following the crash, Jadallah said, although it remains unclear how long they were stuck or the extent of any injuries they suffered.

Flight 7598, operated by cargo carrier 21 Air, had flown from San Juan, Puerto Rico, before landing at Miami International Airport.

The Boeing 767-300 overran the runway before smashing through the airport perimeter and striking multiple vehicles.

News.title: At least 10 dead and 64 injured after massive fireworks explosion at packed festival in Mexico
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FESTIVAL BLAST At least 10 dead and 64 injured after massive fireworks explosion at packed festival in Mexico

A HUGE firework explosion has killed at least ten people and injured 64 at a festival in central Mexico, officials say.

The huge blast collapsed a wall near the Nuestra Seora de la Luz church in Temascalcingo during a religious festival.



Hundreds were preparing to watch the firework show when the explosion occurred on Saturday night.

Two priests are among the injured, according to a local bishop.



It is not yet known what caused the fireworks to erupt in the deadly explosion.

Mexico State Attorney Generals Office has launched a probe into the blast.



Temascalcingo, around 100 miles northwest of Mexico City, is home to 66,000 people.

Dozens of people scoured the debris for survivors.

Photos show the aftermath of the explosion, the air thick with smoke.

Nearly four years ago, a powerful fireworks explosion rocked a in Huejutla, Mexico, injuring 17 people.

News.title: M1 closed after car flips in major crash as emergency crews flood scene and commuters hit with long delays
News.content:
A MAJOR UK motorway has ground to a halt after a serious collision caused a vehicle to flip in the road – sparking long delays.

The M1 southbound lanes one, three and four have all been closed between J15 and J14 near Northampton.

Emergency services have been scrambled to the chaotic scene and are working to reopen the road.

Drivers are currently facing around 35 minutes of delays along the busy route.





Commuters are being advised to check ahead of travelling to avoid delays.

Pictures from the scene show a large emergency services presence with a car in the middle of the carriageway.

Crews are working to remove the debris and the flipped motor and reopen the road.

National Highways said: “Lanes 1, 3 and 4 are closed on the M1 southbound between J15 and J14 near Northampton due to a collision resulting in an overturned vehicle.



“Emergency services are on scene dealing.

“There are delays of 35 minutes on the approach.”

News.title: Woman ‘sexually assaulted’ while walking home from shops by man ‘carrying can of lager’ as cops release e-fit in hunt
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

'ASSAULT' PROBE Woman ‘sexually assaulted’ while walking home from shops by man ‘carrying can of lager’ as cops release e-fit in hunt

POLICE have released an e-fit image of a man after a woman was allegedly sexually assaulted while walking home.

The victim was said to be approached by an unknown man in grey tracksuit bottoms and carrying a can of lager.

This ‘”worrying incident” occurred in the Merthyr Dyfan area of Barry, South Wales, sometime between 5.30am and 8am on Sunday, July 12.

The suspect is described as a white man with light brown hair around 5ft 4in tall and of stocky build.





Police have launched an appeal and urged anyone with information to come forward.

A spokesperson for South Wales Police said: “Detectives investigating a sexual assault in Barry have released an e-fit of the suspect.

“It happened in the Merthyr Dyfan area sometime between 5.30am and 8am on Sunday, July 12.

“A thorough investigation, including CCTV examination and house-to-house enquiries, has been carried out since this worrying incident was reported.



“Detectives are now making a public appeal for information.

“A woman was walking home from a nearby shop when she was assaulted by an unknown man.

“The suspect is described as white, 5ft 4in to 5ft 6in tall, aged in his 20s, of stocky build, with light brown hair and was clean shaven.

“He was holding a can of lager and was wearing grey tracksuit bottoms.



“There have been no further similar incidents reported in the area.

“Anyone who thinks they recognise the suspect or has any information, or footage, is asked to contact South Wales Police quoting 2600222188.”

News.title: Chancellor John Healey unveils £150m growth fund for North as he pledges to steer Britain through economic turmoil
News.content:
JOHN Healey will today gamble on growth to steer Britain through money market turmoil.

The Chancellor is betting on an economic boom in the wake of City jitters and Iran War fall-out.



He is under pressure to boost defence spending and faces putting up taxes in late October’s Budget.

Mr Healey will present Britain as “turning a corner” despite a slew of Labour taxes.



He will put more power in the hands of local leaders and say that growth can offset persistent inflation triggered by rising oil and gas prices.

He will say: “A new story about Britain. An optimistic story. One of resilience. Pride. Huge latent potential. A country turning a corner. A country whose people, businesses and communities are ready to seize the opportunity of new technologies and new ideas.”

The Chancellor will announce a £150million fund to help businesses in the North grow and create jobs.

Labour has already pledged to save small firms £450million by slashing form-filling.

Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith branded Mr Healey’s announcement a “policy-light word salad”, adding: “It’ll do little to comfort hard-working families and businesses worried about more tax rises.”

Reform’s Robert Jenrick said: “Even Rachel Reeves had more vision than this guff.”



Meanwhile, the British Chambers of Commerce says Employer National Insurance should be axed for under-25s to make it cheaper fto hire youngsters.

It could be paid for by scrapping the triple lock, the group claimed.

And a consultancy says households would see a boost of £2,800 a year if the country emulates Greater Manchester’s growth since devolution.

Mandala Partners says £8.5billion handed to mayors could unlock 100,000 homes and support 70,000 jobs.

News.title: Chancellor finally sees the light on Labour’s war on business – now he must go even further
News.content:
Tape squirm

CHANCELLOR John Healey’s move to cut red tape is at least a glimmer of recognition Labour is throttling small businesses.

But what about the rest?



What about the disastrous hike in Employers’ National Insurance contributions — and the self-harming minimum wage rise — that continue to make jobs for youngsters too expensive?

What about Angela Rayner’s spiteful Employment Rights reforms hampering growth in order to appease Labour’s union paymasters?



What about the energy costs crippling industry and households because of Labour’s Net Zero obsession? What about the failure to get a grip on the unsustainable welfare bill bleeding Britain dry?

Labour MPs love to crow that Liz Truss’s infamous mini-Budget “crashed the economy” as the yield on long-term UK Government bonds soared to 4.99 per cent in 2022.

They’re not so noisy since the yield shot up to 5.89 per cent last week — the highest in 28 years — because investors doubt Labour’s ability to service the country’s debt and have been spooked by Andy Burnham’s determination to take Britain back to the 1970s.

The people-pleaser PM shows scant sign of saying “No” to further taxing and spending even with debt interest already costing more than £110billion a year.

If Labour can’t see all this is the problem preventing growth — rather than just some red tape — then they really have no clue.

Troubling time

AS the Government is urged to get on with the deeply flawed Troubles Bill, Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant insists he “has veterans’ backs”.



His words ring hollow, not least because former Armed Forces minister Al Carns resigned this summer, branding the Bill “unfit for purpose”.

While terrorists enjoy immunity from prosecution, old British soldiers face a hounding in decades-old witch-hunts.

Those who break the law should be held to account, but veterans who acted lawfully — under government authority, in accordance with rules of engagement — should not face repeated investigations and legal proceedings even when there is no new or compelling evidence.

This pernicious lawfare hits not only those who served, but also the recruitment of future soldiers who know they can’t trust the Government to “have their backs”.

Lose your Ed

NOT content with the harm he caused with his Net Zero obsession, Ed Miliband seems intent on destroying relationships with key allies now he is Foreign Secretary.



He has put the country on a collision course with both the US and Israel with his video attack on the treatment of Gazans, which the US Ambassador to Israel says is contrary to the facts.

He really is a Milistone around our necks.

News.title: Hero cop swims through Thames in full kit to save unconscious colleague after police boat crash
News.content:
AN armed police officer has been hailed a hero for saving a drowning colleague despite being seriously injured himself.

He fractured his pelvis and badly injured his spine when their Thames police boat crashed.



Weighed down by his uniform, sub-machine gun and kit, he swam to his unconscious pal, who was face down after they were thrown out of their rigid inflatable boat at Westminster Bridge.

He flipped him over and kept him afloat until help arrived.



One source said: “The guy saved his colleague’s life even though he had terrible injuries himself. It was an extraordinary thing to do.’’

The hero officer is still in a wheelchair facing months of recuperation before being able to walk properly again.



In July, he was part of an anti-terror patrol called to help a lifeboat save a person in the water by Battersea Bridge, three miles up river.

But their boat hit an arch under Westminster Bridge at high speed.

Tourists watching above feared there had been an explosion on board.

The lifeboat turned round and plucked the officers from the river.



They were taken to hospital with three other colleagues, including the seriously injured driver.

An investigation is under way.

News.title: Two Border Force officers arrested at Heathrow over alleged drug trafficking
News.content:
TWO Border Force officers based at the UK’s biggest airport were nicked on suspicion of drug trafficking, The Sun can reveal.

A woman was arrested at Heathrow Airport and her male colleague detained at home on the same day because he was off sick.



The joint August 26 raids have stunned aviation colleagues and baffled irate bosses.

National Crime Agency officers were involved as the woman staff suspect was handcuffed as she went about her duties in Terminal 3.



The arrested duo were part of the law enforcement command within the Home Office responsible for immigration, passport control, and customs security across all four operating Heathrow terminals.

Both have been suspended from Border Force while investigations continue.



A source told The Sun yesterday: “These arrests have sent shockwaves through the Heathrow community.

“Border Force staff perform important duties including detecting and stamping out drug use and importation into the UK.

“The fact that two officers have been nicked on suspicion of drug trafficking is frankly astonishing.

“This has been a complex and forensic investigation, which is ongoing. It has left colleagues open-mouthed and in disbelief at what has happened.”



A Home Office spokesperson told The Sun yesterday: “We expect the highest standards from our Border Force officers in their vital role to protect our borders.

“We are unequivocal that where unacceptable behaviour is found, it will be subject to robust disciplinary proceedings.”

News.title: Anak Krakatau eruption - live: Airports close due to volcanic ash as 170,000 passengers stranded
News.content:
Indonesia's Anak Krakatau volcano erupted this weekend, sending a cloud of ash 50,000ft into the sky and forcing the cancellation of all flights at the country's main airport

More than 270,000 passengers have been stranded after Indonesia's Anak Krakatau volcano erupted, blasting ash 50,000 ft into the sky and grounding more than 2,300 flights.

Seven airports, including Jakarta's main international hub Soekarno-Hatta International, remain closed this morning as volcanic ash blankets the capital and surrounding areas.

Operations have been suspended until at least 6pm local time (12pm UK time), with passengers left scrambling for refunds and alternative flights.

Anak Krakatau had shown signs of activity since Friday before erupting twice on Sunday, Indonesia's Geological Agency said.

The volcano - which translates to "child of Krakatoa" in Indonesian - was formed following the eruption of Krakatoa in 1883, one of the most violent volcanic events in recorded history.

News.title: Woman sent £170 bill after five-minute drop-off at airport
News.content:
Woman sent £170 bill after five-minute drop-off at airport

Jopsie Eccles says they were told to pay £170 or go to court

Woman sent £170 bill after five-minute drop-off at airport

A mum has blasted the “ridiculous” £170 airport parking fine she received after a five-minute drop-off led to the threat of court. Josie Eccles had travelled to the airport with her husband, 33, to catch a flight to Malta with her mum and three-year-old son.

‌



The 32-year-old claims her husband pulled into the drop-off zone at around 2pm, unloaded their luggage and said goodbye before heading off. But the couple later realised they had forgotten to pay the airport's £5 drop-off charge within the required 24-hour period.

‌



Josie says they accepted they would have to pay a penalty and even tried checking the airport's payment portal for the charge – but no fine appeared. “My husband was there for under five minutes,” said Josie, a marketing consultant from Cheshire.

‌



View 3 Images Josie Eccles says ther weren't given a chance to pay before the threatening letter

“A couple of days later, I was still in Malta and was speaking to my husband on the phone and asked if he had remembered to pay the charge. I was frustrated that both of us had forgotten to pay within the allocated window, but aware that these things happen and just accepted we would probably have a penalty to pay.

‌



“My husband then checked the payment portal on the website where you usually pay the charge and entered the vehicle details, expecting to see a penalty fine, but nothing was there. I tried again a few days later, and still no charge appeared, so we thought we’d just wait and see if we got a letter in the post.”

But it wasn't until almost two months later that Josie says she opened a letter from a debt collection firm. The letter claimed she had ignored previous correspondence and said the charge had risen to £170. Josie was given the option of paying the £170 in full or £42.50 over four months, while the letter warned the amount could increase further and potentially lead to court action.

She says she was stunned because she had never received the original parking charge notice. Josie said: “I was very confused, as it had been two months since the airport drop-off and I had received no correspondence at all so to receive a letter from a debt recovery company seemed rather extreme. At this point, I thought it must be a misunderstanding, and I would be able to resolve the issue by speaking with them.”

‌



View 3 Images Josie Eccles

Josie claims she immediately tried to appeal the charge through Manchester Airport's car parking operator, APCOA. But she says she received an automated response telling her that she had missed the appeal window and that the matter had already been passed to debt collectors.

‌



She then called the debt recovery firm to explain what had happened. According to Josie, they told her that Manchester Airport had evidence that a letter had been sent to her on June 5. But when she asked whether it had been sent by tracked or recorded delivery, she was allegedly told it hadn’t.

Josie says this left her in an impossible position because the original letter contained the information she needed to pay the penalty. She said: “Not at any point did I try to get out of paying anything. I just wanted the opportunity to pay the initial fine, which would have been £60 if paid within 14 days.

“The only way I would know how to pay the penalty fine was by reading the instructions sent in the letter, so without the letter I had no chance of ever paying the charge before it was handed over to debt recovery. He said my options were to either pay the fine in full, which is £170, or I could seek independent legal advice and email in a dispute that they would look into it.”

‌



In the meantime, Josie says she received two further letters threatening potential court action and warning that the amount could rise to up to £235. Josie claims she contacted the debt firm again and says a member of staff confirmed that her emails had been received but told her the company would not investigate disputes.

View 3 Images Josie Eccles had travelled to the airport with her husband, 33, to catch a flight to Malta

‌



She says she was told her choices were to pay £170 or go to court, where the charge could potentially rise. She alleges she was then told that Manchester Airport would be responsible for taking any court action. Josie said: “I completed an online enquiry for Manchester Airport explaining I wanted to pay the £60 fine, detailed my communication with the debt company and reattached the dispute I had submitted to them with all the legal grounds.

“Within 10 seconds of submitting, I had received an AI response stating this had been handed over to debt recovery and I should liaise directly with them. I then forwarded that response along with my online enquiry submission to the complaints department, saying that was not an adequate response and I would like somebody to review the case so I can resolve this and pay the £60 fine.

“I have still not had any response or acknowledgement.”

‌



Josie insists that she accepts responsibility for forgetting to pay the original £5 charge on 30 May but she believes the escalation is unfair because she claims she was never given the opportunity to respond to the original penalty.

She said: “I’m extremely frustrated. I hold my hands up; we forgot to pay the standard £5 charge within the next 24 hours, so a fine was expected, but to increase it to up to £235 was ridiculous. If I had been ignoring communication, it would maybe be justified, but I have responded to every bit of communication I have received, which surely shows I would have responded had I received the initial letter.

“I can afford to pay the fine; it's not about financial difficulty. It's about the principle of the system being set up to catch you out and the lack of reason they have. If the letter is so important, surely it would be sent tracked?

‌



“Or at least they would try a few attempts before sending it over to debt collectors.”

She believes airports should introduce a free grace period for motorists who are only at the terminal for a few minutes. Josie added: “I’ve used Manchester Airport many times both before and after this encounter and always paid the drop-off charge on time.

“They’ll have a record of this on their system, which validates the fact I did not intentionally avoid paying. Sometimes people forget and these things happen. Other passengers could easily make the same mistake.

‌



“It's very easy to forget. There’s no option to pay at a machine or barrier while you’re there, so they are relying on people remembering to pay later on, which, whether you’re the person travelling through the airport or the person doing the drop-off, it’s easy to get distracted.

“I'm sure that’s why they removed the barriers, as they knew it would catch people out. The cars are logged using ANPR on their registration plates, so surely you should be able to pay on the same payment system even if outside the 24-hour window, with an additional penalty charge added.

“I think it’s ridiculous airports charge you for drop-off and pick-up. I think under 10 minutes should be free, but unfortunately all airports in the UK at least charge these days.”

Article continues below

An APCOA spokesperson said: “We have been in contact with the customer and offered the original charge of £60. The customer has since made payment of the £60, and the matter is now resolved.”

Manchester Airport has been contacted for comment.

News.title: Five killed as Amazon plane overshoots runway and crashes at Miami airport
News.content:
Five people died after an Amazon Air cargo plane overshot the runway while attempting to land at Miami International Airport on Sunday

Five killed as Amazon plane overshoots runway and crashes at Miami airport

An Amazon Air cargo plane overshot the runway and burst into flames while landing at a major Florida airport on Sunday.

Five people were killed and another five injured during the incident, which occurred at Miami International Airport at around 2pm local time.

Thick black smoke and huge flames could be seen engulfing the Amazon plane as emergency services raced to the airport.

The crash brought operations at Miami International Airport to a standstill, however flights have since resumed.

Amazon said it is "working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened".

News.title: Woman loses 120lbs in a year without jabs, pills or surgery
News.content:
Woman loses 120lbs in a year without jabs, pills or surgery

Jenny Lee says she didn't even resort to counting calories

View 8 Images Jenny Lee before her weight loss

A woman has lost 120lbs without counting a single calorie or using weight loss jabs or surgery, achieving the transformation with 'old-school' methods. Jenny Lee says she struggled with her weight from the age of 14 and eventually found herself wearing a UK 26.

‌



The 30-year-old says she was relentlessly bullied and mistreated due to her size, was pre-diabetic and was considered morbidly obese. Now, she is almost unrecognisable, wearing a UK 6-8. “My life used to truly revolve around food and I used to live to eat,” said Jenny, a corporate communications worker.

‌



Her relationship with food first began to spiral after she got her driving licence and suddenly had the freedom to buy whatever she wanted. Despite growing up in a household where her mother prioritised healthy food and fitness, Jenny found herself increasingly turning to fast food, sweets and fried meals.

‌



View 8 Images Jenny had been putting on weight since she was at school

A typical day could begin with a Venti Starbucks Frappuccino and pastry, followed by a snack. Lunch would often be fried chicken, large fries and a large soda, followed by a huge dessert. Dinner was usually another fried meal with mashed potatoes, rolls and butter, before another sweet treat to finish the day.

Before long, the weight piled on. Jenny said: “My weight affected almost every aspect of my life. I was physically uncomfortable, but the mental and emotional side was so much harder. I thought about my weight constantly, what I was wearing, how I looked sitting down, whether I would be the biggest girl in the room, whether someone was looking at me or judging me.

‌



“There were times I didn't want to participate or be seen because I was so uncomfortable in my own skin.”

View 8 Images The weight was impacting Jenny's health and wellbeing

After years of feeling trapped, Jenny had an epiphany. Jenny said: “I had this epiphany that this is the only body I'm ever going to have. I was 22 years old and it just hit me that this was all in my control and I was the only one who could change my predicament.

‌



“I'm going to live in it for the rest of my life, and I finally realised I needed to start taking care of it instead of constantly fighting against it. I also had to be honest with myself and realise that I was the one who had gotten myself to this point, which meant I was the only person who could get myself out of it.

“No one was going to walk in and change my life for me. If my choices had gotten me here, then my choices could take me somewhere different. That was when my mindset really changed.”

View 8 Images Jenny was unhappy at her heaviest

‌



Rather than setting herself the daunting target of losing the daunting amount of weight needed, Jenny committed to following Whole30 and moving her body every day for just 30 days. She began by spending 20-30 minutes on the treadmill or elliptical daily, before joining a gym and discovering a passion for fitness.

Over the course of a year, she had lost 120lbs naturally. Jenny said: “It felt completely impossible. I had convinced myself that because I couldn't go back and undo what had already happened to my body, there was no point in taking care of the body I had now.

“Eventually, I had to ask myself what was scarier: starting a journey that felt impossible, or looking back years from now wishing I had started today. I made the deal with myself that I would give it 30 days – just 30 days where I would stop making excuses, stop starting over and truly show up for myself.

‌



View 8 Images Jenny began by spending 20-30 minutes on the treadmill or elliptical

“If I got to the end and hated it, I never had to do it again. But somewhere in those 30 days, something clicked. I started feeling proud of myself and I started believing that maybe I really could do this. By the end of the 30 days, I was hooked.

“And I was so hooked to how empowered I was feeling, I didn’t ever want to lose that again.”

‌



Jenny focused on whole foods and daily movement, while removing refined sugar, grains, dairy, soy and gluten from her diet. She began preparing protein-rich meals and keeping healthy snacks ready in the fridge so that making a better choice was easier.

Breakfast could be scrambled eggs with meat, while lunch might be eggs with turkey and sweet potatoes. Dinner typically consisted of a protein source, potatoes, vegetables and fruit. S he also does at least 10,000 steps a day and loves strength training and Pilates.

View 8 Images Jenny focused on whole foods and daily movement

‌



Crucially, Jenny says she never tracked calories or macros throughout her journey. She said: “I know calorie deficits work amazingly for some people, but the way my brain works, it never clicked. I couldn’t keep track of the micros and macros and would stress too much over the numbers.

“I realised that for me, counting chemicals in food mattered more than counting the calories. I would so much rather eat my classic stuffed dates that are more calories than someone’s protein ice cream, because eating whole, healthy foods that aren’t super processed, full of fake ingredients and fillers and gums, is so much better for you.

“Paying attention to the ingredients in foods, rather than the calories, made the biggest difference in my life. I don’t weigh myself, but focus on how I am feeling. My priority is being strong and healthy, not necessarily as thin as I can be.”

‌



Since losing weight, Jenny has noted a huge change in the way other people approach her. She said: “I spent so much time trying to make myself valuable in other ways before losing weight. I would do anything for anyone, rarely say no and constantly put other people's needs before my own. I picked myself apart and genuinely believed that my weight determined how other people saw me and how worthy I was of being liked.

View 8 Images Jenny is more confident

“After I lost the weight, some of those friendship dynamics completely changed. I felt like people who had never compared themselves to me before started seeing me differently, and in some relationships I began to feel a sense of competition that had never existed before.

‌



“Some friendships survived that change and became even stronger, while others didn't. One of the strangest parts has been seeing how differently some of the boys I grew up with interact with me now. The popular boys who would have never looked twice at me, let alone gone out of their way to talk to me, suddenly knew exactly who I was after I lost the weight and started reaching out.

View 8 Images Jenny lost 120lbs

“Girls who would have never wanted to hang out with me also reached out to say we should hang out. They would have never wanted to hang out before I lost the weight. It's such a strange feeling because I'm still the same girl they went to school with.

‌



“Experiences like that have made me realise just how differently the world can treat you when your appearance changes.”

She added: “My life has changed in almost every way. I'm more confident, but more than that, I feel empowered. When something feels impossible, I can look back at what I've already done and remind myself that I can do hard things.

“There's also a freedom in my life now that is hard to explain unless you've lived without it. I don't walk into a room thinking about how my clothes look on me, how I'm standing, how I'm sitting or whether someone is judging what I'm eating.

Article continues below

“I don't spend every moment trying to make myself look smaller or worrying about how much space I'm taking up. I can just be present.”

News.title: Iran to announce a new 'exclusion zone' near Strait of Hormuz as war continues
News.content:
Iran to announce a new 'exclusion zone' near Strait of Hormuz as war continues

Around 20% of global oil traded passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the war, which sparked after joint US-Israeli strikes were carried out on several key Iranian site in February

View 3 Images Three boys play in the shallow waters of the Strait of Hormuz, as a plume of smoke rises from an explosion in July (Image: AP Photo/Razieh Poudat)

The new head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council said an "exclusion zone" will be announced outside the Strait of Hormuz aimed at vessels it believes are attempting to transit the waterway.

‌



Speaking to Iran's state broadcaster on Sunday, September 6, Mohsen Rezaei's said Tehran plans to announce an "exclusion zone" but provided few details.

‌



Just one day earlier, the US hit three Iranian oil tankers in response to Tehran launching ballistic missiles at American warships.

‌



View 3 Images The United States said it struck and destroyed three Iranian oil tankers on September 5 in response to attempted missile attacks on naval vessels (Image: US Central Command (CENTCOM)/AFP via Getty Images)

Experts called the launches a dangerous escalation after Iran's previous attacks at sea targeted commercial shipping.

The US and Iran have been at war since February 28, when joint US-Israeli strikes were carried out on several key Iranian site.

‌



Iran retaliated by striking US allies in the Middle East and closing the Strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of global oil passed before the conflict.

The US in turn implemented a blockade on Iranian ports in the strait.

The new zone should be announced in the coming days and weeks.

‌



It "will begin from the line of the US naval blockade, extend toward the Strait of Hormuz, and from this side continue into the Persian Gulf," Rezaei said.

"Any ship that enters this area with the intention of passing through the Strait of Hormuz and is identified will be placed on our sanctions list."

It is not clear where Iran defines the location of the US blockade.

‌



View 3 Images Fuel prices have climbed again as traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains slow (Image: AP Photo/Vahid Salemi)

The American military has said over 20 warships are supporting the blockade.

As of Sunday, the blockade had redirected 92 commercial ships and disabled three.

Article continues below

Also on Sunday, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said that on average, nine million barrels of oil a day are getting through the strait. This should help to relieve pressure on energy prices.

Wright told CNN that with oil also flowing through pipelines in the region, "we're probably two-thirds or more of pre-conflict flows."

Meanwhile, Rezaei in his interview with state TV claimed that "every day we are selling one million, one and a half million (barrels), as if Iran's oil production and trade are continuing as usual."

News.title: Sickle cell breakthrough transformed patients' lives - but thousands more blood donors needed urgently
News.content:
Sickle cell breakthrough transformed patients' lives - but thousands more blood donors needed urgently

On Sickle Cell Awareness Month, patients revealed how donated blood has transformed their lives - as the NHS urges thousands more donors to donate

View 5 Images Nikki relies on donated blood for regular red cell exchanges (Image: Supplied)

When Caroline Fyneface was born, a simple heel prick meant doctors knew she was living with sickle cell before she was old enough to experience its devastating effects.

‌



The 23-year-old was among the first generation of babies to benefit from England’s newborn screening programme, which this year marks 20 years since its nationwide rollout was completed. But knowing what lay ahead could not prepare Caroline for the reality of the condition. She was 13 when she suffered her first serious sickle cell crisis and, in the years that followed, hospital admissions became increasingly frequent - at times happening every month.

‌



Sickle cell is an inherited blood disorder where red blood cells become sickle-shaped rather than circular, causing agonising blockages which can damage organs and lead to serious complications including blindness and strokes.

‌



View 5 Images Caroline's sickle cell was detected through the newborn screening (Image: Supplied)

Simple 10 minute procedure helps save 50,000 lives in a year READ MORE :

Caroline told the Mirror: “I think my life would be different [without the screening]. I don’t think I would have known about sickle cell until that time when I was 13 and having that first crisis . It would’ve been even scarier having to navigate that at that age.”

Her health continued to take its toll while studying Law with Criminology at Oxford Brookes University. Caroline said: “In my undergraduate I spent more time in hospital than I did at lectures, and I feel like I missed out on so much of the university experiences.”

‌



But two years ago, Caroline began receiving regular red cell exchanges, which replace sickled cells with healthy red blood cells from donors. She relies on seven to eight bags every seven weeks.

She said: “I get exchanges every seven weeks where I’m left with bruises and sores all over, but when I get my energy back - it’s almost like I’m a new person.”

View 5 Images Caroline receives seven to eight bags of donated blood every seven weeks (Image: Supplied)

‌



Caroline has now started her Master’s degree in Legal Practice as she works towards qualifying as a solicitor. Her admissions have fallen from almost every month to about five in two years.

She said: “I feel like I’ve had a new lease of life because I’ve been hospitalised less. I’ve definitely had more time to be a young a young person rather than a young sick person.”

Her story is one example of how life with sickle cell has changed for a generation diagnosed earlier and were able to benefit from advances in specialist care and treatment. Before newborn screenings became universally available, some children were only diagnosed after becoming seriously ill, sometimes with life-threatening complications.

‌



Now, more than 19,000 people in England live with sickle cell, with earlier diagnosis and advances in treatment helping more patients receive specialist care. The milestone comes during Sickle Cell Awareness Month, which aims to increase understanding of the condition and the experiences of those living with it.

But the progress which has helped Caroline and thousands of others live fuller lives has brought with it an increasingly urgent problem - there is not enough donated blood to meet demand. The NHS can currently supply only about half of the blood needed by people with sickle cell, and urgently requires at least 16,000 additional Black heritage donors, as they are more likely than white donors to have the RO blood subtype, which is vital in treating patients.

View 5 Images Yann-Elie was inspired to become a blood donor after sickle cell touched his life (Image: Supplied)

‌



Caroline said: “We really need more and more blood, and especially from Black heritage communities. Idon’t think I can imagine how i would feel having to be turned away because there’s not enough blood for me to take it.”

Behind every bag of blood Caroline and other patients receive is another person who has chosen to donate. For 22-year-old politics student Yann-Elie Asket, from Greenwich, that decision is personal.

He was still at primary school when his younger cousin died from complications of sickle cell – years before he fully understood the condition which had taken her life.

‌



Yann-Elie told the Mirror: “I remember being in Year 4 and hearing that my cousin passed away due to sickle cell complications, and seeing the effects that sickle cell actually had before even understanding what it was. But it was not until Year 10 that I properly understood what sickle cell actually does to someone. Unfortunately that was after I already felt the effects of it.”

Years later, seeing his close friend Abby live with sickle cell prompted Yann-Elie to research how he could help. He discovered the importance of donation and that his O positive blood had the highly-sought after RO subtype.

He said: “If given a little bit of my time and a little bit of my blood can be someone else’s suffering even in a small way, then that’s something I want to do and really advise other people to do as well."

‌



View 5 Images Nikki turned her experiences of living with sickle cell into her one-woman play (Image: Supplied)

For Nikki Fagbemi, donated blood has meant fewer days in a hospital bed and helped turn those experiences into a story now being told on stage. The writer and actor receives about 10 units of blood every six weeks through regular red cell exchanges.

Those experiences inspired Bed Five, the one-woman play she took to the Edinburgh Fringe Festival. It was also shaped by the death of her friend Isau, who lived with sickle cell, which forced Nikki to confront her own “mortality”.

‌



Nikki said: “Taking Bed Five to Edinburgh feels incredibly special because it’s an opportunity to tell an authentic story that isn’t often seen on stage. If audiences leave understanding sickle cell a little better, or if someone decides to become a blood donor because of it, then that’s an amazing result.”

She added: “It was the last few years that I’ve kind of realised that my sense of humour is really what gets me through life. I’m in a space that is like if you don’t laugh you’re going to cry and I’m tired of crying.”

Sickle Cell Society Iyamide Thomas, NHS Engagement Lead for Screening Programme said: "The past 20 years have brought significant progress for people living with sickle cell disorder. Newborn screening means babies can be diagnosed before they become seriously unwell and connected to specialist care from the very beginning of their lives. Early diagnosis is only the start of a person's journey with sickle cell.

Article continues below

"We are now seeing the benefits of advances in treatment, including red cell exchange, which can make a profound difference to people who experience frequent and severe sickle cell crises. But these treatments depend on having access to a reliable supply of closely matched blood.

News.title: One of Britain's worst sex predators Zhenhao Zou could face even more charges after raping 10 women
News.content:
One of Britain's worst sex predators Zhenhao Zou could face even more charges after raping 10 women

CPS lawyers examined claims relating to seven more women, after Zhenhao Zou, 28, was jailed last year for life with a minimum of 24 years for drugging and assaulting 10 victims

View 2 Images Zhenhao Zou, 28, was jailed last year for life (Image: PA)

One of Britain's most prolific sexual predators could face further charges, as prosecutors examine rape and abuse claims related to seven more women.

Zhenhao Zou, 28, was jailed last year for life with a minimum of 24 years for drugging and assaulting 10 victims. Engineering PhD student Zou befriended fellow Chinese nationals online before inviting them for drinks at his flats in London or an unknown location in China.

Zou filmed some attacks and kept a trophy box of victim mementos. Only three of the 10 victims he was convicted of attacking have been identified, but police fear he could have targeted more than 60. Detectives appealed for women to come forward after he was jailed at Inner London Crown Court.

Now a file submitted to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) contains evidence of alleged rape and administering a substance with intent to commit a sexual offence.

Zhenhao Zou: Inside dark twisted life of perverted student jailed for raping 10 women READ MORE :

Serial rapist could face dozens of fresh charges as 24 more women come forward READ MORE :

View 2 Images Zhenhao Zou, 28, could face further charges (Image: PA)

It relates to reports made by five women who contacted police following the appeal, as well as two further alleged offences of rape involving two unidentified women. A charging decision has not been made and detectives continue to liaise with the CPS as prosecutors consider the evidence.

Separate enquiries continue into allegations involving women who were allegedly sexually assaulted in China. British detectives are working to obtain evidence through formal international legal processes.

Det Chief Supt Angela Craggs said: "I would like to thank the women who have come forward and spoken to our officers since our appeal. We recognise how difficult it can be to report offences of this nature and every woman who has contacted us has shown considerable courage.

"The submission of this file of evidence marks a significant step in our investigation. While we await a decision from the CPS in relation to allegations concerning women in the UK, our enquiries remain ongoing.

"We remain committed to supporting victim-survivors and pursuing all available lines of enquiry. I would encourage anyone who believes they may have been affected, or anyone with information that could assist our investigation, to contact us.

"Every report will be treated seriously, handled with care and sensitivity, and investigated thoroughly by specially trained officers."

Zou's crimes began to emerge in November 2023, when a woman went to police. There was not enough evidence to charge him over the claim, but when his phone was examined, officers found videos of him raping unconscious women.

Pipettes and drugs including ketamine, Xanax and MDMA were later discovered in his London flat. After a month-long trial, Zou was found guilty of raping three women in London and another seven in China between 2019 and 2023.

He was convicted of 11 counts of rape, with two of the offences relating to one victim.

Zou was also convicted of three counts of voyeurism, 10 of possession of an extreme pornographic image, one of false imprisonment and three of possession of a controlled drug with intent to commit a sexual offence. Sentencing him, Judge Rosina Cottage said Zou, who most recently lived in Elephant and Castle, South London, planned and executed a campaign of rape, treating women as sex toys for his own pleasure.

Article continues below

Reports can be made by emailing survivors@met.police.uk or by calling 101 from within the UK, quoting CAD1258/04SEP26.

News.title: A&E heroes under attack with workers kicked in the face and racially abused
News.content:
A&E heroes under attack with workers kicked in the face and racially abused

At least once a week A&E staff suffer violence and aggression at work prompting a call for action

View 4 Images Stressed NHS staff are facing 'intolerable' violence and aggression at work

Shattered A&E staff face violence or aggression on a daily or weekly basis, with some workers kicked and others racially abused, health leaders have said.

‌



The NHS has become a 'dangerous place to work' it was claimed, after a shocking new survey by the Royal College of Emergency Medicine (RCEM) revealed three quarters of A&E staff witness “appalling and intolerable” violence and aggression at work.

‌



One consultant told how he'd been kicked in the face by an aggressive patient lying on a trolley that he was trying to help.

‌



A resident doctor, speaking anonymously, said: "Working in the emergency department, you brace yourself for a lot, but nothing truly prepares you for direct, hateful verbal abuse, especially when it's racially charged."

The RCEM are now calling for the Government to take “immediate action” after quizzing 2,126 staff in emergency departments. They found 96% have experienced violence or aggression from patients or other members of the public.

And some 73% said this happened weekly or even daily. Two thirds said the incidents involved discrimination against them.

‌



They now say "it’s time for action" and Governments, employers and organisations need to "stand up for NHS staff" and those who "intimidate, abuse or assault" staff face "meaningful" consquences.

Unison, described the violence faced by staff is "deplorable' and said the country needs "better systems for reporting and investigating incidents".

View 4 Images Violence against staff has become 'intolerable' (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Mass 'stabbing' at Essex hotel event with 100 guests as police swoop on suspects READ MORE :

Volodymyr Zelensky welcomes Donald Trump's envoys for first Kyiv visit since Russia invaded READ MORE :

The Royal College of Nursing, responding to the findings, said the NHS "is becoming a more dangerous place to work" and the RCEM fear staff will quit the NHS as they feel no ‘meaningful action’ is taken after attacks by either their bosses or the justice system.

NHS workers have suffered shocking abuse and violence in recent years including broken bones, a finger bitten off, broken jaws, punching, spitting and even gun and acid attack threats.

But now according to a survey by the RCEM, who have launched a ‘Safe to Care’ campaign, only four per cent said they always felt safe working in ED, and barely more than half (57%) felt safe most of the time.

‌



They point out if this is left to continue, the impact this will have on the workforce “could be devastating for Emergency Medicine” as 75% of staff reported short-term stress and anxiety, 40% are experiencing burnout, 14% taking time off work and 28% experiencing long-term stress or anxiety.

Meanwhile, many staff said they had little confidence that reporting incidents will lead to action, with fewer than half (41%) of staff who made a report saying their trust took ‘meaningful action’.

View 4 Images NHS staff are facing an "appalling" level of violence in emergency departments (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Dr Ian Higginson, President of the Royal College of Emergency Medicine, said: “No one should go to work fearing or, worse, expecting, to be attacked, intimidated or abused. Nor should they lack confidence that their employers have their backs, or that the judicial system will kick in.

“Yet, that’s the reality faced by the majority of my colleagues in EDs across the country. They often do not feel safe to care for patients.

“It is an appalling state of affairs which is contributing towards many people seriously considering whether Emergency Medicine – or even healthcare in general – is for them.

‌



“Tackling violence and aggression is crucial for the wellbeing of staff, whose dedication to the NHS is all too frequently being repaid in kicks, punches and abhorrent verbal abuse.

“We know that long waits and crowding are key drivers of this, but that is not the fault of staff – that's on our governments. Every hour of every day, our Emergency Medicine teams are there for patients. It’s time staff received the respect and safety they deserve.

“This should not be a novel concept to anybody. Much has been said by us and other organisations over the years about violence and aggression towards healthcare staff. But the problem seems to be getting worse, not better.

‌



"It’s time for action, time for governments, employers and organisations stand up for NHS staff, and time to ensure that those who intimidate, abuse or assault those who are trying to care for them face meaningful consequences for their actions.”

Workers quizzed pointed out that long waiting times (90%), overcrowding (85%), staff shortages and corridor care (both 65%) was “making the problem worse”.

“Tackling these issues will undoubtedly create a calmer environment in A&E, which provokes fewer incidents,” the REM said.

‌



They are asking for the Government to prevent violence and abuse before it occurs,by getting rid of long waits to be seen, crowding and corridor care, whilst strengthening security standards

Supporting staff through better training, reporting, follow-up, and links with the police.

Improving accountability of organisations to protect and support NHS staff, with better working across systems to ensure perpetrators face justice

‌



Dr Catherine Hayhurst, co-chair of the RCEM Quality in Emergency Care Committee, said: “Safe to Care has a very clear goal: make EDs a place in which you can work without fear of intimidation or attack.

“Some of the stories that our members have told the campaign so far have been heartbreaking – but not surprising. Whilst most patients and relatives continue to be a pleasure to treat, it is true that we are seeing increasing levels of unacceptable behaviour from a significant minority.

“Anyone who works in ED knows that violence and aggression towards healthcare staff has become normalised. That must end and we call on policymakers and NHS leaders to help us make EDs a safer place for staff.”

‌



The survey was the result of 2126 responses received between April 27th and May 31st this year.

Responding to the results. RCN General Secretary and Chief Executive Professor Nicola Ranger said: “These figures are profoundly shocking and show the torrent of abuse that health workers face, sometimes on a daily basis.

"We know the NHS is becoming a more dangerous place to work, and this falls especially hard on female dominated professions like nursing. Far too many are being forced to take time off or even leave the profession because of the physical and mental scarring that can result from these attacks.

‌



View 4 Images The NHS has become a 'dangerous place to work' (Image: Getty Images)

“Employers have a legal duty to protect their staff. Tackling this emergency isn’t easy, but employers, those at the top of the NHS and the government must face it head on. The starting point for employers has to be transparency and accountability and that means acting, being seen to act, and empowering staff to speak up.

"At a national level, we need strong urgency from the government on addressing the rising pressures on services which are catalysing this appalling behaviour.”

‌



A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: "Any acts of violence, abuse or harassment towards NHS staff are completely unacceptable and will not be tolerated.

"Everyone working in our national health service has a fundamental right to be safe at work, and it is deeply concerning that so many emergency department staff continue to experience this behaviour.

"That is why this government recently introduced new NHS staff standards, which set out the steps that every NHS employer across the country must take to prevent and reduce violence and abuse against their staff and help ensure they can do their jobs safely."

Article continues below

UNISON head of health Helga Pile said: “Nobody should face violence or abuse while simply doing their jobs. For aggression to be aimed at NHS workers who’re trying to provide care and save lives is even more deplorable.

“Pressures on the NHS mean staff are working in an ever more stressful environment, and the threat of attack or abuse is rising. That needs to be tackled immediately to stop workers leaving essential roles.

“Better systems for reporting and investigating incidents are needed. And far more must be done to prevent and reduce violent attacks, with procedures put in place to deal with them.”

News.title: Watch: Anti-migrant boat protesters block roads in Portsmouth
News.content:
Police faced off with hundreds of protesters in Portsmouth, in the second large-scale anti-migrant protest of the weekend.

Demonstrators blocked roads and tried to prevent around 140 migrants, who had crossed the English Channel in a single dinghy, from leaving the city.

Hampshire Police urged people to avoid the Eastney Landing ferry port area, where the migrants were brought ashore, and said a dispersal order was in place, meaning anyone failing to comply could be arrested.

The government condemned "the intimidating and thuggish behaviour" of the protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore masks.

News.title: New videos of man at centre of 9/11 lawsuit reveal links to extremists and Saudi state
News.content:
The man at the heart of a $1 trillion (Â£733bn) lawsuit brought by 9/11 families had extensive links to Saudi government officials and went paintballing with one of al-Qaeda's future leaders, video obtained by the BBC reveals.

The footage, which the FBI had within days of the 2001 attacks, stands in stark contrast to Omar al-Bayoumi's 25 years of denials that he was an extremist and a Saudi spy.

Bayoumi, who claimed to be a student when he was in the United States, is seen in one clip embracing Anwar al-Awlaki, who would go on to lead al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula. In another, Bayoumi and Awlaki are paintballing near San Diego with an official from Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Islamic Affairs.

The videos form part of the 9/11 families' lawsuit against Saudi Arabia and have never been shown publicly before.

The lawsuit argues Saudi Arabia was complicit in the attacks and that Bayoumi aided two of the 19 hijackers who flew planes into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon - with another crashing in Pennsylvania.

Bayoumi was arrested in the UK by the Metropolitan Police days after the attacks and the videos were found among his possessions, along with other crucial evidence.

This included a diagram of a plane with a flight descent equation written alongside.

Multiple FBI agents received copies of the diagram, but it was never shared with the British interrogators, even though it had been couriered to the police station where Bayoumi was being held in custody.

The diagram was also kept from some FBI agents investigating Bayoumi, as well as from the 9/11 Commission - the independent inquiry into the largest mass murder in US history, in which nearly 3,000 people were killed. Bayoumi was never prosecuted.

He and the Saudi government did not respond to the BBC's requests for comment, but both have always denied any involvement in, or prior knowledge of, the attacks. The FBI declined to comment.

After a judge ruled the lawsuit could go ahead in 2018, thousands of documents, as well as videos and photographs, have been released to the court and also declassified through an executive order made by former President Joe Biden.

BBC Panorama and Radio 4 have examined these documents, and spoken to dozens of special agents and investigators, to trace the evidence the FBI gathered about Bayoumi and Saudi Arabia's alleged involvement in 9/11 - and to understand why it was never fully pursued over 25 years.
