News.title: Chancellor to say UK economy 'turning a corner' despite debt concerns
News.content:
The chancellor is set to give an upbeat view of the state of the UK economy ahead of next month's Budget, building on a recent uptick in consumer and business confidence.

In a speech on Monday in Coventry, John Healey will talk of a "new story" of the economy not just turning a corner but being resilient, optimistic and "ready to seize the opportunities of new technologies and ideas".

But nearby, Jaguar Land Rover is planning to cut thousands of jobs to save costs following competition from China for cheap cars, US tariffs on UK vehicles and the after effects of a cyber attack.

Healey is also facing concerns about government borrowing costs and the inflationary impact of the Iran war.

In his speech, Healey will unveil a Â£150m fund for companies in the north of England, which is part of a wider plan to generate more economic growth around the UK.

The Conservatives said Healey's plans would "do little to comfort hard-working families and businesses".

Healey will detail plans to use public investment to "unlock private investment, to support our innovation economy, and to create the new jobs their areas need".

The fund, from money already allocated to the British Business Bank, will provide investments of between Â£5m and Â£15m to the "most innovative and fast-growing firms".

It is expected to back university spin-outs and other "ambitious businesses" across the north.

Describing a country "turning the corner", the chancellor is expected to say: "The prime minister laid out a clear diagnosis of what has gone wrong in the past. The solution is a fundamental shift that starts with putting power in the right places.

"The next chapter of Britain's growth story will be written in more places."

Recent ructions in government debt markets have made constrained public finances worse, with the Treasury needing to fill possible multi-billion pound gaps caused by rising borrowing costs, and the need to fund higher defence spending.

As he prepares to deliver his Budget on 28 October, the chancellor has said he is as committed to balancing the books as his predecessor, Rachel Reeves.

But the tone matters. To get high saving consumers spending, and cautious businesses investing, Downing Street wants to point to sunnier times ahead for now, more than the prospect of tough Budgetary medicine.

It would also contrast with former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, who was accused of talking down the UK economy after Labour won the election when he warned the government would have to make "difficult decisions" to boost growth and "fix" the country's finances.

Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: "Economic growth in every postcode sounds great and is something we would all love. I think it'll actually be much harder to achieve in practice."

She said it would be easier to see how the government could make stronger second and third cities than to see "how it would drive growth in literally every postcode", as Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised.

During his first Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, Burnham faced scrutiny over rising UK borrowing costs.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch urged him to say how he would deal with the UK's increasing debt, after the cost of borrowing for the UK reached a new 18-year high.

Burnham blamed the previous Tory administration, and said his government would be "grounded in fiscal responsibility".

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said Healey's plan would do "little to comfort hard-working families and businesses across the country who are worried about more tax rises or the fact that government borrowing rates are near a 28-year high".

He added: "We are facing serious threats from Russia and Iran on our doorstep, as well as threats to the Falkland Islands.

"Yet the chancellor, the man who resigned over defence spending, seemingly does not want to mention our armed forces or how we will reach 3% of GDP on defence."

Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said: "Re-announcing Â£150m across the entire north of England will barely shift the dial on growth."

Robert Jenrick, Reform UK's economic spokesman, said: "Days after a market meltdown, when grip and direction are required, John Healey has revealed himself to be an empty vessel with no idea about how to rescue our economy."

News.title: BBC News presenter Maryam Moshiri reveals she has blood cancer
News.content:
BBC News presenter Maryam Moshiri has revealed she is living with blood cancer.

Moshiri, who joined the BBC in 2003 and is one of the news channel's best-known anchors, told the BBC she wanted to share her diagnosis to raise awareness about the disease.

"It's been two years since my diagnosis and I've felt that I've started to understand the disease a lot better and the way it affects my life. I've got a handle on it to a degree now, so I felt it was really important to raise awareness," the 49-year-old said.

"I'm going to have to spend the rest of my life being treated for this," she added.

Moshiri was diagnosed in November 2024 with polycythaemia vera (PV) - a rare, treatable blood cancer. Although it cannot be cured, it can be managed effectively.

In PV, your body makes too many red blood cells, which makes the blood thicker than normal.

It leads to a higher risk of developing blood clots, which can cause a stroke, heart attack or deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

Symptoms can include headaches, confusion, dizziness and blurred vision.

"I was told by my consultant that I have this incurable blood cancer," she said.

"Mostly I had no symptoms and that's one of the problems with this disease.

"The only reason mine was caught was because my GP was so fastidious in the way she did my routine blood tests and immediately sent them for further diagnosis."

As part of her initial treatment, the BBC News chief presenter underwent several "debilitating" hour-long sessions of venesections.

Venesection is a procedure where a needle is put into a vein in the arm to slowly draw the blood out.

This blood letting can be an effective way to reduce the thickness of the blood.

"In about a space of five months, I had venesection seven or eight times. So you can imagine my iron levels hit the floor and I felt even more exhausted," she said.

"After a while I started feeling extremely unwell and tired. I started losing my hair, I got itchy all over my body, but the main symptom was fatigue."

Later, Moshiri was able to get on an immunotherapy treatment called interferon through the NHS, and after some tweaks, she says she is in a better place.

"I've only needed one venosection in about 15 months, so that's been really good. The last couple of months have been better than the last two years," she said.

"I think it's really important people understand that this blood cancer is incurable but it's manageable with the right treatment and you can lead a relatively healthy life.

"It's just a question of finding the right treatment and making sure it works for you."

She admits she is "not the person I was two years ago" but says she feels "much better".

News.title: Jaguar Land Rover boss to meet minister as thousands of job cuts expected
News.content:
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds will meet the bosses of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) and the Unite union to discuss the impact of thousands of expected job cuts at the car maker.

JLR confirmed to the BBC it is opening a voluntary redundancy programme, a year on from a cyber attack which brought production to a halt for more than a month.

The company did not confirm the numbers but the Times reported as many as 4,000 jobs may be lost due to the impact of tariffs and a drop in sales.

Reynolds told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg the meeting early next week will focus on ways to "mitigate any job losses" but ruled out a bailout for the company.

Asked about the cuts, which are believed to impact mainly white collar workers, Reynolds said: "A company the size of JLR, which is a huge British success story, at various times in its business cycle, the number of, directly, people it employs will change.

"If this is about making sure over time that the workforce is right to make the business as competitive as possible, that's the conversation we need to have."

He said there would be no support "if it's to bail people out", but opened the door to a "long-term investment in the future" of the company.

The cuts come as Chancellor John Healey is preparing to deliver a speech in the Midlands on Monday promising to boost economic growth by changing how the government values investment in infrastructure such as transport and housing. JLR is based in Coventry, in the West Midlands.

The Liberal Democrats said the news would be "devastating" for JLR staff and called for Healey to use his speech to offer "support for those jobs at risk".

"This development lays bare that the government's growth mission is falling far short," the party's business spokesperson Sarah Olney said.

News.title: The £70 refund letter that isn't a scam
News.content:
You may be among the one million people, mostly women, who will receive letters explaining how you are eligible for top-up pension payments - and it's not a scam.

Those entitled are low earners who have missed out on the money because of the way their pension is administered.

HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) will write to people over the next few months, explaining how to receive the payment. Typically they will be due Â£70, but that may vary considerably depending on their circumstances.

Anyone eligible will be contacted automatically but, if you receive a letter, there are various checks you can do to ensure the letter is genuine so you don't get hoodwinked.

News.title: Rapist serving life may face more assault charges
News.content:
A convicted serial rapist described by police as "one of the most prolific predators" in the UK could face further charges after fresh allegations involving seven more women were passed to prosecutors.

Chinese national Zhenhao Zou is serving a life sentence with a minimum term of 24 years after he was found guilty of drugging and raping 10 women in London and China between September 2019 and May 2023.

Believing Zou had committed further crimes, police appealed for more potential victim-survivors to come forward.

The Metropolitan Police has sent a file containing the new allegations of sexual crimes to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which will decide whether to bring further charges.

According to the Met Police, the file contains evidence relating to several alleged offences, including rape and administering a substance with intent to commit a sexual offence.

It relates to reports made by five women who contacted police following the appeal, as well as the alleged rape of two women who remain unidentified, the force said.

A total of 23 women contacted police following the appeal, but most of them did not want to pursue criminal charges, the force added.

The Met said separate inquiries were ongoing into allegations involving women who were allegedly assaulted by Zou in China, with officers working to obtain evidence from the Chinese authorities.

News.title: Andrew Scott feels the Pressure as 'unsung hero' in WW2 thriller
News.content:
Andrew Scott says he loved the challenge of his latest acting role in the film Pressure, as the meteorologist key to the success of World War Two's D-Day - the largest seaborne invasion in history.

âGroup Captain James Stagg may not have been the most charming person, but I think he had a huge amount of humility in the face of nature. And that's one of the themes I think of the film," Scott tells the BBC.

"He appeared to me to be an extraordinarily interesting cinematic character, as well as an unsung hero from history."

Stagg played a crucial advisory role when US General Dwight D Eisenhower invaded Normandy, laying the foundations for the Allied victory in World War Two.

"It was a wonderful part to play," he says, while painting a mixed picture of Stagg, calling him "very chilly", while also "forthright, direct, obsessed with weather - and not afraid to speak truth to power".

News.title: Cooler temperatures with wet and windy weather forecast for UK this week
News.content:
Meteorological summer is over, schools are back and so is the UK's unsettled weather.

After a heat spike on Sunday, low pressure systems will continue to bring wet and windy conditions, especially to the north of the UK at the beginning of the week, before things settle down on Wednesday and Thursday.

It will also feel cooler for many places across England and Wales, after Sunday's temperature approached 29C (84F) in south-east England.

Despite a mostly dry weekend for many, last week was the wettest week in England since early February, according to the Environment Agency.

Spain recorded 45.7C in Huelva last week, which was the country's highest temperature of the year so far.

News.title: Drug rape killer should never have been freed, says victim
News.content:
A man who drugged multiple women over a 40-year period and eventually killed his partner should never have been released from prison, according to one of his victims.

Richard Scatchard was jailed twice but released from prison on licence in 2013.

He went on to kill Kelly Faiers in 2023, by coercing her into taking sleeping tablets after drinking alcohol.

Some experts and a former police detective believe he should not have been free to kill her, having shown signs he was a danger to women.

Krystyna, 70, has waived her legal right to anonymity to speak publicly for the first time about her abuse by Scatchard.

He went on the run after Kelly's death, and was found dead in a caravan park six months later.

The National Crime Agency has said there is an "urgent need" to deal with what it said is a growing international issue of men drugging and raping women - sometimes filming the assaults and posting them online.

News.title: Pioneering fossil hunter recognised with blue plaque
News.content:
A pioneering fossil hunter who was one of the first women to be employed by the National History Museum has been recognised with a national blue plaque.

Dorothea Bate, who died in 1951 aged 72, "transformed our understanding of prehistoric animals and ancient environments" through her research, Historic England said.

She has been recognised with a plaque at the National History Museum, in Tring, Hertfordshire, which notes in its inscription that the palaeontologist was the "Officer-in-Charge of this museum from 1948".

Bate was born in Carmarthen, Wales, in 1878 and developed a fascination with the natural world from an early age.

She moved with her family to rural Gloucestershire as a young woman and spent hours exploring the surrounding countryside and caves, collecting fossils.

She had little formal education, instead largely teaching herself, and in 1900 asked for work behind the scenes at the Natural History Museum in London.

Her determination impressed museum staff, earning her a position as an assistant and beginning an association with the institution that would last more than 50 years.

She published her first scientific paper, A Short Account Of A Bone Cave In The Carboniferous Limestone Of The Wye Valley, in 1901.

Bate went on to undertake expeditions across the Mediterranean, often travelling alone to remote caves in search of evidence of ancient life.

In Cyprus, she discovered a previously unknown species of dwarf elephant and in 1909, while in the Balearics, she discovered the myotragus - an extinct goat-like antelope.

She achieved more than 80 published scientific papers, despite spending most of her career without a permanent paid position.

In 2017, a blue plaque was dedicated to Bate at Napier House in Carmarthen where she was born.

News.title: Baby girl dies while camping with family in woods
News.content:
A three-month-old girl has died while camping in woodland with her family, police have confirmed.

Emergency services were called to land off Strawberry Lane, near Cheslyn Hay, Staffordshire, at 08:45 BST on Saturday, to a report of a child in cardiac arrest.

An air ambulance was sent to the scene but the child was pronounced dead by paramedics a short time later, Staffordshire Police said.

"While the investigation remains at an early stage, this is an isolated incident," Det Insp Katie Gregory said. "The death is being treated as unexplained at this time."

People living in the close-knit community, a village of around 7,000 people, have been left shocked by the child's death.

News.title: Jamaica to hand slavery reparations petition to King Charles
News.content:
The Jamaican government will highlight to King Charles a petition over slavery reparations on Monday, the country's culture minister Olivia Grange has said.

It will ask the King, who serves as Jamaica's head of state, to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the country's highest court, over the legality of the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica.

Grange said it could pave the way for a "long outstanding settlement for the hundreds of years of the most horrific abuse that our African ancestors endured".

She will also meet with British Museum officials to discuss the repatriation of artefacts taken during the colonial era.

The three questions which the Jamaican government is asking the King to refer to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC) are: whether the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica was legal under English law, whether it broke international law, and whether Britain now has a legal duty to provide redress.

The petition, which is not a demand for payment, goes to the King who then refers it to the JCPC.

King Charles has no personal discretion in deciding whether to make a referral.

Grange said: "Once we get the answers, or once we get a response to those questions, then the next steps will be determined."

Buckingham Palace has been working closely with the Governor General of Jamaica to ensure the petition is correctly lodged.

A Palace spokesperson said: "His Majesty has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today."

News.title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' during foreign donor talks filmed undercover
News.content:
There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.

Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days".

They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats.

They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029.

They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest.

Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage.

But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.

What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.

At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake.

One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions".

No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty".

And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.

Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.

A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up â sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage".

Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said.

But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera â Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say."

But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"

This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing.

Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling â to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

News.title: Raise the Colours founder charged with 14 offences
News.content:
The founder of an activist group which has been putting Union Jack and St George's Cross flags on lampposts has been charged with a string of offences including racially aggravated harassment, threatening behaviour and assault.

Ryan Bridge, 45, of Blackwell, Bromsgrove, Worcestershire, has been erecting flags in the Midlands and the south of England since last summer as part of Raise the Colours.

Thames Valley Police said Bridge had been charged with 14 offences from a two-month period in Oxfordshire earlier this year.

He is due to appear at Oxford Magistrates' Court on 3 November.

The offences are:

Seven counts of using threatening words or behaviour to cause harassment, alarm or distress

Three counts of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour with intent to cause fear of, or provoke, unlawful violence

Two counts of racially aggravated intentional harassment, alarm or distress

One count of racially aggravated fear of violence

One count of common assault

In July, Oxfordshire County Council was granted a High Court injunction to stop people placing flags near highways because of safety concerns, trespass and obstruction.

Birmingham City Council has applied for a similar injunction which will be heard at the High Court on Tuesday.

News.title: Three charged with attempted murder after shooting
News.content:
Two adults and a teenager have been charged with attempted murder after a shotgun was fired in a town centre.

Police were called to Market Place in Braintree, Essex, at about 22:10 BST on Monday following what officers described as a "targeted attack".

Two teenagers sustained serious injuries to their face and upper body, while a third person was also injured.

Destiny Ema, 23, of Meadgate Avenue, Chelmsford, Kayden Brown, 18, of Noaks Avenue, Chelmsford, and a 17-year-old from Braintree who cannot be named for legal reasons are due to appear at Chelmsford Magistrates' Court on Monday.

A 16-year-old boy previously arrested in connection with the incident has been released on police bail until 30 November.

Ema was also charged with numerous other offences connected to separate investigations including:

Attempted grievous bodily harm with intent

Possession of a firearm with intent to cause fear of violence

Possession of a firearm while committing an indictable offence

Possession of a firearm while prohibited for life

Harassment

Malicious communications

Possession of a shotgun with intent to cause fear of violence

This year’s rapidly intensifying, climate change-fuelled “super” El Niño is on course to be the strongest on record – and potentially the most powerful in centuries.

“We should be clear that this is an unprecedented event”, said Professor Adam Scaife, head of long range forecasting at the Met Office. “I have never seen an El Niño signal this intense in our forecasts.” Others have described the event as “ truly mind-blowing ” and “ Godzilla-level ”.

Tens of millions of the world’s poorest people are also expected to be plunged into humanitarian crisis as the extreme weather event hits - just as vital support for health, nutrition and disaster response is being gutted by devastating foreign aid cuts from wealthy countries. Britain, for example, is currently slashing bilateral aid to eight African countries by more than 80 per cent.

Torrential rains and flooding are expected to come to parts of East Africa, while droughts are expected to intensify across southern Africa - threatening food supplies and livelihoods on both sides of the continent.

Already, the impacts are being felt in other parts of the world, from unusually weak monsoon rains in India, to catastrophic wildfires in Indonesia.

In the UK, still reeling from a summer of heatwaves that has killed thousands and pushed water levels to critically low levels, the Met office has forecast a particularly wet and stormy winter due to the El Niño. But perhaps the biggest impact will be felt in people’s pockets. Around one quarter of UK food imports – including rice, coffee, cocoa, and tropical fruits – are from parts of the world most exposed to the El Niño, according to research from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit.

The impacts will come on top of an ongoing cost of living crisis that experts say has been exacerbated by climate change. Poor harvests drove a 77 per cent rise in the price of coffee imported into the UK from Brazil in 2025, while cocoa bean prices from Côte d’Ivoire have doubled.

But it is people on the ground across Africa and Asia that will feel the most critical impacts.

“The world is heading into this El Niño at precisely the wrong moment,” Dr Philip Goodwin, CEO of Unicef UK, told The Independent. “We can see the warning signs coming, yet humanitarian agencies are being asked to prepare with fewer resources.”

MPs from across the political divide are now calling on the government to step up its support, as aid groups warn that countries set to be most impacted by the super El Niño are also those bearing the brunt of the global aid squeeze.

“We must change course in order to meet the scale of this crisis,” Dr Ellie Chowns, Green MP for North Herefordshire, told The Independent. “The government must turn all of their efforts to urgently reducing emissions at home… and restore development aid to ensure the Global South is not abandoned to face the worst realities of a crisis they did so little to cause.”

Wildfires, which scientists say are being fuelled by El Niño, are seen burning across Indonesia earlier this month ( AFP/Getty )

Andrew Mitchell, Conservative MP for Sutton Coldfield and a former development minister, added: “It is the poorest in the world who suffer first and hardest from climate change and this summer has shown the rich world, too, the grave climate threats that await us .

“Cuts to Britain’s development budget - as both Prime Ministers Johnson and Starmer did - were acts of the greatest folly… Britain needs to reinvigorate this international leadership if we are to tackle at their roots the threatening evils of climate change, illegal migration, starvation, water shortage and pandemics.”

Comments come as this week the UN warned that this year’s El Niño - an event caused by unusually warm temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific - is already exceptionally strong. “El Niño is being supersized before our eyes… The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up,” said UN secretary general António Guterres.

Occurring on average every two to seven years, a typical El Niño will see sea surface temperatures in a specific patch of the tropical Pacific rise by 1-2C, with 2C considered a very big event.

This year, the temperature has already crossed 2.6C above the El Niño - and current forecasts suggest it could peak at around 4C in November.

Speaking of the super coming El Niño, Dejene Dadi, the general manger of a coffee-growing cooperative in Ethiopia, said: “We aren't ready for this kind of disaster… We can do climate adaptation activities like soil and water conservation, shade management, managing pests and diseases, and water harvesting and irrigation. But it is not possible without more help from coffee companies and governments like the UK.”

For its part, the UK government carried out a “responsible business conduct review” as part of its trade strategy published last year, which advocacy groups understand contains plans that would compel companies to better respond to environmental and human rights concerns in their supply chains. However, the publication of that review has been continually delayed.

“The super El Niño urgently need businesses to invest in their supply chains: paying fair prices, tackling human rights abuses, and safeguarding the environment. And the UK Government must also stop delaying publication of its Responsible Business Conduct review,” said Dr Carley-Jane Stanton, from the Fairtrade Foundation.

The most urgent El Niño concern, however, remains around the impact that El Niño-fuelled weather events will have on food systems at a time when there is very little money available to help the world’s poorest.

The UN’s World Food Programme (WFP) has projected that an additional 49 million more people could be pushed into hunger globally.

“The places most affected by El Niño are often those already facing some of the worst food crises - and over the past year we have already had to make incredible choices on prioritising populations on the brink of famine and starvation,” Richard Choularton, director of WFP's Climate and Resilience Service, told The Independent.

“We simply do not have enough resources. This year we estimate that we need around $13bn to meet emergency food needs around the world, but we expect to only get around six and a half billion,” he added.

A major WFP appeal to donors for $200m to fund “anticipatory action” – programmes that provide families with cash ahead of climate shocks, allowing them to weather the crisis without leaving their communities – has also met with a muted response. “We asked for 200 million for about 22 countries… and we still need over 150 million. And the window for putting those funds to good use is rapidly closing,” said Mr Choularton.

Ummy Dubow, the country director for Somalia at the global development charity CARE, described the super El Niño as a “disaster” for her country during a briefing with journalists this week - in which she emphasised how Somalia is already reeling from crises including the impact of aid cuts as well as the knock-on effects of the War in Iran.

“Somalia is facing a very severe and compounding humanitarian crisis… 3.3 million people are already internally displaced, and 1.88 million children under five in Somalia are acutely malnourished,” she said. “Meanwhile, while CARE used to operate 150 health facilities, this has come down to 50 due to the aid cuts - and food prices have risen between 10 and 20 per cent and fuel costs have gone up by 10 per cent due to the War in the Middle East .”

Unicef’s Dr Philip Goodwin added that it is “children who are paying the highest price” despite the fact that they did not create the climate crisis.

Pippa Heylings, Liberal Democrat MP for South Cambridgeshire and net zero spokesperson, also called on the government to better prepare for the climate crisis and restore the foreign aid budget.

“We cannot afford to abandon our reputation as a global climate leader by betraying our pledges to countries that desperately need climate resilience,” she said.

“The Liberal Democrats want to see the government reverse their cuts. Burnham must set out a roadmap to restore the aid budget back to 0.7 per cent [of Gross National Income, GNI], as well as convening cross-party talks on climate resilience."

The UK retained its aid budget at 0.7 per cent of GNI for a number of years, before Boris Johnson cut it to 0.5 per cent in 2021, and Keir Starmer announced further cuts to 0.3 per cent last year, cutting billions of pounds from the budget.

Sarah Champion, Labour MP for Rotherham and chair of the International Development Committee, echoed warnings that cuts to the UK aid budget are misguided at a time of such severe global danger, suggesting that “successive cuts to overseas development aid... are increasingly undermining good intent” from the government when it comes to international development.

She added: "Climate change is rapidly undermining development gains across vulnerable countries, as we have recently witnessed with the disaster in Nepal... We must recognise El Niño risks further worsening food and water security, and will exacerbate poverty and humanitarian need.”

In response to this article, a spokesperson for the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) said: “Climate is an urgent national security threat. The Foreign Secretary will bring international leadership on this issue to the FCDO as the UK works with international partners on a coordinated response.

“As we transition away from high levels of grant overseas development aid, we are using all available levers on El Nino, focused on strengthening systems, mobilising finance and working with partners to build resilience and support those most at risk."

A UK government spokesperson added that the UK is a “world leader in tackling the climate crisis, including preparing for extreme weather and acting to protect people and places from the very real impacts of climate change which are already becoming more common.”

Tyson Fury has claimed that his long-awaited heavyweight showdown with bitter rival Anthony Joshua is off and has instead challenged Oleksandr Usyk to a third fight.

Joshua and Fury have been mooted to square off at New York City’s Madison Square Garden on 20 November, despite their bout being the biggest between two British stars this generation.

Negotiations have proven difficult, however. Joshua’s promoter Eddie Hearn has said “AJ”’s contract is for a fight in the UK, while Fury’s promoter Frank Warren has said the “Gypsy King”’s deal is more flexible.

open image in gallery Tyson Fury has suggested his fight with Anthony Joshua is off ( PA Wire )

Fury appears to have grown impatient over the lack of confirmation, calling Joshua “a coward” last week and now taking to social media to say the Matchroom star has “s**t his pants” over the bout and instead calling out Usyk, to whom he lost twice on points back in 2024.

“AJ has s**t his pants again, yet again,” Fury said in a post on Instagram stories. “After 11 years he has finally s**t his pants yet again.

“This will only lead me to a fight with Oleksandr Usyk. Oleksandr you’re his (Joshua’s) trainer and his sensei and you know he is a weak minded piece of s**t and that he would never fight the Gypsy King, which you have had the guts to do twice.

“You got the decisions last time, fair play to you. Good luck to you, let’s do it again. Let’s run it back in November. The ball is now in your court… do you want to fight me this year, 2026, or are you calling quits? Let me know because I am now looking for a new opponent.”

open image in gallery Fury (right) twice lost on points to Oleksandr Usyk (left) ( PA Wire )

Fury’s brother Shane recently insisted that Tyson will box on 20 November regardless of whether Joshua is the opponent and the “Gypsy King” doubled down on that idea shortly after, naming Agit Kabayel, Filip Hrgovic and Daniel Dubois as potential replacement opponents.

The 38-year-old Fury last boxed in late July, stopping a 46-year-old Mariusz Wach in seven rounds. The fight, which took place in Thailand, did not air live anywhere.

One day later, Joshua stopped relative unknown Kristian Prenga in two rounds in Saudi Arabia. However, Prenga floored the 37-year-old twice in the first round.

open image in gallery Joshua’s contract is for a fight in the UK, claims promoter Eddie Hearn ( PA Wire )

Those two bouts were seen as warm-ups for Joshua vs Fury, but that week news emerged that ring walks would need to place at 2am in London if Wembley Stadium were to host the fight. Subsequently, Madison Square Garden was made the frontrunner to host the battle of former world champions.

Hearn has previously said an agreement hinged on his client’s net purse and while he insists Joshua’s contract is for a fight in the UK, Sela – the Saudi state-owned promotional company financing the fight – reportedly want a bigger American audience on Netflix and are thus targeting New York for the showdown.

The results from Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt regional election are likely to be a major political headache for Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU) have governed the eastern state for more than 20 years.

Sunday evening’s exit poll showing the far-right, pro-Russian, Alternative for Germany (AfD) potentially gaining 44.5 per cent of the vote is beyond the 40 per cent recent opinion polls had been showing and well in excess of the 20.8 per cent the party secured in 2021. Mr Merz’s CDU fell to 18.5 per cent in the exit poll from 37.1 per cent in 2021. The CDU currently leads a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the free-market Free Democrats (FDP).

About 1.7 million people were eligible to vote in the east-central state of 2.1 million residents. Participation was at a record high of 76.5 per cent.

AfD had been looking to secure an absolute majority of above 50 per cent, to ensure they could try and implement their own radical agenda.

So what happens now?

1. AfD seizes power

If AfD were to take control of the regional parliament, they would be the first far-right party to have power in either a regional or the national parliament since the Second World War. If this were to happen, what is known in Germany as the “firewall” – where parties create coalitions to keep far-right parties from power – would be breached for the first time.

open image in gallery Ulrich Siegmund, top candidate in the Saxony-Anhalt state election for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) ( AFP/Getty )

AfD has been clear about what it would do if it were to take power. It seeks to restrict immigration, quit the Euro and restore ties with Russia as most of Europe rallies around Ukraine.

Based on the party’s “Vision 2026” election manifesto, victory in Saxony-Anhalt could invite sweeping reforms around state policy on migration, education, culture and the family.

Under Germany’s federal system, state governments sit in the upper house of parliament, the Bundesrat, and also have wide powers in education, domestic security and culture.

An AfD-led state would launch a crackdown on migration, with a task force set up to coordinate quicker deportations.

The children of refugees would be placed in separate classes at school to prevent what the party claims are “stresses” on the other children from being around different cultures.

Meanwhile, children with disabilities would no longer be taught in the same classroom as those without, instead being sent to new schools.

Schools would also be banned from flying rainbow flags, and the government would exhaust “all legal avenues” to limit Islamic expression.

The party has claimed greater acceptance of what it offensively labels as “sexual deviations and non-reproductive lifestyles” has contributed to sinking birth rates and promises to aggressively promote “traditional” family structures consisting of a mother, father and children. An AfD government would see major changes to the school curriculum around a “patriotic cultural policy”, extended to raising the German national flag daily and singing the national anthem at school celebrations.

open image in gallery Alternative for Germany (AfD) co-leader Alice Weidel ( AFP/Getty )

It would also advocate for removing war refugee status for Ukrainians in Germany as long as the conflict remains concentrated in eastern Ukraine, arguing they should seek refuge in western Ukraine.

The current structure of the public broadcasting system would be dismantled and funding withdrawn for some cultural institutions.

In terms of domestic security in Saxony, AfD in the state is assessed by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency as a “far-right extremist” group, which would create concerns about the intelligence AfD would be able to see if it was in charge of the regional parliament.

However, AfD will likely need the support of another party, depending on how many smaller parties pass the five per cent threshold needed to get seats. In Saxony-Anhalt, all the parties except the small far-left BSW party have ruled out joining a coalition with AfD.

If some smaller parties do not pass the threshold though, it would make AfD’s job easier, as it would make the chance of a coalition against it less likely.

The party will talk to any sensible party with whom it can find common ground on policy positions, said AfD national co-leader Alice Weidel after the exit poll

2. The CDU pulls together a coalition

The CDU has been hit hard, but may yet be able to pull together a “firewall coalition”. That is what happened in the state of Thuringia in 2024, where AfD gained more than 30 per cent of the vote, but not enough for an absolute majority.

However, American think tank the Brookings Institution believes this will be difficult. “The task of organising a CDU-led governing majority faces almost insurmountable difficulties,” it said in a recent briefing note, exacerbated by the CDU’s ruling out of any coalition with the staunchly socialist party Die Linke (The Left). With exit polls predicting a 9.4 per cent share of the vote for The Left behind the CDU’s 18.4 per cent, the party leadership has indicated it would be open to an arrangement formalising support for a CDU-led government over AfD. But the CDU faces internal divisions over a possible alliance with a party on what it regards as the far left.

open image in gallery German Chancellor and Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party leader Friedrich Merz ( Reuters )

Mr Merz said ahead of the election last Sunday that they would “assess the situation in light of the election results” and “do everything we can to prevent Saxony-Anhalt from falling into the hands of the radicals”.

State premier Sven Schulze congratulated AfD in the wake of the exit poll and acknowledged the result showed it was the strongest party. If AfD is unable to rule outright, it could trigger a protracted process of coalition building by mainstream parties who are determined to keep a party under investigation for right-wing extremism by Germany’s domestic intelligence service.

3. The German government takes a hit regardless

However the political wrangling in the wake of the Saxony result ends up, it is clear that the manner of AfD’s win is important for their national standing and a blow to Mr Merz’s coalition government.

Nationwide, AfD has swollen to become the most popular party, polling at 29 per cent, while Mr Merz has become the most unpopular chancellor since the founding of the Federal Republic, with 85 per cent of voters dissatisfied.

Lars Klingbeil, co-leader of Germany’s centre-left SPD party and vice chancellor in Mr Merz’s governing coalition, said after the exit poll that the result of the Saxony-Anhalt state election is a signal for Berlin politics. The result is ⁠a reason to reflect on the federal government’s policies, Mr Klingbeil told public ‌broadcaster ZDF. “And ​rest ‌assured, that ⁠is what ⁠we will ‌do.”

Mr Merz has already sought to create a harder line on immigration, in a move designed to try and stem the rise of AfD. There will no doubt be a greater push from AfD to try and move the needle on national policy, while their pro-Russia stance could be an issue when it comes to European support for Ukraine, given the nation has previously been accused of moving cautiously when it comes to handing Ukraine weapons to fight off Russia's invasion.

Mr Merz will face an increasing level of political pressure about his own job and government, something AfD will be all too happy to try and press home in both future regional elections and the wider national polls.

News.title: Two cyclists killed and three arrested after crash in Kent village
News.content:

Three people have been arrested after a car hit three cyclists on a road, killing two of the riders.

Kent Police said the incident occurred in the Kent village of Cobham near Gravesend at around 7.47am on Sunday, when a white Ford Focus travelling along Sole Street towards Meopham collided with the cyclists.

Two of them – a man in his 60s and a woman in her 50s – were confirmed dead by paramedics attending the scene near the junction with Round Street.

The third rider was taken to hospital for treatment for injuries police said were minor.

Two men aged 20 and 21 were subsequently arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.

A 19-year-old woman was also detained on suspicion of assisting an offender, according to Kent Police.

open image in gallery The incident occurred in the village of Cobham near Gravesend at around 7.47am on Sunday, when a white Ford Focus travelling along Sole Street towards Meopham collided with the cyclists ( Google )

The road was closed for several hours while officers investigated the circumstances of the crash. The force’s Serious Collision Investigation Unit (SCIU) is now appealing for anyone who has either witnessed the collision, or saw the car or cyclists prior to the incident, to come forward.

Motorists with dashcam equipment or residents with private CCTV have also been urged to get in touch with the force.

Members of the public with relevant information can contact the Kent Police SCIU by calling their appeal line on 01622 798538, quoting reference RY/KA/071/26.

The NHS is currently able to meet only around half the demand for blood required to treat patients with sickle cell disease, according to health experts.

NHS Blood and Transplant (NHSBT) has issued an urgent appeal for donors, specifically encouraging individuals of black heritage to step forward, as an estimated 16,000 additional volunteers are needed.

The request coincides with the 20th anniversary of the nationwide rollout of newborn sickle cell screening across England.

An inherited blood condition, sickle cell disease causes the body to produce abnormally shaped red blood cells that can restrict blood circulation.

The illness is particularly prevalent among individuals with African or Caribbean ancestral backgrounds.

Symptoms include pain, fatigue, and painful swelling in the hands and feet, with treatment comprising medication alongside ongoing blood transfusions.

open image in gallery Black people are much more likely than average to have the type of blood needed for sickle cell patients ( NHS Blood and Transfusion Service )

Screening is offered to every newborn via a heel-prick test, typically administered when the baby is around five days old.

According to NHSBT, the screening initiative has transformed early diagnosis and ongoing management, with more than 19,000 individuals presently living with the disorder in England.

At present, the health service is only capable of providing roughly 50 per cent of the blood required by patients who depend on regular transfusions.

To address the shortfall, NHSBT projects that at least 16,000 new donors of black heritage are required to fulfil current medical needs.

Meeting this figure would require expanding the existing donor pool by three-quarters.

Symptoms of sickle cell disease NHS The main symptoms of sickle cell disease are: painful episodes called sickle cell crises, which can be very severe and last for days or weeks

an increased risk of serious infections

anaemia (where red blood cells cannot carry enough oxygen around the body), which can cause tiredness and shortness of breath

Black donors are especially vital because they are significantly more likely to provide a precise match for those suffering from sickle cell.

This is largely because they are 10 times more likely than white individuals to possess the Ro blood subtype, an essential component for treating the disorder.

Gerry Gogarty, director of blood supply at NHSBT, said: "With improvements to both diagnosis and treatment of sickle cell over the past twenty years, we now have more people with sickle cell reliant on regular blood transfusions than ever before.

"Blood donors play a vital role in keeping these patients alive and as well as possible, but the demand for blood to treat these patients is currently growing faster than we can collect and supply it.

"We have seen an incredible response from our amazing donors across the country, with the number of donors of black heritage rising by 120% over the past decade – but we still urgently need more people to come forward to become regular donors and help us give the very best treatment to even more patients."

open image in gallery More individuals have been encouraged to give blood ( PA )

Yann-Elie Asket, a 22-year-old politics student living in Greenwich, south London, registered to donate blood after losing his cousin to the condition.

"I still remember how much her passing changed our family and how deeply it affected the people closest to her, especially her parents," he said.

"When you lose someone so young, you realise just how precious life is and how important it is to do whatever you can to help someone else keep theirs."

With a friend also living with the condition, Mr Asket noted that blood donation offered a direct, practical way to help.

Iyamide Thomas, of the Sickle Cell Society and NHS engagement lead for the screening programme, said: "The past 20 years have brought significant progress for people living with sickle cell disorder.

"Newborn screening means babies can be diagnosed before they become seriously unwell and connected to specialist care from the very beginning of their lives.

"We are now seeing the benefits of advances in treatment, including red cell exchange, which can make a profound difference to people who experience frequent and severe sickle cell crises. But these treatments depend on having access to a reliable supply of closely matched blood.

"As the number of people living with sickle cell continues to grow, it is vital that we have enough blood donors to meet this increasing need.

"We particularly want to encourage more people of black heritage to come forward and donate. By giving blood regularly, donors can play a direct role in helping people with sickle cell live healthier and more independent lives."

Tackling the growing Neets crisis will be easier for the universities of Kent and Greenwich following their merger into the UK’s first "super-university", according to the group’s leadership.

Known as the London and South East University Group (LASE), the institution is now the third largest in the UK, accommodating more than 50,000 students across four campuses in London, Medway and Kent.

The chief executive said the merged institutions are "much stronger" together as the higher education sector faces ongoing financial strains.

University of Greenwich vice-chancellor and chief executive of LASE Professor Jane Harrington said the move enables the group to meet regional needs in ways they could not independently.

"If I was to look through south-east London going out we’ve got areas of urban deprivation, then you go out into Medway and Kent you’ve got areas of rural deprivation and then we’ve got areas of coastal deprivation," she said ahead of LASE’s official launch on Monday.

"It’s a real opportunity for us to address the very people that the government’s worried about.

open image in gallery Jane Harrington unveiling the 'LASE Gateway' ( PA )

"Everyone probably now is starting to be familiar with the term Neets – basically people who are not in employment, education, or training – and it’s those very young people that we can now actually really start to look at what skills do they need?

"How can we upskill them? How can we reskill them? How can we go out and actually attract them and work with our FE (further education) colleges so that they’ve got pathways that are accessible to them in ways we just couldn’t do on our own."

Between April and June, an estimated 981,000 young people aged 16 to 24 were classified as Neets. While down 30,000 on the previous quarter, the figure remains 30,000 higher than a year ago, according to the Office for National Statistics.

Prof Harrington said the merger has also reinforced the universities’ financial positions. It comes amid escalating financial pressures across the UK sector, with MPs on the Education Committee warning earlier this year of a "real risk" an English university could close due to insolvency for the first time.

The Office for Students, the higher education regulator in England, cautioned the committee that 24 providers risked insolvency and closure in the 12 months from last November, warning 45 per cent of higher education providers could face deficits for 2025/26.

Prof Harrington said: "International students are more difficult to bring into the UK; the cost of living’s gone up constantly; we’ve got more costs within the university; student fees after 12 years are now in a position where they can increase slightly but we don’t know what will happen after two years; and then we’re going to have an international levy imposed on us.

"So if you combine all of that, there isn’t a university in this country that doesn’t have to really look at their costs."

open image in gallery It is hoped that the merger will help tackle the Neets crisis in local areas ( PA )

Institutions are bracing for the international student levy, which will charge them £925 per student annually from 2028-29.

"We are much stronger now we’re together," Prof Harrington added.

"It doesn’t mean we’re immune to the changes; we’re not, but I do believe we’ll be able to get ourselves in a much stronger, firmer position more quickly."

LASE is drafting a lessons learned "blueprint" for the Department for Education to serve as a "model" group structure for other institutions. Prof Harrington admitted the undertaking was "not for the faint-hearted" but insisted it was worthwhile.

Following their legal merger last month, Kent and Greenwich universities will operate as distinct academic divisions under their current names, with students continuing to apply to and graduate from their chosen institution.

However, the unified structure allows the group to offer subjects previously unavailable to them individually, alongside shared access to campus libraries and wellbeing services.

In May, King’s College London and Cranfield University, based in Bedford, announced plans to merge in August 2027.
