Sports.title: Coleman: Ireland's new generation not scarred by past World Cup play-off pain
Sports.content:
Seamus Coleman insists the Republic of Ireland's new generation will not be scarred by the bitter pain of World Cup play-off defeat as they attempt to book a ticket for this summer's finals.

Ireland face the Czech Republic at Prague's Fortuna Arena on Thursday evening attempting to go one better than they did in 2009 against France and in 2017, when Denmark shattered their dreams with a 5-1 demolition job in Dublin.

However, Everton defender Coleman, who was not in the squad on that fateful night in Paris and was injured for the game with the Danes, is confident there will be no hangover, with the Czechs standing between Heimir Hallgrimsson's men and a winner-takes-all match with either Denmark or North Macedonia in Dublin on Tuesday.

Asked if the pain of those near-misses was fuelling the latest bid to make it to the finals for the first time since 2002, the 37-year-old said: "It's difficult to say if it's fuelling the players, they're all so young.

"Obviously the nation was hurt massively, but in terms of the current group of players I don't think they're dwelling too much on that hurt.

"To be honest, we're just riding the wave of the confidence we've got as a group - which I think this young group deserves - from the last two games and we're looking forward to Thursday night and then see what comes after that.

"But to see how the nation is feeling now is incredible and we've got a duty to try and make them even happier."

Image: Troy Parrott's goals inspired Ireland to stunning wins over Portugal and Hungary that secured a play-off spot

Ireland are only in Prague because they backed up a scratchy Group F victory over Armenia with an unexpected 2-0 win against Portugal in Dublin before going to Hungary and coming out on top in a five-goal thriller in which Troy Parrott scored the decisive goal with the last kick of the game.

Coleman is one of only two players - 34-year-old Robbie Brady is the other - in the current squad to have been to a major tournament, and the experience they had in earning their trip to Euro 2016 in France could prove invaluable this time around.

Image: Coleman and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson are bidding to lead Ireland to World Cup qualification for the first time since 2002

Martin O'Neill's team reached the finals by beating Bosnia and Herzegovina 3-1 on aggregate in a play-off after a hard-fought 1-1 draw in Zenica in the first leg.

Coleman said: "Maybe two years ago it would have been a lot for the young lads to take.

"But everyone now has stepped up and are prepared for what's to come and we absolutely, no doubt about it, understand it's going to be a tough game for us, but it's also going to be a tough game for them as well."

Head coach Hallgrimsson, who is without suspended defender Liam Scales and injured midfielder Josh Cullen, as ever exuded calm as he fulfilled his media duties on Wednesday morning, simply asking for more of the same from his players.

He said: "We all know by now why we got good results and good performances, and that's the key, not be over-ambitious tomorrow, stay on point, focus on why we are here and trying to improve that, not only this game, continuously."

Czech boss says Soucek still key player despite not being captain

Image: West Ham's Tomas Soucek is no longer captain of his country

Czech Republic boss Miroslav Koubek said "full-fat" Tomas Soucek remains a key player for his country despite being stripped of the captaincy.

The 31-year-old West Ham midfielder has been replaced as skipper by Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci after being removed from his position amid the fall-out from the 2-1 defeat by the Faroe Islands in October.

However Koubek, who himself took over from Ivan Hasek as head coach in December, still counts Soucek among his most important players ahead of Thursday night's World Cup play-off semi-final against the Republic of Ireland in Prague.

He said: "Tomas Soucek is an outstanding player with a great career. He doesn't have the captain's armband at this moment for reasons you all know, but nothing changes.

"It does not mean he will lose his value. He is still a 'full-fat' player, if I can use these words."

Image: Miroslav Koubek's first game in charge of the Czech Republic is against Ireland

Soucek's removal as captain has prompted speculation in the Czech media that he could even lose his place in the team, although Koubek remained coy over his team selection.

The 74-year-old said: "I don't read the newspapers, so I don't know. You will see tomorrow."

Koubek's side will welcome Ireland to the Fortuna Arena, the home of domestic champions Slavia Prague, knowing they will have to find a way to stop in-from striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in his country's last two qualifiers against Portugal and Hungary to get them to the play-offs.

Asked about his analysis of Heimir Hallgrimsson's team, he said: "One thing I noticed: they put a lot heart into their game. Ireland will definitely be a very tough opponent.

"But we will have a similar mindset, it will be a hard match, definitely.

"As for Parrott, he is outstanding, he is doing great. He is very fit, we know how he works. We do have some information, so now it will all be about eliminating him in a smart way. We will just have to stop him."

Krejci, however, has little doubt that it will be he and his team-mates who ultimately fight it out with either Denmark of North Macedonia for a trip to the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

He said: "We will make it. We will reach our goal. We will qualify for the World Cup."

Sports.title: Time is running out for Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury: AJ is still yet to sign Battle of Britain deal, reveals Frank Warren
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua has still not signed the contract, so the Battle of Britain against Tyson Fury remains in jeopardy.

Time is running out.

Promoter Frank Warren, who suggested that in reality boxing's longest hatching deal had to be finalised by this weekend, says: 'AJ hasn't signed yet.

'Tyson signed in January. He's training in Miami for the fight in early November and doesn't care where it takes place. '

The original agreement stipulated England, putting Wembley Stadium on alert.

But Netflix, the mega-paymasters for the broadcast, have joined their Saudi partners in insisting on New York's fabled Madison Square Garden so as to maximise US revenue.

Anthony Joshua (pictured) is still yet to sign the deal to fight Tyson Fury, Frank Warren has revealed

Warren (right) said Tyson Fury (left) has signed and is already in training for a potential bout

Joshua will need at least a two-month training camp for a fight of this magnitude and ideally nine to ten weeks.

It comes after Joshua was given 10 days to agree a deal on August 26 - seven days ago - with Warren previously warning: 'Unless AJ commits by the end of next week I'm afraid this will slip away like so many of those great fights which never happened.'

He added: 'At some point everyone has to say the most important thing is that it happens. Not this bulls*** about money.

'That everyone wants the fight. Does AJ really want it? I don't know. He's been through that tragedy of the car crash which killed two of his closest friends. Only he knows what he wants.'

Sports.title: Katie Taylor is crowned undisputed champion for a THIRD time with unanimous decision victory over Flora Pili - as Irish boxing icon, 40, enjoys fairytale end to her career in front of 82,000 fans at sold-out Croke Park
Sports.content:
There will never be another night quite like this for Katie Taylor… or, for that matter, for boxing itself.

Under the lights at Croke Park, in front of 82,000 delirious fans, Ireland's greatest fighter walked into the ring for the final time and left it as a three-time undisputed world champion after defeating Flora Pili on points.

Taylor had dreamed of this moment for much of her life. She had spent more than a decade rewriting the history of women's boxing, collecting world titles, conquering America, avenging the only defeat of her professional career and becoming the undisputed champion not once, but twice.

But nothing could have prepared her for this.

The noise inside Croke Park was deafening as Taylor made her final walk to the ring, the 40-year-old receiving a hero's welcome before facing the undefeated Frenchwoman in the last fight of a career that has transformed boxing in Ireland and beyond.

And when the first bell rang, Taylor set about doing exactly what she had come to Croke Park to do.

Katie Taylor celebrated victory on her farewell fight to become a three-time undisputed champion

Taylor overcame the challenge of Flora Pili, who had been unbeaten in 12 fights as a professional

Taylor appeared in the ring with family and friends are wrapping up her career in style

From the opening round, she demonstrated her speed deploying a lightning-quick jab despite being 11 years older than her opponent.

It was in the second round Pili really felt Taylor's power after taking a strong right hand to the temple.

It got the fans excited but the Frenchwoman weathered the storm before receiving a slap across her face from her trainer in the corner as he urged her to 'wake up'.

Knowing she was down heavily on the scorecards Pili showed conviction in the seventh round but it was never going to be enough to topple the Irish champion.

As the tenth and final round rang in, both fighters touched gloves as a sign of respect. The crowd cheered their champion home as she drew the curtain on her career.

Taylor did everything she could to get the stoppage in the dying seconds of the fight but she had to settle for a points victory.

There was a moment after the final bell when Taylor simply stood and took it all in.

The noise, the tears, the Irish flags, the thousands of people on their feet inside Croke Park and the knowledge that this really was the end.

Taylor emerged to a stunning ovation at a sold-out Croke Park, with 82,000 in attendance

Taylor's husband Sean McCavanagh was among those watching on ringside at the venue

Westlife performed in the build-up to Taylor taking to the ring for the last time in her career

Michael Flatley was among the well-known faces in attendance on the historic night

She had wanted one final night. One final fight. One final chance to walk into the ring in front of her home crowd and remind the world exactly who she was.

She got all three.

Taylor leaves boxing as a three-time undisputed world champion, an Olympic gold medallist and one of the most important figures the sport has ever produced.

But her legacy cannot be measured in belts alone.

She changed women's boxing forever. She gave a generation of young girls a reason to believe that they belonged in a boxing gym. She carried Irish boxing on her shoulders for years and became a sporting icon far beyond the ring.

And perhaps most fittingly of all, she signed off where she had always wanted to be.

At Croke Park. In front of her people. With another world title wrapped around her waist.

The final chapter could not have been written any better.

Katie Taylor came home, became undisputed for the third time and walked away on top.

A champion to the very end.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua's conqueror Andy Ruiz is PUMMELLED with punches and brutally beaten on his return to the ring after two years - but incredibly insists he WILL keep fighting
Sports.content:
Andy Ruiz, the man who condemned Anthony Joshua to his first ever professional defeat, suffered a horrific loss of his own on Friday night.

The 36-year-old Mexican was left bruised and bloodied as he lost to Poland's Damian Knyba on his return to the ring after two years out.

Knyba unleashed heavy punch after punch in the seventh round but Ruiz managed to ride it out, after being saved by the bell, to lose by a unanimous points decision.

Ruiz, who is now signed to British promoter Eddie Hearn, vowed to carry on despite losing his comeback fight to Knyba. The Pole now has a record of 18 wins and one defeat.

Rewind to June 2019, and Ruiz shocked the boxing world by upsetting the odds to knock Joshua out in the seventh round at Madison Square Garden.

Ruiz was a late stand-in for Jarrell Miller, who had failed a drugs test, and wasn't seen as a threat to Joshua's chances of remaining unbeaten and hanging on to his then IBF, WBO and WBA world heavyweight titles.

ANDY RUIZ IS SAVED BY THE BELL 🤯🤯🤯#TheFight | #RuizKnyba | Live NOW on DAZN and TNT ▪️ pic.twitter.com/JVQjG3KQM3 — DAZN Boxing (@DAZNBoxing) September 5, 2026

Andy Ruiz kneels down in front of the referee after being on the receiving end of heavy blows

Ruiz feels the full force of Poland's Damian Knyba during Friday's fight in New Jersey

Ruiz famously defeated the then undefeated Anthony Joshua back in June 2019

Joshua exacted revenge six months later and Ruiz has gone on to have just four more fights since due to injury problems, beating Chris Arreola and Luis Ortiz before drawing with Miller and now suffering his third loss.

Ruiz said after Friday's defeat in New Jersey: 'It was just a long layoff, and it was a great opponent.

'I didn't want to take an easy fight, so that's why I took Damian. He's a big guy. But we've got to take risks. I've still got it in me, man. I've just got to stay active and I want to fight again.

'Every time I tried to come in, he'd hold me really tight, and I just couldn't let my combinations go.

'He played a good game plan, but I'd love to run it back and do things a lot different.'

The judges scored the fight 117-110, 114-113 and 114-113 in Knyba's favour.

It wasn't the night Hearn was hoping for after signing Ruiz this summer but much of his current focus is on trying to finalise Joshua's highly anticipated fight against British rival Tyson Fury.

The bout has been proposed to take place in November after years of negotiations but the location of the fight appears to be a major sticking point.

Hearn and Joshua are said to want the fight to take place at Wembley Stadium in London while the Fury camp are reportedly leaning towards Madison Square Garden in New York City.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury attacks Anthony Joshua and questions his 'love' of England over his speech calling for a block on spending in white-owned shops - in bitter feud over moving their fight away from the UK
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury has picked apart Anthony Joshua's 'love' of England and desire to fight his great boxing rival on home soil - by dredging up his speech appearing to call for a block on spending in white-owned shops.

Fury, 38, and 36-year-old Joshua are embroiled in a bitter tug-of-war over their heavyweight superfight - largely centring on a debate around hosting it at London's Wembley Stadium or broadcaster Netflix's choice of Madison Square Garden in New York City.

Yesterday, Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn said Wembley talks had 're-opened', weeks after the fight looked set to be signed off in New York in November - in what has become a crusade towards keeping the event at 'home' for the two fighters.

But today, Fury was keen to make clear Joshua is not motivated by a love of his country. Earlier this year Daily Mail Sport revealed Joshua had in fact quit the UK to move to Dubai - even as thousands tried to flee amid rising panic in the Middle East warzone.

And Fury, a tax exile to the Isle of Man himself, brought up a 2020 speech at a Black Lives Matter march, where Joshua read out a letter from his friend Reece Campbell to urge attendees to stop spending money with white-owned shops and businesses.

'Show them where it hurts,' Joshua had said. 'Abstain from spending your money in their shops and economies, and invest in black-owned businesses.'

Anthony Joshua's 2020 Black Lives Matter speech has been brought back up by his great boxing rival Tyson Fury

A shirtless Fury was relentless in his criticism of Joshua and his perceived dodging of the fight

Fury re-posted the video of the speech, writing: 'This is the man who loves England, absolute s*** bag! Total peice of s*** bully with zero guts! Don't let them deceive you! & Living in Dubai.'

In an address to camera, Fury accused Joshua of trying to derail their fight to avoid being embarrassed: 'If I agreed to tie both hands behind my back and wear solid cement boots, Anthony Joshua would never get in the ring with me because I'll annihilate him.

'And he's a piece of s*** bully, and that's his game—bullying people like he tried to do to Daniel Dubois, and he got knocked spark dead out.

'The latest news from them is, "Tyson don't want to fight in England". Why the f*** wouldn't I want to fight in England, you sausage? "Tyson only wants to fight in America". Are you joking or what?

'Tyson is not in charge of this fight. Tyson didn't put the money up for this fight. Tyson is not the paymaster. Netflix are and Turki Al-Sheikh. Lovely. If it's in England, even better. I'll knock the motherf***er out even quicker. Prime time England, 10 o'clock, Wembley Stadium, 100,000 people. Why the f*** wouldn't I want it in England? Doesn't make any sense, does it?

'Like I said, who do you think you are? You and your little pathetic puppet Eddie Hearn trying to save you. There's no escaping, you know. I'll come to Watford (Joshua's hometown) and I'll set about you. I'll batter you in your own front garden, you piece of s***.'

'There is no getting out of this one. There is no getting out of this one. Get ready for this fight. I've had enough of your sauce to last me 11 years. I'm battering the f*** out of you, you useless dosser, piece of s***. That's what you are. And you know it as well, and everybody else knows what you are: a coward.'

Fury posted this video where Joshua called for 'abstaining on spending' from a friend's letter

Roaring out his title of the 'Gypsy King', Fury added: 'You's are going down, and the cash cow is getting knocked out. Because after this, he won't be able to show his face in public ever again.

'You're a useless dosser, a big bodybuilding piece of s***. Too many weights, not enough speed. When I crack a big right hook off it, you'll go over like spaghetti legs Deontay Wilder. But he's 10 times the man you'll ever be, because he's got a pair of b*****ks like King Kong, and you've got a pair of b*****ks like two f***ing garden peas, you piece of s***.'

Joshua has still not signed his contract for the Battle of Britain fight. Promoter Frank Warren, who suggested that in reality boxing's longest hatching deal had to be finalised by this weekend, told Daily Mail Sport's Jeff Powell: 'AJ hasn't signed yet.

'Tyson signed in January. He's training in Miami for the fight in early November and doesn't care where it takes place.'

The original agreement stipulated England, putting Wembley Stadium on alert.

But Netflix, the mega-paymasters for the broadcast, have joined their Saudi partners in insisting on New York's fabled Madison Square Garden so as to maximise US revenue.

Joshua will need at least a two-month training camp for a fight of this magnitude and ideally nine to ten weeks.

It comes after Joshua was given 10 days to agree a deal on August 26 with Warren previously warning: 'Unless AJ commits by the end of next week I'm afraid this will slip away like so many of those great fights which never happened.'

He added: 'At some point everyone has to say the most important thing is that it happens. Not this bulls*** about money.

'That everyone wants the fight. Does AJ really want it? I don't know. He's been through that tragedy of the car crash which killed two of his closest friends. Only he knows what he wants.'

Much of the discussions around Wembley centre on a willingness to allow a late start time - and late curfew - to suit the American TV market. Mayor Sadiq Khan this week stated that he is keen to host the fight and find a solution.

Sports.title: Sugar Ray Leonard's 'violent' son was arrested for alleged possession of dangerous cocktail of drugs just weeks after trying to break into boxing icon's home
Sports.content:
The troubled 25-year-old son of boxing legend Sugar Ray Leonard was arrested with several dangerous illegal drugs earlier this summer, according to Santa Monica Police.

As first revealed by The California Post on Wednesday, an officer witnessed Daniel Leonard and another man 'walking with an inflated balloon and a large cylindrical container believed to be a nitrous oxide tank' in the early morning hours of July 7.

'As the officer approached, one man attempted to conceal the balloon behind him before dropping it to the ground,' the SMPD rep told the Post. 'The second man appeared to conceal the container at his side. Officers detained both men and confirmed the container was a nitrous oxide tank.'

The pair was arrested for possessing nitrous with the intent to inhale before Daniel was additionally charged with possession of methamphetamine and sedatives/benzodiazepines. In total, he was charged with four misdemeanors for possession of nitrous oxide, a substance containing nitrous oxide, MDMA, alprazolam and dextroamphetamine.

He is due back in court in LA County on October 12, according to the Post.

The Daily Mail has submitted a records request with the SMPD for further information. Daniel did not immediately respond to The Daily Mail's requests for comment on Wednesday night.

Daniel Leonard (left) is seen alongside his father, former Olympic gold medalist Ray Leonard

Daniel Ray Leonard is pictured with his dad Sugar Ray and mom Bernadette back in 2017

This marks the latest arrest for the son of Ray Leonard, a former five-division world champion and Olympic gold medalist, who served as America's most popular boxer in the immediate aftermath of Muhammad Ali's retirement.

In May, TMZ reported Daniel was arrested for violating a restraining order at the family's home, although that protective order was later dropped.

According to the Post, it was a 'violent' incident involving Daniel and Ray that led the father to file a protective order against his son.

The Post later produced Ray's restraining order request in which he describes his youngest son as an addict and thief, who steals 'every day.' In a handwritten declaration, Sugar Ray wrote: 'He has overdosed 4 times. They had to bring him back to life 2 times at the hospital!

'He has stolen extreme amounts of money valuable items! He [illegible] steals every day for years! My son Daniel Leonard has been a drug addict for 7 or 8 years at least. His behavior has gotten worse over the years!'

'I love my son but he has become a danger not only [to] himself but to his family! My wife is extremely afraid along with [my] daughter Camille!' Sugar Ray continued. 'His behavior has gotten worse every day. We haven't had a day of peace in 9 years which is the reality of his addiction! Scared for my family!'

More recently, Daniel (R) was pictured alongside the family - and Magic Johnson - last August

The Leonards live in a sprawling $46.5 million estate in the Pacific Palisades, California

Daniel is the youngest son of Sugar Ray Leonard and his second wife Bernadette Robi, and his third son overall.

Sugar Ray, now 70, had his first son - Ray Jr - with his first wife Juanita Wilkinson in 1973, before adding a daughter - Camille - with Bernadette.

In February of last year, Daniel's mother Bernadette posted a cryptic caption on Instagram alongside a photograph of Sugar Ray and Daniel - her husband and son.

A photo showed the pair standing together on a beach with Sugar Ray's arm around Daniel's shoulder, and the caption read: 'Happy Valentine's to my hearts!!! Love you both beyond and we will get through this faze (sic)!'

Sports.title: Fabio Wardley launches impassioned defence of Moses Itauma's trainer after heavy criticism over his crushing world title defeat by Filip Hrgovic
Sports.content:
Fabio Wardley has sprung to the defence of trainer Ben Davison against the barrage of criticism which followed his stablemate Moses Itauma's crushing world heavyweight title defeat on Saturday night.

Davison has been eviscerated for 21-year-old Itauma subsiding with exhaustion in the ninth round against Croatia's first world heavyweight champion Filip Hrgovic.

Davison may find himself fighting to keep Itauma on his roster at an imminent council of war with promoter Frank Warren

But Wardley - who is in training for the October 17 rematch of the slugfest in which Daniel Dubois took his WBO belt - says: ‘I just can’t believe so much hostility and so much stick being thrown at Ben. He’s been my trainer for seven years and he’s brought me through from my unusual background (white collar boxing) to winning a world title.

‘He doesn’t become a bad trainer because Moses had his first defeat against a really tough opponent.

‘Ben has shown there’s so much more to boxing at the higher levels than just my power to knock people out. Taught me so much. It wasn’t his fault I lost to Daniel. I beat myself,

Fabio Wardley (above) has sprung to the defence of trainer Ben Davison after 21-year-old Moses Itauma's crushing world heavyweight title defeat against Filip Hrgovic on Saturday

Davison (left) has been blasted for Itauma (right) subsiding with exhaustion in the ninth round

‘And Ben is now adding the nuances I never knew anything about so I can adapt for the rematch and win this time.’

Warren, however, says: ’Ben and I will have to have a chat. Was there a plan B for when Hrgovic simply refused to be knocked out through eight rounds of punishment?

‘Or did Moses not listen, like footballers who go out on the pitch and don’t do what the manager tells them?

‘Losing happens but they should have managed the fight when so many rounds ahead. Moses should have stayed behind his terrific jab and boxed his way to a decision. He was too obsessed with getting another knock out.

‘So he just kept his foot hard down on the accelerator from start to finish and punched himself out.

‘Of course at 21 Moses can come back to be a world champion but there’s work to be done.’

The unanswered question is whether Davison will be the man doing it.

Sports.title: Emotional Eddie Hearn reveals why he was in 'floods of tears' in build-up to Katie Taylor's retirement fight - and predicts event could be the biggest of ALL time
Sports.content:
Eddie Hearn has admitted he was reduced to 'floods of tears' watching the promo video for Katie Taylor's retirement fight, before predicting her final ring walk at Croke Park could become 'one of the greatest moments sport has ever seen'.

Taylor will call time on her glittering career on Saturday night when she faces unbeaten Frenchwoman Flora Pili in front of an expected 80,000 fans in Dublin.

The 40-year-old will bid to become a three-time undisputed world champion in the 27th and final fight of her professional career, with the vacant WBC title also on the line alongside her WBO, WBA and IBF belts.

And Hearn, who has promoted Taylor throughout her professional career, is already struggling to contain his emotions ahead of the occasion.

'I've got my daughter with me, and we came through the airport, and it's like every other person knows about Saturday,' he said. 'Everyone knows about Saturday. It sounds like everyone's going. So I just can't wait. I just can't wait to feel it, and it'll be unbelievably emotional.

'I mean, that promo video… I'm not afraid to say it. When I say I cried, I am not exaggerating. This is a bit embarrassing but I bawled my eyes out. Not like, 'Oh, a tear came out', literally floods of tears.

Eddie Hearn (pictured above) has admitted he was reduced to 'floods of tears' watching the promo video for Katie Taylor's retirement fight

Taylor will call time on her glittering career on Saturday night when she faces unbeaten Frenchwoman Flora Pili (pictured on the right) in front of an expected 80,000 fans in Dublin

The 40-year-old (pictured above) will bid to become a three-time undisputed world champion in the 27th and final fight of her professional career

'I can't stop thinking about the ring walk. I truly believe it will be one of the greatest moments sport has ever seen.

'Yes, it's going to be one of the biggest events Irish sport has ever seen, one of the biggest female boxing events ever seen, but honestly I think it could be the biggest sporting event of all time. It's going to be one of those events where everyone's going to go, 'Wow. I can't believe it's happening.'

For Hearn, the scale of the occasion is all the more remarkable given that he once doubted whether Taylor would ever get the chance to fight at Croke Park.

The Matchroom promoter admitted he is disappointed with himself for allowing those doubts to creep in, particularly after previous attempts to Taylor's dream location had failed to materialise.

'I'm disappointed in myself, actually, that I allowed that to happen, because maybe we could have done it earlier,' Hearn said. 'But I probably didn't have the confidence that I had going into it this time, with Peter, with the Serrano three-fight deal and all that.

'If Croke Park had originally gone, 'Yes, this is going to be massive,' I would have gone, 'Wow you're right' and we would have done it. But I was like, 'I don't know' and I was thinking blimey, if they're not sure, do we really want to be gambling with these costs?

'But, they listened, they helped out as well. They were fantastic in the end.

'Saying all of that though, I never thought we'd do 40,000 on a pre-sale. It's honestly blown my mind how passionate the fans are for Katie and how much they support her and show up for her.'

For Hearn, the scale of the occasion is all the more remarkable given that he once doubted whether Taylor would ever get the chance to fight at Croke Park

Taylor pictured inspiring the next generation during her open working in Dublin on Wednesday

The demand has left Hearn wondering just how many more fans could have packed into Ireland's national stadium.

'We're getting hundreds of messages every day from people saying, 'Please, I want to bring my daughter. It's heartbreaking in a way because we'd love for everyone to get a ticket and be there to watch it live but that's just the way it is.'

Hearn is delighted that DAZN will broadcast the fight, while also praising the decision to allow Irish broadcaster RTE to show the event.

'I'm so happy that DAZN are broadcasting the fight,' he said. 'But I think the RTE thing is incredible as well. I was shocked, but very grateful that DAZN allowed that to happen because I think it's very important for Ireland.'

And while her journey to the Olympics and gold medal at London 2012 remains the defining chapter of her amateur career, Hearn believes it is what Taylor has achieved as a professional that will shape her legacy for generations to come.

Taylor won Olympic gold before turning professional, but went on to conquer the sport at the highest level, headlining at Madison Square Garden, fighting on Netflix and beating virtually every major opponent put in front of her.

Hearn believes her battle with Chantelle Cameron, including the rematch in which she avenged the first defeat of her professional career, are particularly underappreciated.

'She won that gold medal, but I think when you look back on everything that she's done, from starting out fighting on the AJ cards to headlining MSG, fighting on Netflix, you know, and she's beaten everybody,' he said.

Taylor won Olympic gold before turning professional, but went on to conquer the sport at the highest level, headlining at Madison Square Garden and fighting on Netflix

She has beaten virtually every major opponent put in front of her - including Amanda Serrano

'By the way, when you look back, you see Chantelle Cameron beat Mikaela Mayer last Saturday. She's a strong, big, big, big girl. And Katie's rematch victory over Chantelle Cameron, I think, is so underrated, especially at the stage in her career that Katie was at.

'There are so many things. I think the Olympics will always be the Olympics, but there are a lot of people that don't remember the Olympics or weren't around in 2012. The younger generation now that are following Katie, I don't think they're necessarily reminiscing about the Olympics.

'These are girls that are eight, 10, 12, 16. They weren't even born when she won the Olympics. So I think what she's done in the pro ranks will be remembered forever. Honestly, it's just everything that she's done across the board. We are so lucky to have had a fighter like her.'

Hearn also believes Taylor has fundamentally transformed women's boxing.

'She changed women's boxing forever,' he said. 'Whether I did it or not, she was going to convince probably someone to do it, right?

'Now, whether they would have done it the same way as us, I doubt it. But this wasn't me going, 'I'm going to try and change women's boxing.' This was me going, 'I believe in you, and I want to come along for the journey.'

'So what led from there is the doors opening and watching…'

Hearn remembers just how different the landscape was when Taylor turned professional.

Serrano and Taylor fighting in their IBF, WBA, WBC, WBO, and Ring super lightweight title bout during Netflix's Katie Taylor vs Amanda Serrano 3 at Madison Square Garden on July 11, 2025

'When she turned pro, there were some weight classes in women's boxing that had four fighters at a professional level,' he said. 'You could fight for the world title in your second or third fight. And now it's really hard to win a world title. There are some brilliant fighters.'

Perhaps most tellingly, Hearn says Taylor has achieved something that goes beyond titles, records and money: she has earned the respect of virtually every fighter in the sport.

'There isn't one female fighter you could find that wouldn't go, 'She's incredible,' he said. 'She's just so loved. And there's no airs or graces. She's not there for the fame. She's not there for the money. It's just pure - purely a faith, the love of the sport, and trying to set an example.'

Yet amid all the emotion and celebration, Hearn knows Taylor cannot afford to lose sight of the woman standing opposite her on Saturday night.

Pili is unbeaten at 12-0 and, while she does not possess Taylor's experience or pedigree, she is younger, strong and willing to trade.

With Taylor fighting for her third undisputed crown and Pili seeking to pull off the biggest upset of her career, Hearn insists the retirement celebrations must wait.

'You know, today really the switch has got to focus on the fight because this girl's decent,' he said. 'She's big. She's 12-0.

'I'm not saying she's got the pedigree of Katie Taylor, but Katie's 40 years old, right? She's fighting a young, strong girl who likes to trade.

Pili (pictured above) is unbeaten at 12-0 and, while she does not possess Taylor's experience or pedigree, she is younger, strong and willing to trade

While Taylor's final fight will inevitably dominate the night, Hearn insists the rest of the card has been designed to make the occasion worthy of Croke Park

'And so does Katie.'

'She's IBO world champion, European champion, decent amateur, who, by the way, can become undisputed herself on Saturday,' Hearn said. 'So I think today there needs to be a little bit of a switch from this whole, 'Oh, euphoric, this is going to be amazing.'

'I just walked into her BBC interview there, and she was saying, 'I need to prepare myself for war here.' Because she can't walk out and get caught up in the emotion. She can't get in the ring and the start of the fight just passes you by.

'She's got to go in there, and prepare for it to be a war from the opening bell.

'And it will be an all-out war because it's the only way she knows how to fight. She's not going to try and box a moon because she'll want to leave it all in the ring.'

And while Taylor's final fight will inevitably dominate the night, Hearn insists the rest of the card has been designed to make the occasion worthy of Croke Park.

There will be major music acts, a host of Irish talent and a series of intriguing fights before Taylor takes her final walk to the ring.

'I'm not going to give too much away… I want you all to see it unfold on the night,' Hearn said. 'But there's definitely people everybody's heard of in this country who are going to be performing on Saturday night, and a number of different things going on during the night.'

Sports.title: Tyson Fury delivers brutal verdict on Moses Itauma - and claims agonising defeat against Filip Hrgovic could cost British star £100m
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury believes fellow British boxer Moses Itauma fought Filip Hrgovic too soon in a decision that could 'cost him £100million'.

Itauma, 21, fell short in his world heavyweight title bout against the Croat when he was stopped in the ninth round at The O2 on Saturday night.

Britain's talented young boxer was ahead on the cards and looked destined to claim the vacant IBF heavyweight title before Hrgovic, 34, mounted an impressive comeback to stage the shock victory.

Fury, who is gearing up for an expected showdown with long-time British rival Anthony Joshua in November, believes Itauma's first shot at a world title came 'too early' and it could ultimately deny him a huge payday.

'I said it was too early – and it could cost him £100m,' the former heavyweight champion told The Telegraph on Thursday, who famously defeated Wladimir Klitschko to win three world-title belts at the age of 27 in 2015.

'If I had boxed him aged 21, Klitschko would have knocked me out,' the Gypsy King recalled. 'Moses is a brilliant talent. I've had him in camp and sparred him many times.

Tyson Fury (above) believes fellow British boxer Moses Itauma fought Filip Hrgovic too soon

Itauma, 21, lost his world title bout against the experienced Croat at The O2 on Saturday night

'Moses is very talented but also very young and raw. Whatever Moses is at 21, in five years' time, 10 years' time, he'll be 10 times better, 10 times stronger, more experienced. He's an amazing boxer, talented.'

Despite waxing lyrical about Itauma's raw ability, Fury believes he wasn't ready to face a 'battle-hardened veteran' such as Hrgovic, who has fought hundreds of fights at differing levels around the world.

'As we saw for the first six, seven rounds, Moses outclassed him,' the 38-year-old said. 'But when it came to the stretch, the championship distance, the young man wasn't ready to go down the straight with a veteran who trained hard, looked in fantastic shape, dedicated himself, and is in the prime of his life at 34.

'I said to everybody who would listen, this is too soon. This guy needs another four, five fights. What's the rush? He's 21. Not only has it cost Moses the hundred-million-dollar career as a superstar athlete – like (NBA star) LeBron James and all those people – when you've been banjoed like that it's difficult to turn that around mentally.

'It's not rocket science. If you go from not going past four rounds to jumping into a 12-round world-title fight without winning anything along the way... if you look at my career, I won English, Irish, British, Commonwealth, European, every international belt there was along the way and every world-title belt, too: Lineal, Ring Magazine, everything you can think of... I did it the traditional route.'

Itauma, who went into the title fight unbeaten, won every round heading into the second half of the bout before momentum swung drastically in the Croat's favour.

Fury believes he wasn't ready to face a 'battle-hardened veteran' such as 34-year-old Hrgovic

Fellow British boxer Chris Eubank Jr posted on X after his defeat: 'Not sure what happened tonight. Moses was fighting well & then gassed out it seems… at his young age this should simply not be happening.

'Time to rethink his training camp moving forward I think. Congratulations to Filip Hrgovic becoming the new heavyweight champ.'

Sports.title: Hamilton says Ferrari has left it "too late" to back him in F1 title fight
Sports.content:
The Italian Grand Prix is probably the worst venue for a spat to brew up between team-mates but that is what happened at Monza as Lewis Hamilton finished a distant sixth after Charles Leclerc barged him into the gravel on the opening lap.

Leclerc then spun off into the Parabolica barrier at high speed at the end of the second lap, inducing a red flag. The outcome of the weekend was that Hamilton lost more ground to Mercedes team-mates Kimi Antonelli and George Russell in the title race, while Ferrari slipped 122 points behind Mercedes in the constructors' standings.

Antonelli is now 66 points ahead of Russell and 76 clear of Hamilton, while Leclerc lies fifth, 112 points adrift of Antonelli.

Hamilton has been critical of Ferrari's execution on several occasions this year, especially when dealing with team orders in scenarios where the drivers are on different strategies. In the Dutch GP, he felt a podium finish was left on the table when the team appeared to dither over how to get Leclerc out of his way at a point where Hamilton was running faster on fresher tyres.

Hamilton clearly feels that he should have been prioritised, given he is closer to the Mercedes drivers than Leclerc in the drivers' championship, but the opportunity has slipped away.

Hamilton spoke frankly about his championship prospects after finishing sixth in Monza Photo by: Getty Images

"I think from today, we've just lost so much ground to them [Mercedes] on points," he told media including Motorsport.com at Monza.

"It's far too late for those decisions to come. It's many, many weeks too late.

"All I can do is just try and turn up. I'll get up tomorrow morning and I'll give it my best. Ultimately today, I feel massively gutted for the tifosi, who showed up for us today.

"The guys back at the factory, who really, really are giving it everything. You know yesterday we didn't really execute that well. I think the same today.

"It's tough. I'm giving it everything I can, but sometimes it's just not enough. You need all the other stuff to come together.

Ferrari might not have had a car quick enough to challenge for outright victory at Monza, but it made the job of maximising it potential needlessly difficult. Throughout qualifying it struggled to orchestrate its drivers to provide a slipstream for one another – essential at this circuit, given the number of straights – to the point where Hamilton was almost eliminated in Q2.

In his first Q3 run, Hamilton was sent out of the pits late, so he struggled to pick up a slipstream from the cars ahead. He did obtain a tow from Leclerc on his second run and lined up just behind his team-mate on the grid as they were promoted to third and fourth by Oscar Piastri's impeding penalty.

Hamilton appeared to get his nose ahead on the inside line into Turn 1, then was still ahead at Turn 2 only for Leclerc to push him wide, onto the gravel. Leclerc held on to third while Hamilton dropped to 10th.

After the race, Leclerc framed the incident in terms of mutual responsibility, saying, "we went too far". But Hamilton saw otherwise – although taking the inside line into the first part of this chicane tends to put the driver on the outside line into the left-hander that follows, inviting collisions such as this.

Diversion via the gravel dropped Hamilton to P10 Photo by: Getty Images

"I was ahead in Turn 2. By the apex, I was ahead. There was no 'we' in it.

"Look, I don't race dirty. I've always raced clean and fairly and always left space.

"I've come into the team and tried to be respectful of space and definitely not put the team in jeopardy. I stand by that and all I can talk about is on my side. You have to speak to Fred [Vasseur, team principal] about the other side and decisions that are taken there.

"Ultimately it comes from the top. It trickles down, decisions. It starts with Fred.

"There's only so much you can say, so much you can push and shout from the mountain top. Yesterday, I said we've got to look at how we communicate. If we continue to travel the same path, we get the same result.

"We keep getting the same result. We've got to change things because it's not helping us move forward. I think they're receptive to it and we'll take it offline over the next, probably not next week, but particularly after the next race, to try and look at how we can procedurally make things different so that the same thing can't happen.

"I think the guys in the factory are doing a really great job. We're not executing as cleanly as well as we can. Easily not as well as now the other teams are. But we were at some points in the season."

Executing team orders is a challenging proposition for Ferrari, given Leclerc's status within the organisation. It's understood that his management was instrumental in Vasseur's appointment, having convinced senior management that regime change was required when Mattia Binotto was team principal.

But if team-mates take points off one another, the damage can extend beyond the race to the drivers' title. The constructors' trophy may be less important to fans, but the order of that championship determines the team's share of the commercial revenues. Indiscipline can therefore have a direct effect on the balance sheet.

"I think it comes down to rules of engagement," said Hamilton.

"When I was at Mercedes, we had a written rule of engagement. We never really had it too bad. Maybe moments with me and Nico [Rosberg] a couple of times. But more often than not it was good.

"Here, there are no rules."

Sports.title: Audi signals appeal over Tsunoda’s Italian GP non-penalty
Sports.content:
The Audi Formula 1 team has notified the FIA of its intention to appeal against Yuki Tsunoda's non-penalty in the Italian Grand Prix.

Amid confusion over where he was supposed to line up on a lap 6 restart, Tsunoda parked in his correct 14th grid slot, but at an angle towards the inside wall. Race director Rui Marques was "not comfortable" with Tsunoda's position, so imposed an extra formation lap.

According to Article B5.9.4 of the F1 2026 sporting regulations, "any driver who caused an extra formation lap, and is then able to start the, or any subsequent, extra formation lap must enter the Pit Lane at the end of the lap and must start ... from the end of the Pit Lane."

But according to the FIA race stewards, Tsunoda didn't technically cause the extra formation lap because the race director acted out of an abundance of caution, Tsunoda wasn't out of his grid slot and didn't impact other competitors. The crux of the issue is that race control hadn't informed Racing Bulls that its driver had caused the extra formation lap either, so therefore the team had no reason to tell Tsunoda to start from the pitlane.

Tsunoda escaped a stop-and-go penalty and went on to score the final point in 10th. The decision not to punish the Japanese driver impacted Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto, who crossed the line in 11th.

As a result, Audi has notified the FIA of its intention to appeal against the non-penalty for Tsunoda.

"Following the Italian Grand Prix, we raised a concern regarding the application of Article B5.9.4, which requires a driver who causes an extra formation lap to enter the pit lane and resume the race from there," Audi said in a statement. "The Stewards issued a decision of No Further Action, and we have notified our intention to appeal. As the matter is now subject to the FIA appeal process, we will not comment further at this stage."

Gabriel Bortoleto would have gained a point in Monza if Yuki Tsunoda had been handed a penalty. Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Per article 15.4 of the FIA's International Sporting Code, competitors have one hour after the stewards' decision to notify their intention to appeal. That does not mean Audi is actually appealing against the verdict just yet. But it gives the team an additional 96-hour time window to further study the case to see if there is an element to appeal against before following through on it.

In their verdict, the stewards wrote: "The extra formation lap resulted from the Race Director’s assessment of the situation, rather than being directly caused by the driver of Car 22.

"Further, Article B5.9.4 goes on to specify that if a driver who causes the extra formation lap and is then able to start the extra formation lap, he must enter the Pit Lane at the end of the lap and start from the Pit Lane. It is only then, if the driver fails to do this, that the mandatory penalty of a Stop and Go penalty is imposed.

"In other words, the penalty is for failing to come into the Pit Lane and start from there. The penalty is not for causing the extra formation lap, if indeed, he caused the extra formation lap in the first place.

"A critical issue emerges here, in that in order to comply with the requirement to enter and start from the Pit Lane, a driver would need to know that he was the cause of the extra formation lap."

The stewards added: "The team, based on the fact that the car was positioned within its starting grid box in compliance with the regulations, had, in our determination, no reason to instruct its driver to enter and start from the Pit Lane.

"Accordingly, irrespective of whether or not the driver directly caused the extra formation lap, the team and driver were unaware that they were being considered as the cause, therefore we determine that we are unable to impose a Stop and Go penalty in this case, and decide to take no further action."

Sports.title: Why Mercedes didn't pit Russell under virtual safety car in Italian GP
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli's sensational win from the back of the grid in the Italian Grand Prix was thanks to a great drive, but perhaps also a little help from strategy and a timely virtual safety car.

The Italian was the only Mercedes driver to make a pitstop during the race - and ultimately defeated his team-mate and championship rival George Russell.

Mercedes split the strategies between its drivers, putting Antonelli on mediums after the early red flag. That was the only option for the Italian to go to the end without stopping, having started the race on hards. Russell, on the other hand, started on mediums and switched to hards after the race was stopped following Charles Leclerc's crash - and stayed on that tyre for the rest of the distance.

For Antonelli, Mercedes used the opportunity to put him on a new set of mediums when Lance Stroll's stoppage caused a virtual safety car on lap 27.

By that point, Antonelli had already made his way through the field and was battling Russell for the lead - although Mercedes asked him not to attack his team-mate after the initial phase of the fight, allowing them to try to build a gap to Max Verstappen.

Then came the call for Antonelli to pit. And although the Italian was able to come back and overtake his team-mate on fresher tyres, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff said the team itself didn't know which strategy would ultimately prove better.

“We didn't know what was the better strategy," he told the media, including Autosport, after the race. "At that stage, the system said that the one-stop [for Russell] comes out ahead. That two-stop was coming close to the end, but wouldn't catch. So that's what the software said.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

“It was also the right thing to split the strategies because it was unknown what the better one would be. In the morning meeting we said the hard tyre is going to go forever. You can start on it and finish on it and you can see with George it was a forever tyre but it didn't have the performance that of the medium.”

The decision to stop Antonelli was made despite him reporting that his tyres were in good shape.

“We didn't talk to Kimi about the stop," Wolff confirmed. "We asked for the state of the tyre and he said, 'Well it's actually good' but it was clear that we saw abrasion and I think it was on Lewis' car. We saw some abrasion on a McLaren. So it was the right thing to do. And that's why it didn't need any big discussion.

“But then having said that, Kimi was able to extract 35 laps or 40 laps from that tyre in a consistent way and that's certainly his skill.”

Russell himself believes he had enough pace to win the race had Antonelli stayed on the same strategy.

"I would have loved to have continued on the same strategy," he said during the post-race press conference. "Because I felt in a good position in that battle. I knew exactly what I needed to do with the energy management to defend but also when to attack and make those moves and I put a lot of preparation into this race in that regard.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

"Then of course when the VSC came out, it came out at that perfect point for the drivers to pull the trigger and take the pitstop."

Asked whether he had considered stopping for fresh rubber at that point, Russell said: "I didn't. I actually thought the guys behind me were going to stay out as well but I'm sure the team were quite nervous on the pitwall watching our battle and were probably quite happy to send us on different strategies.

"When we had Max in the mix as well from a team perspective, you're covering off both scenarios. So, today Kimi did a great job.

"I was on the hard tyre and Kimi was on the medium tyre. So if either of us were to pit, it was going to be Kimi. And that's why I was just a little bit annoyed with the timing of that VSC, because I think it would have been tough for those guys on the medium to have competed with anybody on the hard tyre.

"But, it takes nothing away from Kimi's drive altogether. It would have been very interesting to see how the race would have panned out if there was no VSC."

After the race at Monza, Russell trails Antonelli by 66 points in the championship.

Sports.title: After Antonelli’s Italian GP win, is the F1 title fight over? Our writers have their say
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli’s Italian Grand Prix win from 19th on the grid was a statement performance and extends his lead in the Formula 1 world championship to 66 points.

With a maximum of 10 rounds left – subject to the Qatar and Abu Dhabi GPs and the situation in the Middle East – the Italian driver is in a supremely strong position to seal the 2026 world title.

So, is the 2026 F1 world title fight over? Our writers have their say.

It’d need to be a generational choke for Antonelli to lose it from here

I don’t want to say it is done and dusted before the European stretch of the season is over but this felt monumental. To go from 19th on the grid to victory, against the likes of George Russell and Max Verstappen at the front of the pack, is going to go down in history as the first moment Antonelli demonstrated his F1 world champion credentials.

A gap of 66 points with 10-ish rounds to go isn’t impossible to overturn – just two DNFs and the pressure is right on top of the 20-year-old – but he just doesn’t seem phased by any of it and, if anything, is driving better now than at any point in his burgeoning career in F1.

Antonelli has shown already he can bank solid results when needed, and also charge for the win when it is there for the taking; he effectively did both one after the other at Monza this weekend.

Yes, finishing second to Russell in every race still isn’t enough to mathematically seal the title, but with his team-mate expected to serve a back of the grid penalty for an engine change in Azerbaijan, he has a great opportunity to make that scenario a reality.

– Haydn Cobb

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Rose / Formula 1 via Getty Images

It’s not over – but Russell will need luck

Antonelli definitely dealt a sizeable blow to Russell’s title hopes in Monza but, as of today, there are 10 rounds to go – 258 points to score.

Russell’s deficit is up to 66 points, and the dynamic isn’t favourable to him, as frustration will understandably be growing – though he was very gracious in defeat on Sunday.

In order to make up such a substantial gap, Russell will need the stars to align. Antonelli doesn’t have many off days; in 13 grands prix so far this season, he has finished on the podium 11 times to Russell’s seven.

That remarkable consistency typically leads to a world title, with few examples to the contrary. Coincidentally, it happened just last year. Oscar Piastri also had 11 podiums from the first 13 rounds, by which time he was 16 points ahead of team-mate Lando Norris and 81 points clear of Max Verstappen, but he ended up outscored by both.

Other than that, the most recent one was Nico Rosberg in 2014. The German had recorded 11 podiums in the first 13 races, but team-mate Lewis Hamilton had 10 podium finishes himself and was just 22 points down in the standings. Three times fewer than the current gap, in other words.

So, such a recovery wouldn’t be unprecedented, as shown by Verstappen – but it wasn’t comparable given Russell and Antonelli have the same car, unlike the Red Bull racer and the McLaren drivers last year. So, while there’s hope, the Briton really is a long shot by now.

– Ben Vinel

Antonelli’s rivals have too much to do

There’s really very little to suggest anything can still stop Antonelli from clinching the title this year after his Monza victory. If anyone had doubts before, this weekend probably removed the last arguments for predicting any other outcome - barring something going completely wrong for the Italian off track.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

After all, Isack Hadjar didn’t exactly plan to miss a couple of races. So, as long as Antonelli stays away from boxing gloves for the next couple of months, he should be fine. If he shows up on the grid - regardless of where he starts, apparently - he looks set to become world champion at the age of 20.

It’s not only about Antonelli, either. Russell, still his closest rival, doesn’t just need to close a massive points gap - he has to do something even more difficult: maintain the belief that he can still beat Antonelli on any given weekend.

Given how this season has unfolded, and the speed of the Italian’s progress, it must be daunting for the Briton to see just how brilliant his young team-mate has become.

Monza also confirmed Ferrari is probably out of the picture. Charles Leclerc never really was in it, and now he’s simply too far behind to seriously think about the title. And Hamilton doesn’t appear to have a car capable of challenging the Mercedes drivers consistently. The same applies to Norris and McLaren, whose weaknesses were exposed again this weekend.

– Oleg Karpov

I am going to call it here

I just don't see a way back for Russell. I really don't. Yes, there are a lot of points on the table, stranger things have happened in F1, and those formidable Mercedes power units have been glass cannons. I get all that.

But the manner in which Antonelli has been amassing race wins, and collecting whichever result is available when Mercedes doesn't enjoy its usual supremacy, is a quite a marvel for a 20-year-old.

Russell is turning things around, but even that doesn't appear to be enough to be beating Antonelli on a regular basis and that's exactly what he would have to do. Not keeping pace, as he is roughly doing now, but battering Antonelli.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Rose / Formula 1 via Getty Images

I just don't see it happening, because I'm afraid Russell has met his match in the young Italian.

What's more, the Italian Grand Prix was supposed to be Antonelli's mulligan, his joker race where taking his fifth power unit meant an exercise in damage limitation. Instead of sustaining damage, he has dealt Russell a mental hammer blow. Meanwhile, Russell still has to take his engine penalty later on, and there isn't a circuit left where overtaking will be this easy.

The conclusion to last year's title race has shown that 10 races is an eternity, but that was when the best driver of his generation was doing the chasing. Now, the best driver of the next generation is out in front, and he looks bulletproof. I am going to call it here.

– Filip Cleeren

Sports.title: F1 Italian GP: Antonelli stuns from 19th on the grid to win home race
Sports.content:
Formula 1 world championship leader Kimi Antonelli has taken a sensational home win at the Italian Grand Prix, coming from 19th on the grid to defeat Mercedes team-mate George Russell.

In an action-packed display of battery-led yo-yo racing, Antonelli overcame a grid penalty and a mid-race pitstop to scythe through the field and defeat long-time leader Russell, with Max Verstappen beating the McLaren to the final podium spot.

The race started with a huge blow for the sold-out tifosi-filled grandstands. As shock polesitter Pierre Gasly held firm against Russell, Lewis Hamilton attempted to pass team-mate Charles Leclerc down the inside of the tight Turn 1 chicane, with Leclerc pushing the Briton wide on exit, costing Hamilton six positions as he dropped to 10th.

The incident was noted by race control, but on the end of lap 2 Leclerc suffered a huge crash on the exit of the Parabolica corner as he fended off McLaren's Oscar Piastri. Leclerc skated across the gravel and veered into the outside wall at high speed, escaping unhurt but bringing out the red flag for lengthy barrier repairs.

Read Also: Formula 1 Leclerc needs further health checks after heavy Italian GP crash

Russell had been able to pass Gasly on the front straight earlier on the lap, ensuring the Mercedes driver would take the restart from pole, while Verstappen and Franco Colapinto worked their way up to third and fourth at the expense of Piastri.

All drivers were afforded a free tyre change under the red flag, with Verstappen the only frontrunner to pick mediums instead of hards. Following an extra formation lap for Yuki Tsunoda being out of position, Russell defended the lead from Gasly, while Colapinto passed Verstappen in the second Alpine for third. But after Verstappen retaliated with a trademark move around the outside of the second chicane, Colapinto went off the track in the first Lesmo right-hander, dropping the Argentinian down to 16th.

In the melee behind the pair, Hamilton moved up to fourth at the expense of Piastri, who was battling team-mate Norris and Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad. After a rocket start, Antonelli took advantage of that fight to motor to sixth with a double pass on Norris and Lindblad on the main straight.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images

On lap 7 Alpine's hopes of a shock win for Gasly dwindled further when he was passed for second by Verstappen. Three laps later the Frenchman also lost third to Hamilton, and he was powerless to keep Piastri and Antonelli behind as the Alpine man dropped to sixth.

Clearing Gasly quickly was supposed to hand Russell a clear path to victory, but on an afternoon where slipstreaming was key, the Mercedes man was unable to break away from Verstappen and instead started coming under pressure from the Dutchman, with the pair trading the lead two more times on lap 12 and 15.

But rather than Russell, Antonelli quickly emerged as the more likely of the two Mercedes drivers to take victory despite starting from 19th. As the last driver of a gaggle of three cars, some two seconds behind the leaders, Antonelli had already picked off Hamilton and Piastri in quick succession.

Russell's jousting with Verstappen allowed Antonelli to rapidly close in on the lead battle, snatching second away from the Red Bull man on lap 16. Antonelli only needed one attempt to pass Russell for the lead, claiming control on lap 18 at Turn 1.

The yo-yo racing, with battery levels dictating straightline speeds, continued at a breathless pace, with Russell twice retaking the lead on lap 22 and 23. Suggestions from the pitwall to halt the yo-yo racing and build a gap to Verstappen were met with a grumpy reply from the young Italian, but he did comply as he tucked in behind Russell and conserved his more brittle medium tyres.

The story of the race changed when Lance Stroll ground to a halt in his Aston Martin, with Antonelli and Verstappen using the virtual safety car to rid themselves of their medium tyres and switch to new rubber. The pair came out in sixth and seventh, just 15 seconds behind Russell, who was nursing his hard tyres to the end.

By lap 37 of 53, Antonelli had worked his way past Hamilton and then Piastri to second place, giving himself 16 laps to close the nine-second gap to his leading team-mate while Verstappen followed him through into third.

George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

Antonelli was quick but not initially catching Russell fast enough to close the gap, as the Briton escaped for action for a suspected yellow flag infringement. But Russell's hard tyres started showing worsening signs of wear towards the end of the race, allowing Antonelli to close the gap by the end of lap 47.

The first clash followed at the start of lap 49, with Russell cutting Turn 2 as he desperately tried to keep Antonelli behind. But the Italian went off as well, drifting through the gravel trap on the outside, allowing Russell to retain the lead.

Not best pleased by the Turn 1 skirmish, Antonelli tried again on the following tour but opted for a more straight-forward pass between Lesmo 2 and the Variante Ascari.

The 19-year-old held onto his hard-fought lead until the finish, winning his home race at the second time of asking. Russell was a defeated second, with Verstappen joining them on the podium.

Norris beat Piastri at the line for fourth, while Hamilton dropped back on worn medium tyres to finish sixth. From pole, Gasly eventually salvaged seventh at the finish ahead of Lindblad and Colapinto, with the second Racing Bulls car of Tsunoda claiming the final point in tenth on his second weekend as a replacement driver.

In breathtaking fashion, Antonelli is the first Italian winner of the Monza race in 60 years as he reinforces his championship lead by seven points, now heading Russell by 66 points into next weekend's Spanish Grand Prix on the newly-built Madring in Madrid.

Sports.title: Leclerc needs further health checks after heavy Italian GP crash
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc says he needs “a few additional checks” following his Italian Grand Prix crash, in order to make sure he’ll be fit next weekend for Formula 1’s Madrid round.

Leclerc lost control of his Ferrari SF-26 at high speed in the Parabolica at the end of lap two and suffered a hefty impact against the wall, which caused a red flag.

The Monegasque was taken to the medical centre, which he was released from in the absence of any detected injuries.

“The neck was OK, it was just the vision a little bit at first,” said Leclerc. “The right eye was not showing me great vision, but now it's all good, so that's the thing I was most worried of getting off the car.

“Then after that everything, a bit of pain here and there, which is normal after a crash like this, so nothing more.”

However, this doesn’t mean the 28-year-old emerged from the accident fully unscathed.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari crash

“I think I'll have quite a few additional checks that we still have to do on my side, probably tonight and tomorrow, to make sure that I'll be fully fine for Madrid,” he added. “It should be the case, but better be safe than sorry.”

As to why he lost control in the first place, Leclerc suggested "a difference in power delivery", but insisted he wanted to look at the data rather than make uninformed comments. He also admitted to his disappointment.

“Yeah, it's very frustrating, but it's the way it is now, I cannot change the results. I'll have to look forward and hopefully bounce back in Madrid,” the Ferrari racer concluded.

Sports.title: Huge crash knocks Leclerc out of F1 Italian GP
Sports.content:
Ferrari Formula 1 driver Charles Leclerc crashed out of the Italian Grand Prix, bringing out the red flag after two racing laps at Monza.

At the end of the second lap, Leclerc was defending fourth position from McLaren's Oscar Piastri when the Ferrari driver suffered a snap of oversteer and lost the rear of his Ferrari through the fast Parabolica right-hander.

Leclerc spun in the outside barriers at high speed, but walked away unhurt. But a safety car turned into a full red flag so race officials could repair the barriers.

It was a huge blow for Ferrari at his home race, which had already suffered a poor start when Leclerc pushed team-mate Lewis Hamilton wide at the start. Hamilton was demoted to eighth, with Mercedes' George Russell taking over the lead from surprise polesitter Pierre Gasly in the Alpine.

On the team radio Hamilton fumed that "Charles pushed me off", an incident that was noted by the stewards but no investigation was called for.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

Drivers are expected to take a standing restart at 15:39 local time, with teams allowed to make a tyre change during the stoppage.

Russell will lead the restart from Gasly, Max Verstappen, Franco Colapinto and Piastri, championship leader Kimi Antonelli worked his way up to 12th after starting down in 19th due to an engine penalty.

Given the severity of the impact, Leclerc headed to the medical centre for precautionary checks, but was cleared and released without injuries.

Sports.title: Alpine brings back folding rear wing at Italian GP as Gasly grabs pole
Sports.content:
There are magical days, but there are also special places. Monza is one of them for Pierre Gasly. Six years after his triumph with AlphaTauri, in what was one of the most unpredictable Formula 1 races ever, the Frenchman took the first pole position of his career in the most unexpected way possible.

Even Alpine itself had not predicted that it could get involved in the fight for the very top positions, especially considering that the target at the start of Saturday had been to make the top 10 in qualifying. That was a more than realistic and achievable goal based on what was seen in practice, with the team fighting Racing Bulls and, albeit inconsistently, Audi.

The final classification was much more favourable than anyone could have expected, but this was not a pole position produced by chance. It was deserved and earned on track. Certainly, the slipstreaming games played their part, and it cannot be denied that Mercedes realistically had more margin with George Russell had he not been involved in a fracas with Max Verstappen on his final attempt. But you have to capitalise on such opportunities.

That is exactly what Alpine did. The A526 is a car that, particularly in the configuration brought to Monza, generates relatively little aerodynamic drag compared with other teams, and that undoubtedly helps on the long straights. Even in practice, it was possible to see that the Enstone team was recording excellent top speeds on the straights. The challenge was finding the right balance through the corners without giving too much away.

There is, however, an interesting aspect to this weekend’s pole position, because the low-downforce package also featured an old acquaintance: the rear wing that opens in reverse, causing the two flaps to collapse. This solution had been seen in testing and during the first three races of the season – Australia, China and Suzuka – before being set aside in favour of a more conventional opening mechanism similar to last year’s DRS.

Alpine novel rear wing assembly made a comeback in Monza Photo by: Marcel van Dorst / EYE4images / NurPhoto via Getty Images

The low-downforce package has therefore brought back the early-season wing, while all the additional elements on the wing actuator have been removed. Alpine was actually the first team this season to introduce dedicated structures around the wing-opening mechanism at Suzuka in order to find more aerodynamic load, starting a trend that was subsequently adopted by all the other teams.

On a circuit like Monza, however, all those additional elements aimed at generating more downforce were not considered necessary and were removed, effectively returning to the very first specification from the beginning of the year. That version was considered more efficient, including in its interaction with the diffuser.

It is worth remembering that at Zandvoort two weeks ago, Alpine introduced a major package of long-awaited technical upgrades. With it, the A526 found some of the downforce it had been lacking, and this was particularly useful in the high-speed corners.

That does not mean that Alpine has suddenly become a benchmark car in terms of cornering performance. Rather, it has managed to find those few extra km/h needed to avoid throwing away what it gains on the straights.

“The new package we put on is not very draggy, which is good here. Our top speed is no secret. You can see that. It's competitive. So, who knows? Let's see what we can do,” explained Alpine managing director Steve Nielsen.

Sports.title: Audi to appeal stewards’ decision not to penalise Tsunoda over start error | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Audi have informed the FIA they intend to appeal against the stewards’ decision not to penalise Yuki Tsunoda for his error at the restart of the Italian Grand Prix.

Tsunoda lined up in his grid box incorrectly before the restart of the race. The race director therefore abandoned the start and ordered an extra formation lap.

Ordinarily this would result in the driver who caused the delay having to start the race from the pit lane. Tsunoda did not do this.

The stewards took no action against Tsunoda. They ruled it was the race director’s decision to order an extra formation lap (below).

Tsunoda finished the race in 10th place, seven seconds ahead of Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto, who was a second ahead of his team mate Nico Hulkenberg.

Car 22 [Tsunoda] approached the grid initially heading for the left hand side of the grid, then

realising he was headed for the wrong grid position, the driver changed direction and positioned his car in the correct grid box and in the correct position within the grid box. This was verified by the stewards with video from multiple camera angles.

The race director, in evidence, stated that it was his call, based on the behaviour of the car on the approach to the grid box, to commence an extra formation lap. He stated he was not comfortable starting the race with the car in that position.

The team representative stated that:

(i) The car was not in a “false start” position – referring to Article B5.1.1c of the F1 regulations, because no contact patch of the front tyres was outside the grid box lines (front and side)

(ii) At the drivers meeting, the race director advised that for the start, the track limits were the pit walls and in this case, even though the car was pointed to the right, it had at least four metres of space to move off from the start

(iii) No other driver was impacted by the position of car 22

(iv) The driver of car 22 was not the “cause” of the extra formation lap.

(v) At no time was the team advised that race control considered car 22 to be the cause of the extra formation lap.

The Stewards agree with the points above and consider that the extra formation lap resulted from the Race Director’s assessment of the situation, rather than being directly caused by the driver of car 22.

Further, Article B5.9.4 goes on to specify that if a driver who causes the extra formation lap and is then able to start the extra formation lap, he must enter the pit lane at the end of the lap and start from the pit lane. It is only then, if the driver fails to do this, that the mandatory penalty of a Stop-and-Go penalty is imposed.

In other words, the penalty is for failing to come into the pit lane and start from there. The penalty is not for causing the extra formation lap, if indeed, he caused the extra formation lap in the first place.

A critical issue emerges here, in that in order to comply with the requirement to enter and start from the pit lane, a driver would need to know that he was the cause of the extra formation lap. The team representative quoted situations where extra formation laps have been commenced due to extraneous circumstances such as the position of a photographer etc. In this case, no message was sent to the team or the driver, advising them that they were the cause of the extra formation lap.

The team, based on the fact that the car was positioned within its starting grid box in compliance with the regulations, had, in our determination, no reason to instruct its driver to enter and start from the pit lane.

Accordingly, irrespective of whether or not the driver directly caused the extra formation lap, the team and driver were unaware that they were being considered as the cause, therefore we determine that we are unable to impose a Stop and Go penalty in this case, and decide to take no further action.

We note that the race director acted in good faith and out of an abundance of caution in ordering an extra formation lap.

We further note that the FIA might wish to consider implementing a process to advise teams and drivers if they are considered to be the cause of an extra formation lap, so that they are then able to comply with the requirements of Article B5.9.4

Sports.title: Domenicali hails F1’s ‘incredible racing’, Norris says it’s ‘just who presses a button when’ | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula 1 CEO Stefano Domenicali and reigning world champion Lando Norris gave strikingly different assessments of the racing in today’s Italian Grand Prix.

Prior to the race, several F1 drivers predicted they would see “yo-yo racing” at Monza . This was expected as their energy-starved cars would swap positions repeatedly on the high-speed track while the Overtake Mode boost button would hand a valuable advantage to those following within a second of another car.

However Domenicali claimed the opposite, insisting there had been pre-race predictions of a processional race. He said the repeated positions swaps therefore represented a welcome surprise.

“In Monza, a lot of people yesterday were saying, maybe we’re going to have a lot of trains, one behind the other,” Domenicali told Sky. “And actually we had incredible racing.”

Several drivers have criticised the “yo-yo racing” produced by the current cars at some tracks, particularly the quicker ones. Norris gave a candid assessment of the racing today when asked by the official Formula 1 channel whether he enjoyed it.

“It’s good fun in parts,” Norris replied, “of course a lot of it’s just who presses a button when and so forth.”

His team mate Oscar Piastri agreed it had been “a very different race in Monza compared to what we’ve seen previously.”

Piastri repeatedly swapped positions with Lewis Hamilton during the race. He said that made it difficult to make progress.

“A lot of yo-yo battling, which [made it] quite difficult to know what exactly the right thing to do was. Because obviously you can’t just give up an easy overtake, but you also don’t want to be losing race time, you want to just going with whoever you’re racing.

“So that was quite difficult to manage. Definitely some lessons learned from that one.”
