World.title: Europe cannot afford to lose the race for biomedical innovation
World.content:
This is not a theoretical risk. The pandemic exposed how reliance on external supply chains can threaten access to essential medical products, underscoring why the pharmaceutical industry is now recognized as strategic for Europe’s competitiveness, security and autonomy. A strong biopharmaceutical industry is therefore not only an economic asset; it is essential to health security and to Europe’s ability to respond to future crises.

Every clinical trial that moves away and every patent filed outside Europe mean a real loss of knowledge, skilled jobs and opportunities for Europeans.

Much of Europe’s declining appeal can be explained by developments across the Atlantic. The U.S. represents a much larger share of the global pharmaceutical market and has long offered stronger incentives for innovation, steadily attracting research investment. New measures to reinforce domestic production and draw further investment to the U.S. risk accelerating this trend. For Europe, the message is clear: strengthening our own regulatory and fiscal incentives for innovation is no longer optional — it is urgent, and it is entirely in our hands.

Greater competitiveness also requires faster and fairer access to treatments by removing unnecessary restrictions. Access to innovation is not only an industry issue; it is also a societal one. Scientific investment must reach patients, because better health also strengthens the economy.

Europe still has an exceptional scientific and academic base, but it has not always translated that knowledge into innovation that delivers wellbeing and social progress on the same scale. The priority now is to build a life-sciences ecosystem that translates research into tangible solutions for citizens.

Developing a medicine takes 10 to 15 years, which is why companies need predictable regulation, legal certainty and policies that recognize the value of innovation.

Spain illustrates this paradox clearly. It is Europe’s fourth-largest pharmaceutical market and a leader in clinical trials, yet patients still wait too long for approved treatments. Scientific excellence does not automatically translate into timely access; closing that gap is a challenge for all of Europe, not Spain alone.

Developing a medicine takes 10 to 15 years, which is why companies need predictable regulation, legal certainty and policies that recognize the value of innovation. Intellectual property protection is central to this. Weakening it will not sustainably lower medicine costs; it will only reduce the incentive to research and develop new treatments in Europe.

World.title: Poland’s anti-Ukrainian turn spills into violence
World.content:
Warsaw has been one of Kyiv’s strongest supporters against Russia since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. But the nationalist camp, which Nawrocki seeks to lead, has sought to capitalize on tensions over the Ukrainian presence in Poland and the wartime massacres.

Anti-Ukrainian rhetoric is already intensifying ahead of the fall 2027 parliamentary election, when Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s broadly pro-Ukraine coalition will face the nationalist Law and Justice party and two other far-right parties. Polls show Tusk is far from certain of victory.

The libertarian Confederation party denounced Ukrainians getting social welfare, while Gregorz Braun, the European Parliament member who leads the far-right Confederation of the Polish Crown party, said: “The Kyiv regime is neither our ally nor our friend, it is our enemy,” during a summer gathering commemorating the wartime killing of Polish civilians by Ukrainians.

Przemysław Czarnek, the candidate for prime minister from the Law and Justice party, said July: “Military aid to Ukraine must be suspended until that country changes its historical policy.”

Rafał Pankowski, a sociology professor at Warsaw’s Civitas University and co-founder of the Polish anti-racism group Never Again, believes that while the Polish population is broadly supportive of Ukraine, fissures are beginning to show.

“Solidarity with Ukrainians remains strong among many Poles, but populist anti-Ukrainian rhetoric has created fertile ground for attacks, turning a large and visible minority into a target and helping verbal hostility spill into violence. Russian propaganda seized on the opportunity, too,” he said.

World.title: Russia has entered Sweden’s election campaign, center-left front-runner warns
World.content:
Åkesson said his party had been unaware of the pro-Kremlin posts by Malaberg but conceded “we have to look at this and sort this out,” adding that the party was investigating the claims and that Malaberg could not continue to work for them if she maintained her pro-Russian views.

But these answers aren’t enough, said Andersson, a former finance minister and prime minister of Sweden. “When did the prime minister’s office become aware of this, and what information has been given to the prime minister?” she asked, adding: “This is about Sweden and the security of the Swedish people.”

Speaking to POLITICO from her parliamentary office in Stockholm, Andersson argued that the risks of having the Sweden Democrats in government go beyond security. “We’ve seen journalists threatened” since Kristersson started ruling with backing from the Sweden Democrats, she said. “NGOs are threatened if they criticize what the government is doing. They’ve been threatened to have their state support withdrawn.”

Ulf Kristersson has been in power since 2022. | Pool photo by Jaimi Joy via EFA/EPA

“There could be a Swedish government where half of the ministers, including the foreign minister and the EU minister, come from a party that thinks we should have an inquiry on exit” from the European Union, she added.

The question is whether Swedish voters will agree with Andersson that it’s time for a change (Kristersson has been in power since 2022).

Security and migration remain top campaign issues. Kristersson’s camp vows to crack down harder on gang violence while ramping up deportations, including plans to deport some migrants who have been schooled in Sweden when they turn 18.

World.title: Kallas scraps new high-level European defense group in fresh blow to her leadership
World.content:
Kallas has been in intense competition with the Commission over these plans, but an EU official said the reason for the cancellation was pressure from some capitals.

“Some member states felt this was not the right path to pursue at this moment,” said the official. “After some discussion with ministers, we have decided not to proceed with the initiative, we are looking at new ways of engaging with member states.”

The presentation had been meant to take place in Brussels at the Bibliothèque Solvay on Monday morning, with some 150 people from EU institutions, think tanks, academia and NATO expected to attend.

The names of group members were kept under wraps by Kallas’ office, but three diplomats said the group was expected to be chaired by former NATO Secretary General Anders Fogh Rasmussen and to include former defense ministers, like Estonia’s Jüri Luik, who also served as NATO ambassador, and France’s Florence Parly, a former minister of the armed forces.

Germany was expected to have a representative, as were other countries from outside the EU such as the U.K. and Ukraine, other diplomats said. Rasmussen was then expected to be tasked with writing a report on the outcome of the group’s work.

The EEAS did not confirm any of the names.

World.title: Germany’s far-right AfD scores its biggest win
World.content:
“We’ve made history. We’re taking back our country. It starts here in Saxony-Anhalt,” Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s candidate for regional premier, said at a victory event in the city of Magdeburg where a crowd chanted his name — “Uli, Uli” — in unison.

With almost all of the ballots counted, the AfD was set to win some 44 percent, a landslide on high turnout which would give it 39 seats in the regional parliament — just shy of the 42 seats needed to rule outright.

The political haggling over whether the AfD can wield power is now likely to center on whether it can come to an arrangement with the BSW, a populist-left party founded by a former member of East Germany’s communist party. The alternative is to persuade lawmakers from other parties to defect.

Sunday’s election is a catastrophe for the Christian Democratic Union of Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Its support crashed to less than 18 percent — a devastating implosion from the 37. 1 percent it scored in 2021.

The success of the AfD in this small state of just 2.1 million inhabitants has even sparked speculation about a potential Kanzlertausch, or chancellor swap.

Siegmund argued the result was a direct signal to Merz.

World.title: German startup makes European space history with first successful orbital launch
World.content:
We made history. On just our second flight, we became the first commercial space company from Europe to deliver satellites into orbit. Mission 'Onward and Upward' successfully lifted off and deployed payloads into orbit. A new chapter for European spaceflight. More:… pic.twitter.com/AWvqG2l8Mn — Isar Aerospace (@isaraerospace) September 5, 2026

Germany’s Ministry for Research, Technology and Space hailed the launch as a “milestone that impressively demonstrates our country's innovative strength and technical expertise.”

Europe is trying to reduce its reliance on non-European launch providers, particularly Elon Musk’s SpaceX. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the Norwegian launch site in March and warned Europe has been “dependent on other supply chains and other countries in the world for far too long.”

The two-day International Space Summit will be held in Paris on Wednesday and Thursday with delegations from more than 120 countries. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is set to give her first speech solely about space policy, as the Commission prepares to unveil its European Space Shield, an action plan aimed at protecting the bloc's satellites.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration is discouraging American companies from attending the conference.

Isar’s first launch, in March last year, ended with the rocket crashing into the sea shortly after liftoff.

Calling Saturday night’s successful launch “historic,” European Space Agency Director General Josef Aschbacher said it was “yet another step towards a more diverse autonomous European launch service sector.”

Isar is one of several European startups seeking to break into the orbital launch market, alongside Spain’s PLD Space and France’s MaiaSpace. Arianespace, a Paris-headquartered company, has long operated from France’s overseas territory of French Guiana.

Based near Munich, Isar plans to move toward serial production of its Spectrum rocket, with a target of manufacturing over 30 a year, and is developing a second launch site in Canada.

World.title: AfD's historic win splits Europe as populists cheer and Warsaw warns of 'traitors'
World.content:
Alternative for Germany's dominant showing in Sunday's Saxony-Anhalt election has triggered starkly divided reactions across the continent, exposing the widening fault line between Europe's establishment centre and its emboldened populist right.

 

AfD won 43.8% of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago in the region of 2.1 million people west of Berlin.

That was far ahead of Merz’s Christian Democratic Union, which polled 17.2% — losing about half its support — and won 15 seats. The center-left Social Democrats polled 9.3%, the Greens 8.9% and the Left Party 8.6%, winning eight seats apiece.

In Berlin, the result landed as a direct blow to Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who watched the count from CDU headquarters without addressing the public.

General secretary Franziska Hoppermann called it "a very difficult result for us," while state premier Sven Schulze offered only muted congratulations to AfD.

AfD Co-leader Alice Weidel declared "we have received a very clear mandate to govern here."

“We ran on a clear platform of representing the interests of our country, not those of Ukraine or any other country," Weidel told reporters.

"If we receive the mandate to govern at the federal level and assume governmental responsibility, we will cut all unnecessary spending. We will control our borders. We will deport all those required to leave the country and all criminals. We will close the borders.

"I also expect early federal elections, and I expect the current chancellor to be replaced before Christmas."

Lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund also needled Merz, saying "a very good campaigner for us in this election campaign was Friedrich Merz. Every day this man is in the chancellery is one too many."

Reaction from Warsaw was openly critical. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote on X that "only idiots or traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD," naming members of Konfederacja and PiS among them.

Elsewhere on the continent, Europe's populist right treated the outcome as validation. Italian Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini declared that "another Europe is possible."

Spain's Vox leader Santiago Abascal called the result "a great hope for Germany and for Europe," while Portugal's André Ventura hailed AfD's "historic" victory, linking it to public anger over immigration.

The split reactions underline how a single German regional vote has become a proxy battle for Europe, with mainstream leaders alarmed and nationalist movements energised heading into a string of more German state elections this month.

World.title: How can the EU help you repair your broken electronics? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot
World.content:
Throwing away your broken washing machine seems easier because it’s quicker and cheaper than fixing it. This is changing as the EU wants you to use your goods for longer.

 

The EU's Right to Repair Directive encourages consumers to repair broken products rather than replace them by making repairs easier, more accessible, and more appealing. The directive was adopted in June 2024, and member states had until 31 July 2026 to transpose it into national law.

The goal is to keep products for longer, reduce e-waste, promote sustainability, and help consumers save money. The rules cover appliances such as washing machines, vacuum cleaners, mobile phones, and tablets.

Under the directive, manufacturers must repair fixable products, can’t refuse repairs for economic or prior repair reasons, and must offer spare parts at fair prices. Repairs should be free or fairly priced and completed quickly. They must provide spare parts and repair information to independent repairers and clearly display repair service and price information online or in manuals.

The rules also extend the legal warranty by an extra year. If goods are under warranty and consumers opt for repair, they get an additional 12 months of protection.

The European online repair platform helps consumers find local repair shops, refurbished goods sellers, buyers of defective items, and community-led repair initiatives. Customers can also use a European information form to discover and compare repair offers and services.

Do you want to know more about your rights under the Right to Repair Directive? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot!

World.title: Turkey lifts inflation forecast to 28.4% as Middle East conflict pushes outlook higher
World.content:
Turkey has raised its year-end inflation forecast to 28.4%, Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said on Sunday when he unveiled the country's medium-term economic programme for 2027-2029.

 

"We expect inflation to start declining again in the fourth quarter of 2026 and to reach 28.4% by the end of the year," Yilmaz said in a televised address.

The new forecast is significantly higher than previous projections.

In last year's medium-term programme covering 2026-2028, the government had forecast year-end inflation at 16%.

Under the new programme, inflation is projected to fall to 21% in 2027, 13.5% in 2028 and 9% in 2029.

Turkey's annual inflation rate eased to 31.51% in August from 31.75% in July, according to official data.

Yilmaz said the war in the Middle East had played a key role in the upward revision of the inflation outlook.

"According to our central bank, the direct and indirect effects of the war on inflation have been estimated at approximately seven percentage points," he said.

Annual inflation, which has remained above 30% since December 2021, peaked at more than 75% in May 2024 before beginning to slow.

Yilmaz said the government had made "significant progress in combating inflation", which remains the top priority of its economic programme.

"Inflation, which had risen to 75.5% in May 2024, has begun to show a clear downward trend as a result of the policies we have implemented," he said.

World.title: Germany seeks to quash 'facilitating genocide' in Gaza case brought by Nicaragua at top UN court
World.content:
Germany will ask the top United Nations court to toss out a case brought against it by Nicaragua on Monday, which accuses Berlin of "facilitating genocide" with its support of Israel.

 

Lawyers for Germany will kick off four days of hearings at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the court based in The Hague that rules on disputes between countries.

The case dates back to 2024, following the start of Israel's offensive in Gaza. Nicaragua urged ICJ judges to impose emergency measures to force Berlin to halt all aid to Israel, in particular military equipment.

The court threw out Nicaragua's request in April of that year, saying "the circumstances, as they now present themselves" did not justify emergency orders.

The case is nevertheless ongoing and Germany is now seeking to have it removed, either by persuading judges they do not have the power to rule in the case or that Nicaragua's argument does not stack up.

Palestinians gather and inspect the rubble of a building destroyed in an Israeli airstrike in Gaza City, 24 August, 2026 AP Photo

Berlin has filed so-called "preliminary objections to the jurisdiction of the Court and to the admissibility of certain claims" presented by Nicaragua, according to an ICJ statement.

The detail of Berlin's case has not yet been made public.

Genocide claim

After Germany presents its case on Monday, Nicaragua will respond before both countries get another chance to address the court on Wednesday and Thursday.

It takes on average six months for the court to hand down a ruling in such cases.

The court could either side with Germany and throw out the case completely or rule against Berlin, meaning the case would then be considered "on the merits" in more detail.

During hearings at the court in April 2024, Nicaragua said Germany was "pathetic" to provide aid to Gaza while also simultaneously furnishing Israel with weapons.

Palestinians gather around the burning wreckage of a car after an Israeli army strike in Gaza City, 31 August, 2026 AP Photo

Nicaragua's ambassador to the Netherlands, Carlos Jose Arguello Gomez, told the court: "Germany seems not to be able to differentiate between self-defence and genocide."

Germany retorted that Nicaragua's case was "grossly biased," strongly denying the accusations that it was in breach of the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.

Israel launched its offensive in Gaza in response to the deadly 7 October 2023 attacks against it by Hamas-led militants.

Due to its Nazi past, Germany has placed Israel's security "at the core" of its foreign policy, its representative told the court in the 2024 hearings.

Germany said its arms trade with Israel was subject to "detailed scrutiny...that far exceeds the requirements of international law."

This procedure is separate from a high-profile case also before the ICJ, in which South Africa has accused Israel of perpetrating genocide in Gaza, which Israel denies.

The ICJ's rulings are binding but it has no power to enforce them.

For example, it ordered Russia to stop its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, a demand that has been ignored by Moscow.

World.title: EU diplomatic service scraps new high-level defence group amid pressure from member states
World.content:
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas announced the new group just last week to advise on Europe's defence needs, but the initiative was scrapped following strong opposition from member states.

 

At an informal meeting of defence ministers in Ireland last week, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas announced a new advisory body bringing together political and military leaders to help design a new approach to European defence.

"The aim is to have some of the brightest minds on security and defence come together and really provide out-of-the-box solutions on how we can be faster in fulfilling these gaps and how we can be more effective," Kallas said during the press conference.

Only days later, the initiative was quietly shelved. Invitees to the launch event, a fireside chat with Kallas, due to take place on Monday in a cosy venue in Brussels, received word of the cancellation on Sunday afternoon.

The abrupt decision came after several member states opposed the move, viewing it as the wrong path to pursue, despite the group having been intended solely as an advisory body rather than one empowered to make decisions on behalf of member states.

"The diagnosis has not changed that Europe needs to deliver faster on defence. Europe still needs to confront the question the group was designed to address, how to strengthen European defence faster," an EU official told Euronews, asking not to be named.

The European External Action Service (EEAS) is already under pressure, as Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has steadily sought more say over the bloc's foreign policy, clashing with Kallas over major issues such as relations with Israel.

The latest Franco-German proposal would place the EEAS under the direct supervision of the President of the European Commission, though it would also give the High Representative a much broader portfolio.

The pressure to scrap the initiative before it was even launched — before the names of its participants had even been announced — is a significant political defeat for Kallas, who had only recently put in place a new EEAS leadership to shore up her position.

World.title: Witches, tapestries and a suspended horse: The best things to do, hear, see or watch in Europe this week
World.content:
September is in full swing, and we're ringing in the autumn vibes with a line-up of events and new releases that will give you goosebumps.

 

From the Bayeux Tapestry's first appearance in the UK in nearly 1,000 years, to the provocative works of Maurizio Cattelan, and spellbinding magic of Practical Magic 2, this week's offerings conjure all kinds of wonder and awe.

There's also the release of indie band Bloc Party's new album, along with a new teen drama Netflix show that calls for evenings spent snuggled under blankets — hot drink in hand, remote in the other.

Keep scrolling to find out more.

Exhibitions and events

Maurizio Cattelan: Night

Maurizio Cattelan, Novecento, 1997, Castello di Rivoli, Torino. Foto / Photo: Paolo Pellion di Persano.

When: 10 September - 7 March 2027

Where: Neue Nationalgalerie (Berlin, Germany)

Italian artist Maurizio Cattelan has become a mischief maker within the art world. From his banana duct-taped to a wall, to a child-sized statue of Hitler in prayer, to an 18-karat gold (and fully functional) toilet that was installed at the Guggenheim — his creations have proven polarising, but also often funny, inspiring, and always challenging. One particular theme that runs throughout his career is the tensions between innocence and violence, and how we balance our identities with the collective discomfort of historical memories. This is the focus of the Neue Nationalgalerie's latest exhibition, which brings together some of Cattelan's most seminal works, along with new and never-before-seen commissions. Find out more here.

The Bayeux Tapestry

A detail of the Bayeux tapestry before its transfer to the British Museum, at the Bayeux Tapestry Museum, in Bayeux, northwestern France, Thursday, Sept. 18, 2025. Lou Benoist, Pool via AP

When: 10 September - 11 July 2027

Where: British Museum (London, UK)

Nearly 1,000 years ago, the Bayeux Tapestry was commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux. It has not been seen in Britain since — until now.

Following an unprecedented agreement with France, the 70-metre-long tapestry, which depicts the events leading up to the Battle of Hastings and Normal Conquest of England in 1066, has been transferred to the British Museum. It's a once in a lifetime event that allows visitors to see in person a piece of astonishing medieval history; a representation of one of, if not the most, defining moments of the England's past. It's also estimated to have cost the UK around €20 million to transport and exhibit the tapestry — a worthy investment judging by the ticket sales so far. Find out more here.

Bonus highlight: Timeless Tintoretto, a showcase of the works of Jacomo Robusti, opens at the Musée Jacquemart-André in Paris on 11 September.

Movies

Practical Magic 2

Where: Cinemas

When: 11 September

Midnight margaritas, anyone? The iconic Owen's sisters (Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman) are back — 28 years after they first appeared on screen in what has become a cosy classic among Halloween-loving Millennials. The plot centres around a centuries-old family curse: Any man the witches fall in love with is doomed to die. While seemingly broken by collective love at the end of the first movie, the sequel grapples with its seeming return, as Sally's (Bullock) daughters reckon with its consequences and the emergence of their own powers. Based on Alice Hoffman's The Book of Magic, it's a return to that nostalgic '90s fall feeling — suburban streets, candlelit laughter, black cats in lap — and a cinematic world where whimsy and women rule.

To find out more about other upcoming movie releases this autumn, take a look at our preview list here.

Bonus highlight: A new documentary about Britpop band Oasis, Don't Look Back in Anger, is released on 11 September. Stay tuned for our full review later this week.

TV series

Crew Girl

Where: Netflix

When: 10 September

Netflix's new sports drama follows a teenage elite rower named Teagan Tao (Miku Martineau), who relocates to a small town with her mother following a family scandal. However, after joining an all-boys varsity crew as their coxswain, she finds herself in even more uncharted waters: navigating being an outsider, school rivalries, romantic dramas and the strain of emotional grief. A throwback to teen dramas of the late 2000s/early 2010s, it's perfect binge-watch material as the colder nights set in.

Bonus highlight: A police dispatcher (Patrick Brammall) sets out on an all-consuming quest to find his missing daughter in Apple TV+'s compelling new drama, Last Seen. Stream from 9 September.

Music

Bloc Party: Anatomy of a Brief Romance

When: 10 September

The seventh studio album from British indie band Bloc Party arrives after an almost 4 and a half year hiatus, which followed their polarising last, release 'Alpha Games'. A lot has happened in that time — especially in frontman Kele Okereke's life. After his 11 year relationship ended, he began a whirlwind romance with someone else, the intensity of which forms the crux of the band's latest songwriting. From the percussive punchiness of 'Coming on Strong' to the jittery harmonies of 'Love Bombs', each track takes listeners through the highs and lows of falling for someone: from excitable infatuation to crushing disappointment to difficult but necessary realisations.

To find out more about other upcoming albums this autumn, take a look at our preview list here.

Bonus highlight: British musician Simon Charles Green, who goes by the stage name Bonobo, releases his eighth studio album on 11 September, 'Distance in Static'.

World.title: Trial begins in Finland of man accused of abusing 361 children online over three years
World.content:
A man goes on trial in Finland on Monday charged with sexually abusing hundreds of children aged nine to 15 on social media platforms including Snapchat.

 

A public presentation of the case was to take place at the Pirkanmaa district court on Monday, before continuing behind closed doors on Tuesday.

The man has been charged with carrying out various sexual offences on 361 children between 2019 and 2022.

According to Finnish public broadcaster Yle, the victims were boys living across the country.

In December 2025, Finnish police announced they were investigating a 27-year-old man suspected of 364 sexual offences against children.

The National Prosecution Authority then said in June that prosecutors had decided not to press charges in three of the cases.

The introduction page for Snapchat shown in a mobile phone displayed at Apple's App Store in Chicago, 30 July, 2019 AP Photo

Thousands of videos and images of unidentified children had been found on the man's mobile phone in 2022, when police searched his phone in connection with another criminal case, police said in December.

The man had allegedly contacted the children via Snapchat, asking them to take and send him photos or videos of themselves wearing very little clothing or naked.

He had also asked them to perform sexual acts, police said.

The main charges against him were aggravated sexual abuse of children, sexual abuse of children and aggravated distribution of an image depicting children in a sexual manner, the prosecutor told the AFP news agency ahead of the trial.

The man partly admitted to the offences during the investigation.

With approximately 45 hearing days dedicated to the case, the proceedings are expected to last "at least until the end of this year," according to the court.

World.title: Turkey seeks Black Sea shipping deal as attacks threaten grain trade
World.content:
Turkey is racing to restore safe passage for cargo ships in the Black Sea as attacks on shipping disrupt grain exports and push up prices. Russia and Ukraine are major global wheat exporters, but Black Sea trade has been severely disrupted as both sides step up attacks on shipping and port infrastructure.

Advertising

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan announced this week that Turkey was working on a plan to ensure safe passage in the Black Sea for commercial shipping and said he was in touch with both Ukraine and Russia.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan confirmed that he raised the issue with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, on the sidelines of a gathering of regional leaders in Kyrgyzstan.

The Turkish move comes as Ukraine and Russia have ramped up their attacks on shipping and ports in and around the Black Sea. In 2022, Turkey and the United Nations brokered a deal between Ukraine and Russia to ensure safe passage for Ukrainian grain exports through the Black Sea.

The agreement lasted a year.

While Turkey has maintained good ties with both sides, reaching another agreement will be much harder, warned international relations professor Huseyin Bagci of Ankara’s Middle East Technical University.

“The tension is increasing more than ever before,” Bagci said. “It's not enough to have good relations, because the two sides – the Ukrainians and Russians – should sit down and talk about a common solution to this problem. Turkey cannot solve this problem alone.”

What the SDF’s dissolution means for Syria’s Kurds and neighbouring Turkey

Growing attacks

In August Ukraine offered a ceasefire on commercial shipping, but the offer was rejected by Moscow, which said it wanted a broader deal. Ukrainian drones continue to strike Russian shipping, while Russia has continued missile attacks on Ukrainian ports and ships.

This surge in attacks comes as both nations rush to export their grain harvests.

Grain prices have risen sharply, by as much as 30 percent, international grain broker Can Atbasoglu said, even as both sides scramble to find new routes for their exports.

“Russia will do their best to export as much as they can, both from Russian Baltic ports and EU Baltic ports like Latvia and Lithuania; they're also exporting,” Atbasoglu said.

“Ukraine will also export as much as they can from Romania as well and through the Danube ports. But the export pace will be definitely lower. So it will definitely stay bullish for the markets. Prices are definitely going to stay like this or can have a further increase.”

Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea

Ships staying put

At one of Istanbul's many shipyards, the docks are crowded with ships that once braved the Black Sea. One vessel bears the scars of a drone attack and is under repair. Others undergo routine maintenance as shipowners hesitate to risk new journeys into dangerous waters.

The superintendent of one ship, speaking anonymously, says repairs are nearly finished, but uncertainty clouds the future.

“We wanted to take the ship out to the Black Sea before entering the shipyard, but because of that risk, we didn’t enter the Black Sea and didn’t take on any cargo. We’ve been in the shipyard for 50 days for repairs, but we don’t know what will happen once the repairs are finished,” the superintendent said.

Turkish shipowners warn that many are on the brink of bankruptcy, as idle ships rack up costs of up to 50,000 euros a month in mooring and crew expenses.

Ziya Ustel, CEO of Turkish shipping company VI-ZA STAR, says high freight rates are being offered for Black Sea routes, but the risks are too great.

“They are offering high freight rates, etc,” Ustel said.

Without a diplomatic solution, few shipowners will be prepared to risk their vessels, Ustel warned.

“The main thing is to find out a real solution,” Ustel added. “Otherwise, no one will try anything anymore.”

Turkish diplomacy

Ankara is expected to step up its efforts to find a solution.

Grain brokers say hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough may be one reason prices have so far remained below the record highs seen at the start of the war.

But if Turkish efforts fail and attacks on Black Sea shipping continue, higher grain prices could have a considerable impact, especially on the world’s poorest nations, many of which depend on Russian and Ukrainian grain.

World.title: Saxony-Anhalt: Germany wakes up to 'unsettling' AfD victory
World.content:
09/07/2026 September 7, 2026 AfD faces uncertain coalition options after Saxony-Anhalt win

According to preliminary official results, the AfD emerged as the largest party but fell short of a governing majority in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament. The far-right party therefore faces challenges in forming a government.

AfD lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt Ulrich Siegmund said his party’s result represented "a clear mandate to govern."

The far-right AfD faces challenges in forming a coalition government in Saxony-Anhalt Image: Sebastian Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance

At the same time, the 35-year-old said he currently saw no potential coalition partners. However, he added that he did not know what might happen in the coming days.

"I don’t know whether there are individual lawmakers who might say: 'That’s it, I’m not playing along with this anymore,'" he said, adding, "A lot can still happen." Following the historic win, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said: "Ulrich Siegmund will definitely run as a candidate for state premier in the state parliament. That much is certain."

If efforts to form a government fail, Siegmund said a new election could also be an option. "In the worst-case scenario, there would simply be new elections, and then we would get 50% or 55%," he said.

Is coalition without AfD possible?

The only coalition that would have a numerical majority without the AfD would be an alliance of all the other parties. However, under a resolution adopted previously, the center-right CDU rules out not only a coalition with the AfD but also with the Left Party. This policy is known as the " political firewall."

That would also be a stumbling block for a CDU-led minority government. In addition, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) could potentialy hold the balance of power with five seats. Its leadership has ruled out supporting CDU.

Following the election, the previously governing coalition of the CDU, SPD and FDP will end. However, state premier Sven Schulze and his Cabinet will remain in office in a caretaker capacity until a new state premier is elected.

World.title: Von der Leyen in Greenland with EU investments amid Trump pressure
World.content:
The EU is preparing a major investment package and closer political ties with the Danish Arctic territory amid Donald Trump's demand for greater US control of the mineral-rich island.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is in Greenland for a two-day visit as the European Union plans a major boost in investment in the region amid threats of US annexation under President Donald Trump.

Alongside the EU investments, she is expected to announce closer political ties with the autonomous Arctic territory which is part of the Kingdom of Denmark.

The European Commission head arrived in Greenland's capital Nuuk on Sunday in a show of support for Greenland and Denmark, and was received by Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.

In a post on X, Von der Leyen said the EU is committed to "contributing to a safe, peaceful Arctic and to the security of Greenland."

What does the EU investment package include?

The EU package is expected to include hundreds of millions of euros in investment in:

critical minerals,

satellite communications

renewable energy

Von der Leyen said the package would be "substantial" but gave no details.

Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen described the visit as an opportunity to deepen the territory's "close friendship and good partnership" with the EU.

The largely autonomous Greenland left the EU in 1985, although its population of about 57,000 are EU citizens through Danish citizenship.

Why is Trump demanding 'total access' over Greenland?

Von der Leyen's visit comes as the Arctic gains strategic importance for the US, Russia, China and Europe, with melting sea ice opening new shipping routes and increasing access to the region's mineral resources.

Trump has repeatedly stated that the US "needs" Greenland for its "national security," pointing to his claims — without providing evidence — that the island is "covered with Chinese and Russian ships all over the place."

Trump has maintained that Denmark cannot adequately defend the island against China and Russia.

His campaign bid to gain "total access" to the Danish territory has strained US-European relations and raised tensions within NATO as both Greenland and the Danish government have rejected Trump's demands.

World.title: Several killed in Amazon cargo plane crash in Miami
World.content:
At least five people have died after a cargo plane crashed at Miami International Airport. The aircraft overran a runway, struck several vehicles and caught fire.

An Amazon cargo plane barreled off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing at least five people as it struck vehicles and burst into flames, authorities said.

The aircraft overran the runway around 2 p.m. local time, or 18:00 GMT, after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico. Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalized with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials said at a press conference.

"Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being and care of everyone involved. We’re doing everything we can to support those affected," officials said, adding that it was too soon to determine whether those killed were on the plane or in vehicles struck by the aircraft.

According to the authorities, the crash sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky and trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit, as well as some people in cars.

Investigation launched into cause of crash

The Prime Air aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.

The NTSB said in an X post on Sunday the B-767-300 cargo airplane was flying into Miami from San Juan, Puerto Rico and they have "launched a go team to investigate Sunday's runway excursion accident."

The flight was operated by 21 Air, a North Carolina-based cargo carrier. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to Flightradar24.

Amazon said it would cooperate with the investigation.

The National Transportation Safety Board said it was sending a team to Miami to investigate. Amazon said it would cooperate with the investigation Image: Marco Bello/REUTERS

“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport,” the company said in a statement. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones and all those affected by this devastating loss."

About 250 flights were delayed at the airport by late Sunday afternoon, according to FlightAware. Fire crews were still dealing with a fuel leak several hours later, according to reports.

Eyewitness say they saw 'thick black smoke billowing into the sky'

Jackson Lee, who runs an electronics shop near the crash site, told news agencies that he went outside with four colleagues after the crash and saw smoke rising near the airport’s fences.

"We hear planes taking off and landing every five minutes. I thought I’d got used to it," Lee said. "I never thought it could come this close to us."

World.title: US envoys Witkoff and Kushner hold Ukraine talks after meeting Putin
World.content:
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv, seeking to revive efforts to end the war. But the latest diplomatic push seems to have produced no breakthrough.

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held "encouraging" talks in Kyiv on Sunday during their first official visit to Ukraine, but made no breakthrough toward ending Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Despite the renewed diplomatic push, Moscow and Kyiv remain divided over key issues, particularly territorial concessions. Kushner acknowledged the challenge, saying the US was working "behind the scenes" to create the conditions for a possible deal.

"It’s a very, very hard problem, but we’re going to try," Kushner said.

As Ukraine's airspace remains closed due to the conflict, the pair arrived in Kyiv by train from Poland, having held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow a day earlier.

Putin had declared a three-day ceasefire to ensure the envoys' safety.

Ukraine peace push? Trump envoys hold talks with Kremlin To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Zelenskyy: We will need a 'winter package'

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held three rounds of talks with the US envoys, the final one joined by national security advisers from the United Kingdom, France and Germany.

After meeting with Witkoff and Kushner, Zelenskyy said the talks focused on military aid, including Patriot missile systems and other weapons Ukraine will need in the coming months. He said Kyiv was seeking "serious volumes" of US support, with backing from its European partners.

"If the war drags on until winter — and that is how things currently look — we will need a 'winter package'," he said.

The Ukrainian president also expressed gratitude that representatives of European nations were in Kyiv.

"Here we are all on the same side," he said.

What did Russia say about Moscow talks?

Momentum by US President Donald Trump to end the four-and-a-half-year-old conflict has stalled in recent months after talks with Putin at the Kremlin in January failed to produce a result.

Despite hopes of a breakthrough with the Russian leader on Saturday, there were no announcements after the meeting.

Putin's foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov described the Moscow talks as constructive, frank, and useful but didn't discuss specific outcomes.

Ushakov said the talks also focused on economic issues and potentially large Russia-US projects.

During previous talks, negotiators have struggled to bring both sides together on a range of key issues, including the future of the industrial Donbas region of eastern Ukraine.

The US and Russia have been discussing tie-ins for months to try and end the war Image: Sputnik/Kremlin Pool/AP Photo/picture alliance

Ukraine war escalating in recent months

For Ukraine, hard security guarantees from its European allies and Washington are crucial to deterring Russia ​from further aggression.

Kyrylo Budanov, Zelenskyy's chief of staff, told the New York Times last weekend that he did not expect the fighting to end before spring 2027.

He also predicted further Russian strategic air strikes on Ukraine this winter.

The war has escalated in recent months, with Putin seeking the complete conquest of Donbas and Russian drones targeting the Ukrainian capital.

Meanwhile, Ukraine has focused its drone attacks on Russia's energy sector. It has also targeted online retailers deep inside Russia to try and bring the war home to the public.

World.title: AfD wants to form a government in Saxony-Anhalt — but how?
World.content:
Following its record-breaking success in the state election, the far-right AfD in Saxony-Anhalt is aiming to form a government.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) achieved its best-ever election result in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, winning well over 40% of the vote and leaving all other parties far behind.

However, the party lacks the majority of seats in parliament needed to govern on its own. Because the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been classified as "confirmed far-right extremist" by the domestic intelligence agency, other parties announced that cooperation with the AfD was out of the question. This will make forming a government in this eastern German state quite difficult.

On election night, Ulrich Siegmund announced on public broadcaster ARD: "As a democrat, I will reach out to all those who wish to work with us to bring about a fundamental political turnaround." At the same time, he acknowledged that there are currently no political parties that he considers suitable for a coalition government.

Above all, he was referring to the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which currently holds power in coalitions both in Saxony-Anhalt and on the federal level in Germany. Siegmund, along with the entire AfD leadership, has characterized the CDU's policy of refusing to work with the AfD a failure.

On public broadcaster ZDF, AfD party co-leader Alice Weidel sharply criticized the CDU for stonewalling the AfD: "The CDU will not win another election — not a federal election. And this clearly gives the AfD a mandate to govern. Because we are democrats, we do not refuse to work with others."

On election night, Ulrich Siegmund emphasized that implementing the AfD's platform was more important to him than the prospect of power: "There will be no compromise with me." Leading up to the vote, the 35-year-old AfD lead candidate repeatedly stated that he was only interested in governing alone in order to usher in a fundamental political change in Germany.

The AfD's radical governing platform

For months, the AfD's political program has sparked heated debates across Germany. That's because the party wants to drastically tighten asylum and immigration policies. It wants to speed up the deportation of illegal asylum seekers and introduce a general work requirement for all other asylum seekers.

Above all, however, it wants to make Saxony-Anhalt and Germany less attractive to immigrants and is calling for a "180-degree turnaround in migration policy." During its election campaign, the party repeatedly blamed migrants for crime in German cities and for the housing shortage.

What's more, the AfD is planning a radical restructuring of society: it has declared war on public broadcasting, wants to cut funding for democracy projects, intends to establish a kind of vigilante group against migrants and aims to combat social diversity — all of which is laid out in its platform. And Ulrich Siegmund emphasized in an ARD interview that these issues are non-negotiable.

Now, one option involves a minority government led by the AfD, in which it would need to secure support from other parties to advance its policies.

AfD: Saxony-Anhalt result will 'shake all of Germany' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

AfD Chairwoman Alice Weidel told ZDF television: "Who ultimately forms the government — perhaps through a tolerance agreement or even a coalition — remains to be seen."

On behalf of the CDU, the party's secretary-general, Franziska Hoppermann, categorically ruled out a coalition: "There will be no cooperation with the far left or the far right."

Will the BSW decide on the government of Saxony-Anhalt?

The biggest unknown in this power struggle is the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), should it manage to move into the state parliament.

The small party campaigns primarily on a left-wing economic platform and — similar to the AfD — calls for a foreign policy that is more friendly toward Russia. In the past, party founder and former member of the socialist Left Party, Sahra Wagenknecht, has repeatedly expressed openness to substantive cooperation with the AfD. However, for ideological reasons, the party is not considered a particularly attractive partner within AfD circles.

As the AfD celebrated its victory into the night and even before the vote count was complete, some AfD state politicians announced that, if necessary, they intended to remain in the opposition and keep the other parties on the defensive until they could secure a majority of their own.

Take, for example, Oliver Kirchner, co-chair of the AfD caucus in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt: "If we end up behind the lectern as the opposition, it will be brutal for the others," he warned during an AfD livestream.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Saxony-Anhalt: Digesting the AfD's landmark election win
World.content:
With well over 40% for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), Saxony-Anhalt has witnessed a landmark election night. DW's reporters were on the ground.

After an unusually quiet evening at the press center for the Saxony-Anhalt state election, journalists, camera crews and technicians were suddenly running around, jostling and shouting. Ulrich Siegmund, the leading candidate of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), went running off with his bodyguards, looking for the best place to stand so that he would be clearly visible on camera when the election projections started appearing on the screens.

And then, a few minutes later, the commotion started up again, as AfD party leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla arrived, beaming just as broadly as Siegmund. Another scramble ensued, and the bodyguards shouted: "Stay back!"

At 6 pm, when the preliminary results finally came in, the AfD was well above 40%. For the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which governs the region between the Elbe and the Harz Mountains, it is a nightmare — there's no other way to put it. Weidel subsequently declares the result a clear mandate for her party to form a government. It's hard to disagree with her on that. She tells reporters that even before Christmas rolls around, Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) will be replaced following this election result.

Weidel: 'This is a mandate for us to form a government!'

After all, Merz, whose popularity has hit record lows across the country, was rarely seen during this election campaign. And his party here in Saxony-Anhalt was glad about that.

AfD co-chair Tino Chrupalla also spoke of a blow to the chancellor, who he said only makes grandiose announcements. He also accused the chancellor of "unnecessarily escalating" tensions with Russia recently. Once the cameras were off, Chrupalla admitted that even he hadn't expected such a clear victory.

The AfD, which the domestic intelligence agency classifies as "confirmed far-right extremist," held its election party at the Altes Theater, just a stone's throw from the press center. Before entering the building, journalists and visitors were searched by police dogs, and bags were checked twice.

"This feels less like a state election and more like a G7 summit," said DW correspondent Matthew Moore, after finally getting into the Altes Theater. To maintain order over the weekend, 1,800 additional police officers were dispatched to Saxony-Anhalt from other federal states.

'Like a trip to the dentist': The CDU at the Maritim Hotel

And what about the CDU, which has governed Saxony-Anhalt for the last 24 years? The voters' rejection of the party could hardly be more decisive. That Sven Schulze, the incumbent premier, did not resign immediately could even be seen as an act of bravery. With a stony expression, he told his supporters: "This is democracy!"

At the beginning of the year, Schulze succeeded Reiner Haseloff as head of government in Saxony-Anhalt. Seventy-two-year-old Haseloff was highly respected in the state and yet did not wish to run for another term. But when he stepped down, it was too late for Schulze to counter the force of support for the AfD.

The CDU election party — which turned out to be not much of a party at all — was held at the four-star Maritim Hotel. In the hotel ballroom, only die-hard CDU supporters remained to witness the debacle. This year's results were half of what they were in the previous state election. It was a difficult defeat for the party that remained the strongest political force in Saxony-Anhalt for the last twenty years. "It's a bit like being in the dentist's waiting room," a CDU supporter told DW reporter Bernd Riegert with a bitter smile. "You know it's going to hurt, but you can't run away."

Uncertainty regarding the BSW

No matter how big the right-wing populists' election victory may be, the AfD has little chance of governing with an absolute majority. And so far, all other parties have ruled out entering into a coalition with it.

It will likely come down to the economically left-wing and politically conservative Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which could narrowly make it into the state parliament.

Meanwhile, Eva von Angern, the leading candidate for the socialist Left Party in Saxony-Anhalt, spoke of a "dark day" for the state, because of "the consequences this result could have for Saxony-Anhalt and the people of Saxony-Anhalt." And by that, she was also referring to the AfD's hardline policy toward refugees. During the campaign, the AfD made it clear time and again that asylum seekers whose applications were rejected would be deported on a large scale "from day one."

What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hope within the SPD for a majority without the AfD

As for the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), the junior partner in Chancellor Merz's federal government struck a surprisingly optimistic tone. Despite predictions that they would fare much worse, the Social Democrats are now assured of representation in the state parliament. In distant Berlin, SPD Secretary-General Tim Klüssendorf was not yet ready to give up hope that a coalition of all mainstream parties might be able to bypass the AfD and form a coalition: "If such a majority exists, then it should be formed with the participation of all the parties represented in this state parliament," he said.

Greens between euphoria and shock

The environmentalist Greens spent election night somewhere between euphoria and shock. Actually, the party should be delighted with such an unexpected result. Predictions had long suggested they might fail to clear the five-percent threshold, but now they're safely in. DW reporter Giula Saudelli said that some staff members at the Green Party's election party had tears in their eyes when the projections appeared on the screens: tears of relief for their own party and tears of shock at the AfD's gains.

"There's no reason to jump for joy when it's still unclear whether far-right extremists will be able to govern this state," party co-leader Felix Banaszak told DW. He had spent a lot of time campaigning in Saxony-Anhalt. Videos on social media showed him being openly attacked and verbally abused. But he continued nonetheless. People close to him say that this may have contributed to the Greens' election success — a success that doesn't quite feel like one.

… and in Berlin, the chancellor remains silent

But this much is clear: it was an historic evening in Saxony-Anhalt: a defining moment. Much remains unclear, such as who will eventually govern the state and what consequences this will have for Chancellor Friedrich Merz. A press conference has been scheduled with him for midday on Monday.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Fact check: Election fraud claims spread in Saxony-Anhalt
World.content:
False and misleading claims are raising questions about the integrity of the election in Saxony-Anhalt. DW Fact Check takes a closer look.

On Sunday, Saxony-Anhalt held one of Germany's most consequential elections in years. The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won a decisive lead, putting the party in a position to potentially form the first far-right state government in Germany since World War II.

In the days before the vote, false and misleading claims seized on the election's importance, with social media users alleging fraud, vote-rigging and irregularities in the handling and counting of ballots.

DW Fact Check previously documented some of these tactics as part of Matryoshka, also known as Operation Overload, a Russian-linked influence operation targeting German elections.

Below, we take a closer look at some more recent claims.

Fake video shows election workers destroying AfD ballots

Claim: "German election workers recorded themselves outright destroying ballots that were cast for the populist party 'Alternative For Germany' (AfD), during Germany's recent elections," reads a post viewed 10,000 times on X, posted by a QAnon-associated account, a far-right American political conspiracy theory and political movement.

A one-minute video shows a white-gloved man unpacking ballots from red envelopes, laying them on a table, and drawing a black X through ones that select the AfD. A ballot marked for the CDU is set aside, as a voice says in German, "these are OK."

The same video was shared by numerous other accounts, in German and English across social media platforms X and YouTube.

Verdict: False

There are several telltale signs that this video is staged. Most obviously, all three crossed-out ballots contain the same name.

They're also missing a hole punch in the top right corner, a regulation that ensures ballots can be used with a template for blind or visually impaired voters. The envelopes are also already unsealed.

The Gnida Project, a Russian disinformation watchdog group, said the video was part of the Storm-1516 campaign.

Storm-1516, a unit controlled by Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, was also active ahead of Germany's 2025 federal election.

Read more on disinformation around Germany's postal voting system

Though a false claim purported that AfD ballots were destroyed, the AfD in fact won a huge share of the vote on Sunday Image: Fabrizio Bensch/REUTERS

Russian disinfo campaign alleges CDU fraud

Claim: The CDU is engaging in fraud in the Saxony-Anhalt election. "The social media pages of deceased residents of Saxony-Anhalt have become a platform for the #CDU's election campaign," reads one post on X, sharing a spoofed DW video.

"According to T-Online, non-existent citizens are set to vote by post for the #CDU in the Saxony-Anhalt election," reads another.

Verdict: False

DW Fact check reviewed five videos following a near-identical template: each was about a minute long and was posted by an account with zero followers and nearly no other posts. The videos feature a reputable news outlet's logo in the corner — including DW, ARD, WIRED, and BBC — and make claims about the CDU committing election fraud.

The claims range from the CDU using a database of Nazi soldier names to register fake ballots, to residents receiving campaign messages from deceased relatives.

Each video ends with a message urging viewers to "share this video with your family and friends in any way you see fit".

One of the videos claims T-Online disinformation reporter Lars Wienand had "obtained evidence that the CDU will attempt to rig the election." Wienand confirmed he had reported no such thing, writing to DW that "it's not the first time that suspected Russian disinformation had misused my name and image."

Julia Smirnova, disinformation expert and senior researcher at the Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy, told DW the posts were part of the Matryoshka Russian disinformation campaign, also known as Operation Overload.

"As with other Matryoshka videos, the reach is mostly inauthentic," she wrote in an email to DW.

DW Fact Check has previously documented the same operation targeting candidates in Germany's state elections. We identified more than 180 fake posts on X, Bluesky and TikTok, many of them using the logos and formats of established media outlets to spread fabricated allegations about politicians.

Read more on Russian disinformation targeting German elections

A misleading claim alleged that postal ballots were being counted before polls closed Image: Michael Bihlmayer/Bihlmayerfotografie/IMAGO

Did Halle start counting ballots too early?

Claim: "Unbelievable scandal! In Halle, absentee voting ballots are already being counted before 6 p.m. That's blatantly illegal!" reads a post on X with over 160,000 views, posted by a right-wing journalist.

Below is a screenshot of German newspaper ZEIT's online news blog, with an entry, originally written in German, titled: "Counting of absentee ballots from 60 polling districts begins in Halle-Neustadt".

Verdict: Misleading

The screenshot accurately shows a screengrabbed ZEIT liveblog entry, published at 3:15 pm.

Only ZEIT made an error, with the reporter clarifying to DW over email that their reporting was just describing "preparatory tasks" and not the actual counting of ballots.

The ZEIT blog entry has since been corrected with a "transparency note" that reads, "An earlier version of this blog post stated that the count had already begun. In fact, preparations were only underway. We have corrected the error."

The Saxony-Anhalt's state election regulations specify that ballots are not supposed to be officially counted until the voting period ends at 6 p.m. They can, however, be opened in advance to facilitate later ballot-counting.

World.title: Saxony-Anhalt's state election will have a nationwide impact
World.content:
The election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt could have dramatic consequences for Germany's federal government. Pollsters point to dissatisfaction with Chancellor Merz as one reason for his party's poor showing.

Only 1.6 million eligible voters were called to choose a new state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, September 6. The region between the Elbe River and Harz Mountains in eastern Germany is outnumbered in population by 10 of Germany's total 16 federal states.

For weeks it was clear that the vote had become a major challenge for the federal government coalition of the conservative Union — of the Christian Democrats and their Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) — and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD). In the last few months, there were even rumors in Berlin that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the CDU could step down following this vote — or that he would be forced to by his own party.

The in-part right-wing extremist Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the election, doubling its percentage compared to the last election five years ago, while the ruling CDU lost half of its support. If the AfD now manages to form a government, the election would have serious consequences for the federal government in Berlin.

A threat to Chancellor Friedrich Merz?

Political scientist Carsten Koschmieder from the Free University in Berlin does not believe Merz will give up.

"I do not have the impression that he is a person who would resign," Koschmieder told DW before the election. "Rather, he is very glad to be chancellor and has long worked toward that." In addition, there is currently no ready successor to Merz in the CDU and CSU, he added.

Koschmieder also predicted that a strong showing by the AfD would intensify pressure regarding the correct way to deal with the AfD, which is in parts right-wing extremist. The CDU has categorically ruled out working with the AfD, as have all other established German political parties.

Most analysts believe that engaging with the right-wing populists would massively damage the CDU/CSU. "There are many conservative democrats in the CDU who say: We have nothing to do with the AfD. They want to abolish our democracy; they support Russia's President Putin and oppose Western integration and European unity," Koschmieder explained.

Before he was elected chancellor in May 2025, Merz set the goal of halving support for the AfD, in part by adopting a tough migration policy. The fact that this has not succeeded, and instead the CDU has lost support, has yielded him much criticism within his party.

Could a CDU government get support from the Left Party?

It's also possible that the CDU in Saxony-Anhalt ends up forming a minority government with the SPD and the environmentalist Greens. But even such a three-way coalition is unlikely to have a majority in parliament.

This would mean it has to be tolerated, ironically, by the socialist Left Party. Ironic, because the CDU also wants to avoid any cooperation with the Left, as the chancellor reiterated in an interview with regional newspaper the Mitteldeutsche Zeitung: "Both the AfD and Left Party have such fundamental differences with the Union that cooperation is out of the question," Merz said on Tuesday.

Here, Koschmieder said, a double problem arises for Merz: Many local-level CDU politicians, especially in eastern Germany, consider cooperation with the AfD quite possible, and have categorically rejected working with the Left Party.

Saxony-Anhalt election: Can the CDU stop the AfD? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Merz: Government stability not at risk

Amid far right's rise, is Germany at a breaking point? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video





The chancellor seems resolved to carry on with his government, even amid growing dissatisfaction and rising pressure. This year, he still plans to bring his controversial reforms of the old age pension system through parliament, which have been heavily criticized by members of his own party on the campaign trail in Saxony-Anhalt.

But that hasn't discouraged Merz. "The pension system is no longer sustainable because of demographics, and we have known this for years," he said.

What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

SPD hopes for success in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania

What about the Social Democrats? They have remained at around 8% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt. This is a great improvement on what was being predicted six months ago.

In addition, the Social Democrat premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Manuela Schwesig, has good odds of a renewed mandate in state parliament elections there on September 20. The SPD has made a strong comeback in the polls in the coastal state since last year; with around 30% of the vote, they could form a government with the Left Party, the CDU or potentially both.
