World.title: Leucemia linfocítica crónica: cuando la investigación equivale a supervivencia
World.content:
Del total de personas a las que se diagnostica leucemia linfocítica crónica, un tercio no necesita tratamiento y la decisión de aplicarlo depende de que la enfermedad esté activa o no, según establecen las guías clínicas de esta patología. /GETTY IMAGES

La supervivencia a cinco años sitúa la leucemia más habitual en adultos entre los cánceres con mejor pronóstico. La incorporación de tratamientos de duración limitada ha permitido, además, reducir la toxicidad y facilitar una mejor calidad de vida a los pacientes

La historia de la oncología se ha escrito con avances paulatinos que han supuesto un aumento en la supervivencia del cáncer en general, y además con grandes saltos terapéuticos, como la medicina de precisión, que han marcado un antes y un después en el abordaje de algunos tipos de cáncer. Uno de ellos es la leucemia linfocítica crónica (LLC). Los datos de supervivencia a cinco años de los pacientes con LLC revelan ese impacto: ha pasado de un 59% en 2005 a un 85% en la actualidad, según datos recogidos por la Sociedad Española de Hematología y Hemoterapia en su informe Avance en los cánceres hematológicos.

Francesc Bosch, jefe del servicio de Hematología del hospital Vall d’Hebron de Barcelona, sitúa el punto de inflexión definitivo en la última década: “El conocimiento de la biología de la LLC se ha traducido en el desarrollo de medicamentos muy dirigidos que van a buscar las debilidades de la enfermedad”.

La combinación de mutaciones que se registran en un cáncer es única en cada persona y la medicina de precisión aplicada a la oncología se basa en buscar esas alteraciones genéticas tumorales para predecir la respuesta al tratamiento. En la LLC ha supuesto, en la práctica, pasar de la quimioterapia que se aplicaba a todos los pacientes a un tratamiento personalizado. Los avances terapéuticos han supuesto, además, menos efectos secundarios y, como consecuencia, mejor calidad de vida para los pacientes.

En qué consiste la leucemia linfocítica crónica Fuente: Instituto Nacional del Cáncer (NIH) de EE UU y elaboración propia a partir de las fuentes consultadas.

Las leucemias se clasifican según la rapidez con la que se desarrollan y la célula en la que se originan. Francesc Bosch explica que “la leucemia linfocítica crónica afecta a los linfocitos y a los órganos donde se ubican estas células y, a diferencia de la leucemia aguda, que se manifiesta de forma abrupta, la LLC aparece lentamente, por lo que muchos pacientes no van a necesitar tratamiento para su enfermedad”.

Cuando una persona escucha en la voz de su médico la palabra leucemia, no espera que la indicación sea una cita a los tres o a los seis meses. En la mente de esa persona se instala la idea del cáncer, un diagnóstico que todo el mundo asocia automáticamente con recibir tratamiento urgente. Pero, en el caso de la LLC, la espera activa forma parte del proceso. Jesús Pérez Viejo, psico-oncólogo y profesor de la Universidad Nacional de Educación a Distancia (UNED), ha comprobado esa perplejidad inicial en numerosos enfermos: “A veces es difícil integrar palabras como cáncer y enfermedad crónica porque el paciente no espera convivir con la leucemia de por vida; la idea generalizada que tenemos de un proceso oncológico es que, si no te curas, te mueres”.

“La leucemia linfocítica crónica es de los cánceres con mejor pronóstico y la incertidumbre del diagnóstico desaparece si sabes que estás en buenas manos y si hay información sobre el camino por el que vas a pasar” Julio González González, presidente de la Asociación de Pacientes con Leucemia Linfocítica Crónica (ASPALLC)

Cómo gestionar esa incertidumbre es, según los clínicos y las asociaciones de pacientes, uno de los retos en la LLC. Julio González, presidente de la Asociación de Pacientes con Leucemia Linfocítica Crónica (ASPALLC), convive con ella desde hace 12 años y pone especial énfasis en la importancia de que la persona diagnosticada conozca lo mejor posible la enfermedad para despejar las nubes oscuras que tienden a instalarse en la mente y hallar respuesta a las docenas de preguntas que le surgen: “La leucemia linfocítica crónica es de los cánceres con mejor pronóstico y la incertidumbre del diagnóstico desaparece si sabes que estás en buenas manos y si hay información sobre el camino por el que vas a pasar”.

Un paciente implicado y una responsabilidad compartida

Los propios equipos sanitarios, cada vez más multidisciplinares, propician la implicación del paciente. Les corresponde ese protagonismo y asumirlo repercute, entre otras cosas, en la adherencia terapéutica. “Cuanto más formado e implicado esté el paciente, mayor es la adherencia”, señala el doctor Bosch. Jesús Pérez Viejo, por su parte, incide en que los beneficios alcanzan a todos los implicados en la LLC: “La participación de los pacientes, sobre todo en la toma de decisiones, mejora su capacidad de afrontamiento de la enfermedad y ayuda al personal sanitario a que su responsabilidad sea compartida”.

“Con los tratamientos que tenemos, basados en las características genéticas de la enfermedad en cada paciente, la respuesta es muy rápida: al cabo de un mes o dos desaparecen los síntomas y el paciente nota que mejora mucho” Francesc Bosch, jefe del servicio de Hematología del hospital Vall d’Hebron de Barcelona

Del total de personas a las que se diagnostica LLC, un tercio no necesita tratamiento y la decisión de aplicarlo depende de que la enfermedad esté activa o no, según establecen las guías clínicas; es decir, que el paciente presente síntomas asociados a la leucemia, como crecimiento de los ganglios, anemia o descenso de las plaquetas. Si se ha iniciado el tratamiento, la adherencia es muy importante porque hay un grupo de enfermos en los que la terapia será de por vida, igual que ocurre en enfermedades como la diabetes o la hipertensión.

Aunque los efectos adversos de estas terapias están lejos de los que producía la quimioterapia, siguen existiendo, como en cualquier tratamiento crónico. De ahí que los especialistas ponderen el valor de uno de los cambios que se ha registrado en los últimos años: la incorporación de tratamientos limitados en el tiempo a partir de la combinación de diferentes terapias ya existentes. “Con un terapia de duración fija se ahorra toxicidad para el paciente y se evita la posibilidad de que genere resistencias al tratamiento”, apunta Bosch.

La leucemia linfocítica crónica (LLC), en datos Fuente: Fuente: Elaboración propia a partir de las fuentes consultadas.

De la mano de los avances terapéuticos en los últimos años ha llegado también una atención cada vez más integral a los pacientes. Jesús Pérez Viejo precisa: “El cáncer afecta a todas las áreas de la vida, desde la familiar a la laboral y hay momentos en que los tratamientos o el avance de la enfermedad requiere un soporte emocional especializado”.

Los profesionales de la psico-oncología tienen cada vez mayor protagonismo en ese acompañamiento. Se trata de vivir y hacerlo con calidad de vida, y en el logro de ese objetivo el bienestar emocional es fundamental. Pérez Viejo comenta que el psico-oncólogo puede resolver muchos de los temores que viven el enfermo y su entorno: “La LLC conlleva síntomas que generan retos psicológicos, pues hay inmunosupresión y se deben cuidar las infecciones. A veces, esto genera inseguridad en muchos pacientes porque tienen miedo a contagiarse y eso les hace evitar determinados lugares y el consiguiente aislamiento”.

“La participación de los pacientes, sobre todo en la toma de decisiones, mejora su capacidad de afrontar la enfermedad y ayuda al personal sanitario a que su responsabilidad sea compartida” Jesús Pérez Viejo, psico-oncólogo y profesor de la Universidad Nacional de Educación a Distancia (UNED)

Con la experiencia de 12 años conviviendo con la LLC, Julio González recomienda disponer de “una caja de herramientas propia” para afrontar una relación no querida pero inevitable, como es la de la leucemia. Esa caja le sirve para afrontar las repercusiones de la enfermedad en todos los ámbitos en los que se desenvuelve. Así, para las personas que todavía están trabajando recomienda tener claro que “el diagnóstico forma parte de la información médica privada y es el paciente quien decide qué compartir, con quién y cuándo hacerlo”. Si se necesita flexibilidad para revisiones o pruebas, señala que lo mejor es ser práctico: “Necesito tal día o tal franja horaria. Hay que proponer soluciones. Menos drama, más claridad”.

Los pacientes, las asociaciones como ASPALLC y los profesionales que atienden a las personas con LLC consideran que todavía quedan necesidades no cubiertas, que tienen que ver, sobre todo, con la falta de equidad en el acceso a un soporte integral. “Hay sitios donde la posibilidad de recurrir a un psico-oncólogo simplemente no existe y la información para los pacientes se limita a una consulta cada cuatro meses aprisa y corriendo”, apunta Julio González. Las otras necesidades por cubrir alcanzan a otros ámbitos muchas veces ignorados, pero importantes, que precisa Jesús Pérez Viejo: “Tienen que ver con el trabajo, el gasto económico que supone una enfermedad oncológica o incluso con problemas sexológicos que pueden aparecer y que en un primer momento no son prioritarios, pero afectan a la calidad de vida”.

Todo suma en el abordaje integral de una enfermedad, la LLC, cuyo horizonte se tiñe cada vez más de verde. La investigación y los profesionales implicados en el proceso oncológico han conseguido prolongar drásticamente la supervivencia y mejorar la calidad de vida de los pacientes, pero no se han olvidado del objetivo final, que apunta Francesc Bosch como médico: “Se investiga mucho la LLC porque no deja de ser la leucemia más frecuente en adultos, pero nuestro fin último es curarla”.

World.title: Un verano en Wolfgangsee: aguas cristalinas y pueblos de cuento en el lago más bonito de Austria
World.content:
Encajado entre montañas, este enclave de la región de Salzkammergut ha sido fuente de inspiración para el arte, la música y la literatura. En los meses estivales, además, se suma todo un catálogo de actividades náuticas, incluyendo una travesía en barco de vapor

Hay en la región austriaca de Salzkammergut una expresión popular que los vecinos emplean para expresar que todo está “simplemente bien”: “Alles gschmah”. Esta viene a definir ese estado en el que todo fluye de manera natural, en el que cada elemento tiene su propio ritmo, en el que la vida, aunque solo sea por un instante, puede concebirse como relajada y serena.

Esta sensibilidad especial se atribuye al influjo del Wolfgangsee, el lago al que muchos identifican, más que por su abrumadora belleza, por la calma que favorece con su propia presencia. Hasta hay quien dice que las pulsaciones descienden solo con contemplarlo.

Encajado en un cuenco entre majestuosas montañas y rodeado de bosques en los que se ocultan pequeños pueblos recostados sobre la orilla, lo cierto es que este lago, ubicado a menos de una hora en coche de la ciudad de Salzburgo, dibuja una postal idílica. Especialmente por el color de sus aguas, a las que las partículas de cal confieren unas tonalidades que van desde el zafiro hasta el esmeralda. Es en estos meses estivales, con el sol proyectando sobre su espejo destellos plateados, cuando mejor se aprecia su intensidad. Y también cuando más se disfruta de las actividades en la naturaleza.

El puerto de St. Gilgen, localidad situada a orillas del lago Wolfgangsee, en el estado austriaco de Salzburgo, en la región del Salzkammergut. Darren Edgell ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Un verano en Wolfgangsee pasa por darse cada mañana un chapuzón refrescante en las áreas de baño que dibujan una suerte de playas de interior, con césped en lugar de arena y tumbonas a la sombra de los árboles. Pero también por surcar las aguas sobre un hidropedal o por empujarse con el viento para navegar a vela, o por aprovechar las corrientes térmicas para practicar surf, windsurf y paddle surf.

Para los de secano, no faltan las rutas de senderismo por prados exuberantes y pastizales alpinos, siempre con vistas a las cumbres imponentes.

El lago que cuenta historias

El conocido como el lago camaleón (así lo llaman los fotógrafos por el cambio de luz) tiene miles de historias sumergidas. Como aquella leyenda que convirtió en santo al obispo Wolfgang de Ratisbona, que había llegado a este lugar para vivir como un ermitaño. Cuentan que construyó una iglesia en el mismo punto donde cayó el hacha que había lanzado montaña abajo y que después hizo brotar agua de una roca plana. Gracias a este milagro, la ermita se convirtió en uno de los centros de peregrinaje más visitado por los católicos.

Hotel Schafbergspitze, en lo alto del monte Schafberg, con espectaculares vistas panorámicas sobre los Alpes y el lago Attersee, cerca de Sankt Wolfgang, en la región del Salzkammergut (Austria). MIKALAI ZASTSENSKI ( GETTY IMAGES )

Tiempo después, la región de Salzkammergut, compuesta por 76 lagos, viviría el esplendor de la sal que le da nombre. Eran los tiempos del Imperio Austrohúngaro, cuando los soberanos europeos descubrieron los poderes curativos de las salinas de la ciudad austriaca de Bad Ischl. La misma emperatriz Sissi disfrutó de estos baños terapéuticos y frecuentó el lago Wolfgangsee en sus muchas escapadas libres del riguroso protocolo de la corte.

Como ella, ya en el siglo XIX, artistas e intelectuales vieron en estos parajes todo un caudal de inspiración. Gustav Klimt pintó una serie sobre el lago Attersee, que forma parte de la colección permanente del Leopold Museum de Viena. El escritor Stefan Zweig ensalzó la belleza de la zona en sus múltiples cartas y diarios, y la recordó con nostalgia en sus memorias póstumas, tituladas El mundo de ayer. También Johann Strauss, Gustav Mahler y Johannes Brahms alumbraron célebres melodías con el marco de las montañas. Hasta el hotel Im Weissen Rössl inspiró una famosa opereta, La Posada del Caballito Blanco, que, con su estreno en Berlín en 1930 (y su posterior adaptación cinematográfica) colocó en el mapa turístico la estampa bucólica de estos paisajes.

Del barco de vapor al tren cremallera

Nada como navegar por el lago, solo durante los meses de verano, a bordo del histórico barco de vapor llamado Kaiser Franz Josef I, tal y como se hacía en la época imperial en lo que supuso, para su tiempo, todo un triunfo tecnológico. Una travesía nostálgica que acerca a pintorescos pueblos como St. Gilgen, en la orilla norte, donde se esconden las raíces de un genio: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. Aquí nació su madre, Anna Maria Pertl, y vivió su hermana, Nannerl, en una casa que hoy es utilizada para eventos, conciertos y seminarios, aunque hay quien también la elige para casarse por lo civil.

Estatua de Mozart frente al Ayuntamiento (Rathaus) de St. Gilgen. Adwo ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Más allá de la huella del músico (no falta su escultura en la plaza que lleva su mismo nombre ni las placas en la iglesia de San Egidio, donde se casaron sus abuelos), St. Gilgen es un pueblo encantador en el que las fachadas lucen los coloridos frescos de lüftlmalerei, una técnica de pintura mural y trampantojo típica de Austria y Baviera. Un buen plan es visitar el curioso Museo del Instrumento, donde Askold zur Eck no solo ha reunido más de 6.000 ejemplares procedentes de todo el mundo, sino que hasta se atreve a tocarlos si el visitante se lo pide. E imprescindible es subir al pico Zwölferhorn a través de un teleférico alimentado por placas solares, desde el que se obtienen fabulosas vistas sobre el entorno.

St. Wolfang es otro pueblo de cuento, también a la vera del Wolfgangsee y desparramado por las laderas del monte Schafberg, a cuya cima (1.783 metros) llega el Schafbergbahn, el tren cremallera con mayor desnivel de Austria. La estación desde la que parte no solo fue reconocida con el prestigioso Prix Versailles 2024 de la Unesco por su arquitectura rompedora, sino que es considerada por muchos rankings viajeros como una de las estaciones de pasajeros más bellas del mundo. Una vez en las alturas, además de disfrutar de la más hermosa panorámica, lo suyo es tomar algo en el Schafbergspitze, el hotel alpino más antiguo del país —abrió en 1862—, para después volver a descender hacia el lago milenario que es uno de los grandes tesoros de Austria.

World.title: Calpe, renovarse a la sombra del Peñón
World.content:
Además de por su paquidérmica y famosa formación rocosa, la ciudad alicantina merece una visita por las Salinas, el conjunto arqueológico Baños de la Reina y una gastronomía en la que destaca la gamba blanca

Siempre que vuelvo a Calpe (cosa que pasa menos veces de las que querría) me sorprende y me exalta la colosalidad irredenta del peñón de Ifach. Esta paquidérmica protuberancia, ocasionalmente envuelta de nubes como la aureola de un santo, parece siempre a punto de saltar sobre el mar, que le es refugio y no abismo. Y, en efecto, ese tosco poliedro es una prolongación de la cordillera Bética, que se sumerge audazmente bajo las olas para dirigirse a Mallorca. Un tótem prodigioso, una ofrenda desmesurada y, quizás, en su priapismo cósmico, un tabú.

El parecido de esta gran roca con la de Gibraltar ha propiciado teorías diversas, normalmente descabelladas pero siempre amenas. Que Gibraltar e Ifach estuvieron unidos físicamente antes de abrirse el Estrecho es una de esas leyendas. Sí que es cierto que, en la antigüedad, el nombre Calpe designaba al peñón de Gibraltar. En un tiempo tan dado a las supercherías y otros golpes en el pecho de la ignorancia suprema me extraña que nadie haya propuesto que este titánico pedrusco pueda ser una ofrenda a algún dios. O quizás un monumento obra de los extraterrestres, como algunos partidarios desaforados del delirium tremens dicen que son las pirámides de El Cairo. Ajeno a todas nuestras elucubraciones, el Peñón sigue aquí, como el dinosaurio de Monterroso: una erección ciclópea, una insurgencia calcárea insolente y retadora, un desorbitado capricho morfológico.

Con este atractivo paisajístico, la ciudad alicantina necesita poco más para atraer visitantes. Y, sin embargo, las calidades de su oferta no dejan de aumentar. Ya se sabe que desde hace décadas recibe un elevado número de turistas extranjeros (muchos, hoy, residentes permanentes), principalmente procedentes del Reino Unido, Alemania, Bélgica y los Países Bajos. Este carácter cosmopolita no le ha hecho perder personalidad. Su casco antiguo con restos de los muros medievales resulta muy evocador, con sus calles estrechas, sus plazas tradicionales y edificios históricos como la iglesia Antigua (del siglo XV) y el Torreó de la Peça (baluarte defensivo de la antigua muralla). A esto une una variada oferta de restauración y comercio, amén de las actividades náuticas de su puerto deportivo o el senderismo que puede practicarse en el Peñón.

Torreó de la Peça, baluarte defensivo de la antigua muralla, en Calpe. TONO BALAGUER (GETTY IMAGES )

Entre sus atractivos naturales están las Salinas y el conjunto arqueológico Baños de la Reina. Las Salinas son parte de una antigua bahía cerrada por una barrera de dunas que unía el Peñón con el continente. La explotación de sal se cerró en 1988, así que, clausurada la industria, ha florecido la biodiversidad: allí viven 173 especies diferentes de aves. En cuanto a Baños de la Reina, es un yacimiento arqueológico, anexo a las Salinas, donde debió vivir un noble romano. Además de su lujosa villa, incluye una piscifactoría (donde se llevaba a cabo la salazón del pescado), unas termas, una noria y cuatro aljibes.

Esta antigua actividad pesquera ha llegado hasta la actualidad. A diferencia de otros destinos muy orientados exclusivamente al turismo, Calpe ha mantenido una flota de arrastre significativa. Su puerto alberga una de las lonjas más importantes de la zona, donde se realiza la ancestral e imprescindible subasta del pescado y el marisco locales.

Vista de Las Salinas, parte de una antigua bahía cerrada por una barrera de dunas que unía el Peñón con el continente. Jacek Krysciak ( GETTY IMAGES )

Su gran tesoro marino es la gamba blanca. Aunque la gamba roja de su vecina Dénia tiene una fama más consolidada, las propiedades de la blanca (su dulzura natural, su carne firme y sedosa, el suave aroma a yodo acabada de pescar) no son precisamente despreciables. Desde 2025, este fruto del mar goza de marca de calidad propia. Según el Portal Agrari de la Generalitat, ese año se capturaron y comercializaron más de 1.600 toneladas de gamba blanca en la Comunidad Valenciana (casi toda en la costa de Alicante). Es la tercera especie local en número de capturas (después del boquerón y de la sardina): genera 13,5 millones de euros, superando a la gamba roja y al boquerón, que hace años lideraban el ránking marino. Y ahora ese tesoro, que era cuantitativo, ha empezado a volverse cualitativo.

Parte de los Baños de la Reina, un yacimiento arqueológico anexo a Las Salinas. Teo Moreno ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Es precisamente en la gastronomía donde Calpe ha afinado más su renovación en los últimos tiempos. La versatilidad culinaria de ese prodigioso crustáceo ha llamado la atención de los chefs más reputados de la zona. Dos ejemplos: los restaurantes Onami y Beat.

Marisco fresco expuesto en el puerto pesquero de Calpe, Alicante. Manoli Perez ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Onami abrió este pasado mes de junio en el hotel AR Diamante Beach. Este imponente establecimiento ya disponía de otros dos locales de restauración, el Audrey’s (el primer local con estrella Michelin de Calpe) y el Amas. Onami comparte chef con Amas: Diego Laso. La diferencia entre los dos —inspirados ambos en la cocina japonesa— es que en Onami no hay carta y se come en la barra. El servicio está concebido como un menú degustación al estilo kaiseki-ryori: la forma más refinada y tradicional de la alta gastronomía japonesa. Onami es un juego de palabras entre ona (ola, en valenciano/catalán) y nami (mismo significado en japonés). Esto da la medida de su filosofía: ofrecer un diálogo entre la cocina valenciana y la nipona. De aquí la receta de gamba blanca en Amas (curada con sake y servida con crema inglesa y algas de Galicia), o el nigiri de este mismo crustáceo en Onami, simplemente pelado y servido sobre arroz.

Segundo ejemplo: el restaurante Beat (una estrella Michelin), ubicado en The Cookbook. Este hotel acaba de renovarse en profundidad. En Beat reina desde hace diez años José Manuel Miguel, el único cocinero valenciano que ha obtenido estrellas Michelin en Francia y en España. Si en Onami dialogaban la cocina local con la nipona, aquí la fusión está protagonizada por lo valenciano y lo francés. El gran referente de José Manuel Miguel es Paul Bocuse, emblema de la nouvelle cuisine gala. El bogavante lo cocina a la manera de la Salade de homard à la française de Bocuse, pero la gamba blanca no requiere mayor transformación: su hechizo radica en la ausencia de cocción.

Con todo esto ya se puede volver a visitar Calpe y saborear algo más que la siempre imponente vista de su Peñón. Tradición y modernidad, lo llaman.

World.title: Israel tiene un problema con su principal aeropuerto
World.content:
Una huelga sitúa el aeródromo de Ben Gurión en la cúspide mundial de alteraciones del tráfico y pone de relieve el reto que afronta el pequeño país con sus infraestructuras de transporte

El 27 de agosto, una fotografía de decenas de maletas al sol en el principal aeropuerto de Israel, Ben Gurión, circuló con indignación por las redes sociales. Seguían en tierra una semana después de la huelga que convirtió el aeropuerto en un caos de anulaciones y retrasos. Ben Gurión, puerta de entrada y salida a un país que adora presentarse —a menudo para desviar la atención de todo lo otro que hace— como una start-up nation tecnológica e innovadora, se convirtió aquel día en el aeropuerto de todo el mundo con más alteraciones de tráfico, según la famosa página de seguimiento de vuelos en tiempo real Flightradar24.

La huelga atrajo toda la atención, pero el aeropuerto llevaba semanas con dificultades para acomodar la demanda, con retrasos, colas y esperas de hasta tres horas para recibir el equipaje. En parte porque, pese a ser civil, sigue alojando a plena vista aviones militares estadounidenses de repostaje y carga, que llegaron antes de que EE UU e Israel atacasen a Irán y siguen ahí por si acaso seis meses después, aunque ahora menos y más distribuidos.

Estalló en verano porque es cuando sus empleados añaden tres horas extra pagadas a su turno, de nueve horas, bajo el agobiante y húmedo calor de la zona, a fin de que los vuelos puedan salir. Tras meses advirtiendo de la situación, aquel 20 de agosto (en el que más de 106.000 pasajeros tenía previsto tomar 620 vuelos y justo tras una visita del primer ministro Benjamín Netanyahu y de la ministra de Transportes, Miri Regev) los empleados dijeron basta. Simplemente, se marcharon al terminar su jornada. El resultado: durante dos horas y media nadie cargó maletas, alimentando un cuello de botella. Algunos aviones que volaban hacia Israel dieron media vuelta.

El caos ha vuelto a poner el foco en la disonancia entre la imagen de país occidental (“la vanguardia de la civilización en medio de la barbarie”, como decía el fundador el sionismo, Theodor Herzl) que gusta proyectar Israel y el estado de sus infestadas infraestructuras de transporte clave.

Más aún en los últimos tres años de incendio de Oriente Próximo, en los que la imprevisibilidad se ha vuelto la norma. Los que vivimos aquí hemos normalizado situaciones que afectan mucho a la vida y al bolsillo. Iberia acaba de prorrogar hasta el 30 de septiembre su suspensión de la ruta Madrid-Tel Aviv, con Air Europa yendo y viniendo, según el grado de peligrosidad. Ryanair ha dejado de operar rutas a Israel; e Easyjet, American Airlines o British Airways siguen sin retomarlas, tras cuatro rondas de misiles y drones iraníes contra el país, y uno lanzado en 2025 por los hutíes de Yemen que cayó en el aparcamiento del aeropuerto.

En algunos meses enteros desde 2023, la única forma de entrar o salir de Israel ha sido consiguiendo una plaza cara en una aerolínea nacional (que primaban traer a los israelíes atrapados en el extranjero o que querían volver a alistarse), volar en Business o hacerlo a través de la vecina Jordania, cruzando por tierra.

En el diagnóstico, todos están de acuerdo: al aeropuerto de Ben Gurión le aprietan las costuras. En el tratamiento, ya divergen porque entran en juego las ideologías.

El sindicato, por ejemplo, cifra entre 400 y 500 las contrataciones que necesita y recuerda que 100 de sus operarios están de uniforme militar, sirviendo como reservistas. La Autoridad Aeroportuaria responde que el número de empleados este agosto (con 2,67 millones de pasajeros) es el mismo que el de 2019, el mes récord para la aviación israelí, con 2,8 millones de viajeros, justo antes de la pandemia. El problema reside, según la Autoridad, en que hoy son fijos un 10% más, y cobran mejor, son más reacios a hacer horas extra y presentan mayores índices de absentismo que los temporales. Algunos analistas describen el sindicato, que dirige Pinchas Idan ―miembro del partido de Netanyahu, Likud, hasta que el primer ministro lo expulsó por la huelga— más como un grupo de interés preocupado por proteger sueldos muy por encima de la media del sector (25.000 séquels, 7.230 euros u 8.400 dólares brutos mensuales) que como un sindicato de clase. El Ministerio de Finanzas (que dirige el ultranacionalista Bezalel Smotrich) quiere, de hecho, otorgar la gestión de los terrenos de expansión del aeropuerto a una concesionaria privada.

La situación es insostenible para Israel, un país pequeño, de 10 millones de habitantes y un turismo formado por judíos de otras partes del mundo, peregrinos musulmanes o cristianos y empresarios. Se prevé que Ben Gurión, su único aeropuerto de peso, alcance su tope ya en 2034: 40 millones de viajes al año. Tras una década de debates y planes, el Gobierno ha aprobado construir otros dos internacionales: en el sur (Ziklag, en el desierto del Neguev) y en el norte, Ramat David, pero aún no está claro quién los levantará ni operará.

Mientras, el aeropuerto que más crece, en la ciudad de Haifa, data del protectorado británico de Palestina, antes de la creación de Israel en 1948. Solo vuela a Grecia, Chipre y Bulgaria y acaba de presentar como un éxito sus 250.000 viajeros en lo que va de año. Es el equivalente a los que reciben en España ciudades como Melilla o San Sebastián.

World.title: Dutch schools must make space for languages spoken at home
World.content:
Dutch primary schools are now expected to make room for the languages pupils speak at home, like Turkish, Polish and Arabic. New national curriculum standards will encourage teachers to allow students to use their mother tongue to prepare for class or better understand material if it helps them.

The change comes from updated core objectives (kerndoelen) for the Dutch language, which became law in August and set out what children are meant to learn. Current affairs programme Nieuwsuur reported on the new rules on Friday.

About a quarter of people aged 15 and over mainly speak something other than standard Dutch at home – a dialect, a regional language such as Frisian or Limburgish, or another language such as English, Turkish or Polish, according to the national statistics office CBS.

What the schools actually do with the new standards is largely up to them. Attention to multilingualism and pupils’ linguistic identity is obligatory, but the more concrete idea – letting children talk through difficult material in their home language, or prepare for a lesson in it – is advice rather than a strict requirement.

Not everyone agrees

Language expert Joanneke Prenger, who advises on primary education, said parents should “speak the language you know best” with their children, reversing years of guidance to use Dutch at home. Doing so, she told Nieuwsuur, gives pupils a richer base for learning Dutch and other languages.

Thomas Hendriks, who teaches Dutch in an Amsterdam bridging class for pupils with a language gap, said the steady stream of new advice “comes across as a whim, a trend”, even as more young people leave school unable to read and write properly. In his classroom, he added, letting pupils switch languages also means losing track of what is being said.

The debate comes amid years of concern about basic Dutch skills. The Netherlands was once seen as a strong performer in reading, but scores have fallen sharply, and a national programme worth hundreds of millions of euros has yet to turn things around.

A tougher line elsewhere

The classroom shift runs alongside a harder line on Dutch in other areas. Ministers want to raise the language level required for naturalisation to B1, and are drawing up stricter rules for welfare claimants who do not speak adequate Dutch.

For international families, the change means a child’s English, Turkish or Polish is now something schools are meant to work with rather than discourage. Regional languages count too – Friesland already requires schools to actively teach Frisian.

Schools have until 2031 to fold all the new objectives into their teaching, and for now decide for themselves how to handle home languages.

World.title: The Hague’s historic jenever distillery is fighting for its life
World.content:
The iconic Van Kleef Distillery dates back to 1776. It’s faced countless challenges since then, but the latest round could force it to close or substantially change.

For over two centuries, the Van Kleef Distillery in The Hague has been mixing up unique liqueurs and genever made with time-tested recipes. Vincent van Gogh is one of the customers known to have sampled its spirits.

Despite its rich history and status as the last remaining distillery in the city, owner Fleur Kruyt says Van Kleef is currently facing a series of setbacks that could shut down its long-time location on the Lange Beestenmarkt.

“Right now I have the same colour hair as my grandmother at the age of 96,” she told DutchNews during an interview in the distillery’ tasting room.

Kruyt has spent the past several years trying to come up with solutions to appease her landlord and city officials as she strives to expand Van Kleef’s operations, modernise its museum, and, more than anything else, prevent its doors from closing altogether.

It’s all enough to turn the hair of even the most steadfast and indomitable of small business owners completely white.

But these challenges are only the latest in Van Kleef’s tumultuous history. Over the years, it’s contended with the sudden death of an owner, a crime wave, overzealous safety inspectors, and the Covid pandemic.

The first few centuries

The distillery dates all the way back to the late 18th century. It originally opened in 1776 as Distilleerderij “Anker” before being taken over by the Van Kleef family in 1842.

Kruyt is convinced Van Gogh stopped by at least once. The famous artist may have even been a regular given his proclivities. He lived down the street from 1869 to 1873 and spent those years working at Goupil & Cie, an art business in The Hague owned by his uncle.

Along with the rest of the Netherlands, the distillery managed to endure the impacts of the Spanish flu pandemic and two World Wars, but it was a safety inspection in 1986 that came much closer to shutting it down.

Explosive concerns

The officials declared the 40,000 litres of alcohol sitting in the distillery’s vats were a huge safety risk that made it an almost literal ticking time bomb. They decided it was no longer safe to distill alcohol on the property.

At the time, Van Kleef was teetering on the edge of bankruptcy. The surrounding neighbourhood was considered a “no-go zone” for many of the city’s residents and the distillery wasn’t getting much foot traffic.

“If you walked these streets as a woman at night back then, you were either a prostitute or tired of your life,” Kruyt said. “There was lots of criminality. No one came here anymore.”

After much discussion and planning, production was moved off site. The building itself was purchased by a local development company called Stadsherstel Den Haag and Van Kleef officially became a tenant in its long-time home.

The books were eventually balanced after it attained historical status and Van Kleef finally reopened as a multipurpose operation in 1995. Along with the museum and a tasting room, Van Kleef’s liqueurs are bottled and labelled there to this day.

Even more setbacks

The construction of a tram tunnel and the redesign of the street out front dragged on for over a decade and further drove customers away.

The distillery’s revenue dropped by 80% when the city began installing barriers around the neighbourhood to discourage auto traffic in 2009. Its suppliers and customers had to navigate a maze every time they tried to go there.

Kruyt, who was operating Van Kleef with her husband Louis Centazzo at the time, was forced to use their house as collateral on a loan to keep it open. Then he suddenly died in 2015, leaving her to manage the distillery on her own.

Foreclosure followed and Kruyt moved into an apartment on the property. The hits kept coming as gentrification quickly transformed the neighbourhood and raised the distillery’s monthly rent along with it.

Then the Covid crisis began, which forced Van Kleef to shut down its tasting room. Undaunted, Kruyt and her crew came up with clever ways to ensure revenue would keep coming in.

She joked that “booze was declared a necessity” during the pandemic. Kruyt developed a “vaccine” after inspiration struck while she was giving her dog injections for arthritis. “The Van Kleef Vaccine” is a mix of Limoncello, Vitamin C, and ginger-infused liqueur.

At first, Kruyt fretted that it wouldn’t go over well with customers who had spent weeks social distancing and worrying they’d be the next ones to catch Covid. Those fears proved unfounded.

“And the first people who bought it? Doctors and pharmacists,” she recalled. “They found it really cool. I thought, ‘If these people find it funny, I don’t care about the rest!’”

A “ginitiser” sold in spray bottles soon followed. It, too, was a hit.

The current dilemmas

“We’ve always managed and, whenever I feel bad, I turn on the television and see how it could be a lot worse,” Kruyt said before discussing the latest round of threats to the distillery.

The city’s decision to impose a flat €50-a-day parking fee has taken another bite out of Van Kleef’s revenue. The policy was so controversial it was even covered by The Guardian in 2023. If all this wasn’t enough, Kruyt broke her ankle while on a summer holiday and the recovery process required several surgeries.

Determined to keep the distillery where it’s been for over 200 years, Kruyt has been combating another wave of financial woes coupled with bureaucratic headaches, soaring energy bills, and other increased costs. Even the price of the glass that goes into Van Kleef’s bottles has gone up recently.

A crowdfunding campaign has been underway since 2025. Plans were also made to expand operations to attract more visitors, but negotiations with Stadsherstel Den Haag have proven challenging.

After over two years of discussions about everything from the future of the museum to renovations for the apartments on the property, Kruyt said the situation has been handed over to a new director named Jan-Willem de Bruijn.

“Stadsherstel Den Haag is currently taking a comprehensive look at the complex,” De Bruijn told DutchNews. “This means that, in addition to the shop and the tasting room, we are also focusing on the redevelopment of the museum and garden as well as upgrades in the apartments. In doing so, we aim to invest sustainably in the preservation of this unique and characteristic part of The Hague.”

Delays with permitting haven’t helped. DutchNews contacted the office of Alderwoman Saskia Bruines for comment about this and other matters concerning the distillery, but had not received a response as of press time.

Fighting onward

Regardless of what happens next, Kruyt says Van Kleef will continue in one form or another, even if that means turning it into a distillery-and-wholesaler-only operation at a facility closed to the public and likely located on the outskirts of The Hague.

“But all of this history would go away,” she said as she gestured towards the centuries-old equipment in Van Kleef’s museum.

Takeaway liqueurs and tastings have covered the costs of maintaining the distillery’s historical inventory, but the current circumstances have made that impossible to continue. As Kruyt faces another round of discussions with Stadsherstel Den Haag, she’s determined to stay optimistic.

“We met with Jan-Willem a few weeks ago,” she said. “We’re really happy that he is taking everything seriously and trying to preserve the heritage that we have here.”

Still open for business

Visitors to Van Kleef can currently visit the small museum, enjoy drinks and snacks in its tasting room, host gatherings in a former storage cellar turned conference room, and purchase bottles of liqueurs made with recipes that date back to the 17th century.

Among them is Bridal Tears, which contains flakes of 24-carat gold. It was once a popular wedding gift. The bawdy tales and traditions surrounding it and two accompanying liqueurs could fill an entire book.

In an age of alcoholic beverages with preservatives and other ingredients that are difficult to describe, let alone pronounce the names of, Van Kleef is still doing things the old-fashioned way.

“All of our recipes have been preserved,” Kruyt said. “We have an archive full of them that began in the 1840s. Everything you’re tasting is real in the sense that there’s no artificial flavouring or colourings.”

The distillery continues to attract international visitors and aficionados of liqueurs. Kruyt said a few of them are household names, but she demurred when asked for the details.

“What happens at Van Kleef, stays at Van Kleef,” she said. “So any celebrities out there, you can come here and we won’t talk about you.”

World.title: The Many Lives of Anne Frank: a fascinating work
World.content:
The Many Lives of Anne Frank is a biography, of the German Jewish teenager herself, of her famous diary and, also, of her legacy. Ruth Franklin’s innovative approach to the most famous work of the Holocaust is fascinating, thought-provoking and well worth the read.

The Diary of Anne Frank has been assigned to thousands of students and has sold millions of copies. The annex where the teenager hid with her family during the Second World War is visited by a million tourists a year, whose queue snakes along the canal in Amsterdam for blocks.

Published in 2025, the first half of the book is a classic biography. We follow the Frank family from Germany to exile in the Netherlands and then to further banishment above a warehouse on the Prinsengracht. Franklin brings the story to life, with minute details (it was raining on the evening the Franks walked across the Dutch capital to their hiding place) and wider context (the ongoing round-up of Jews by the occupying Nazis.)

The biography does not end, as most biographies do, with the subject’s death. The young girl died somewhere in March or April of 1945 at Bergen-Belsen concentration camp, possibly just weeks before it was liberated by the British army.

Her legacy lives on, in her diary published, following edits from her father, shortly after the war. Anne herself also edited the work, inspired by a 1944 appeal from the Dutch minister for education diaries and letters documenting the German occupation. The teen aspired to get her thoughts and feelings into print.

The second half of the book follows the legacy of the diary, how it came into being and how it became a phenomenon, vaulting Anne Frank to an epic level of fame.

Franklin delves into the details of the book’s publication journey, raising questions about what it means for something to be “authentic.”

Anne’s father Otto sends a translated (and edited) version to relatives in Switzerland, who encourage him to publish the work. A composite of Anne’s two versions, plus her father’s edits is submitted to a publisher, who suggests certain cuts as to not offend more conservative readers. A longer, critical edition was published in 1986 and, based on that, the English-language version was published in 1989.

The first German-language version edits a passage Anne wrote taking a dig at the country. She writes “Only civilized languages are permitted [in the Annex], therefore no German,” which is changed to “all civilised languages may be spoken.” The occupants made an effort to speak to one another in Dutch, rather than in their native German, as a form of resistance.

The chapters are all titled with descriptors of the various versions of Anne. The final one is called “Pawn” and addresses her legacy. Otto intended for the diary to “promote peace and tolerance,” Franklin writes, but he couldn’t control his daughter’s celebrity.

The adaptation of the diary in a play in the United States is complicated by differing artistic versions of the work, the iconic image of Anne is used by those protesting South African apartheid and later, Israel’s war on Gaza. Franklin’s chronicle leaves the reader with many questions about how to contextualise the diary of a teenage girl.

A prize-winning literary critic, Franklin is a former editor at The New Republic. Her first biography, Shirley Jackson: A Rather Haunted Life, won multiple awards. The Many Lives of Anne Frank was a finalist for the 2025 Los Angeles Times Book Prizes.

The Many Lives of Anne Frank is deeply researched, well-written and stimulating.

You can get your copy at the American Book Center.

World.title: Amsterdam travel app leaked users’ personal data for months
World.content:
Polarsteps, an Amsterdam-founded travel app used by more than 23 million people, left users’ photos, locations and home addresses reachable by anyone through an unsecured data feed – including trips put on private mode – and had known about the flaw for months, an investigation by Follow the Money (FTM) has found.

The investigation found that anyone could connect to the free app’s data feed and pull users’ names, 230 million photos and videos, and 1 billion GPS locations from nearly 2 million trips – enough to plot journeys on a map and follow many of them close to real time.

More than a million of those trips had been shared only with followers. Even accounts set fully to private gave away who a user followed, who followed them and which device they logged in from. And once FTM held the link to someone’s trip, removing it as a follower changed nothing.

Home addresses were among the most sensitive details exposed. FTM pinned down dozens from the exact location saved inside users’ photos – a shot of packed suitcases taken at home, for example, and worked out many more from the spots people returned to each night.

That photo-location data appeared nowhere in Polarsteps’ privacy policy, and was missing from the file the company released when FTM asked to see its own records.

A year’s warning

The problem was first flagged last year by a French cybersecurity researcher who said Polarsteps told him it already knew what was happening. He took his findings to FTM, which said the data stayed exposed for at least six months.

Marc Schuilenburg, a professor of digital surveillance at Erasmus University, called the company negligent, and warned that leaked location data can be used to stalk, harass or threaten people.

The leak was not from a hack – no passwords were taken and no accounts entered. Anyone with basic technical skill could connect to Polarsteps’ servers and scrape the data, with none of the request limits, CAPTCHAs or login walls.

Company response

Polarsteps, which has grown from 1 million users in 2019, said no passwords or accounts were compromised and that it is in contact with the AP.

Chief executive Clare Jones, appointed in 2024, said the company should have caught the problem itself and was working out what went wrong. It has since tightened its systems, and noted that much of the exposed data had been made public by users’ own choice.

The company’s own website warns travellers that sharing location details in real time “can make you a target.” FTM said a second part of its investigation, on dozens of military personnel it tracked to bases and missions at home and abroad, would follow on Saturday.

World.title: Prosecutors hold 32 over Overasselt attack, including two minors
World.content:
Public prosecutors are detaining 32 people on suspicion of murder or manslaughter in connection with the killing of a security guard in Overasselt on Tuesday.

Thirty-four people were initially arrested in the area surrounding the Gelderland village but two were released as there was insufficient evidence to hold them. CCTV footage shows dozens of masked men getting out of a truck outside the property, some heavily armed, before one shoots a man sitting in a car.

They also opened fire on police shortly afterwards, injuring two. Of those arrested, two are minors aged 16 and 17, the rest are men from France, Netherlands, Algeria, Libya, Belgium and Ukraine – all aged between 18 and 32.

Footage emerged online after the attack purportedly by a drugs gang, threatening the resident of the property that was attacked and saying that he had stolen a large quantity of goods from them.

That man, known as Jan G. Jr, has been barred from entering the council around Overasselt for at least two weeks and will not be allowed back to live in the property for at least a year.

He has been linked to the drugs trade before and the house was shot at last year with an AK-47 by a young man from Amsterdam, said to be a drug addict who was paid to carry out the attack. He never named who paid him.

World.title: Public officials among those abusing Jetten online, AD finds
World.content:
A council official, a police employee and a member of the Dutch air force are among thousands of people posting homophobic abuse under prime minister Rob Jetten’s social media messages on X, an investigation by the Algemeen Dagblad (AD) has found.

The paper analysed 45,860 replies to 323 posts sent from the prime minister’s official account during his first six months in office. One in 20 – 2,293 replies – was homophobic, it said.

The abuse appeared under routine posts, from a congratulatory message for Queen Máxima to a post about Amsterdam Pride, and did not depend on the topics Jetten was writing about.

AD identified two recurring forms of abuse. The first was crude slurs and the second, far more common, was a single insinuating question posted in Dutch hundreds of times: “Did you tell them you’re gay?”

Hard to prosecute

Most of the accounts did not belong to anonymous trolls, AD said. The large majority left a single homophobic reply and never returned, and the 10 most persistent accounts together produced less than 6% of the total.

Only a handful of repeat posters could be traced, among them the council, police and air force employees. Marloes van Noorloos, a professor of criminal law at Leiden University, told the paper that the insinuating questions were hard to prosecute as hate speech or criminal insult, because it depends largely on wording and context.

Civil servants, she said, could face disciplinary action under the rules governing public employees.

Jetten’s response

Jetten is the Netherlands’ first openly gay prime minister, and has said he files a police report every week over the abuse he receives about his sexuality. At the WorldPride conference last month he said big social media companies were “barely moderating content for hate speech”.

X’s own rules prohibit attacking users over their sexual orientation, but the company has taken little action, according to AD.

Dutch acceptance of homosexuality has stalled after years of progress. Jetten has said the Netherlands needs to get back on track and return to the top 10 countries for LGBTQI+ rights, from where it fell to number 13 after 2018.

World.title: Farmers face livestock cuts as nitrogen plan falls short
World.content:
Dutch farmers are still facing a compulsory cut in the number of animals they can keep as livestock, after the government’s environmental assessment agency found the cabinet’s nitrogen plan would fall just short of its own 2035 target.

The agency, PBL, assessed the €20 billion nitrogen plan at the cabinet’s request and called it an important step that could bring the farming emissions target within reach.

But it found the measures worked out so far leave a gap, and that an across-the-board cut of 5% to 10% in farmers’ livestock rights, the permits that cap how many animals a farm may hold, is still needed.

The coalition has always said that a blanket cut is a last resort, to be used only if the targets are missed in 2035. Agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen called it an “emergency brake” on Friday and “a no-go for the cabinet.”

Farmers must reduce ammonia emissions by 42% to 46% by 2035, against 2019 levels, under the package agreed in June. PBL expects the herd to shrink further regardless as farms adapt to those rules, with some businesses forced to close.

The agency was more positive about the plan’s benefits for the environment, but warned the nitrogen problem will not just disappear. On more than half the area of the most sensitive protected sites, deposition is still expected to breach the critical threshold in 2035.

Nature groups called the plans the minimum needed to start repairing decades of damage. The farmers’ party BBB and the farm lobby LTO said the extra cut was unacceptable, though LTO is staying at the table to negotiate the rest of the package.

World.title: Poland’s oldest operating electric train, 63-year-old “Granny”, returns to the tracks after a refurb
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Poland’s oldest operational multiple-unit electric train, a 63-year-old vehicle nicknamed Babcia (meaning “Granny”), is returning to service after refurbishment. The train, whose official name is EN57-038, rolled off the production lines on 9 May 1963 at a factory in the city of Wrocław belonging to Pafawag, a state locomotive manufacturer. For decades, it served in the southern Małopolska province, transporting passengers in cities including Kraków, Tarnów, Nowy Sącz and Sucha Beskidzka. In 2003, it was transferred to Masovia, the province around Poland’s capital, Warsaw, where it has operated ever since. “Masovian Railways continually invests in modern rolling stock, making our fleet among the most modern in Poland,” said Czesław Sulima, the operations director for the regional rail operator. “However, we fully understand the importance of tradition and sentiment.” “Babcia has become a permanent fixture in Polish railway history,” he added. “We are delighted that after a major overhaul, this unique vehicle will once again serve passengers and delight lovers of old-time travel, combining history with modernity.” Babcia has previously undergone periodic modernisation and maintenance, most recently in 2022, when she regained her original yellow and blue livery associated with the historic Pafawag factory. The latest work included upgrades to the train’s monitoring system and toilet, which now operates in “closed circulation” (a polite way of saying that waste is no longer dropped directly onto the track). State rail operator PKP has for years been promising to phase out the few remaining old “open” toilets. Now that Babcia has been refurbished, she will return to service early on Saturday morning, running a 10 km route on weekends between the town of Tłuszcz and village of Mostówka, just northeast of Warsaw. Babcia is one of the EN57 class of electric multiple unit trains produced by Pafawag between 1961 and 1993. A total of 1,429 were manufactured, with many still in use – though none as old as EN57-038. The history of the Wrocław factory itself dates back to the 1830s (when the city was part of Germany and called Breslau), making it one of the oldest manufacturers of rolling stock in Europe. After World War Two, when Wrocław became part of Poland following border changes, the factory came under the ownership of the new communist state. In the 1990s, after the fall of communism, it was privatised, being acquired in 1997 by German company ADtranz, which was in 2001 itself taken over by Canada’s Bombardier Transportation, which was then acquired in 2021 by France’s Alstom. Train travel has been booming in Poland in recent years. In the first half of 2026, a record 44.7 million passengers travelled with PKP Intercity, the main long-distance operator, more than 10% up on the previous year’s record and some 45% higher than three years earlier. While the country is seeking to expand its high-speed rail network and increase train speeds up to 320 km/h (199mph), there has also been a growing interest in older trains. That prompted PKP to launch a special “unhurried” service earlier this year, allowing passengers to travel along scenic routes in restored 1980s trains. World.title: Poland to begin using sewage water to cool power plants
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland will begin using reclaimed sewage water to cool power plants from the start of next year. The measures are intended to reduce the use of fresh water and make the power system more resilient to increasingly frequent droughts. The change comes after some of Poland’s power plants were partially shut down this summer amid a series of heatwaves and lack of rain that led to record-low water levels in many rivers. 💧⚡ Otwieramy sektor energetyczny na wodę odzyskaną. Od 1 stycznia 2027 r. polskie elektrownie i elektrociepłownie będą mogły wykorzystywać wodę odzyskaną ze ścieków komunalnych w systemach chłodzenia. Nowe rozwiązania przedstawiliśmy dziś wspólnie z ministrem energii… pic.twitter.com/qRDOgjcDwb — Dariusz Klimczak (@DariuszKlimczak) September 3, 2026 “This may seem to many like a minor change, but it is of fundamental importance for many power-generating units in Poland,” said energy minister Miłosz Motyka. “Thanks to this, we will be even more resilient and even better prepared for crises of all kinds.” The legislation was first proposed by a group of MPs from The Left (Lewica) and the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), two members of the current ruling coalition, in May, and was then approved by parliament in July. Last week, President Karol Nawrocki signed it into law. The law, which will come into force at the start of 2027, introduces a definition of water recovered from municipal sewage, which, in turn, will allow its use in the cooling circuits of power stations and combined heat and power plants. Power stations require large amounts of water to help cool and condense steam, which drives the turbines, back into liquid form so that it can be reheated into steam once more. Orlen Termika, a subsidiary of state energy giant Orlen, has announced that it plans to invest more than 1 billion zloty (€230 million) over the next four years to maximise the benefits of the change by connecting sewage treatment plants with three of its power and heat plants around Warsaw. According to Andrzej Gajewski, the CEO of Orlen Termika, one of the plants, Żeran, will be able to save up to 80% of previous water use. Another, Siekierki, will save up to 20%. The company also plans to install heat pumps to extract heat from sewage, which can then be used to help supply heat to residents of Warsaw before the water is then used to cool down the plants. Sewage is relatively warm, typically between 10°C and 20°C, making it a good source of recoverable heat. “From the point of view of security of supply for Warsaw’s residents and from the point of view of efficiency – that is, the price of heating – this is the best and most advantageous solution,” emphasised Gajewski. Poland’s power grid operator has, for the second time in three days and third time this summer, invoked emergency measures to ensure supply amid a heatwave. Before this summer, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced https://t.co/fIDR4SimgG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 6, 2026 Poland has experienced increasingly hot temperatures in recent years. This summer, the country broke its all-time record, as temperatures reached more than 40°C. That, along with low amounts of rainfall, has seen rivers reach record lows. As a result, Poland’s power grid operator has this summer been forced three times to invoke emergency measures to ensure supply. Previously, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced. Last month, state power supplier Enea announced that it had reduced operations at two of its coal-fired plants due to the low level of water in the Vistula. Around 1.1 gigawatts (GW) of capacity, just over 1% of Poland’s total, was taken offline. World.title: Prime minister’s “right-hand man” elected as Polish constitutional court judge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has succeeded in having Maciej Berek, whom he recently described as his “right-hand man”, elected by parliament as a Constitutional Tribunal (TK) judge, staving off a rebellion from some members of his own coalition. Critics argued that the nomination violated the government’s pledge to “depoliticise” the TK, including by banning recently active politicians from sitting on it. Berek served as a government minister from 2023, when Tusk came to power, until last month, when he stepped down in order to run for the TK. However, it is far from clear what will happen next. Opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has this year refused to swear in four TK judges chosen by parliament, and he has made clear that he also opposes Berek’s candidacy. ✅Sejm dokonał wyboru Macieja Berka na stanowisko sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. pic.twitter.com/ek0ak9C33v — Sejm RP🇵🇱 (@KancelariaSejmu) September 4, 2026 In mid-August, Berek announced that he was leaving the government, where he had served as minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy. Shortly afterwards, Tusk confirmed that Berek would be nominated to fill an upcoming vacancy on the TK. The prime minister argued that, during his time in government, Berek had undertaken a technocratic role that was “apolitical and nonpartisan”. He said that Berek’s extensive experience in constitutional law and the legislative process made him an ideal candidate. However, some MPs from Tusk’s junior coalition partners publicly opposed the nomination. They noted that the government’s parliamentary majority had, in 2024, approved a law banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. The law never went into force as it was effectively blocked by a combination of then-President Andrzej Duda and the TK itself, which were both aligned with the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party from 2015 to 2023 and now the largest opposition group. Polish NGOs have urged Tusk's "right-hand man" to withdraw his Constitutional Tribunal candidacy, warning his political ties could undermine efforts to restore the court’s independence. The nomination has also exposed tensions within the ruling coalitionhttps://t.co/jQn0MyuS7G — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 21, 2026 Ahead of today’s vote in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, it remained unclear if Berek’s candidacy would be approved. In the end, he obtained the necessary majority, receiving the support of 226 MPs among the 437 who voted in the 460-seat chamber. Within the ruling coalition, only four MPs voted against Berek’s candidacy, including one from Tusk’s own centrist Civic Coalition (KO), Klaudia Jachira. Another opponent was Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is the leader of The Left (Lewica), one of Tusk’s junior coalition partners, and the speaker of the Sejm. Eleven MPs from the ruling coalition did not take part in the vote. The entire right-wing and far-right opposition voted against Berek’s candidacy. Berek is now meant to join the TK after the next vacancy on its 15-person bench opens up on 18 September, when the nine-year term of an existing judge, Justyn Piskorski, ends. However, under Polish law, a new TK judge must first swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki has used this requirement to refuse to swear in four of the judges chosen by the ruling majority in the Sejm this year. He has, however, sworn in three others. Nawrocki argued that there were legal doubts over the appointment of the quartet whose oaths he refused to receive. However, the government says that the president does not have the right to assess their candidacies and that the swearing-in is merely a formality. The crisis around Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has deepened further after the tribunal ruled that the president is not obliged to swear in new TK judges appointed by parliament. President Nawrocki last month refused to swear in four new judges https://t.co/ycnweW9pSR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 13, 2026 The four judges instead organised their own swearing-in ceremony in the Sejm before a notary, after which they forwarded their oaths to the president and attempted to take their seats on the TK. However, the tribunal’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, refused to allow them to serve, citing their failure to swear an oath before the president. Święczkowski previously served as a deputy justice minister in the former PiS government and is still seen as loyal to the party. In May, the European Court of Human Rights issued an interim order requiring that the four judges be allowed to take up their positions. However, Święczkowski has ignored it, arguing that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 It appears likely that Nawrocki will refuse to swear in Berek. “I think the last thing the TK needs is another politician, especially a politician who is a close collaborator of Prime Minister Donald Tusk,” said Nawrocki on Thursday. On Friday morning, ahead of the Sejm vote, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, addressed the chamber to outline the president’s opposition to Berek’s candidacy. He said that, as well as Berek’s political association with the government, there are doubts over whether he even meets the formal requirements to sit on the tribunal, in particular the need to have practised the law for at least 10 years. Berek says he does meet that requirement. Adding to the confusion is the fact that Tusk’s government does not regard the current TK as legitimate because of the presence of judges, including Piskorski, who were unlawfully appointed when PiS and Duda were in office. It ignores all TK rulings. Tusk has emphasised that one of the reasons he wants to appoint Berek to the TK is to help “fix” the tribunal. Berek’s nomination means that there are now eight TK judges chosen by the ruling coalition, giving them a majority on the court. However, with Nawrocki and Święczkowski refusing to accept four of them, and likely to reject Berek too, some kind of drastic action would be required to allow them to begin to serve. The proportion of Poles who negatively assess the justice system has increased under the current government, despite its promises to restore the rule of law. When deciding which businesses to invite on the trip, the presidential chancellery says it would seek “well-established companies with the potential to grow in the US market and seeking new partners and opportunities for collaboration” Those selected will be invited to travel on the presidential flight from Warsaw to New York and back, and will also receive local transportation. In recent years, a growing number of Polish companies have expanded abroad, helped by the country’s strong economic growth over the past three decades. Poland has summoned Russia’s ambassador in response to recent hostile actions against Germany. “[We] expressed our strong condemnation of state terrorism perpetrated by Russia – because what is a problem for one ally is a problem for the entire alliance,” said Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. “Putin’s Russia remains one of the most serious security threats – not just for Europe, but for the entire world order,” he added. “Its goal is to permanently destroy the European security architecture.” 💬 Nie ma zgody na podpalenia, ataki na kolej, morderstwa i inne prowokacje. Polska też wezwała ambasadora Rosji po to, aby wyrazić nasze stanowcze potępienie dla terroryzmu państwowego autorstwa Federacji Rosyjskiej. | wicepremier, minister spraw zagranicznych @sikorskiradek… pic.twitter.com/LChAjwsX8H — Ministerstwo Spraw Zagranicznych RP 🇵🇱 (@MSZ_RP) September 3, 2026 On Tuesday, the German government announced that it held Russia responsible for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport last month. In response, it ordered the closure of Russia’s consulate in Bonn and a Russian cultural centre in Berlin. This week also saw attempts to sabotage Germany’s electricity network in two locations. While they are still being investigated, on Wednesday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggested that they may also be part of “Russia’s escalatory actions throughout the region”. On Thursday, the spokesman for Poland’s foreign ministry, Maciej Wewiór, confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that Russia’s ambassador to Warsaw, Georgy Mikhno, had been summoned to the ministry. Wewiór said that Poland wanted to convey “our firm opposition to the escalation of Russia’s aggressive actions” as well as to show solidarity with Germany. A number of other European leaders have also this week expressed solidarity with Germany, including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. Poland has itself been a major target for Russia. Earlier this year, a report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland was the “primary focus” of Russian sabotage. It has also suffered cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns, and “weaponised migration” on its eastern border. In response, Poland has successively closed down all of Russia’s consulates in the country, with Moscow responding by doing the same with Polish consulates operating on its territory. This week, after a fire broke out at a drone factory in Poland, Tusk said that there is “no doubt” it was caused deliberately and suggested it was also likely carried out on behalf of Russia. World.title: Poland moves to allow local communities to ban short-term rentals
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals – the type of privately owned accommodation offered through services such as Airbnb and Booking.com. Such services have boomed in Poland in recent years, like in other parts of the world. But that has prompted a backlash from many communities, which argue that short-term rentals can cause disruption, reduce the availability of housing, and drive up prices. However, the proposed measures have already caused divisions within the ruling coalition and must still be approved by parliament, where the government has a majority, and by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of bills. ❗ Rada Ministrów przyjęła autopoprawkę do projektu ustawy dotyczącego najmu krótkoterminowego. Nowe rozwiązania dadzą mieszkańcom i samorządom konkretne narzędzia do reagowania tam, gdzie najem krótkoterminowy powoduje problemy z bezpieczeństwem i porządkiem publicznym. ➡️… pic.twitter.com/7KvW2O4AKW — Ministerstwo Sportu i Turystyki (@SPORT_GOV_PL) September 2, 2026 Speaking ahead of a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk confirmed that, following a “difficult process” of discussion, his coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, had agreed on the measures. They would grant “greater rights for residents, communities, housing cooperatives and local authorities regarding the situation in the short-term rental market”, said Tusk. “Wherever order, safety and basic comfort of life are threatened, decisions can be made to exclude these types of businesses.” The new rules would allow homeowner associations (wspólnoty mieszkaniowe) and housing cooperatives (spółdzielnie mieszkaniowe) to prohibit short-term rentals. If a majority of members voted to adopt such a ban, operators of short-term rental properties would have six months to end operations. Municipal councils (rady gmin), at the request of the mayor, would also be given the power to designate specific areas within their territory in which short-term rentals would be banned or restricted (for example, to a certain number of days a year). There would also be greater powers for residents and housing groups to initiate official inspections of properties if they believe there are violations of public safety and order rules. If a property violated such regulations three times within six months, it would be banned from operating for a year. Tusk noted that, if the bill becomes law, it would not fully go into force until 2028, in order to give enough time for businesses and communities to adapt to the new rules. If Poland does introduce the new measures, its cities could follow the example of many of their European counterparts, such as Barcelona, Paris and London, which have introduced various restrictions on short-term rentals. The European Union has also moved to more tightly regulate the sector. EU to help tourism hotspots crack down on Airbnb-style holiday rentals https://t.co/0Y5nzfZZYF — Financial Times (@FT) August 30, 2026 The measures have been subject to intense debate within the ruling coalition. When the legislation was first submitted to parliament in July, some parts that had previously been included, such as provisions allowing municipalities to ban short-term rentals in certain areas, were removed. That prompted a backlash from two junior coalition partners in particular, The Left (Lewica) and the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), prompting further discussions over the summer, resulting in the bill now being toughened again. The Left celebrated the government’s decision to restore tougher elements of the bill, saying it would help avoid “situations where short-term rentals turn into a nightmare, stripping residents of their peace”. The leader of Poland 2050, Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, declared that they had “scored another goal against the lobbyists” by toughening the legislation. Previously, her party had accused the government of watering down the original bill due to industry lobbying. Znowu wbiliśmy lobbystom gola. Właśnie spłynęła nowa wersja rządowej ustawy o Airbnb. Jest decyzyjność wspólnot, spółdzielni i samorządów. Patohotele strzeżcie się – idziemy po was. Czasem warto być „kłótnicą” rządu 😉@PL_2050 — Katarzyna Pełczyńska (@Kpelczynska) August 31, 2026 It also appears that the bill could obtain support from the opposition. In July, after the government initially removed parts of the legislation, the largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), called for them to be restored, saying that power should be put in the hands of local communities. If the bill is approved by parliament, it also requires the signature of Nawrocki, who was elected last year with the support of PiS, before becoming law. He has vetoed a record number of government bills, but has signed an even larger number. It remains unclear what his position on short-term rentals is. ‼️ To mieszkańcy najlepiej wiedzą, co służy ich wspólnocie. Dlatego wspólnota powinna mieć prawo powiedzieć NIE, jeśli chodzi o najem krótkoterminowy. 👉 Udostępnij! pic.twitter.com/dWURZ9awAY — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) July 27, 2026 Poland has seen a boom in tourism in recent years. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-largest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation. Its increase of 7% was behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta (9.9%). However, the growth in tourism has also prompted tensions. In 2024, Kraków, which is Poland’s second-largest city and its main tourist destination, appointed a new “night mayor”, who is responsible for reconciling the needs of the city’s residents, business owners and tourists. Previously, in 2020, the city formed a partnership with Airbnb to promote responsible and sustainable tourism. The following year, it launched a “tourist patrol scheme” to inform visitors of the “rules and norms they should follow”. In 2024, Kraków also appealed to the government to allow it to introduce a new tax on tourists. It warned that “overtourism has led to tensions and social discontent in many places in Europe…because residents increasingly feel like tourists in their own city”. World.title: NfP podcast: How small towns became a testing ground for Poland’s far right
World.content: In our new podcast, Notes from Poland’s editor-in-chief Daniel Tilles speaks with deputy editor-in-chief Alicja Ptak about her research into how four contentious issues – migration, women’s rights, Jewish heritage and LGBT+ rights – have played out in 19 smaller towns and cities in Poland. They discuss how national far-right talking points are being imported into smaller towns, how these issues are covered and contested at the local level, and what this all means ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections. Speaking ahead of a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Tusk noted that there had been “some very disturbing incidents and events in Poland and Germany over the past few [days]”. “This is a continuation of Russia’s escalatory actions throughout the region,” he continued. “Unfortunately, these are not the first cases and, even worse, they certainly won’t be the last.” 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Najbliższe tygodnie i miesiące będą krytyczne nie tylko jeśli chodzi o zdarzenia na froncie i w ogóle całą wojnę rosyjsko-ukraińską, ale te tygodnie i miesiące będą także bardzo dużym wyzwaniem dla wszystkich państw w tej części Europy, ze względu na… pic.twitter.com/ZcjVMjhWc0 — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 2, 2026 On Sunday, a fire broke out at a production facility in the Polish city of Lublin belonging to JFG Composites, a company that produces components for the aerospace industry, including for military helicopters. It supplies the armed forces of Ukraine and Poland, among others. By Monday afternoon, Polish prosecutors and the security services had confirmed that they were investigating the Skarżysko-Kamienna fire as a potential “crime of a terrorist nature” carried out with the involvement of “foreign intelligence”. On Tuesday, improvised explosive devices were found at one electricity substation in Germany near the border with Poland while another substation in the west of the country was attacked.
