World.title: Martin Romualdez charged with plunder
World.content:
FORMER SPEAKER. Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez tenders his resignation as speaker during the plenary session of the House of Representatives on September 17, 2025.

(2nd UPDATE) The President's cousin and former House speaker is tagged as the 'central figure' in the alleged scheme involving 'diversion of public funds meant for flood control projects'

MANILA, Philippines – The Office the Ombudsman filed a plunder case against former House speaker Martin Romualdez over the flood control scam.

The Ombudsman charged Romualdez before the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan on Monday, September 7, making the former speaker one of the highest officials to be charged over the multi-billion flood control anomaly.

According to the Ombudsman, Romualdez, the cousin of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., is the “central figure” in the alleged scheme involving “diversion of public funds meant for flood control projects.”

The plunder case also includes former Ako Bicol representative Zaldy Co and private individuals Joselyn Serenio and Felicito Guevarra.

Earlier, the investigative body said the allegedly anomalous projects supposedly reached P56 billion.

The Leyte lawmaker denied masterminding the alleged kickback scheme, claiming that the national budget process is done not by the House speaker alone but by the entire House, the Senate, and the executive branch.

The Ombudsman filing was the latest blow against the once powerful speaker.

A source told Rappler that the money laundering allegation – which is originally part of the Romualdez complaints – was returned to the fact-finding phase. This means the Ombudsman investigators are seeking additional evidence and may include additional respondents in the complaint if ever.

“Investigators found more personalities should have been further investigated and then included in the charge,” said the source.

A source said the plunder case “absorbed” the bribery complaints. Bribery is a predicate crime of plunder.

To put this into perspective, Senator Jinggoy Estrada was acquitted of plunder in connection with the pork barrel scam in 2024, but the court convicted him of three counts of bribery. Although the prosecution failed to establish plunder, it was able to prove that bribery existed. However, the bribery conviction was later reversed as well.

In April, the Court of Appeals ordered the freezing of assets linked to him after finding probable cause to believe they were connected to alleged plunder, graft, and direct and indirect bribery. He has also been placed under a preliminary hold departure order that month.

Romualdez asked the anti-graft court to lift his travel ban, but the Sandiganbayan denied the request.

The US government has also canceled Romualdez’s diplomatic and tourist/business visas.

As of April 22, Romualdez has already been barred from leaving the Philippines – the Sandiganbayan granted the Ombudsman’s precautionary hold departure order request against Marcos’ cousin.

A Rappler investigation revealed there were multimillion-peso properties linked to Romualdez, including a P445-million mansion in Sotogrande, Spain. Another investigation also recently showed that the former speaker has ties to Tropics Hotel and to the Tacloban Golf and Country Club.

The Ombudsman’s latest ammunition against Romualdez is former public works secretary Manuel Bonoan, whom it sought to be a state witness.



It believes that Bonoan’s testimony can pin Romualdez and shed light on how lawmakers allegedly inserted allocations in the national budget through the Department of Public Works and Highways.



“We are requesting the Ombudsman to inform us if there is any allegation from Secretary Bonoan against former Speaker Romualdez and to give us ample time to comment on it,” Romualdez lawyer Ade Fajardo said.

“There is also the report that the Ombudsman has 28 new witnesses. We would like to know if there is any statement from them against our client, and we would like as well to have the opportunity to respond,” he added.

The case was raffled to the Sandiganbayan’s 3rd Division shortly after 1:30 pm on Friday. The same division handles the cases of Senator Rodante Marcoleta and former senator Bong Revilla.

In July, the division granted Revilla’s request for bail in a split decision. The division chairperson, Associate Justice Karl Miranda, dissented, but he was outvoted by Associate Justices Ronald Moreno and Fritz Bryn Anthony delos Santos. – Rappler.com

World.title: Big fuel price hike set for September 8 after last week’s rollback
World.content:
NOT AVAILABLE. Signs are posted on fuel dispensers at a gas station in Quezon City due fuel shortages, on March 26, 2026.

Despite last week’s price cuts, diesel and gasoline are again under pressure from Middle East tensions, tight fuel supply and a weaker peso

MANILA, Philippines – Fuel prices are set to rise again starting Tuesday, September 8, undoing last week’s rollback as global and regional fuel markets remain under pressure.

In a press conference on Monday, September 7, the Department of Energy announced the following fuel price adjustments for the week of September 8 to 14:

Gasoline – increase of P4.69 per liter

Diesel – increase of P5.18 per liter

Kerosene – increase of P5.58 per liter

The adjustments will take effect on Tuesday, September 8.

Photo from Department of Energy

Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said that the fuel price hike comes “following renewed tensions, affecting energy flows through the Middle East.”

The energy secretary also pointed to the depreciation of the Philippine peso against the US dollar, which she said has “also added pressure on domestic pump prices,” given that fuel in the Philippines is mainly imported and paid for in US dollars.

The latest increase follows last week’s fuel price rollback, when gasoline prices went down by P0.32 per liter, diesel by P3.83 per liter, and kerosene by P3.84 per liter

That rollback offered motorists a brief break from two straight weeks of fuel price hikes. On August 25, pump prices rose by P1.08 per liter for gasoline, P2.31 per liter for diesel, and P0.95 per liter for kerosene.

The latest pressure comes from renewed tensions in the Middle East, where developments involving Iran, Israel, and the United States have again raised concerns over oil and fuel supply. Traffic along the Strait of Hormuz has dropped to its lowest point since May following strikes on tankers by the United States and Iran.

The DOE specifically pointed to renewed geopolitical risk after no confirmed peace deal emerged from US and Iran talks, coupled with the US Treasury’s sanctions under Operation Economic Outcast, which targeted financial channels allegedly used by Iran to move oil revenues and evade sanctions.

The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman, remains one of the world’s most important oil shipping routes, and any disruption to tanker traffic can quickly affect global crude and refined product prices.

Fuel markets in Asia have also remained tight due to constraints on Middle Eastern fuel exports, disruptions in Russian refinery operations, and limited supply from other global suppliers.

A weaker peso against the US dollar can add further pressure on local pump prices because imported crude and refined fuel products are priced internationally in dollars.

For these reasons, local pump prices remain far above levels seen before fighting involving Iran and US-Israeli forces broke out on February 28. In the last full week before the conflict, DOE data showed common retail prices in Metro Manila at P56 per liter for gasoline RON95, P54.70 per liter for gasoline RON91, P55 per liter for diesel, and P83.47 per liter for kerosene.

The Philippines is a net importer of petroleum products, making local pump prices vulnerable to global oil price swings, foreign exchange movements, regional refined fuel prices, and disruptions in international supply routes. – Rappler.com

World.title: Butuan’s state of calamity declaration to hasten emergency response
World.content:
Butuan City Mayor Lawrence Fortun said the state of calamity declaration will allow the city government to accelerate emergency spending, mobilize more agencies, and establish temporary water systems as the area continues to grapple with its water supply crisis. (Photo by Butuan City PIO page.)

SAN FRANCISCO, Surigao del Sur – Butuan City Mayor Lawrence Fortun said the state of calamity declaration will allow the city government to accelerate emergency spending, mobilize more agencies, and establish temporary water systems as the area continues to grapple with its water supply crisis.

In a video posted Monday morning by the Butuan City Public Information Office, Fortun explained that the declaration was a necessary step to strengthen ongoing interventions and prepare the city for similar disruptions in the future.

The city council approved the declaration last Saturday through an urgent resolution after the water supply situation showed no significant improvement.

Article continues after this 

READ: Butuan’s state of calamity declaration to hasten emergency response

Fortun said the city government had already activated a task force in anticipation of the worsening crisis affecting the Butuan City Water District (BCWD) service areas.

He met with BCWD officials last Friday, which led to the deployment of additional water tankers, equipment, and logistical support for rationing and other emergency initiatives.

“We need to intensify our intervention,” Fortun said.

According to the mayor, the calamity declaration will allow immediate access to emergency funds to purchase more water tanks and rent pumps and generators, among others.

Article continues after this 

The calamity status will also enable a whole-of-government response, Fortun said, adding the water crisis should not be addressed solely by the city government and BCWD but must also involve national government agencies and others willing to help.

The declaration will also help the city intensify measures to protect public health, Fortun said, noting that prolonged water shortages can affect household sanitation, hygiene and access to safe drinking water.

Article continues after this 

Fortun said the city’s efforts would continue even after normal water service is restored.

The city government plans to establish more permanent or standby water supply systems in affected barangays to improve their readiness for future disruptions, he revealed.

READ: El Niño takes toll on Bukidnon rice farms

Fortun said long-term solutions also include exploring alternative water sources outside of the Taguibo watershed.

The mayor acknowledged the frustration aired by residents affected by the water crisis, but appealed for patience, understanding, and cooperation while emergency measures are being implemented.

World.title: Adult dugong found dead off Antique town
World.content:
A large adult dugong (Dugong dugon) lies along the coast of Barangay Aras-Asan in Sebaste, Antique, where it was found dead on Monday, Sept. 7, 2026, a day after a juvenile dugong was rescued from a low-tide stranding in Caluya town. Fisheries technologist and biodiversity researcher Flord Nicson Calawag said strong waves associated with the prevailing southwest monsoon may have washed it ashore. But a necropsy is needed to determine the animal’s cause of death. (Photo courtesy of Rey Tan Cadiena)

ILOILO CITY — A day after residents of an Antique island helped a stranded juvenile dugong return to the sea, another of the threatened marine mammals was found dead along the coast of the province.

The dugong, or sea cow (Dugong dugon), was discovered along the shoreline of Barangay Aras-Asan in Sebaste town on Monday morning.

Authorities responded to the area and examined the carcass to help determine the possible cause of death and arrange its proper handling.

Article continues after this 

READ: Stranded baby dugong in Antique gets help returning to sea

Flord Nicson Calawag, a licensed fisheries technologist and biodiversity researcher, said the animal appeared to be a large adult based on photographs of the carcass.

“From these photos, the dugong appears to be a large adult species. There are some superficial marks and abrasions visible on the body, but the photographs alone cannot establish the cause of death,” Calawag said.

He said the prevailing southwest monsoon, locally known as habagat, could have brought the carcass to the shoreline.

“There is a strong possibility that the adult dugong was washed ashore by strong waves associated with the prevailing Habagat in Antique,” Calawag said.

Article continues after this 

But he stressed that being washed ashore would not explain what caused the animal to die in the first place.

“A proper examination or necropsy is necessary to establish the cause of death and determine whether it may be linked to fishing activities, ingestion of marine debris, vessel collision, disease or other natural or human-related factors,” he said.

Article continues after this 

Authorities had yet to announce the results of an examination or determine when and how the dugong died.

READ: Endangered dugong found dead in Magsaysay, Occidental Mindoro

The discovery came just a day after a juvenile dugong became stranded during low tide on Liwagao Island in Barangay Sibolo, Caluya town, also in Antique.

Residents came to the juvenile’s aid and successfully helped it return to the sea on Sept. 6.

No indication suggested the two incidents were related. But their occurrence on successive days drew attention to dugongs’ presence in Antique waters and concerns about protecting the species and its coastal habitat.

Dugongs are herbivorous marine mammals that depend largely on seagrass meadows in shallow coastal waters. They reproduce slowly, making the loss of breeding adults particularly significant to small or declining populations.

Based on documentation, dugongs are threatened by accidental capture and entanglement in fishing gear, vessel strikes, hunting, and the degradation or loss of seagrass habitat.

World.title: Duterte impeachment trial: Defense says CF payee names are ‘aliases’

Defense counsel Justin Gular. Photo from Senate PRIB

MANILA, Philippines — For the first time since the impeachment proceedings started in July, Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense team stated that the names of those who signed acknowledgment receipts (AR) for confidential fund (CF) payments are “aliases.”

Defense counsel Justin Gular made the revelation during Duterte’s trial on Monday when asked by Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros to clarify the matter.

Over the years, lawmakers and lawyers have questioned the unusual names of those who signed the ARs for confidential expenditures made by Duterte’s offices — the Office of the Vice President and, previously, the Department of Education — such as the infamous Mary Grace Piattos.

Article continues after this 

READ: Duterte trial Day 22: PSA official to testify on CF payees’ identities

“Your honor, given that this has become a material matter, we have to couch this answer that this is classified information, but these are in fact aliases … for the consideration of this court,” Gular said.

“But I hope you understand, your honor, that in threshing out this matter … we will do this at the appropriate time during our presentation of evidence,” he added.

Due to this, Gular said he would “veer away” from drawing conclusions of law and fact, as it is not yet the defense’s turn to present its evidence. /mcm

World.title: Palace distances from Sara Duterte ‘special treatment’ at QC court
World.content:
Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City Hall of Justice on Saturday, September 5, 2026, to post bail following an arrest warrant issued by Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 98. The warrant stems from three counts of grave threats filed against her. (INQUIRER / GRIG C. MONTEGRANDE)

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang on Monday distanced itself from the alleged red-carpet treatment extended to Vice President Sara Duterte when she appeared before the Quezon City Hall of Justice over the weekend.

Duterte arrived at the Quezon City Hall of Justice on Saturday to post bail following the issuance of an arrest warrant against her for three counts of grave threats.

The charges stemmed from her alleged threats against President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former Speaker Martin Romualdez.

Article continues after this 

READ: Arrest warrant issued vs Sara Duterte over grave threats

Photos and videos showing a red carpet rolled out for Duterte as she entered the building, however, raised questions about why such treatment was given to an individual facing an arrest warrant.

When asked about this, Palace press officer Claire Castro cited the separation of powers between the executive and judiciary.

“Wala po tayong masasabi kung ano po ang naging dahilan ng korte [sa paglagay ng red carpet]. Iyan po ay hindi na po saklaw ng ehekutibo,” she said at a briefing.

(We cannot say what the court’s reason was for putting up the red carpet. That is no longer within the scope of the executive branch.)

Article continues after this 

“Kung ano po ang nais nilang isagawa na proseso sa kanilang korte, nasa kanila po iyon,” Castro continued.

(If they wish to carry out a particular process in their court, that is entirely up to them.)

Article continues after this 

Castro said there was nothing wrong with Duterte not having her mugshots taken, after House prosecutor and Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon described the absence of mugshots as “special treatment.”

READ: Palace denies Sara Duterte’s claim on plan to ‘attack’ her

Duterte’s legal team submitted her recent photographs to the court in lieu of police mugshots.

According to Castro, however, an accused person is not required to have their mugshots taken exclusively at a police precinct.

“Sa parte po ng hindi pagkuha ng mugshot, mayroon po kasing proseso na kapag po kayo ay pumunta nang diretso sa korte at naglagak po ng cash bond, ang lahat po ng requirements na maaaring isumite katulad po ng mga larawan, sketch ng tahanan, kung saan iyong address, barangay certificate, at kapag ito naman po ay nakumpleto, hindi naman po niri-require na pumunta pa sa presinto para sa the usual na nakikita nating mugshot,” Castro explained.

(Regarding the part about not having a mugshot, there is a process where, if you go directly to the court and post a cash bond, you can submit all the required documents, such as photographs, a sketch of your residence showing the address, a barangay certificate, and other requirements. Once everything has been completed, you are not required to go to the police station for the usual mugshot that we typically see.)

Duterte posted bail for each of the three counts of grave threats filed against her before the Quezon City Regional Trial Court.

She appeared in person before QC RTC Branch 98, accompanied by her lawyers, Atty. Paul Lawrence Lim and Atty. Michael Poa, to post bail.

World.title: DepEd can’t hire new teachers in 2027 due to budget cuts – Angara
World.content:
Education Secretary Sonny Angara. Photo from DepEd Philippines/Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Education (DepEd) will not be able to hire new public school teachers next year after its recruitment program was left unfunded in the agency’s proposed budget, its secretary, Sonny Angara, said on Monday.

Asked at a congressional budget hearing if funding for hiring new teachers in 2027 had been zeroed out, Angara said: “Yes.”

“Unfortunately, there was none,” he told lawmakers in mixed English and Filipino. “But we’re hoping that it will be hiked in the course of the budgetary process.”

Article continues after this 

DepEd was earmarked P973.40 billion under the 2027 National Expenditure Program, 3.87 percent lower than its P1.01-trillion funding this year.

Angara’s presentation to lawmakers showed that the agency had requested an additional P49.16 billion for its “personnel improvement” program, including P4.29 billion for the hiring of 14,274 teachers.

“This is part of the wish list,” he said.

READ: Angara speeds up DepEd hiring to boost school operations

His appeal comes as legislators review the P7.2-trillion spending plan. Congress is the final arbiter and can cut or tweak funding at its discretion, leaving the door open for amendments to DepEd’s budget proposal.

Article continues after this 

Angara said DepEd hires an average of 20,000 teachers a year, noting that the agency received enough funding to hire 32,000 teachers for 2026.

“We got 32,000 this year, which is above the average hiring [average],” he said.

Article continues after this 

Besides funding for Teacher I posts, Angara also requested P16.64 billion for hiring 39,428 Project Development Officer I staff and P10.52 billion to fund 14,126 School Principal I posts. /mcm

World.title: DOH steps up drive to address low vaccination coverage, hesitancy
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Health (DOH) on Monday laid down its plans to intensify its campaign and measures to address low vaccination rates and vaccination hesitancy.

During the continuation of the House committee on appropriations’ briefing on the proposed budget of the DOH for next year, Rep. Girlie Veloso asked the agency for its concrete actions as she expressed her concern regarding the low vaccination coverage among children aged 12 to 23 months.

Citing the 2025 National Demographic and Health Survey, she noted that 4 out of 10 children among this age group were not fully vaccinated.

Article continues after this 

READ: DOH: 1M NCR children vaccinated vs measles-rubella

DOH Undersecretary Gloria Balboa acknowledged that the agency needs to “sustain and increase public trust” as she shared that one of the reasons behind the low vaccination rate, aside from delays in vaccine procurement, is the “persistent vaccine hesitancy that is brought about by, let’s say, misinformation.”

Balboa underscored the importance of coordinating with local government officials and other authorities to help address vaccine hesitancy among communities by strengthening information campaigns.

READ: Vaccine misinformation hampers measles-rubella drive in Central Visayas

“We have to involve our community leaders, those people that they trust in the community para magtiwala yung ating mga magulang para magpabakuna and improve on our information campaign kasi we really need to do this, medyo matagal na po but then still there is a need to intensify, educate our parents and all the members of the community,” she said.

Article continues after this 

(We have to involve our community leaders, those people that they trust in the community so the parents can trust us to vaccinate their children and improve on our information campaign because we really need to do this, this has been overdue but then still there is a need to intensify, educate our parents and all the members of the community.)

Aside from these measures, Balboa said the DOH will have to strengthen its vaccine supply and cold chain management system, as well as disease surveillance and outbreak response.

Article continues after this 

In the same hearing, Health Secretary Edwin Mercado said early procurement of vaccines for the agency’s immunization programs has been set.

He noted that some vaccines are delivered depending on their seasonality, such as flu and pneumonia vaccines, and the calendar of schools, such as human papillomavirus and cervical cancer vaccines for school girls.

Lastly, Balboa said that there is a need to digitalize the immunization information system.

“This is part of the digitalization that our present leadership will look into para mas maayos po yung ating information that we get especially on the ground that will guide us in our policy and decision making,” Balboa added.

World.title: Expert: Higher Foreign Currency Supply Supports Tenge Strengthening Amid Changing Market Flows
World.content:
ASTANA – The Kazakh tenge strengthened 2.6% against the US dollar in August, reaching 461.57 per dollar at the end of the month, as foreign currency supply continued to exceed demand amid increased market activity and changing capital flows, according to Saltanat Igenbekova, head of the Analytics Center at Halyk Finance.

According to the center’s analysis of the National Bank’s monthly foreign exchange market data, trading activity remained high in August, while the structure of currency flows changed.

The total trading volume on the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (KASE) reached $8.7 billion, up from $8.6 billion in July. Average daily trading volumes increased to $415 million, reads the analysis published on Sept. 4.

The tenge strengthened despite a decline in some traditional sources of foreign currency supply. Net foreign currency sales by the National Bank fell to $284 million in August from $617 million in July.

Sales of foreign currency from the National Fund amounted to $200 million, within the announced range of $200-300 million.

At the same time, the National Bank purchased $721 million in foreign currency for the investment portfolio of the Unified Accumulative Pension Fund, twice July’s $375 million.

Non-resident capital supports tenge

The analysis attributes much of the stronger currency supply to foreign portfolio capital.

“In our assessment, the high level of foreign currency supply on the market was largely supported by the inflow of non-resident capital through several channels,” Igenbekova said.

She linked investors’ interest in tenge-denominated assets to their attractive real returns, growth in Kazakhstan’s combined foreign exchange reserves and the country’s sovereign credit rating upgrade by S&P this year.

The role of the quasi-public sector as a source of foreign currency supply was more limited following the suspension in July of the requirement for quasi-public entities to sell 50% of their foreign currency earnings.

The center also noted that the National Bank conducted no foreign exchange interventions in August.

Trading activity rises

Foreign exchange trading on KASE reached $60 billion in January-August, up $21.8 billion from the same period in 2025.

Unlike the previous year, when higher trading volumes coincided with a weaker tenge, the currency strengthened from 501.2 tenge per dollar at the start of this year to 461.6 at the end of August.

“The observed strengthening points to the continued predominance of foreign currency supply over demand during the period under review,” Igenbekova said.

September outlook

Foreign currency sales from the National Fund are planned at $200-300 million in September. The National Bank also expects to sell foreign currency equivalent to 374 billion tenge under its gold-operations mirroring mechanism.

Igenbekova said it will update the tenge outlook following changes in the expected use of National Fund transfers.

“The main factors influencing the exchange rate remain the balance of foreign currency flows in the domestic market, global oil prices, and the activity of non-residents,” Igenbekova said.

According to the analysis, the interaction of these factors will determine the tenge’s direction in the coming months.

World.title: Kazakhstan Is Upgrading Its Oil Export Strategy—Here’s How
World.content:
Astana is looking for more ways to move its oil.

Russia, its principal export outlet, is rife with disruptions. Damage to the Caspian Pipeline Consortium’s (CPC) Black Sea terminal in November 2025 suppressed exports into early 2026, while the recent July attacks on tankers threatened roughly 1.5 million barrels per day.

The vulnerability would not be so enormous if 80% of Kazakh oil exports did not move through the CPC terminal near Novorossiysk.

But is Kazakhstan merely searching for emergency alternatives amid instability? Or is this a transformation it has been preparing for?

The answer is consequential: Kazakhstan is attempting a wholesale upgrade of its oil-export strategy, one befitting a rising regional power. It is moving from rational efficiency toward strategic resilience, from accepting routes toward shaping them, and from concentrated dependence toward managed interdependence. Although the CPC will remain dominant through 2030, Astana is seeking greater control over the risks, partnerships and infrastructure connecting its oil to international markets.

From rational efficiency to strategic resilience

The CPC transports Kazakh oil, particularly from Tengiz, to global markets, making it the most commercially attractive route.

When it was created in 1992, a fledgling independent Kazakhstan was looking to enter international energy markets. The CPC was the rational choice. It, for instance, transported up to 1.3 million barrels per day back in 2021; avoided the additional loading, shipping and crossing costs of a Trans-Caspian route; and its 1,510-kilometer pipeline, according to area studies analyst Ilya Roubanis, would be extremely difficult to replicate. Astana selected efficiency while adjusting to a new geopolitical environment.

Contrast this with Azerbaijan. According to Ken Moriyasu, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, Azerbaijan chose the expensive option. The Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan (BTC) pipeline through Georgia and Türkiye required what he called an “insurance premium for strategic autonomy” to avoid dependence on competing producers. Kazakhstan captured the CPC’s immediate savings but accepted greater concentration risk.

The stakes will rise alongside production. The KazEnergy 2023 National Energy Report anticipated high output from Tengiz, Kashagan and Karachaganak, with national production potentially reaching 105 million tons. Higher output requires dependable market access; otherwise, its advantage can be undermined by one constrained route.

The lesson is simple: the cheapest route is not necessarily the least costly once the consequences of interruption are included. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev affirmed as much in 2024: “With unprecedented international turbulence, the priority is to further diversify export routes.” Diversification, however, requires more than identifying alternatives. It requires Kazakhstan to help shape the infrastructure and partnerships behind them.

From route-taker to route-shaper

As a landlocked, post-Soviet producer, Kazakhstan has historically been constrained by existing pipelines and neighboring states. Its role was simple: produce oil and insert it into available routes.

But Kazakhstan does not have to remain a route-taker. Although it cannot independently control its export geography, it can shape the terms on which that geography operates. It can negotiate access to multiple corridors, invest in tankers, coordinate with transit states and treat infrastructure as an instrument of foreign policy.

Nowhere is Kazakhstan assuming this route-shaper role more clearly than in the Caspian. Tokayev identified the Trans-Caspian route as a “priority” in 2022. KazMunayGas and Azerbaijan’s SOCAR subsequently agreed to transport approximately 1.5 million tons annually through BTC, while Kazakhstan added the Caspian’s Taraz and Liwa tankers to its fleet, each with an 8,000-tonne capacity.

This gradual Caspianization continues. KazTransOil supplied 155,000 tons of Kazakh oil to BTC through Aktau in July, an 11.5% increase over the previous year. Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov said Kazakhstan plans to transport 2.2 million tons through BTC in 2026. Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan have also discussed using the idle Baku–Supsa pipeline for between three million and five million tons of Kazakh crude.

But this role has limits. According to Andy Kuchins, a senior fellow at the Center for the National Interest, major expansion would require high capital expenditure, long-term purchase commitments and several years of construction. Oil majors like ExxonMobil and BP are “more reluctant now as compared to the 1990s” to finance large projects in remote markets.

The direction is nevertheless clear: Kazakhstan is moving from accepting the routes geography provides toward assembling the infrastructure and partnerships it needs. It is not yet a fully fledged route-shaper, but it is steadily behaving like one—using new routes not to eliminate dependence, but to distribute it more strategically.

From concentrated dependence to managed interdependence

Every export option depends on another state, infrastructure operator, or external market. Self-reliance is not realistic. Kuchins nevertheless argues that Astana can “reduce concentration of its dependence on Russia.”

Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy reported 73.4 million tons of oil exports during the first eleven months of 2025. Separately reported full-year route data show 64.8 million tons transported through the CPC, 9.3 million through Atyrau–Samara, 3.5 million through Aktau, 1.1 million through Atasu–Alashankou toward China, and approximately 100,000 by rail. Of the 78.8 million tons accounted for in this route-level data, approximately 94% moved through the two Russian corridors. Kazakhstan therefore possesses several export routes, but its portfolio remains highly asymmetrical.

Herein lies its greatest oil-policy shift: managed interdependence. This means distributing export relationships so that no transit state possesses overwhelming influence over Kazakhstan’s market access. Each direction performs a different function.

And at the moment, Kazakhstan is assessing four directions—some mainstay, some new.

The Russian route

The CPC will remain dominant because it offers unmatched capacity, established infrastructure and lower costs. Kuchins and Roubanis expect structural dependence to persist through 2030. Following the Tengiz expansion, Kazakhstan may become more dependent on the CPC in the short term even as its long-term strategy diversifies. Diversification does not require abandoning the CPC; it requires making an interruption less damaging.

The Trans-Caspian route

BTC could absorb Kazakh crude as Azerbaijani production declines, while Baku–Supsa could provide another outlet. Neither would match CPC volumes, but together they would widen access to global buyers.

Europe also has a stake in this.

The European Union imported 52.4 million tons of Kazakh crude just in 2024, making Kazakhstan its third-largest external supplier. If Europe wants westward diversification, it must help make projects bankable through financing and long-term commitments. Brussels and its partners are therefore mobilizing 10 billion euros to improve transport connections with Central Asia. According to Roubanis, “building ties with the region in the short run is necessary for the EU’s long-term positioning.” The push indicates that Trans-Caspian connectivity is not just a Kazakh interest, but one shared by the whole region.

The Chinese route

China may offer the easiest immediately available opportunity to reduce dependence on Russia. The Kazakhstan–China pipeline transported 19.5 million tons in 2025, but that included domestic deliveries and Russian transit. Direct Kazakh crude exports through Atasu–Alashankou were planned to be 1 million tons in 2025, compared to the more than 11 million tons per year flowing with non-Kazakh suppliers.

China remains a credible expansion market and willing financier. Yet the fastest way to reduce Russian dependence could deepen dependence on China. Moriyasu similarly argues that Kazakhstan does not want to exchange one concentrated dependency for another. Unlike the Trans-Caspian route, China provides access to one principal market rather than multiple global buyers.

The Southern route

A corridor through Iran—possibly toward Pakistan and India—could be compelling but faces formidable political and economic obstacles. But it should not be dismissed altogether.

Moriyasu suggests that “Iran offers Central Asia one of its shortest routes to warm-water ports.” Although current geopolitical conditions severely constrain this option, he argues that “infrastructure Kazakhstan builds today will still be operating decades from now. Astana should therefore avoid making long-term infrastructure decisions on the assumption that today’s geopolitical map is permanent.”

The southern route’s present value lies in preserving a long-term option, not in providing a realistic alternative before 2030.

From east to west and north to south, Kazakhstan is not moving from dependence to independence. It is moving from one dominant dependency toward a deliberately balanced portfolio of interdependence.

A more advanced role, but not autonomy

Kazakhstan’s transformation should not be measured by whether the CPC ceases to dominate. By 2030, it will likely remain the principal corridor as Trans-Caspian volumes rise incrementally and eastbound capacity becomes more important amid regional instability and escalation. The resulting portfolio will be broader, though still asymmetrical.

The strategy is itself an upgrade—a threefold one. Resilience is becoming the objective, route-shaping the emerging function, and managed interdependence the organizing principle.

Looking forward, Kazakhstan’s strategic upgrade lies not in escaping geography, but in developing the infrastructure, partnerships and political leverage needed to manage geography more effectively.

The author is Joseph Shumunov, a Non-Resident Research Fellow at the Topchubashov Center in Baku, Azerbaijan, and a Fellow at Nightingale Intelligence.

World.title: Kazakhstan Plans $327 Million Expansion of Oil Pipeline Routes to China
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to invest an estimated $327 million to expand two key sections of its oil pipeline system toward China, increasing their combined capacity to 35 million tons annually and strengthening the country’s eastern export corridor.

KazTransOil, the nation’s oil transport company, presented the investment plans to investors on Sept. 2 during the virtual Issuer Day at the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange. The project, scheduled for 2026-2030, is expected to be financed mainly through borrowing, inbusiness.kz reported, citing Interfax.

The capacity of Kenkiyak-Atyrau pipeline that connects Kenkiyak station in the Aktobe Region with Atyrau is planned to rise from around six million to 15 million tons of oil per year, while the Kenkiyak-Kumkol pipeline is expected to increase from 10 million to 20 million tons.

Five new oil pumping stations are planned to support the expanded capacity.

The Kenkiyak-Atyrau pipeline, which runs through the Aktobe and Atyrau regions, can operate in both directions. This allows it to serve both export logistics and domestic refineries by transporting western Kazakh oil toward the country’s processing facilities.

The Kenkiyak-Kumkol pipeline forms part of the eastern route to the Atasu-Alashankou pipeline and onward to China.

The expansion comes as Kazakhstan continues to strengthen alternative oil transportation routes. The Astana Times reported in July that the Kazakhstan-China pipeline system has become an important alternative export corridor amid disruptions affecting other routes. The Kenkiyak-Kumkol pipeline has transported more than 100 million tons of oil since it began operations.

The project has been under preparation for several years. In May 2023, KazMunayGas and China National Petroleum Corporation agreed to conduct a preliminary study on increasing the capacity of the Kenkiyak-Atyrau and Kenkiyak-Kumkol sections.

The latest $327 million estimate moves the project closer to the investment stage, although the final cost may change following project design, feasibility studies and decisions on equipment and financing.

Expanding regional transit

Kazakhstan is also broadening its role as a regional oil transit hub.

In August, KazTransOil transported 35,000 tons of oil to the Kyrgyz Republic, marking the first such transit deliveries through Kazakhstan. KazTransOil dispatched the first shipment on Aug. 15.

Oil is transported through Kazakhstan’s main pipeline system to the Shagyr oil loading facility, where it is transferred into railway tank cars for delivery to the Kyrgyz Republic.

The new route expands Kazakhstan’s portfolio of regional oil transit services and complements its established connections with China and other export markets.

KazTransOil previously reported that it transported 45.12 million tons of oil through its main pipeline system in 2025, a seven-year high.

World.title: Second Przewalski’s Horse Foal Born in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – A second Przewalski’s horse foal has been born in Kazakhstan as part of an international program to restore the endangered species to its historical habitat, the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources reported.

The foal was born to a mare named Umbra at the Alibi Wild Ungulates Reintroduction Center, located in the Altyn Dala State Nature Reserve in the Kostanai Region. Specialists are monitoring the health and behaviour of both the mare and her newborn foal.

The birth comes just days after the arrival of Kazakhstan’s first Przewalski’s horse foal, which was born at the same center on Aug. 22. The first foal was born to Tessa, a seven-year-old mare that arrived in Kazakhstan from Berlin’s Tierpark in 2024.

The two births mark an important milestone for the country’s reintroduction program, demonstrating that the animals brought from European conservation centers are adapting to the Kazakh steppe and reproducing successfully.

The program has expanded significantly since the first horses arrived in Kazakhstan. In June, Astana Times reported on the arrival of four additional Przewalski’s horses to the Altyn Dala Reserve as part of efforts to strengthen the emerging population. The animals were transported from European conservation centers and prepared for gradual adaptation to their new environment.

The reintroduction program began in 2024, when seven Przewalski’s horses were brought to Kazakhstan from Europe. A further seven arrived in 2025, followed by eight in 2026. The program aims to bring approximately 40 horses to Kazakhstan by 2029.

Przewalski’s horse, known in Kazakh as kerqūlan or kertaqy, is the last surviving wild horse species. The species disappeared from the wild during the 20th century but survived through captive breeding programs. Conservation initiatives have since sought to return the animals to parts of their historical range.

Kazakhstan’s project is being implemented through cooperation between the Committee of Forestry and Wildlife of the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources, Prague Zoo, the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan (ACBK), the Frankfurt Zoological Society, Nuremberg Zoo, Berlin’s Tierpark and Hortobágy National Park, with scientific and veterinary support from the Leibniz Institute for Zoo and Wildlife Research.

The Altyn Dala State Nature Reserve in the southern part of the Kostanai Region was selected for its rich pasture land, perennial water sources, and protected status. Spanning 489,000 hectares, the area provides ample room for the reintroduced horses to roam freely. The animals are not confined, but tracked using GPS collars to monitor their movement, health, and habitat integration.

Before transportation, each horse underwent rigorous genetic and health screening to help establish a healthy, resilient population. The selection process prioritized genetic diversity, a balanced mix of ages and sexes, and the animals’ ability to adapt to life in the wild.

“We selected the strongest, most adaptable individuals. We know everything about them from their health history to their genetic traits. Horses are chosen not just for fitness but to avoid inbreeding and ensure long-term viability,” said Endre Só́s, then-chief veterinarian at Hungary’s Hortobágy National Park, in an interview with The Astana Times.

World.title: Kazakh Scientists Develop Drone Technology To Protect Crops From Pests
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakh scientists have developed a drone-based technology to automatically distribute beneficial insects across agricultural fields, potentially making biological crop protection faster and more effective, the Ministry of Agriculture reported on Sept. 2.

Researchers at the Zhiembayev Kazakh Research Institute of Plant Protection and Quarantine developed the BioDrop technology. The system combines biodegradable spherical BioDrop capsules, a specialized distribution device and an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV).

The capsules contain entomophages – natural enemies of agricultural pests. Loaded onto a drone, the capsules are automatically distributed across a field according to a pre-set flight route. Once they reach the ground, the capsules gradually release the beneficial insects, which then seek out and destroy agricultural pests.

The spherical capsule design accommodates the dosing mechanism while preserving the viability of the biological material.

Field trials show higher efficiency

Field trials showed higher biological effectiveness than traditional manual distribution of entomophages.

On the 14th day after distribution, biological effectiveness under the conventional method averaged 70–73%. With BioDrop, the figure reached 81–83%. This represents an average increase of 10–11% compared with manual distribution.

The technology also reduces the time required to treat fields. Manual distribution in the test area took about 1–1.5 hours, while the same work with a drone took 10–15 minutes, including equipment preparation.

According to the researchers, the time savings could make biological crop protection more practical on large agricultural areas and in hard-to-reach locations.

Technology already used by farms

BioDrop has already been introduced and is being used by four agricultural enterprises, demonstrating its potential for practical application in crop protection. The technology could subsequently be integrated into precision agriculture systems and used alongside phytosanitary monitoring technologies.

Using entomophages is part of an environmentally oriented approach to plant protection, reducing reliance on conventional pest-control methods. Automating their distribution could further expand biological crop protection by making it faster and more efficient.

The researchers also see potential in combining BioDrop with digital agricultural technologies to improve the timing and precision of pest-control measures.

World.title: Kazakhstan Races to Top at World Nomad Games
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan leads the overall medal standings at the sixth World Nomad Games with 55 medals, reported the Kazakh Ministry of Tourism and Sports.

As of Sept. 4, Kazakh athletes had won 25 gold, 13 silver and 17 bronze medals.

The Kyrgyz Republic ranks second with 58 medals, including 23 gold, 24 silver and 11 bronze. Russia is third with 23 medals: four gold, six silver and 13 bronze.

Kazakhstan has won medals in audaryspak, kazakh kuresi, alysh, arm wrestling, sambo, tug of war, traditional archery, horse racing, eagle hunting and other disciplines.

Syrym Izbasarov won the audaryspak title in the 100-kilogram division. The world champion and two-time WNG winner defeated his longtime rival from the Kyrgyz Republic in the final to claim his third games title.

Daryn Otkelbai also won gold in the 90-kilogram division, while Nurzhan Erkinuly took bronze in the heavyweight category.

In the eagle hunting competition, Serikbolsyn Zhalgasuly and his hawk, Zhebe, won the gold medal. Arman Koshkarov and his golden eagle, Algyr, took silver. Kazakhstan fielded nine athletes in the eagle hunting competition.

Kazakhstan’s arm-wrestling team delivered the country’s strongest performance, winning 12 medals, including seven gold, four silver and one bronze.

Kazakh women also excelled in archery. Ayash Kabdollayeva won gold in the 60-meter puta target event, while Asemgul Galymzhanova took gold in the 40-meter Central Asian target event.

Kazakh athletes are yet to compete in 11 sports, meaning the standings could still change as the games continue.

The country also won the 300-kilometer long-distance horse race, known as zhoryk. Kazakh riders completed the four-day race first, finishing ahead of the Kyrgyz Republic.

World.title: Kazakhstan to Host Its First Ever ICAO Aviation Security Week 2026 in October
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan will host ICAO Aviation Security Week for the first time on Oct. 20-22, bringing aviation regulators, industry leaders and security experts to the capital to address emerging threats and strengthen international cooperation.

Supported by Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport, the event will focus on the theme Safe Skies in a Complex World: Enhancing Aviation Security for All. ICAO Council President Toshiyuki Onuma, ICAO Secretary General Juan Carlos Salazar and senior representatives of foreign states and international organizations are expected to attend, the Civil Aviation Committee reported.

Kazakhstan reports 95.7% compliance with international aviation security standards, placing it among the world’s top 20 countries and making it a regional leader in Central Asia.

Security as a foundation for aviation growth

The forum comes as Kazakhstan seeks to strengthen its position as a Central Asian aviation hub, with safety and regulatory reliability increasingly viewed as essential to competitiveness.

“The long-term sustainability of a hub depends on trust in the system: trust in safety, regulation and predictable rules,” Civil Aviation Committee Chair Saltanat Tompiyeva said in an interview with The Astana Times.

Tompiyeva, who has worked in civil aviation since 1998 and was appointed an ICAO Global Ambassador earlier this year, identified Kazakhstan’s strong aviation security and safety record as a key competitive advantage. International assessments also show 82% effectiveness of aviation safety oversight.

Addressing emerging risks

The aviation security environment is changing rapidly, with new risks linked to artificial intelligence, cyberattacks, unmanned aircraft, critical infrastructure and geopolitical instability.

Aviation Security Week will address risk management, new technologies, workforce development and stronger information-sharing mechanisms, including approaches to aviation risk assessment in conflict situations.

Discussions will be held within the framework of ICAO initiatives such as the Global Aviation Security Plan (GASeP) and the Universal Security Audit Program – Continuous Monitoring Approach (USAP-CMA).

The Astana forum will also contribute to preparations for the Third High-Level Conference on Aviation Security (HLCAS/3) in 2027.

For Kazakhstan, hosting the global forum marks a step from regional cooperation toward a stronger role in international aviation security dialogue, supporting the country’s wider ambition to develop as a regional aviation hub.

World.title: Cyberport, Astana Hub Deepen Tech Ties Between Hong Kong and Kazakhstan
World.content:
HONG KONG – Cyberport digital technology hub sees its collaboration with Kazakhstan’s Astana Hub IT park as a two-way launchpad, enabling Hong Kong to expand into Central Asia’s growing AI market while offering Central Asian startups a direct corridor into mainland China and the broader Asia-Pacific region.

Cyberport Chairman Simon Chan said Cyberport and Astana Hub share similar development priorities, particularly in finance and information technology making the hub-to-hub partnership a platform for business expansion.

In June, Cyberport signed a memorandum of understanding with Central Asian’s largest innovation clusters Astana Hub and IT Park Uzbekistan during the visit of Hong Kong business delegation to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, led by Chief Executive John Lee. The partnership focuses on technology transfer, supporting tech companies in areas such as AI, fintech, smart city solutions and Web 3, and facilitating overseas expansion and global market access for innovation and technology companies from both regions.

“The finance sector as well as other sectors of the economy are growing fast in Kazakhstan. There’s also a lot of business opportunities. We hope through the collaboration, our companies, stakeholders and startups can open up the business there or find the collaboration with the Kazakh business entities. Astana Hub itself is comprehensive and focused on AI,” Mr. Chan said in an interview for this story.

“Hong Kong is one of the major Asian financial centers, not only Asian but also the international financial center. We hope to build Hong Kong into an international IT hub as well. And Kazakhstan is an ideal place for our companies to open up their businesses or make collaboration with the tech companies or financial companies for more collaboration and widen their scope of business and to seek more business opportunities,” he said.

Cyberport accommodates more than 2,300 companies, including 18 listed companies with a combined market capital of more than 500 billion HK dollars (US$63 billion), nine unicorns worth more than 150 billion HK dollars (US$19 billion). Its innovation ecosystem includes AI, data science, fintech, digital assets and blockchain, cybersecurity, and smart living.

In late August, Cyberport hosted the Digital Entertainment Leadership Forum (DELF 2026) marking this direction as a strategic one.

“DELF is important not only as an event but also its content is evolving every year along with the growth of different types of technology that can be reflected in its solutions. In the past, we focused on digital entertainment and other types of technology. But nowadays, we are focusing on AI and how to incorporate it in promoting the digital entertainment industry. We use this platform to reflect the development of different types of technology and attract guests from overseas to share with us and also to share their experience and insights with our local peers and stakeholders,” said Mr. Chan.

Building a global tech network

The Hong Kong SAR government has taken major steps aligning with the nation’s 15th five-year plan on positioning Hong Kong as a hub for innovative economy in the Asia-Pacific region.

The Cyberport chairman also spoke about the qualities they look for while building connections globally.

“We hope to build a gateway or platform for the different types of companies who can access different countries and industries. The critical success factor of locating a good collaborator or good competitors is the prospects for growth. The mission of the countries or the strategy of the development strategy of the country itself. In Kazakhstan, we have agreed to help make Kazakhstan more AI-oriented.”

Diversity in tech, talent development and different funding schemes for IT building up in Hong Kong are the main advantages.

“Hong Kong welcomes our friends from overseas to open up their office or presence here. We hope for more collaboration ahead. Collaboration is pretty important as the world is changing rapidly. We are looking for more hub-to-hub cooperation to build up more opportunities for the next generations,” said Mr. Chan.

World.title: What do Abkhaz residents expect from Tbilisi? A video discussion with Abkhaz experts
World.content:
De-isolation of Abkhazia

Abkhaz journalist and editor of Chegemskaya Pravda, Inal Khashig, and civic activist Adgur Lagvilava discussed the key challenges facing Abkhazia’s foreign relations, as well as its ties with Georgia’s official authorities in Tbilisi.

Key points and arguments:

Fuel crisis and relations with Georgia: Resolving the gasoline shortage in part through purchases in Georgia sparked absurd accusations from the Georgian opposition regarding supplies to the Russian military.

Resolving the gasoline shortage in part through purchases in Georgia sparked absurd accusations from the Georgian opposition regarding supplies to the Russian military. Distorted perception of Abkhazia in Georgian society: A historically inaccurate narrative prevails in Georgia alleging that Abkhaz are an “alien people,” which is used to justify Georgian claims. Abkhazia has become a political simulacrum for Tbilisi, and ignoring Abkhaz agency hinders dialogue.

A historically inaccurate narrative prevails in Georgia alleging that Abkhaz are an “alien people,” which is used to justify Georgian claims. Abkhazia has become a political simulacrum for Tbilisi, and ignoring Abkhaz agency hinders dialogue. Politicization of history in Georgia: Georgian authorities pragmatically rewrite history and rehabilitate historical figures (such as King Heraclius II) to justify their current political course and rapprochement with Moscow. The speakers view this approach as a dangerous manipulation of the past for the sake of short-term gain.
