The speakers view this approach as a dangerous manipulation of the past for the sake of short-term gain. Prospects for conflict resolution and Georgia’s European integration: To establish relations, Georgia must take responsibility for the 1992 war, officially recognize Abkhaz as an indigenous people, and repeal the “Law on Occupied Territories.” Promises of European integration are a “hollow sound” for Abkhazia, as the country is isolated from Europe and sits within the Russian information sphere.

To establish relations, Georgia must take responsibility for the 1992 war, officially recognize Abkhaz as an indigenous people, and repeal the “Law on Occupied Territories.” Promises of European integration are a “hollow sound” for Abkhazia, as the country is isolated from Europe and sits within the Russian information sphere. Abkhazia’s foreign policy: The Abkhaz authorities show passivity and miss international opportunities (for example, initiatives in the Turkish parliament), positioning the country as Russia’s “zone of responsibility.” The speakers call for actively developing an independent strategy of de-isolation to protect sovereignty and guarantee citizens’ rights.

Full text version of the conversation:

Inal Khashig: Hello! You are watching “Chegemskaya Pravda.” Another anniversary of the recognition of Abkhazia’s independence by Russia has passed. The festive events have once again brought to the forefront the issue of our development—the development of the Abkhaz state. And this topic resonates not only on its own, but also in the context of relations between Georgia, Abkhazia, and Russia, as well as the global situation. One way or another, there is much to think about. Today, our guest is Adgur Lagvilava. Adgur, good afternoon!

Adgur Lagvilava: Good afternoon, Inal.

Inal Khashig: Gasoline has finally reappeared, thank God.

Adgur Lagvilava: But it’s expensive.

Inal Khashig: But expensive, yes. Nevertheless, it is available, and thank God for that. Overall, the situation itself, of course, is far from pleasant. The fact that gasoline is back now does not mean that disruptions will not occur again. How do you view this entire situation when we have to, say, make up for the deficit from Georgia?

Adgur Lagvilava: Gasoline is not just a chocolate bar that you can easily forgo (though it’s probably better to give up chocolate). Gasoline is a strategic resource, the foundation of economic activity. Virtually all freight transport inside Abkhazia depends on fuel. Therefore, in the current situation, to provide the economy and the people with fuel, if we were able to take it from Georgia, I see no problem with that. We could also take it from other countries. We had similar experiences after the war: we bought fuel from Romania. Unfortunately, all these alternative supply routes ceased.

Right now, Russia is experiencing a complex fuel situation, and we ended up dragged into this crisis alongside them. If our fuel companies have the opportunity to get gasoline somewhere else to supply the population, I see no problem with it whatsoever.

At the same time, in Georgia itself, this was perceived very negatively—to the point where the opposition accuses the government, alleging that this fuel is supposedly being bought by the Russians for their military needs. That is entering the realm of clinical pathology.

Inal Khashig: For anyone who served in the Soviet Army, it is clear that little has changed in terms of weaponry systems. Most of the equipment—both Soviet and Russian—runs on diesel. In that light, such statements sound simply absurd.

On the other hand, one way or another, fuel enters Abkhazia from Russia, and it is insufficient for our market. But if the Russian military base were lacking gasoline, Russia would first and foremost take care of its own needs. At the very least, Rosneft, which is the primary supplier of gasoline to Abkhazia, would have supplied the Russian military bases first.

Therefore, such assertions are sheer nonsense. And when you read things like that from people who once held major state posts in Georgia—specifically, comments were made, it seems, by the former chairman of the National Bank of Georgia—it sounds extremely unseemly. I understand there is a domestic political agenda, but you cannot allow it to run on tracks where your statements will simply be laughed at.

Adgur Lagvilava: Incidentally, in this context, we have been observing Georgian discourse for many years. We receive precisely the information that is connected to us and occurs around us. One gets the impression that for Georgia’s internal political agenda, Abkhazia has become a sort of mythical country. It is recalled whenever some tension arises. Some use the topic of Abkhazia to direct negativity against the ruling authorities, while the ruling authorities constantly try to “reconcile” with us—though it is completely unclear on what basis all of this is supposed to happen.

That is to say, Abkhazia today is a simulacrum for Georgia that they created for themselves. The country they invented does not actually exist. Some say their territories are occupied; others claim that we in Abkhazia dream of returning to Georgia. They have their own sort of Abkhazia-Narnia, a Middle-earth of sorts in which they believe. Unfortunately, all these myths they constructed around Abkhazia have now maximumly obstructed our ability to obtain fuel. They bought into their own myths, and now it negatively impacts us because we do not know what tomorrow will bring. Perhaps Russia itself will temporarily run out of fuel, leaving us in a desperate situation. That is why our authorities must look for alternative avenues.

Inal Khashig: In any case, we won’t be left entirely without gasoline.

Adgur Lagvilava: I have serious doubts about that. If nothing is done about it…

Inal Khashig: Yes, but I think one way or another there will be gasoline. I am more concerned about the presence of a distorted understanding of the nature of the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict within Georgian society, government, and political circles. They hold a warped perception of the sentiment in Abkhazia. It seems to me that even the Abkhaz nation itself is perceived there in a distorted light: to them, we are some kind of “Apsuas” who descended from the mountains two or three centuries ago, while the real Abkhazia is allegedly something completely different.

What I am driving at is this: there are opportunistic approaches that clearly get in the way, but on the other hand, there are attempts by Georgia itself to change something, and this applies not only to Abkhazia. I have been observing the current discussions in Georgia surrounding the figure of the former King of Kartli-Kakheti, Erekle II, under whom the Treaty of Georgievsk was signed in 1783, placing Kartli and Kakheti under the protectorate of the Russian Empire. For many years after Georgia gained independence, Erekle II was considered a negative figure. Now, his rehabilitation is underway: last year, I believe, a monument to him was unveiled in Tbilisi, and now discussions surrounding his personality have intensified once more. Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze states that Erekle II effectively saved the Georgian people and their future, and that without the Treaty of Georgievsk, modern independent Georgia would not exist.

Reflections on what might have been are highly debatable, but the fact that Erekle II had very little choice at that moment is indisputable. Nevertheless, when history becomes a tool of political expediency, it is quite dangerous. I do not believe Erekle II wished harm upon his people. Historical facts speak volumes, even though the Treaty of Georgievsk did not save Tbilisi from Persian occupation a few years later. But things could have been significantly worse.

Currently, a segment of Georgian society views the rehabilitation of Erekle II quite negatively, perceiving it as a subtle indicator of a possible restoration of diplomatic relations between Tbilisi and Moscow and the conclusion of an alliance treaty. How do you view all of this? Saakashvili goes even further in his predictions, claiming there will be separate agreements with both Abkhazia and South Ossetia. What is your take on all these discussions, and what do you think about this matter?

Adgur Lagvilava: I am not deeply versed in Georgian history of the late 18th and early 19th centuries, but judging by our experience of living with Georgians in a single state, post-war events, and their historical discourse, Georgians frequently use history as an ideological foundation for the current political environment.

They have their own vision of who the Abkhaz are today. Perhaps it is not the official viewpoint, but a perception has taken root in Georgian society that we are an alien element who assimilated the local so-called “Abkhaz” by force of arms and began calling ourselves Abkhaz. This narrative has persisted from the very moment they developed claims over Abkhazia. Historical science and all kinds of pseudo-theories, such as Ingorokva’s famous concept, were tailored to fit this narrative.

If you look deeper into this process: since 2008, a narrative emerged (including in official documents) that we are a territory occupied by Russia. But that is merely the superficial layer. If the Georgians want to, they can peel it away simply by altering a few laws. At a fundamental level, however, they view us, the Abkhaz, as the occupiers. In their view, we occupied this territory after arriving 300–400 years ago from the North Caucasus and destroying or assimilating the Georgian population here.

When these historical narratives first emerged, they may not have carried direct aggression, but ultimately they led to the 1992 war. The radical segment of Georgian society gained an ideological and historical justification, which, naturally, bears a very distant relationship to genuine historical science. Authentic scholars—Georgian, Russian, and international alike—acknowledge this. Yet within Georgian society, this narrative remains potent, as is clearly visible across social media.

This issue could be resolved at the legislative level. Or the Georgian president or prime minister could simply step forward and state that the Abkhaz are an autochthonous people who have inhabited this land throughout their entire history, which aligns with reality.

Given how Georgians handle history, it seems to me that the current discourse surrounding the Treaty of Georgievsk also rests on political expediency—an ideological justification for the present rapprochement between Tbilisi and Moscow. I view it precisely within this context: in Georgia, history is used to justify the current political agenda or to steer it in the desired direction. I believe that is precisely the case.

Inal Khashig: As for the occupation: yes, according to their version, the Abkhaz once came down from the mountains and assimilated the local population. But regarding the occupation, they still maintain the view that Russia occupied the territory—and, by their logic, not in 2008…

Adgur Lagvilava: By their logic, we are an alien population here and ought to vacate this territory. Since we are an incoming element, we should leave Abkhazia.

Inal Khashig: Even if we were an alien people, how are we supposed to vacate the territory? How is that envisioned?

Adgur Lagvilava: In the manner they attempted in 1992.

Inal Khashig: For a state striving to join the civilized world and having declared a course toward Europe for many years, speculating about being “indigenous” or “non-indigenous” is a foolish endeavor altogether.

On the other hand, the thesis of “occupied territories” was originally launched by Saakashvili based on the events of 2008. But then their appetites grew, and now it turns out that Russia began the occupation as far back as 1992. Sometimes you watch broadcasts on the internet where participants ponder with a wise air that Russia started the war in 1992, as if the government and the State Council of Georgia had absolutely nothing to do with it.

Yes, there are many myths, but they lack a coherent picture. When you start asking questions from different angles, this logic collapses. Since the time of Eduard Shevardnadze, they have asserted that a certain “third force” prevented them from avoiding war. At the same time, they did not deny that they sent in troops. And who were those troops? The Mkhedrioni—criminals released from prisons. They explained that Abkhazia is Georgian territory. But if you send criminals who engage in looting and killing civilians onto your own territory against your own citizens, the state forfeits the moral right to that territory and those citizens.

At one time, Russian journalist Yulia Latynina formulated a statement drawing a bottom line under Georgia’s claims: Georgia lost the moral right to Abkhazia the first time when it sent in troops, and the second time when it lost that war. Frankly speaking, that is the starting point we must build upon.

When they appeal to a “third force,” it becomes a question of responsibility. If you are so easily manipulated that a “third force” can compel you to send criminals and cutthroats from the Mkhedrioni into territory you consider your own, what is your level of responsibility? How will you explain to the Abkhaz: “Sorry, the devil made us do it, it was all a third party”? Suppose we hypothetically resolved the conflict and found ourselves in a unified state. Where is the guarantee that some “third force” will not drive them mad again and lead them to wage war on us once more?

Referencing a “third force” demonstrates the failure of the state itself. How attractive must such a state be to the Abkhaz people, who endured the hell of war and lost 4% of their ethnicity, to spark a desire to unite with Georgia?

Another question: you cannot alter geography, and this conflict must be resolved in any case. Sooner or later, it will be resolved. To achieve this, one must talk to the Georgians—perhaps to win back something for their own citizens residing in the Gali district. Who knows what interests might exist. But all of this is resolved through negotiations. Yet how do you conduct negotiations if they believe their conflict is with Russia, not with us?

Adgur Lagvilava: For them, it is a very convenient position—to blame Russia for everything without delving into our actual relationship, problems, and historical context. After all, if Georgians truly immersed themselves in what transpired, they would have to recall more than just the 1992 war. There was the long Soviet period, the alteration of the status of the Abkhaz Republic within the USSR, assimilation processes, and resettlement.

If they objectively studied this history, they would have to draw certain conclusions and assume the main share of responsibility. But they do not want to do that, because then they would have to take concrete steps. It is far more convenient to blame Russia for everything—especially since the global context right now is such that “Russia is to blame for everything.”

If Georgian society and the state wish to take real steps toward us—we are not talking about recognition right now, which is a long-term prospect—the very first step must be the official dismantling of the narrative regarding the “alien” nature of the Abkhaz population. They could do this at least at the level of speeches by top state officials: officially declare that Abkhazia is the historical homeland of the Abkhaz and cease broadcasting these unpleasant assertions. Ideally, they could codify in their legislative acts that the Abkhaz are an autochthonous population. That would be a first step, and I do not believe acknowledging an objective historical truth is so painful for Georgian society. We are not demanding that they recognize us tomorrow and open an embassy here. One must begin precisely with this. And, of course, it is necessary to repeal the Law on Occupied Territories, which serves as the legal foundation of our international isolation.

Inal Khashig: Yes. You have probably read the transcript of the interview with Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Georgian opposition. He argues that it is necessary to stop picking at the past and reopening the wounds of Georgian society caused by the war and defeat, and instead move forward and speak about the future. As an opposition representative with a distinctly pro-European stance, he speaks about the European Union, the economy, and the need to showcase to the Abkhaz all the benefits the EU provides. How do you assess Georgia’s prospects in the context of the European Union, and how attractive is the European Union itself to Abkhaz?

Adgur Lagvilava: As far as Georgia is concerned, the agenda of European integration sounds much weaker there now than it did 10 years ago, when it was their primary foreign policy strategy. It seems to me that de facto Georgia is moving away from it.

Recall the events in Ukraine: Yanukovych also constantly spoke about European integration, even though he had no intention of executing it. But because a demand existed within society, he was forced to employ at least rhetorical tactics. I compare this to the current situation in Georgia: there is a young population oriented toward Europe, and the authorities cannot simply dismiss their political views, regardless of whether they favor joining the EU or rapprochement with Russia. Therefore, one should view this primarily from a rhetorical perspective.

If we look at the facts of recent years and read international reports on Georgia—European, American—the level of democratization, which is so crucial for the European community, is steadily declining in Georgia. A few years ago, I compared the metrics for Abkhazia and Georgia based on a report by World Vision (I might be mistaken about the organization’s name): our democratization metrics were higher than Georgia’s.

Furthermore, one must not forget that there are dozens, if not hundreds, of political prisoners in Georgia. Many opposition figures are under investigation, and criminal cases are opened over public statements. Georgia may rhetorically articulate plans to join the EU out of inertia, but de facto we see that the country is increasingly closing off.

The European agenda is fading further against the backdrop of cooling relations with the US. American leaders and the Deputy Secretary of State state this directly: a genuine chilling effect is observable. Many experts write that the White House’s focus has shifted further south—to Armenia and Azerbaijan—while Georgia remains on a residual basis. Against this backdrop, rapprochement between Tbilisi and Moscow is taking place. It appears that international support for Georgia today is much weaker than it was 10 years ago.

Inal Khashig: Yes, Georgian Dream lacks a clear goal to join the European Union for quite understandable reasons. After all, it is the party of Ivanishvili—an oligarch who accumulated his fortune quickly. For Europe, a person with such origins of capital looks questionable. On the other hand, without holding any official positions, he is the primary figure in the country, which cannot happen in Europe. With such a status, one is not admitted to the European Union.

However, that is the current situation, and what happens in the long term remains unknown. Georgian Dream is not permanent; sooner or later, the uninterrupted presence of a single political force in power becomes tiresome…

Adgur Lagvilava: Forgive me for interrupting. I do not claim absolute truth and do not consider myself a profound expert on Georgian political processes, but it seems to me that at a fundamental level, the Georgian people approve of Georgian Dream’s policies. Power is maintained not merely through heavy-handed measures. It appears to me that the majority of Georgians do not actually want movement toward Europe and the West, but rather support rapprochement with Russia. Georgian Dream possesses a strong electoral base. To me, this is a bit of a Georgian phenomenon.

Inal Khashig: On one hand, I wouldn’t put it quite like that. When for nearly 35 years—since the late 1980s—a pronounced anti-Russian card was played in Georgia and Russia was consistently portrayed as an enemy, such informational propaganda does not pass without leaving a trace. I see this in the scandals surrounding Russian tourists, where someone might be beaten, insulted, or refused service. On the other hand, a negative image is also forged by the existence of the Law on Occupation, when society is indoctrinated to believe that all problems, including the loss of Abkhazia and South Ossetia, arose because of Russia. Despite the fact that Georgia’s economy interacts closely with Russia’s, the negative image of Russia among the majority of the population persists, and this will be a defining factor for the future of Georgia itself.

Returning to Abkhaz realities: when Georgian politicians speak of attempting to “seduce” us with the European Union, one must understand that the EU has always been closed off to us. Under the Soviet Union, we did not know Europe, and then the war, blockade, and sanctions began. The Law on Occupied Territories prohibits any interaction with Europe, and Europe respects Georgian laws. Residents of Abkhazia are not issued visas, our passports are not recognized, and we have no trade or economic relations with the EU. We have grown accustomed to this; Europe is closed to us.

Adgur Lagvilava: We don’t even know what we are refusing.

Inal Khashig: Exactly. On the other hand, the majority of Abkhazia’s population resides within the Russian information space, where the narratives broadcast about Europe are far from positive. Why would the European Union be attractive to us?

For us to even consider whether we need Europe or not, it would be necessary to repeal the Law on Occupation, allow Abkhaz to travel freely around the world, and trade with European and other countries. Then, perhaps, our horizons would expand and our attitude toward the world would change. But this does not mean that Abkhaz would immediately decide to head toward the European Union. For the idea of European integration to have any prospect at all, they should first open the world to us, and then we will decide for ourselves. For now, while this world remains closed, the European Union is merely an empty phrase to us.

Adgur Lagvilava: It is an entirely dead agenda. It seems to me they formulate these points primarily for themselves, trying to find hypothetical paths to regain Abkhazia: “Let us show the Abkhaz the European Union!” Within Abkhaz society, this topic is not discussed at all.

Inal Khashig: In that same interview, Nika Gvaramia suggests not touching old wounds and speaking about the European Union. He is a politician and understands that describing Abkhazia and South Ossetia as a “lost cause” would mean putting an end to his career.

Nevertheless, a certain thought can be traced in his words: regaining the territories by military force will not succeed; there are no guarantees of victory in a new war. And if Georgia faces a choice—to move toward the European Union or to remain with dreams of restoring territorial integrity—his assertions nudge toward the idea of moving toward the EU, even if without formally relinquishing claims for now.

Europe is unlikely to want to assume responsibility for these unresolved conflicts. Therefore, a pragmatic understanding is emerging among a portion of the Georgian opposition: the perpetual desire to reclaim Abkhazia and South Ossetia hampers the development of Georgia itself. The seeds of this understanding already exist in society. Do you think such a scenario is possible?

Adgur Lagvilava: Regarding joining the European Union?

Inal Khashig: Regarding a pivot toward Europe, if sooner or later such a choice presents itself.

Adgur Lagvilava: It seems to me that in the coming decades, Georgia will not find itself in the European Union. Right now, the country has, one could say, pivoted toward Russia. This is clearly visible in economic relations: Georgia’s economic dependence on Russia today is significantly higher than on the EU.

All logistical projects being implemented in Georgia, even if targeted at Europe, have China and the US as their main beneficiaries. And talk about the EU is a narrative for internal consumption. There is a young segment of the population in Georgia that aspires to the West, travels extensively, and the authorities cannot simply wave away this agenda. They support it at the rhetorical level, but Georgia is taking no real steps toward joining the EU, nor will it in the near future.

The pragmatic element of the Georgian establishment and opposition understands that reclaiming Abkhazia through old Saakashvili-era methods will not succeed. Perhaps they calculate that Abkhazia will open up to Georgia not within a unified state, but on the foundation of some shared integration platform. The European Union in their vision is a structure more akin to the Soviet Union than a union of national states, where Abkhaz borders would open to Georgia. This is a pragmatic approach, but their overarching goal remains unchanged.

At the same time, today we are not prepared to join any integration platforms—neither the European Union nor any others—due to our economic, political, and military vulnerabilities. For us, this represents a colossal risk. We are extremely vulnerable economically: our entire recent political agenda and the resignation of the previous president were linked to economic risks. We are currently not ready for any integration.

If the Georgian authorities truly wish to make correct political moves, they must eliminate the primary landmine planted beneath our future relations—the narrative that we are an alien people. This is a fundamental issue about which the Georgian establishment remains silent. In Georgian society, the perception of us as alien occupiers has become dominant, and that is the bedrock for future conflicts. If they want to demonstrate a constructive approach, it is precisely this stereotype they must combat. The Law on Occupied Territories can be repealed in a single day, but changing society’s perception that Abkhaz are not an alien element is far more difficult. What basis can there be for good-neighborly relations if we are viewed as occupiers?

As for the European agenda, I would not take it seriously. But a major problem lies in how we ourselves behave. Georgians react to our silence: if we do not clearly state our path, where are we actually heading? They, for instance, want to join the European Union or align with Russia, but what is our foreign policy agenda? Our leadership speaks daily about internal issues and expresses gratitude to Russia, but performs no active work toward international recognition. We have found ourselves in the role of passive observers of the geopolitical processes occurring around us. We lack distinct foreign policy initiative.

In such a situation, Georgians interpret our behavior as a weakening of positions and a readiness to concede. A recent example: when a deputy from Turkey made a statement about the possibility of recognizing documents and establishing maritime and air communication with Abkhazia, our authorities effectively ignored it.

Inal Khashig: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Abkhazia came out in support, but not a single pro-presidential or pro-government organization issued a statement.

Adgur Lagvilava: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs made a very vague statement in the spirit of “we favor all good things.” I would not attach great significance to it.

Inal Khashig: Nevertheless, it was stated there that they support it. But what bothers me most of all is that all these pro-government parties and various public organizations, which express their views on any occasion, remained silent in this context.

Adgur Lagvilava: Including the fact that neither the president nor the prime minister spoke out. Officially, only individual deputies stepped forward and expressed their support, whereas parliament itself as an institution did not speak out, even though this falls squarely within its domain. Through the Turkish parliament, it might have been possible to find some useful avenues. But the president remained silent, the prime minister remained silent, and pro-government organizations remained silent. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs issued a statement—and it is good that it did—but it was perceived more as a routine formality.

Inal Khashig: You see, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs did note the existence of the movement and welcomed it. But there is a nuance here: this agenda in Turkey itself is pushed by the opposition, by opposition organizations. I understand why the president or other state bodies might not have spoken out, but other public and political organizations could very well have done so. We have “Amtsakhara,” “Aytaira,” and “United Abkhazia,” which convene round tables every week. They ought to have spoken out!

I consider this a very important point. Remember the thesis pushed during the presidential elections about a certain “pro-Turkish” stance of the Abkhaz opposition or a segment of Abkhaz society? At that moment, all players in that field knew perfectly well that it was a suspicion entirely plucked out of thin air. But now it is working. It is entirely possible these pro-government organizations did not speak out precisely because they are afraid: what if someone dislikes it, what if it is seen as a movement toward Turkey, and so forth? This is a case where you spawn fake narratives and then fall victim to them yourself.

Adgur Lagvilava: That happens often—when you fall victim to your own propaganda.

Inal Khashig: Exactly, your own propaganda. It seems to me it is time to move away from this fake reality, from attempts to constantly portray a situation of perpetual celebration in Abkhazia. We must ensure that our economy develops and our sovereignty and security are strengthened. On this note, I will wrap up, but before doing so, I want to briefly return to your words…

Adgur Lagvilava: You mentioned that in Turkey, this process is being driven by opposition organizations. But after all, the locomotive of this process is the Abkhaz residing there. Sitting here in Abkhazia, I should not divide Turkish Abkhaz based on whether they belong to the opposition or support Erdoğan. Turkey is a large country with a great history; it has both a government and an opposition. Yet this initiative was supported by a third of the Turkish parliament—not five or ten individuals.

I voiced criticism regarding our reaction for this reason. Naturally, our society received this news with enthusiasm: genuine joy arose that at least some process of ending Abkhazia’s isolation had begun. But look at the situation from the outside. Step back from being an Abkhaz journalist and view everything through the eyes of an outside observer from another country who needs to examine what is happening in Abkhazia. In recent years, you do not hear Abkhazia declaring the need for international recognition. The impression is created as though we are already recognized by the whole world and belong to all international organizations, including the UN.

In fact, through our inaction, we position ourselves not as a state that strove for recognition, but as someone’s area of responsibility. Today, we are perceived as a territory within Russia’s sphere of responsibility, rather than an independent state pursuing international recognition and participation in international institutions. Any observer watches how a state reacts to ongoing processes. Our state ignored these events, and the Georgians read this perfectly well too. They see our reaction. I can imagine what a psychological blow the beginning of such processes in Turkey was for them. But then they see that our authorities do not react to it in any way. That is, through our own inaction, we demonstrate that we are prepared to shift our own positions.

That is what I was talking about. The point is not whether someone likes the Turkish position or whether there are hidden traps—nobody disputes that. But our state must react to such processes and demonstrate—even if it has no direct involvement in them—that this is part of our strategy.

Inal Khashig: I think it is important for the authorities in any case to formulate a strategy for ending Abkhazia’s isolation. And this applies to such moments as well. It is not strictly necessary to achieve recognition from yet another small Pacific island nation like Nauru, which might revoke its recognition a few years later. By and large, that is merely an emotional factor that has no bearing on our lives: we do not travel to Nauru, and we have no real contacts with them.

Adgur Lagvilava: Recognition of our passports by Turkey would be far more important than recognition by fifty islands in Oceania or the Caribbean.

Inal Khashig: Yes. That is one effective measure that could truly impact the lives of many of our citizens and numerous ethnic Abkhaz living in Turkey. The ability to travel around the world with Abkhaz passports is significantly more important—with all due respect to all the small states of the world with which, by and large, we have no contacts and are unlikely to have any in the near future, even if they recognize us. When we talk about ending isolation, the most important thing is our residents, our citizens, who will be able to move freely across the globe using Abkhaz documents. That is fundamentally important for us.

On this note, I will conclude our broadcast. Let us fight for the end of our isolation!

Adgur Lagvilava: For now, it seems to me, through our own efforts.

Inal Khashig: How else? Do you want someone else to fight for you?

Adgur Lagvilava: I mean—through the efforts of society itself.

Inal Khashig: That is precisely the point: it is always society itself that achieves these goals. Adgur, thank you very much!

Let me remind you that our guest today was Adgur Lagvilava. I bid you farewell. Goodbye, and until next time!

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website

World.title: Consistency in illusions and inaction out of fear: barriers to Georgian-Abkhaz dialogue. An opinion from Tbilisi
World.content:
Georgian-Abkhaz dialogue

Numerous criticisms are heard regarding the foreign or domestic policy of the Georgian government. One of the main accusations is inattention and inaction toward the topic of conflicts. In an interview with conflict researcher Vano Abramashvili, we attempted to assess the reality in which peace policy finds itself today, to understand the reasons behind this reality, and, most importantly, to discuss future prospects.

Vano Abramashvili

Question: How would you evaluate the currently existing peace policy? Where are we now, and what processes are taking place on both the Georgian and Abkhaz sides?

Vano Abramashvili: Currently, we find ourselves in a paradigm-less peace. Georgian Dream has utilized “peace policy” in an entirely different sense. Issues regarding Georgian-Abkhaz relations are completely sidelined. As a result, the process has been left entirely to drift. There is also a total lack of trust toward this policy.

On the one hand, everyone realizes that the end of the war in Ukraine will have a major impact on what the situation will be in Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region. It will also have a major impact on our policy. We have no guarantee whatsoever that this war will end favorably. Therefore, the Georgian side has entered a spiral of mistrust.

In domestic political discourse, the leading narrative is that we must fortify ourselves like a fortress, that we have no friends, and that everyone has their own interests. This approach has also affected the topic of conflicts.

Every policy and movement related to Abkhazia is perceived as a source of potential destabilization. The attitude is that no way out exists to resolve these problems. There is a feeling that even internal resources do not exist to take these steps.

It is a state of despair and hopelessness.

For our society, this is also an unfamiliar state, because today it seems there are not even alternative visions and ideas. Until now, there existed the idea of Euro-Atlantic integration and, against this backdrop, a vision for conducting peace policy. However, today this Western policy has been suspended. We do not even know how much time and what scale of work will be required of us to restore these damaged relations.

Added to all this is the altered geopolitical situation in the region and globally.

That is why I would call the current state a paradigm-less peace.

Question: Is this paradigm-less state artificially created, or does it simply reflect the reality that took shape after the August 2008 war?

Vano Abramashvili: I think that such a choice was made, and this reality did not create itself.

Any state, no matter what blow it receives, decides for itself what position to place itself in. Back then, the war ended with an undesirable outcome for Tbilisi. The idea of returning the regions through military force became unpopular, and conflict issues shifted entirely into the dimension of Russian-Georgian relations.

Georgian Dream inherited the peace policy of the United National Movement and, in its own way, tailored this policy to its own comfort. It is through this comfort based on nothing that we have arrived at today’s state.

Question: When describing this modern reality, the main attention and responsibility shift to the Georgian side. But if the conflict also has a second side—we must also evaluate the Abkhaz side and its steps. What is their approach and paradigm? What are they doing or not doing that serves to create this lack of perspective?

Vano Abramashvili: The main difference between the Georgian and Abkhaz sides is consistency. The Abkhaz know what they want. Whether it works out for them or not—that does not matter. Their consistent steps obey a logic.

On the Georgian side, it is not like that. Here, policies changed, and individuals changed.

Over the last thirty years, we have clearly seen who is consistent. We must also understand this issue correctly. You can be consistent even in your illusions. The Abkhaz do not have the resources and means to achieve their goals. Creating an independent state is impossible. It is a fact that they are trying to do this, although it is also clear that it is not working out for them.

The Russians also have a consistent vision and plan. There must be an alienation of Georgians and Abkhaz from one another, and Abkhazia must be turned into merely a territory. This territory will ultimately have no ethnic content or purpose.

When the Georgian political class does nothing on a large scale against this and refrains from taking potential political steps due to security risks and fears—this makes it easier for Russia to achieve this long-term goal.

Question: Peace policy must be mutual. Do you notice in Abkhaz political circles or civil society any kind of interest, change, or reflection regarding the policy they themselves carry out toward Georgia? Are there any signs visible that, given a desirable political environment and willingness, peace policy would become mutual?

Vano Abramashvili: A situational alliance with them is possible on many things. We say that peace policy requires two sides, but my argument is that currently not even one side exists.

Both sides today live our own lives; we are in parallel realities.

Let us take even the population of Gali, which is our and the Abkhazians’ natural point of intersection, and assess what special attention they feel from our side.

Neither side is actually interested in a positive peace policy. What we have is a negative peace. And this is merely the absence of war. Real peace requires clarifying where we are, what speaking positions we have, who is ready to concede what, and so forth.

Abkhaz society is even smaller than ours, and they have far fewer resources. Given the established political logic, it does not even surprise me that the first steps do not originate from there.

To evaluate peace steps, those steps must first exist. We cannot evaluate what simply does not exist. And this non-existence has its own understandable reasons.

Question: The architects of the current stagnation are the political forces on all three sides. If political will exists, what topics do you think are practical and future-oriented that would interest the Georgian and Abkhaz sides and “force” them to talk to each other?

Vano Abramashvili: These topics must relate to development – socio-economic and rights-based development, and the improvement of the standard of living.

Everything except status.

I think that even under the conditions of occupation with the Abkhaz, we can talk. It simply requires political will and the correct formats.

On our side, we do not see the ruling party demonstrating political courage, committing to a revolutionary change in a good sense, and taking any step.

Topics with which dialogue can be initiated and which are in the interest of both sides could be a shared living space. For example, energy, climate. Everyone wants to live in a predictable natural environment.

If we explicitly state that in the long-term perspective we aim for cohabitation in a unified state, it is important that democracy, as a political system and a political culture, exists on the ground. Accordingly, this too could be a matter of common touch.

“Georgian Dream” failed to draw the line between strengthening the de facto regime on the ground and protecting human rights, choosing instead to avoid touching this topic altogether in public policy. This, however, is a flawed approach.

Question: Considering the ongoing political processes, do you expect any kind of changes in the direction of peace policy? The war in Ukraine also breeds uncertainty. It is not clear where the processes are ultimately heading.

Vano Abramashvili: We see that conducting the war is costing Russia more and more. This cost is human, political, and economic as well. Accordingly, Russia should likely steer this conflict toward an end; it must end it in some form.

It is natural that the end of the war in Ukraine will exert a major influence on our region—whether it be a temporary freezing of the conflict, a pause, or its final end. But if political initiative is not demonstrated and a vision or formats for a renewed peace policy are not proposed, we may again fail to utilize this new geopolitical reality to strengthen the process of restoring trust.

In peace policy, the human dimension is important – how this policy translates into people’s lives. We are talking about living human beings, about the future. If our policy is not reflected in the lives of the people living there—first and foremost, the population of Gali – then it was never a real and sincere peace policy. It is more indicative of political messaging.

If you speak about poverty reduction, this requires concrete steps and instruments. Peace too is achieved and felt through concrete mechanisms at the human level: through security, social attention, and culture. When this is not present on the ground, a person cannot develop a feeling of peace merely through talks on television.

World.title: “Georgia against Ivanishvili!” – 38th Saturday march in Tbilisi | Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
Protests in Georgia against Ivanishvili

The traditional “Saturday march” in Tbilisi on September 5 was held under the main slogan “Georgia against Ivanishvili”. Speakers said democracy was declining in Georgia, relations with the EU and Western partners had sharply deteriorated, and the country’s EU integration process had been suspended despite Georgia already having candidate status.

Participants blamed the situation on Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder of the ruling Georgian Dream party and an oligarch widely seen as the country’s de facto ruler.

“Protests will continue until the Ivanishvili government leaves office,” march participants said.

The traditional Saturday march was held in Tbilisi for the 38th time. The demands remain unchanged: the release of detained protesters, new parliamentary elections and a return to the path of European integration.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

News in Georgia

World.title: Rights activist Siranush Sahakyan: ‘Lives of all Armenians held in Baku are in danger’
World.content:
Trials of Armenian prisoners in Baku

“The lives of all Armenians held in Baku are in danger. They may even express views that are contrary to their own will,” Siranush Sahakyan, who represents the interests of Armenian prisoners at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), told a news conference.

She said this was also reflected in statements dictated to the prisoners. Many of those who have returned to Armenia told human rights activists that they had signed documents under torture that “in no way reflected the information known to them”.

At the same time, Sahakyan said some prisoners express their views while “being prepared to face the consequences”. She specifically referred to statements from prison by Ruben Vardanyan, Davit Babayan and Davit Ishkhanyan.

“We should be cautious and attentive when analysing these statements. We need to understand whether they were dictated by the authorities in Baku or reflect the prisoners’ free will, because we cannot rule out coercion under torture. Those making these statements are simply in a situation where they have no choice. They are forced to make a statement under threat of reprisals,” the rights activist said.

Responding to questions from Armenian journalists, Sahakyan commented on the trials of Armenian prisoners held in Azerbaijan, described the conditions in which they are being held and detailed alleged violations of their rights.

According to official figures, 19 Armenian prisoners are being held in Baku, including former leaders of the self-proclaimed Nagorno-Karabakh Republic. On 5 February, an Azerbaijani court sentenced former President Arayik Harutyunyan, former Defence Army commander Levon Mnatsakanyan, deputy commander Davit Manukyan, parliament speaker Davit Ishkhanyan and Foreign Minister Davit Babayan to life imprisonment. Former presidents Arkadi Ghukasyan and Bako Sahakyan were sentenced to 20 years in prison. The lighter sentences for the two former presidents were attributed to their age. Under Azerbaijani law, people over the age of 65 cannot be sentenced to life imprisonment. The case of former State Minister Ruben Vardanyan was heard separately from those of the other former Nagorno-Karabakh leaders. On 17 February, he was sentenced to 20 years in prison.

Baku pursues ‘hostage diplomacy’

“The release of the prisoners requires, first and foremost, a political decision, since their detention itself was linked to the conflict,” Siranush Sahakyan said.

Siranush Sahakyan

She argues that resolving the conflict entails an obligation to release the detainees.

At the same time, she believes Azerbaijan is using the prisoners to pursue what she described as “hostage diplomacy”, treating them as a bargaining tool in the conflict settlement process.

According to the lawyer, this applies particularly to the former Karabakh leaders: “Holding them is particularly valuable in terms of hostage diplomacy.”

Charges not supported by any evidence

The representative of the Armenian prisoners at the European Court of Human Rights has not been able to examine the judgments in the cases of 15 of them.

“We only have an extract containing information about the charges and the sentences handed down to those convicted; it is not the full text,” she said.

However, she has access to the indictment and an English translation of the judgment in the case of former State Minister Ruben Vardanyan. The document runs to 3,302 pages.

Sahakyan has studied it and believes it demonstrates an unprecedented violation of the defendant’s rights:

“The entire trial was a farce and its outcome is illegitimate. We have submitted our arguments to the ECHR. Ruben Vardanyan’s case has already been assigned a number and will be considered by the court.”

According to the rights activist, the Azerbaijani authorities, “using an unknown methodology”, calculated the number of victims and declared that more than 18,000 people had been killed during the years of the conflict:

“And because Ruben Vardanyan joined this criminal organisation [meaning the NKR and its leadership] in 2022 and took up a position there, Vardanyan himself is held responsible for all these lives.”

The lawyer says Ruben Vardanyan is accused of crimes that have nothing to do with his activities or reality.

Moreover, according to her, the Baku court regarded the following as “criminal activity”:

implementing various social and charitable programmes in Karabakh,

renovating schools and kindergartens,

funding a large joint wedding for 250 couples.

His Aurora Humanitarian Initiative was also deemed to constitute activity linked to “terrorism”, while award recipients who visited Karabakh were described as members of a “criminal organisation”.

The Aurora Humanitarian Initiative is an international philanthropic project established on behalf of the survivors of the Armenian genocide of the early 20th century. Its founders are Ruben Vardanyan, Vartan Gregorian and Noubar Afeyan. They described the initiative as a gesture of gratitude to all those who sought to save the victims of the tragedy. Each year, the Aurora Prize is awarded to individuals and organisations that have “dedicated themselves to saving human lives and advancing humanitarian causes”.

“For example, one of the laureates is an Iraqi citizen. His receipt of a [monetary] award was classified as financing Iraqi Kurdish mercenaries,” Sahakyan said.

She stressed that Vardanyan’s case goes beyond the fate of one individual. In her view, it concerns the right to a fair trial, the quality of justice and the protection of fundamental human rights and democratic principles.

“The professional community has serious work ahead of it. It must not allow charges and convictions that have no evidentiary basis to become a precedent and standard practice,” the lawyer said.

Prisoners are isolated from outside world

The rights activist stressed that the Armenian prisoners held in Baku have no contact with the outside world:

“They do not see their relatives, consular officials, independent doctors, independent lawyers or representatives of the ICRC. In short, they are being held in conditions of complete isolation from the outside world.”

According to Sahakyan, their only means of communicating with family members is by telephone:

“However, all calls are monitored and permitted at the authorities’ discretion. Depending on their content, they may be forcibly terminated. The permitted frequency of calls also varies. For example, three prisoners are allowed to make a call once every 40 days, while the others are allowed to call once a week. The duration of calls also varies: two minutes, three minutes and, in some cases, 10 minutes.”

Some prisoners suffered fractures after beatings

According to Sahakyan, in recent months the prisoners have frequently spoken during telephone calls about health problems and a lack of medical care:

“After a certain hour, there are no medical staff at the facility. If emergency care is needed, there is no possibility of providing it. At most, they may be given medication to relieve certain symptoms.”

There have also been documented cases of prisoners suffering fractures as a result of beatings. The lawyer said she had information about which prisoners had sustained fractures but could not disclose their names.

Alleged torture over religious symbols

According to Siranush Sahakyan, religion also plays a role in the treatment of the prisoners, with such cases documented in international reports:

“Those who had cross tattoos had them burned, with the crosses removed from their skin through torture.”

She also said that although prisoners had been allowed a limited number of books, they were not permitted to receive copies of the Bible.

“There have been cases, which we have documented, in which they were forced to read the Koran,” the rights activist said.

Proposal by Ruben Vardanyan’s wife

Veronika Zonabend, the wife of former State Minister Ruben Vardanyan, has proposed creating an international women’s humanitarian delegation to travel to Baku in September. Zonabend hopes that a group of female human rights activists, under the auspices of Azerbaijan’s ombudsman, will be allowed to visit the Armenian prisoners and deliver personal belongings, photographs and letters to them.

However, it remains unclear whether the visit to Azerbaijan will take place. The proposal is currently being discussed with the Armenian authorities.

Sahakyan explained that because of visa requirements, security considerations and procedures governing access to prisons, the project could not be carried out as a private initiative.

Representatives of the relevant Armenian agencies have already met Veronika Zonabend and Vardanyan’s defence team.

“We have not yet received an official response. The matter is still under discussion,” Siranush Sahakyan said.

World.title: Drug for Duchenne muscular dystrophy to become available in Georgia early next week
World.content:
Givinostat for Duchenne muscular dystrophy to arrive in Georgia

According to Georgian Health Minister Mikheil Sarjveladze, the drug givinostat, used to treat Duchenne muscular dystrophy, will arrive in Georgia early next week. He said all the necessary preparations have already been completed so that doctors can begin using the drug in the country as soon as possible.

“Today we have another piece of good news: we have received confirmation that the drug givinostat has been sent to Georgia by air mail. This means the medicine will arrive in Tbilisi by the beginning of next week.

We have carried out extensive preparations together with Italfarmaco. In particular, we have recorded patient data with the utmost accuracy, created a dedicated registry, approved the relevant regulations, and had foreign specialists train doctors. Everything is now ready to start using the drug in practice as soon as possible,” Sarjveladze said.

He said parents can call the ministry’s hotline for information and advice on how the medicine will be used.

Sarjveladze also spoke about another drug for Duchenne muscular dystrophy. The ministry has been negotiating with its manufacturer in parallel with the talks on givinostat. The minister said he hoped the two sides would sign an agreement within days.

The drug in question is Elevidys, which doctors use to treat Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

“In this case, I would like to share some good news with the public: we have completed negotiations on all the key commercial issues. We have already prepared and issued all the necessary legal acts on our side and confirmed that we are fully ready to sign the agreement.

We are now waiting for the company’s response and are confident that we will sign the procurement agreement for this medicine within days.

It is worth noting that the negotiations took longer than expected. This was mainly because of our firm position that we must clearly define and insure the responsibilities and obligations of the relevant parties regarding the quality of the medicine,” Sarjveladze explained.

The minister also thanked the parents of children with Duchenne muscular dystrophy for their active involvement in the process.

Background

On 31 July, Sarjveladze announced that the government would purchase givinostat for patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

Parents of children with the condition first met Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze on 3 June. After a second meeting on 4 June, Kobakhidze announced the creation of a working group to address the supply of the medicines the children need.

After the meeting, the parents said the authorities had agreed to provide the medicines. They expected two specific drugs to arrive in Georgia in about two months.

On 8 July, after meeting Health Minister Mikheil Sarjveladze, the parents said negotiations on making one of the drugs available in Georgia had reached the final stage. They added that they would announce details of the talks on the second drug the following week.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy is a rare genetic disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness and muscle damage. It mainly affects boys, with symptoms usually appearing in early childhood. As the disease progresses, it can also affect the respiratory and heart muscles. There is currently no cure, but treatment can slow the progression of the disease.

World.title: Abkhazia to review how effectively agricultural grants are being spent
World.content:
The authorities in Abkhazia plan to review how agricultural grants have been spent. President Badra Gunba has ordered the government to return to the budget any money spent on ineffective projects.

The grants come from the Agriculture Ministry’s “Agricultural Development for 2025” programme and the Economy Ministry’s programme supporting small and medium-sized businesses.

The president’s decision to review how the grants are used was most likely prompted by numerous complaints from farmers on social media, who say the government is providing little or no support to actual producers.

Badra Gunba does not rule out some violations given the large amount of funding involved.

“If violations are found — and with such a huge amount of funding, they are bound to occur — we must respond to them. But most importantly, we should not simply punish those responsible. We must make sure they compensate the state for all the costs it has incurred and return the money to the budget,” the president said.

The opposition media outlet Respublika believes that the president’s decision to order law enforcement agencies to set up an interagency group to oversee state support programmes for small and medium-sized businesses can only mean one thing: something is clearly wrong with these programmes.

“It looks like someone has already decided to make a tidy profit from state support for entrepreneurs. Now law enforcement agencies have several options:

simply scare them so they stop stealing;

investigate what they have already managed to steal;

or get in on the deal themselves.

Which option do you think they will choose?” Respublika asks, making it clear that it believes the answer is obvious.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Agriculture in Abkhazia

World.title: Georgian businessman Elizbarashvili charged over alleged threats
World.content:
Elizbarashvili charged with making threats

Prosecutors have charged businessman and animal rights activist Tamaz Elizbarashvili, who is known for his outspoken criticism of the government, with making threats. He is accused of an offence under Article 151, Part 1 of the Criminal Code, which carries a maximum prison sentence of one year.

According to Elizbarashvili’s lawyer, Lekso Svimonishvili, seven alleged victims are involved in the case. Prosecutors say Elizbarashvili threatened them and that they regarded the threats as genuine.

Svimonishvili said his client categorically rejected the charges and maintained that he was completely innocent.

What do investigators accuse Elizbarashvili of?

According to the Georgian Prosecutor’s Office, an investigation by the Interior Ministry established that at around 2340 on 30 August, Tamaz Elizbarashvili and one of the alleged victims encountered each other by chance at a restaurant in Tbilisi. A verbal altercation broke out over a comment Elizbarashvili had previously posted on social media about the individual and his family.

According to investigators, during the altercation Elizbarashvili threatened the alleged victim and the people accompanying him. In particular, he allegedly said he would not let the matter rest and would return in about 30 minutes, while demanding that they remain at the restaurant.

“Since the alleged victims knew that Tamaz Elizbarashvili possessed a weapon that could be used against them, they had reasonable grounds to fear for their lives and safety and therefore decided to leave the restaurant.

At around 0020, Tamaz Elizbarashvili returned to the scene intending to carry out his threat. He was armed and attempted to enter the restaurant, conspicuously keeping his hand on a weapon tucked into his waistband. He also continued to threaten and insult the alleged victims. Those who had not managed to leave and remained near the restaurant had reasonable grounds to fear that the threat would be carried out.

Despite being barred by security staff, Tamaz Elizbarashvili nevertheless entered the restaurant premises. After establishing that the alleged victims were no longer there, he left,” the Prosecutor’s Office said.

What does the lawyer say?

According to Elizbarashvili’s lawyer, prosecutors cite comments previously made by the businessman on social media as the reason for the confrontation. However, the defence says the indictment makes no mention of any personal conflict between Elizbarashvili and the alleged victims.

“Mr Tamaz does not admit guilt, and his account of what happened is radically different [from the one presented]. During the incident, he left his wife and children at home to shield them from any potential confrontation and returned alone, believing that if anyone had questions, they could put them to him in person. However, no-one was there when he arrived,” Svimonishvili said.

The case materials also refer to a firearm, although Elizbarashvili denies possessing one illegally. According to his lawyer, he has not at this stage been charged with the illegal acquisition, possession or carrying of a firearm.

Svimonishvili said the only firearm seized during a search of Elizbarashvili’s apartment was officially registered in his name and had been sent for forensic examination.

The defence will ask the court not to impose any pre-trial restrictions on Elizbarashvili. Alternatively, the lawyer will request that he be released on bail.

Prosecutors have not yet specified what pre-trial measure they will ask the court to impose.

Background

On 1 September 2026, Elizbarashvili was placed under administrative arrest for allegedly failing to comply with a lawful police order. His arrest followed searches of his car and home conducted as part of an investigation launched under Articles 151 (threats) and 236 (illegal acquisition, possession and carrying of firearms) of the Criminal Code.

Elizbarashvili said the complaint against him had been filed by employees of the Imedi TV channel, with whom he had a verbal altercation at a restaurant on 30 August. He alleged that the Imedi employees had initiated the confrontation and threatened him over his political views.

World.title: Ex-Georgian PM questioned in prison over his statements on a human rights defender who died by suicide
World.content:
Georgia: Gharibashvili questioned in Jorbenadze case

As part of the ongoing investigation into the death of Lazare Jorbenadze, law enforcement officers questioned former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili at Prison No. 12 in Rustavi on September 3.

Jorbenadze had publicly criticised current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze. Gharibashvili recently published a letter expressing doubts about the officially stated cause of the human rights defender’s death — suicide.

Following several hours of questioning, prosecutor Medea Tsiramua and Gharibashvili’s lawyer, Natia Tamazashvili, spoke to journalists.

Former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili was sentenced to five years in January 2026 for legalising illicit income on a particularly large scale. He pleaded guilty and reached a plea deal with the prosecution. On August 24, he was charged with a second offence — accepting a particularly large bribe. Gharibashvili denies the new charge.

What the lawyer and prosecutor said

How it started. On September 1, 2026, Irakli Gharibashvili published another letter from prison on social media, calling on government officials to answer questions about the true circumstances of Lazare Jorbenadze’s death. Gharibashvili pointed out that Jorbenadze, a former human rights defender, had criticised current Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze in an article by journalist Dito Chubinidze and died by suicide shortly after its publication. Gharibashvili also noted that the newspaper Asaval-Dasavali, where the article was published, had publicly questioned the suicide theory.

According to the prosecution, Gharibashvili’s public suspicions about the circumstances of Jorbenadze’s death have no direct factual basis. The prosecutor said the former prime minister provided investigators with no new or significant information.

She said the questioning showed that Gharibashvili was neither a direct witness to Jorbenadze’s death nor someone with specific information about it.

“Gharibashvili’s public letters were based solely on information from various publications, rather than any specific facts. He categorically stated that he has no specific information about Lazare Jorbenadze’s suicide,” prosecutor Medea Tsiramua said.

Gharibashvili’s lawyer, Natia Tamazashvili, who is his wife’s sister, said the former prime minister’s questions arose after he read specific publications while in prison and later learned of Jorbenadze’s death.

“His questions arose after he was sent a letter containing an article by journalist Dito Chubinidze in Asaval-Dasavali. The article was critical of Irakli Kobakhidze. Gharibashvili later learned about Jorbenadze’s death, put the facts together and raised questions publicly. During the questioning, he repeated the same questions he had raised in his public letter,” the lawyer said.

According to the defence, Gharibashvili was not trying to provide investigators with previously unknown sources or information. His questions were based on suspicions about a possible connection between the articles published in the media and Jorbenadze’s sudden death.

Series of interrogations in the Lazare Jorbenadze case

Before Gharibashvili was questioned, politicians and public figures were questioned at the Digomi police headquarters in Tbilisi. They were asked about the former prime minister’s letter published on social media.

Investigators questioned Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the opposition coalition For Change, analyst Gia Khukhashvili and several activists.

Gvaramia said he had no information about the details of the case and knew only what had been published on social media.

Opposition politicians Khatia Dekanoidze and Tazo Datunashvili, as well as journalist Nanuka Zhorzholiani, refused to appear for questioning at the police station. They told investigators they would give evidence only in court, in the presence of a magistrate judge.

World.title: Baku has made a strong contribution to global climate diplomacy, COP31 - official
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 7. Baku’s position in climate diplomacy is commendable, Trend’s correspondent reports.

Fatma Varank, CEO of COP31 and Türkiye’s deputy minister of environment, urbanization and climate change, said this while addressing the opening ceremony of the Fourth Climate Week of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change(UNFCCC).

She noted that Baku’s contribution to the climate agenda has extended beyond a single conference.

“The Baku-to-Belem Roadmap, which aims to mobilize $1.3 trillion annually, was developed in this city. This has provided a strong foundation for us on the road to Antalya.

“The mission of COP31 is clear. We are turning commitments into concrete results, projects and investments. In June, we announced the COP31 Action Agenda in Bonn, covering 10 priority areas. The key areas of this agenda are the transition to clean energy, zero waste, climate-resilient cities, the green industrial transition, youth and education, food security, oceans and seas, dynamic and resilient health systems, bioenergy, and climate implementation centers. This agenda has been designed as a call to accelerate implementation,” she added.

The Fourth Climate Week (CW4) of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change is being held in Baku through September 11, hosted by the Republic of Azerbaijan and organized by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan.

Having become an important international platform on the climate agenda, Baku is hosting discussions during the event on the practical implementation of climate decisions, expanding international cooperation and further strengthening global climate action ahead of COP31.

Government and state officials from various countries, as well as representatives of international organizations, experts, financial institutions, the private sector and civil society, are expected to participate in the events.

Baku Climate Week is designed as an international platform for discussions on combating climate change, the energy transition, renewable energy, sustainable development and accelerating climate action.

The events are expected to further strengthen Baku’s active role in the global climate agenda while making an important contribution to strengthening international climate cooperation ahead of COP31.

World.title: Azerbaijan to launch operation of two green energy corridors from 2032 — minister
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 7. Azerbaijan will begin operating two green energy corridors from 2032, Azerbaijani Energy Minister Parviz Shahbazov said, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

Shahbazov made the remarks during the opening ceremony of Baku Climate Week 2026.

The minister said that another strategic priority is to deliver green energy to international markets through regional and interregional connectivity. Shahbazov noted that the feasibility study for the Caspian-Black Sea-Europe Green Energy Corridor, with a total capacity of 3,900 MW, has already brought the projects closer to implementation. “Starting from 2032, the first phase of this corridor, as well as the Central Asia-Azerbaijan Green Energy Corridor, are expected to become operational.

At the same time, concrete measures are being taken to develop new green energy corridors toward Türkiye and Europe through Georgia, the Zangezur Corridor, and Azerbaijan’s Nakhchivan region. Through the diversified energy links being developed, we will contribute to strengthening interregional energy security and reducing emissions beyond Azerbaijan’s borders — across a wider geography,” he said.

Addressing the participants, the energy minister also touched upon COP31, which will be hosted by Türkiye, noting that the clean energy transition and electrification will remain among its key priorities. “Building on the strong legacy of COP29, Azerbaijan will continue supporting the transformation of the energy transition agenda into concrete projects, regional connectivity, and tangible emissions reductions. We believe that the energy system of the future should be not only greener, but also more secure, flexible, and sustainable,” Shahbazov said.

The fourth Climate Week (CW4) of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change is being held in Baku through September 11, hosted by the Republic of Azerbaijan and organized by the Azerbaijani Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Baku, which has become an important international platform for the climate agenda, is hosting discussions on the practical implementation of climate decisions, the expansion of international cooperation, and further strengthening global climate action ahead of COP31. Representatives of governments and international organizations, experts, financial institutions, the private sector, and civil society from various countries are expected to attend the events.

Baku Climate Week is designed as an international platform for discussions on combating climate change, the energy transition, renewable energy, sustainable development, and accelerating climate action. The events will further strengthen Baku’s active role in the global climate agenda and make an important contribution to strengthening international climate cooperation ahead of COP31.
