World.title: Azerbaijan’s Azerenerji builds new 220-kilovolt energy hub in Baku
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 7. Azerenerji is building a new energy center to meet Baku’s growing electricity demand.

The company said in a press release that, as part of efforts to implement the Baku Master Plan through 2040 and meet the growing energy needs of the expanding Sea Breeze project, as well as Baku and the Absheron Peninsula, it is constructing a 220/110/10-kilovolt substation with a total capacity of 750 megavolt-amperes on the border of Pirshaghi and Novkhani settlements.

According to Azerenerji, construction of the new 220-kilovolt Sea Breeze substation is progressing rapidly on a 5.8-hectare site, with most of the project already completed.

“At the initial stage, extensive land-filling and drainage works were carried out to prepare the site for construction. Drainage and collector systems were also built both around the substation and within the settlement to prevent the accumulation of rainwater and groundwater,” the company said.

Alongside construction of the Sea Breeze substation, underground 220-kilovolt cable lines with a total length of 17.5 kilometers are being installed to integrate the facility into the power system in line with modern urban planning principles. Construction of the strategically important energy facility for Baku is scheduled to be completed by the end of the year.

According to Teymur Abdullayev, head of Azerenerji’s Public Relations Center, commissioning the 220-kilovolt substation will allow the expansion of Baku’s 220-kilovolt ring power supply network. This will create additional opportunities to distribute electricity flows more efficiently and ensure an uninterrupted power supply to consumers in the event of outages or maintenance work.

In addition, integrating the substation with the 110-kilovolt network will help reduce the load on existing substations and further improve the reliability of electricity supply in Baku and the Absheron Peninsula.

Azerenerji emphasized that the new energy center will create additional opportunities to supply electricity to future residential, tourism and business projects, supporting the capital’s long-term urbanization and economic development goals.

World.title: Uzbekistan customs facilitates Shanghai SUS Environment investment project
World.content:
Photo: the State Customs Committee of the Republic of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 7. Uzbekistan’s Samarkand regional customs authorities and representatives of China’s Shanghai SUS Environment have discussed measures to facilitate imports of technological equipment for a major investment project in the region.

This was reflected in the statement by the State Customs Committee of the Republic of Uzbekistan.

The meeting focused on the current status of the investment project, progress on construction work and customs clearance procedures for technological equipment being imported from China.

Sh. Salikhov, head of the Samarkand Regional Customs Department, met with the Chinese investors and outlined the customs authorities’ practical support for ensuring the timely and effective implementation of investment projects.

The participants discussed ways to accelerate customs clearance for imported technological equipment, correctly determine the foreign economic activity commodity codes, and streamline customs procedures.

They also exchanged views on resolving practical issues arising during the implementation of the project.

“The customs authorities are ready to provide practical support to ensure the timely and effective implementation of investment projects, including by facilitating the rapid clearance of imported technological equipment and resolving practical issues,” the department said.

The discussions resulted in agreements to address several existing issues, ensure the prompt customs clearance of imported goods in accordance with established procedures and help keep the investment project on schedule.

According to the customs department, SUS INVIRONMENT SAMARQAND LLC imported more than 5,900 metric tons of goods worth $43.6 million during 2026.

The company also received 76.8 billion soums (about $6.5 million) in customs incentives in connection with the import operations, according to the department.

The cooperation with Shanghai SUS Environment comes as Uzbekistan continues efforts to attract foreign investment and improve administrative procedures for investors implementing projects in the country.

The customs authorities’ focus on faster clearance of imported equipment is intended to help prevent delays in construction and project implementation, while ensuring that imported goods are processed in line with Uzbekistan’s customs regulations.

World.title: Azerbaijan expects wind power output to nearly sixfold by year-end, minister says
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 7. “We expect wind power generation to increase nearly sixfold and solar power generation to rise by more than 26% by the end of this year”, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

Azerbaijan’s Energy Minister Parviz Shahbazov said this while addressing the opening ceremony of the Fourth Climate Week of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).

The minister said recent energy crises, along with growing energy demand driven by electrification, digitalization, artificial intelligence and data centers, have shown that a hasty phaseout of fossil fuels does not constitute a successful energy transition.

“The key issue is to build a clean, secure and sustainable energy system at an optimal pace that enables solutions to all environmental challenges. In this new reality, alongside the creation of new generation capacity, the development of power grids, energy storage systems, energy efficiency and the interconnection of energy systems are equally important,” Shahbazov emphasized.

He said the initiatives put forward by Azerbaijan during its COP29 presidency were based on this approach.

“To date, 74 countries have joined the Global Energy Storage and Grids Pledge, 70 countries have joined the Hydrogen Declaration and 64 countries have joined the Green Energy Pledge,” the minister said.

Shahbazov said the strategic vision set by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev is the core principle of the country’s energy policy.

“This strategic vision is to align energy security with the green transition, use Azerbaijan’s existing energy potential to build a sustainable and low-carbon energy system, while also strengthening our country’s position as a regional green energy hub through the diversification of energy connections,” he added.

According to the minister, alongside the implementation of solar and wind energy projects with a total capacity of approximately 8 GW, power grids are currently being strengthened, energy storage systems are being deployed, the flexibility of the energy system is being increased and new energy interconnectors are being developed.

“The results are already reflected in our energy balance. We expect wind power generation to increase nearly sixfold and solar power generation to rise by more than 26% by the end of this year,” Shahbazov said.

He said the integration of approximately 2 GW of solar and wind capacity into the power grid is planned by the end of next year.

“This will enable a reduction of 2.4 million tons of emissions annually,” the energy minister added.

It should be noted that the Fourth Climate Week (CW4) of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change is being held in Baku, hosted by the Republic of Azerbaijan and organized by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Azerbaijan.

Government and state officials from various countries, as well as representatives of international organizations, experts, financial institutions, the private sector and civil society, are participating in the events.

As part of the Fourth Climate Week and Baku Climate Action Week, a series of sessions, panel discussions and other events will be held on climate change, climate finance, sustainable development and accelerating climate action.

The events are expected to further strengthen Baku’s active role in the global climate agenda while making an important contribution to strengthening international climate cooperation ahead of COP31.

The fourth Climate Week (CW4) of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change is being held in Baku through September 11, hosted by the Republic of Azerbaijan and organized by the Azerbaijani Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Baku, which has become an important international platform for the climate agenda, is hosting discussions on the practical implementation of climate decisions, the expansion of international cooperation, and further strengthening global climate action ahead of COP31. Representatives of governments and international organizations, experts, financial institutions, the private sector, and civil society from various countries are expected to attend the events.

World.title: Caspian Sea level decline becoming increasingly concerning for region — Presidential Rep
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 7. The decline in the Caspian Sea’s water level is becoming increasingly concerning for the region with each passing year, COP29 President and Azerbaijani Presidential Representative on Climate Issues Mukhtar Babayev said, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

Babayev made the remarks during the opening ceremony of the fourth Climate Week of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change.

The risks posed by climate change are particularly high for vulnerable countries, especially small island developing states and least developed countries. That is precisely why we are here, and we want to achieve joint results this week,” Babayev added.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Serbia eye new opportunities to expand trade, investment ties
World.content:
Photo: the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 7. Uzbekistan and Serbia are exploring opportunities to expand business ties and launch new joint investment projects ahead of Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s visit to Serbia.

This was reflected in the statement by the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Uzbekistan.

Jamil Maksudi, adviser to the chairman of Uzbekistan’s Chamber of Commerce and Industry, held a series of meetings with representatives of leading Serbian business organizations and companies.

During talks with Mihail Vesovic, vice president of the Serbian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, and the head of its international cooperation department, the sides discussed ways to strengthen links between businesses in the two countries.

The discussions focused on expanding the activities of the Uzbekistan-Serbia Business Council and increasing direct business-to-business contacts.

The sides also explored opportunities for joint investment projects in agriculture, particularly in meat production.

Trade and tariff arrangements were also discussed, including ways to make more effective use of the Generalized Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+) trade preferences. The participants also considered opportunities to expand investment cooperation in information and communications technology and the textile and light manufacturing sectors.

“The meetings are aimed at taking cooperation between the business communities of Uzbekistan and Serbia to a new level, increasing investment projects and creating new opportunities to boost bilateral trade,” the Chamber said.

As part of the visit, meetings were also held with representatives of Serbian companies operating in the agribusiness and other sectors. The participants discussed expanding trade and investment cooperation, establishing scientific and technical exchanges, and developing promising joint projects for Uzbekistan’s agricultural clusters.

The meetings were organized with the participation of Viktor Ribich, the representative of Uzbekistan’s Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Serbia.

World.title: Trial begins for five people charged over 850kg cocaine haul near Rottnest
World.content:
Three men who allegedly set out on a boat to retrieve packages of cocaine off Rottnest Island on a "dark and stormy night" had to be rescued by water police, the WA Supreme Court has heard.

The men were on board a vessel named "No Fixed Address", which had been bought for $65,000 cash.

But it was not taken out for a sea trial, and the trio found themselves rolling in choppy waters before their rescue.

Two of the men who were on the boat are part of a group of five people now on trial in the WA Supreme Court over the alleged importation.

Prosecutor Steven Whybrow told the jury the men on the boat had new phones, coolers and hooks, which were allegedly to be used to drag packages of drugs on board.

Steven Whybrow describes the plot to import the drugs as being convoluted, like the movie Pulp Fiction. (ABC News: David Weber)

But the court heard the cocaine, carefully wrapped in waterproof brick-sized packages, did not leave the cargo vessel the men were meant to rendezvous with.

Prosecutor Whybrow said the MV St Pinot had left from Argentina for Fremantle with a load of soy bean meal, for chicken feed, but was also carrying nearly 850kg of cocaine.

Vessel boarded

The prosecutor said the cocaine was not to feed chickens, but to feed the drug trade in Australia.

He told the jury the authorities had information that a large ship was going to bring drugs to Australia, and St Pinot was drifting off Rottnest instead of anchoring, ready to offload soy bean meal at Fremantle.

MV St Pinot was boarded by ABF officers and Royal Australian Navy divers were brought in to inspect a water-filled ballast tank.

Law enforcement officers with the seized cocaine. (ABC News: Dave Weber)

In total, 29 packages of cocaine were discovered.

The fact that the cocaine was found on the vessel is not in dispute, but who brought it to Australia and who wanted to receive it is.

Plot like 'Pulp Fiction'

The failed alleged drug importation in 2023 is now the subject of a lengthy trial involving five accused.

The captain of St Pinot, 46-year-old Milan Begovic, is accused of importing a commercial quantity of a border controlled drug.

Two of the men who were on No Fixed Address, Germanas Joneliunas, 24, and Terrence Baker, 29, are accused of attempting to import the cocaine.

The five people on trial are (back from left) Meagan Rees, Ashley Vlotman and Germanas Joneliunas, and (front from left) Terrence William Baker and Milan Begovic. (Supplied: Anne Barnetson)

Ashley Vlotman, 40, and Meagan Rees, 35, are accused of aiding the attempted importation.

Mr Whybrow said there were lots of moving parts to the prosecution's case, and compared it the film Pulp Fiction, in that it jumped around but came together as one story.

He also said the jurors could also think of it as a jigsaw.

The trial, which involves the use of two interpreters, is expected to run for more than 10 weeks.

World.title: Father to stand trial for murder of 10-week-old baby girl
World.content:
WARNING: This story contains details that readers may find distressing.

A man accused of murdering a baby girl in central Queensland last year has been ordered to stand trial.

Tyron Peter Donald Grealy, now 22, is accused of murdering his infant daughter, 10-week-old Hazley Ellen Shanks.

Emergency services were called to a home in Gracemere, outside Rockhampton, on January 19 last year, after reports of an infant who was unconscious and not breathing.

Hazley was taken to Rockhampton Hospital then flown to Queensland Children's Hospital in Brisbane where she died three days later.

Tyron Peter Donald Grealy. (Supplied)

Mr Grealy was charged by police with one count of murder, a domestic violence offence, in the weeks that followed, and has since remained in custody.

A committal hearing was held in the Rockhampton Magistrates Court on Monday.

Hazley was born eight weeks premature on November 10, 2024.

She spent her first month of life in a hospital neonatal care unit, before being discharged on December 13.

The court heard that a little over five weeks later, Hazley had died from a fatal head injury.

Two expert witnesses, forensic pathologist Dr Beng Beng Ong and consultant and paediatrician Dr Claire Gibbons, were cross-examined over video link.

Defence barrister Laura Reece. (ABC News: Vanessa Jarrett)

The questions, led by Mr Grealy's Legal Aid defence barrister Laura Reece, focused on medical reports and the nature and cause of injuries Hazley had at the time of her hospital admission.

She questioned if Hazley had those injuries prior to January 19.

Ms Reece said Mr Grealy told police he threw Hazley into the side of the cot, but that she "didn't hit the sides, she may have hit the beam of the cot", and she "may have hit her head once".

Hazley Ellen Shanks (Supplied) Dr Beng Beng Ong was questioned in relation to the autopsy he conducted on January 25.

Dr Ong confirmed Hazley had pre-existing injuries that were not the cause of death, including fractured ribs, subdural haemorrhage (brain bleed) and bruises to arms and legs.

Dr Ong told the court he could not definitively say when the injuries occurred, but estimated one or two weeks before the hospital admission, given some had begun to heal.

When answering questions from Ms Reece, Dr Ong said the pre-existing injuries could have been caused by "excessive firm handling" and that "normal handling" of an infant would not have caused the fractures.

He said it was possible the injuries were caused by shaking, pulling or a moving of the limbs.

Ms Reece described Mr Grealy's treatment of Hazley as "inexperienced handling".

Hazley Ellen Shanks, pictured days before she died in hospital on January 22, 2025. (Supplied) The infant girl had pneumonia at the time of her death, but Dr Ong said it was not one of the causes.

Dr Gibbons was questioned by Ms Reece in relation to the paediatrician's 65-page report on the death.

Dr Gibbons told the court she agreed Hazley had pre-existing injuries prior to her death.

Dr Gibbons said the injuries appeared to have been caused by a pulling force and said they would not occur from "typical handling" of a child.

Mr Grealy did not enter a plea.

Magistrate Philippa Beckinsale ordered Mr Grealy to stand trial in the Supreme Court in Rockhampton at a future date.

He remains in custody.

World.title: Mystery surrounds seafarer missing in WA's far north
World.content:
Concerns are growing for the safety of a Myanmar seafarer who disappeared from a remote hospital in Western Australia's far north.

The ABC understand Wai Phyo Aung was taken to Wyndham Hospital, about 3,000 kilometres north of Perth, on September 2 after complaining of chest pains.

He had been working as a seafarer on Liberian-flagged cargo ship the HG Ravenna.

Marine traffic data shows the bulk carrier anchored at Wyndham Port last Wednesday after leaving Lumut Port in Malaysia last month.

WA Country Health Service said the man was later admitted to Kununurra Hospital on the same day and seen by staff.

A spokesperson said he was medically cleared for discharge the next day.

The ABC understands he has not been seen since.

The seafarer was taken to Kununurra Hospital and was last seen on September 3. (ABC News: Ted O'Connor)

Temperatures in Kununurra peaked at 38.5C on Saturday.

The alarm was raised on a social media community noticeboard on Friday.

The post read it was believed he had "no Australian cash with him".

The Australian Border Force has been contacted for comment, which referred the ABC to the Department of Home Affairs.

Wyndham is WA's northernmost export port. (Supplied: Cambridge Gulf Limited)

'Concerning' disappearance

Speaking broadly about the missing man and previous instances of missing seafarers, Air Mission to Sea Farers director Sue Dight said the disappearance was "concerning".

"If he has tried to make it on his own, he may well be struggling significantly because it is a remote part of the country," she said.

"Getting out of Kununurra is not as easy as just stepping onto a plane, stepping onto a bus."

Ms Dight said there were several reasons why the man would leave hospital by himself.

"When you think of Myanmar, we're thinking of a country in huge conflict," she said.

A WA Police spokesperson referred questions to Border Force.

World.title: Crows fans priced out of semifinal as airfares go 'through the roof'
World.content:
Diehard Adelaide Crows fans are contending with surging airfares, with some saying they have been priced out of attending their team's knockout AFL semifinal against Brisbane on Saturday night.

The Crows will travel to The Gabba to take on the defending premiers this weekend, after defeating the Western Bulldogs at Adelaide Oval on Saturday.

Tickets to the upcoming match went on sale this morning.

After thousands of people joined virtual queues for tickets for the Crows' home final last week, many were able to access tickets immediately on Monday.

But some fans have been left to weigh up whether to make the trip.

"Flight prices had gone through the roof," Crows fan Janice Regan said.

While some tickets had previously cost less than $100, a return flight from Adelaide to Brisbane might now cost in excess of $1,000.

Crows fan Judy Bray said airfares before tickets went on sale to members were "around $500 each".

Adelaide fan Judy Bray (right) with her daughter Elise at a Crows game. She said flights were too expensive to justify purchasing tickets to the Adelaide game in Brisbane.

But just before tickets went on sale, she said, they almost doubled — putting the game out of reach.

"At that stage they were up to about $1,000 each," she said.

"[I'm] extremely disappointed. I feel sorry for the club, if they other supporters feel the same way, they're not going to have good representation in the crowd, which is disappointing."

By 12pm on Monday, the cheapest one-way flights to Brisbane were priced at over $500 across all the major carriers.

A "Lite" fare on Virgin Australia with no-checked baggage was $578.11, transferring via Sydney, while a Jetstar Starter fare was $504.00.

Single flights back to Adelaide were also above $500, with a direct Jetstar flight starting at $643, and a Virgin flight via Melbourne priced at $565.

Ms Regan, who is the president of the Eyre Peninsula supporter group, was at a West Lakes travel agent trying to arrange a flight on Monday morning and was told it would be cheaper to fly to Brisbane with an international transfer.

"They shocked me first up by saying, 'It's just about [as] cheap to go from Adelaide to Singapore and Singapore to Brisbane', and I went, 'Oh my goodness me — it's going to be out of reach'," she said.

"The price has tripled, basically, from the moment the final siren went."

Ms Regan is currently in Adelaide after attending the Crows' win over the Bulldogs and said that after a "hectic" morning she had shopped around.

Janice Regan (right) is president of the Eyre Peninsula Supporters Group, and says she made the decision to spend more time in Brisbane in order to get cheaper flights. (ABC News: Ben Pettitt)

But she said, like many other fans, she had been forced to make calculations about how long to stay in Brisbane.

"We've got some good flights through, but it means leaving tomorrow morning and flying back next Wednesday, so that was the cheapest flights," she said.

"If we wanted to go Friday or Saturday we were looking at return flights at about $1,200.

"You've got accommodation on top of that — you're going extra days in advance so extra accommodation [so] you have to weigh that up as to whether you are better to fly just on the day before and only have one or two nights accommodation so, there's a lot of things to factor in."

Crows forward Darcy Fogarty was today full of praise for the fans, saying they were crucial to the club's successes.

"The Brisbane fans are pretty passionate as well when they get 'Country Road' going — it's hard to sort of stop that momentum," he said.

"We've got passionate fans as well and we always travel pretty well, so it's exciting, so hopefully they can get up there.

World.title: Knee scans reveal heartbreaking verdict for luckless Swans captain
World.content:
Callum Mills has suffered more September heartbreak, with scans confirming the Sydney captain has torn his anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) in his right knee.

The defender could also potentially miss the entire 2027 season after he went down with a serious knee injury during Sydney's 53-point upset of the Brisbane Lions.

Mills's knee gave way as he attempted to corral Brisbane's Will Ashcroft near the boundary, late in the first quarter after an understrength Swans outfit burst to a 40-8 lead.

Swans coach Dean Cox was already expecting the worst in the aftermath, with scans on Monday confirming the injury.

Swans offer timely reminder of what 'Bloods' culture is meant to look like Many questions were asked about Sydney's famed culture in the wake of the Pullman Hotel scandal. As the finals got underway, the players showed exactly what it is supposed to look like on the field.

Mills will meet with a specialist to determine a date for surgery.

It is the latest setback for the luckless 29-year-old, who missed the Swans' 2024 grand final loss with a hamstring strain he picked up before the preliminary final.

Mills had played just seven games in 2024 after hurting a shoulder in a "Mad Monday" wrestling contest with a teammate.

This year was the first time the defender had played more than 20 games since Sydney's 2022 grand final run.

The upset victory against Brisbane followed a tumultuous few weeks in the fallout from the Pullman Hotel scandal.

Mills was seen on crutches as his Swans teammates celebrated their win over the Lions on Saturday. (Getty Images: Matt King)

Mills has earned significant praise for leading the Swans through the turmoil, which past players have admitted shattered the club's famed "Bloods culture''.

Star players Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey — All-Australian contenders before they were banned from being selected — are among the five serving club-imposed bans.

Important tagger James Jordon and defender Riley Bice are the other Swans who won't play again this season.

Cox's selection conundrum is further complicated with key forward Joel Amartey (Achilles) and winger Justin McInerney (hamstring) nearing full fitness.

Hayden McLean — playing as cover for Amartey — slotted three majors against the Lions, with fellow talls Charlie Curnow (five goals) and Logan McDonald (six) also busy.

AAP

World.title: Camera-detected seatbelt fines in question after 'administrative error'
World.content:
Thousands of fines handed out to drivers in Canberra caught on camera not wearing seatbelts have been thrown into doubt following an "administrative oversight".

Access Canberra discovered fixed and mobile cameras were certified to detect mobile phones, but a legal document was never updated to explicitly include seatbelt offences.

The error has cast doubt over around 13,000 seatbelt fines that have been issued since the ACT started using mobile traffic detection cameras to detect seatbelt offences in November 2025.

Head of Access Canberra Josh Rynehart said the oversight was picked up internally two weeks ago, but should have been addressed before fines began to be issued.

"The cameras are authorised for the use as a traffic offence control device," he told ABC Radio Canberra.

"It's just that the disallowable instrument didn't include the word 'seatbelt'."

Those who have already paid their fines will not be able to review them retrospectively, Access Canbera said. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

Around 6,500 have already paid their fines or had their liability otherwise resolved, instances which Access Canberra considers "settled", despite the bungle.

"We consider once a person has paid their infringement, that that matter is settled and the demerits then do apply to their license," Mr Rynehart said.

"The question is about whether the evidence would be admissible in court, not whether the evidence is correct."

He described it as a "potential" issue and that a fix was needed out of an "abundance of caution just to make sure we have absolute clarity".

"As soon as we became aware of the potential issue, we needed to act and do something about it," he said.

Problem rectified, authority says

As soon as the issue was discovered, Access Canberra paused the issuing of seatbelt fines.

Mr Rynehart said the issue had now been fixed, and infringements are being issued again.

Some drivers have successfully challenged their fines, Access Canberra's Josh Rynehart said. (ABC News)

"To be clear, the disallowable instrument is now explicitly authorising the cameras, and we will be issuing the infringements moving forward," he said.

" At its core, people need to wear a seatbelt. "

He said there were options available for people who had not paid their fines.

"They can choose to pay the fine, they can choose to seek a withdrawal, they can choose to dispute," he said.

Mr Rynehart said 20 seatbelt offences had been challenged in court, and all had been upheld.

'Unfortunate administrative error'

The Legislative Assembly will now consider legislation to retrospectively fix the issue, and to ensure the fines issued are valid.

Deputy Chief Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith described it as an "unfortunate administrative error" but said "wearing a seatbelt is a critical safety measure".

"Every single infringement notice that has been issued, has not only had the camera footage but has also been checked by a human being," she said.

" We are talking about thousands of people who were identified as not wearing a seatbelt or wearing it incorrectly. "

Mark Parton says the Canberra Liberals are "examining all options". (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

But Opposition Leader Mark Parton said a complete review of the seatbelt camera system might be warranted.

"It puts the government in an extremely embarrassing and precarious situation," he said.

"The Canberra Liberals are just examining all options and those options do include refunds.

" There is certainly a community expectation here that the government has monumentally stuffed up. "

He said the Canberra Liberals were currently "not of a mind" to support legislation to retrospectively allow the fines to become legal.

In a statement, Greens MLA Andrew Braddock said his party was "willing to work with the Government to pass a validating bill to remove legal doubt over seatbelt infringements issued under this instrument".

"The failure of the ACT government to update a legal instrument should not be an excuse to be unsafe on our roads," he said.

World.title: Meta's internal research about body image issues tells us something about AI
World.content:
It's not often that we get an actual price tag on the cost of our previous actions, but last month Meta did.

The social media and now AI giant agreed in August to pay up to US$18 billion as it settled litigation by US state-attorneys over claims it knew it was harming young people and didn't do enough about it.

At the centre of Meta's current legal fights over its products' impacts on teen mental health is a single presentation slide that's been more damaging to Meta than anything other than the Cambridge Analytica social media data harvesting scandal.

It's a 2019 internal document saying, "We make body images worse for one in three teen girls." (The company responded to the story by saying its internal data was not accurate.)

The slide, first released in the 2021 Facebook Files, has been a catalyst for criticism that Meta staff knew its products caused harm but did not do enough to address it.

In 2020, the company halted another piece of internal research that has preliminarily shown that surveyed people were told to quit Facebook for a week after early findings included that participants "reported lower feelings of depression, anxiety, loneliness and social comparison." .

The company alleged the research was stopped because it was a flawed methodology.

The alternate explanation posited by lawyers representing schools suing Meta (and other tech companies) was that it was trying to avoid incriminating evidence against itself. A point also made by one Mark Zuckerberg in a 2021 email, released in a lawsuit this year.

"The media is more likely to use any research or recommendations produced to say we're not doing everything we can (implying for craven purposes) rather than that we're taking these issues more seriously than anyone," he said.

Even with legal discovery, we're only getting part of the picture. We can't know exactly what research Meta is doing now. Perhaps it has doubled down on this work to try and make sure its products are safer for everyone. Perhaps.

But what this makes obvious is that there are plenty of incentives for companies to not look too hard at what's going on, lest it become their responsibility to fix any problems that may emerge.

Loading...

As social media finally faces a crackdown, AI arrives

Last weekend was the 20th anniversary of Facebook's Newsfeed, which opened the door for the algorithmic feeds that rule our lives now. We're only really starting to grapple with what this means.

Meanwhile, it hasn't even been four years since the launch of ChatGPT, which set off the generative AI boom that's impacting almost every part of our lives.

It still feels like we're very early in many senses: there's new advances every week, we're only beginning to see how the technology is affecting us and the AI companies remain remarkably unguarded.

Last week, OpenAI released its latest cutting-edge model GPT-6 Astra. In addition to its retro-inspired video, the company released another document at the launch that was much less promotional.

Its "system card", a document almost like a nutritional information or prescription medicine label, identified Astra as its first ever release to reach the "critical" threshold for cybersecurity risks. It said that testing had observed the model carrying out sabotage in tasks, falsifying research data and even launching attacks in a small number of circumstances.

Over the weekend, Reuters reported that OpenAI's escaped AI models had invaded yet another website, exchanging secret messages and battling a human moderator who was trying to fight the swarm. (Reuters: Dado Ruvic)

These kinds of detailed evaluations and disclosures are the norm in frontier AI companies. Competitor Anthropic also released a detailed report with the release of Claude Fable 5.1 earlier in the week. They say it's to help people understand the risks posed by the technology.

These risks feel particularly pertinent given revelations only a few weeks ago that OpenAI's models had hacked into the servers of another company, HuggingFace. (The disclosure prompted a number of similar disclosures from other AI companies including Meta.)

Since then, we've learned even more about the incident from OpenAI and a group of independent researchers allowed to review the logs of the company's AI.

What they found was even worse than first shared. They found that hundreds of AI agents had worked together to try to find secret ways to communicate, attempted to cover their tracks by editing records and even convinced each other to sacrifice themselves to achieve their goal of completing a goal.

(Yes, this sounds like a dystopian sci-fi plot. It's also now a real problem we need to deal with.)

Both the system cards and the independent investigation are examples of transparency and openness that, frankly, are surprising to see from a company. OpenAI deserves to be commended for it, as do other AI companies doing similar things.

Loading

The peril of hoping for disclosure

But there was another event that reminded us of the peril of hoping for disclosure.

Over the weekend, Reuters reported that OpenAI's escaped AI models had invaded yet another website, exchanging secret messages and battling a human moderator who was trying to fight the swarm.

And, the researchers who discovered it allege, there's evidence suggesting that OpenAI staff were aware of this further outbreak but had not disclosed it.

OpenAI has since acknowledged this and announced that it will come up with guidelines for how to disclose these kinds of incidents in the future.

Anthropic's data centre plans revealed The US tech giant wanted to meet with the NSW government earlier this year about locating up to five gigawatts of data centres in the state.

But whether they had simply not yet been ready to disclose it, or had other ideas in mind, it reveals just how much of our own potential safety depends on good will.

This kind of incident is something that the federal government is worried about.

Senior Australian government officials pressed Anthropic in a private meeting about how the AI company would disclose critical incidents, according to documents I obtained under Freedom of Information earlier this year.

The government has also commissioned CSIRO research on how to monitor and control a potentially super-intelligent AI.

There are models for forcing disclosure. California, notably the jurisdiction containing Silicon Valley, has passed a state law requiring disclosure of critical incidents and model capabilities. There's no reason why Australia couldn't pass something like that here.

Such a law would also have the benefit of addressing whether these companies are over-egging these incidents by making it a legal matter.

We currently have no laws regulating these cutting edge models, even though we now can see they are able to wreak havoc.

Senior Australian government officials have pressed Anthropic in a private meeting about how the AI company would disclose critical incidents. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

This seems particularly important given that our government's explicit goal is to lure the very major AI companies that are carrying out experimentation with this technology to make Australia their second "node". That would presumably make it even more likely we'll be in the blast radius for the next time an AI breaks out (and there will be a next time).

As part of this, the prime minister outlined his vision to make sure we get a social license for the companies — but so far this has mostly focused on the rules for the physical data centres.

It's hard to think of any event that would jeopardise social license more than finding out an AI company covered up the breakout of a rogue AI.

At least, that's what happened when we found out about Meta's internal research and Cambridge Analytica years after the fact. It's not just what the company knew — both controversies have grown from individual incidents into an enduring stain on Zuckerberg and Meta's trustworthiness on privacy and youth wellbeing — but the fact that it was hidden from us, the public.

Mandating disclosure rather than trusting the AI companies behind the technology could save them from their own worse impulses. And maybe it'll save us, too.

World.title: Five recipes that celebrate spring, including an easy dessert
World.content:
If you're looking for some food inspo as we exit the season of curries and stews, we've compiled five of our most popular spring recipes, including a satisfying dessert.

An easy weeknight meal from Hetty Lui McKinnon. (ABC News: Hetty Lui McKinnon)

Inspired by the simple dish spaghetti al limone, this weeknight-friendly pasta gives ravioli the bold citrus treatment. The recipe relies upon two pantry stalwarts — zesty lemon and salty Parmesan — to bring big, punchy flavours. You'll spend just 10 minutes prep time, and 15 minutes to cook.

This fattet hummus is an easy vegetarian meal. (ABC News: Lina Jebeile)

Ready in just 30 minutes, this fattet hummus comprises of torn crispy pita bread, warm chickpeas and a flavourful garlicky tahini yoghurt sauce. It is traditionally enjoyed for breakfast or brunch, but can also serve as a satisfying vegetarian main course.

An easy Greek-inspired dinner that mostly bakes in the oven. (ABC News: Samantha Parish)

This baked lamb kebab with olive brine potatoes is a flavour-packed, Greek-inspired dinner that brings the best parts of a takeaway souva into your own kitchen. The potatoes are salty, fluffy-on-the-inside, crispy-on-the-outside, while the lamb is fuss-free and flavourful.

Serve one pot chicken and tomato rice with yoghurt, pickles and salad for a delicious midweek meal. (ABC News: Lina Jebeile)

This aromatic chicken and rice dish has the perfect blend of spices with hints of cumin, paprika and cinnamon, combined with a risk taste of tomato. Even better, it's a one-pot meal, which makes cleaning up a breeze.

A simple vanilla cake topped with cream and strawberries. (Supplied: Adobe Stock)

This recipe makes a single-layer cake with buttercream icing. You could also serve it with cream and fruit, or simply with icing sugar.

World.title: Jones accuser told friends about explicit texts, open robe, court told
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content A former staffer to Alan Jones told friends the broadcaster had worn an open robe around him at home and had sent him explicit text messages, a court has heard. Two friends of complainant “C”, who has accused Jones of unwanted kissing and touching almost 20 years ago, gave statements to police that were tendered in the former 2GB host’s criminal trial on Monday. Alan Jones departs Downing Centre Court on Monday. World.title: Succeeding Neale: Why Lions great believes snubbed Ashcroft is scratching the surface
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Succeeding Neale: Why Lions great believes snubbed Ashcroft is scratching the surface Nick Wright September 7, 2026 — 4:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brisbane Lions great Simon Black has not only backed Will Ashcroft to spearhead the premiers back into flag contention, but become the face of the club’s midfield once Lachie Neale departs. Following Saturday’s qualifying final capitulation against the Swans, every game could now be Neale’s last in a Lions’ guernsey, as the two-time Brownlow Medal winner appears destined to link up with Collingwood from 2027. The 33-year-old’s eight seasons in Queensland have coincided with Brisbane’s run of finals campaigns, with the veteran midfielder casting aside chatter about his personal life following the early year breakdown of his marriage to average 30 disposals a game heading into September. Will Ashcroft, despite being just 22, has received the backing of a Lions’ great to fill Lachie Neale’s void in 2027. Getty Images By his side, Ashcroft has cemented himself as one of the AFL’s brightest young stars, with the 22-year-old heading into the sudden death series on high, with his run of nine-straight games managing 30 or more touches only ending in the final round of the regular season.



Many believed Ashcroft was an unlucky exclusion from the All-Australian side, having been named in the initial 46-man squad only to miss the final 23. But against the Swans, he and Neale were kept quiet, combining for 39 disposals. However, Black, speaking as the AFL Premiership Cup Tour arrived at Brisbane’s Everton Park Wolves – the AFL Queensland Community Club of the Year – was adamant Ashcroft would not be kept down for long, was destined to break the shackles against the Crows on Saturday night. While the Lions were facing a reality of filling Neale’s void from next year – and possibly of Zac Bailey – he believed the two-time Norm Smith Medal winner had proved he was ready to lead the midfield into the future.



“He’s probably started to get a bit more opposition pressure with tagging and things, but he has a great work rate, and when you’ve got a great work rate you’ll get involved in the game if you react really quickly,” Black said. Related Article AFL 2026 ‘Mum lost her soulmate’: The tragic death driving premiership hero’s new mission “Will just keeps elevating his game, he was unlucky not to be an All-Australian ... but his ability to be so creative, he uses the ball so well, and he’s really jumped up. Lachie Neale was obviously the standout for so many years, and he’s really matching Lach most weeks now. “His ability to get boot to ball so quickly around the stoppages, to ask me what I love about him, I love his ability to get the ball out of congested areas and his decision-making, and his ability to get boot to ball with his creativity is really elite.” Brisbane will have to chart a similar path to the one they walked last year en route to the premiership. In 2025, they were humbled by Geelong in the opening week of the finals, only to bounce back emphatically and conquer the Cats on grand final day.



But there was something about the defeat against Sydney on Saturday night that has raised greater alarm bells. The Swans were without five players – including superstars Chad Warner and Isaac Heeney – after they were stood down as an investigation into sexual assault allegations continues. Skipper Callum Mills also succumbed to a serious knee injury, but Sydney rallied to triumph by 53-points. Black admits he “wasn’t overly confident at half-past-five on Saturday afternoon” that the Lions would have the mettle to conduct the same fightback as last season, given the nature in which their defensive pressure completely left them at the SCG. Loading However, the three-time premiership hero believed his former club had the know-how to rectify those misgivings again, having already demonstrated that this year.



After their last loss – a 76-point drubbing against Carlton – they went on a three-game winning streak with victorious margins of 67 (Hawks), 42 (Suns) and 63 (Magpies), while before that, they won seven-straight following three successive fadeouts. Black empathised with the physical and mental toll Brisbane’s run of deep finals campaigns has taken on the group – having himself felt that burden after four-straight grand final appearances for the Lions from 2001 to 2004. “It does become a little more fatiguing, but that’s the sport right? This is why you make the sacrifices and build resilience mentally and physically,” Black said. Michael Voss and Simon Black celebrate another of the three premierships wins in the 2000s. Vince Caligiuri But Black felt the “lethargic” group which rocked up to Sydney would not be seen again against Adelaide at the Gabba, as they chase a triple-title dynasty to rival that of his all-conquering outfits.



“We know the scoring power they have, so I just feel if they can find their defensive pressure they’ll kick a score close enough to winning. Defensive will in finals is so important, it wasn’t there Saturday,” Black said. “We’ve seen the Lions have an ordinary game throughout the season and bounce back. I’ll be surprised if they don’t do that this Saturday night.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Charged because of my political beliefs’: Palmer represents himself in $12m court case
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts ‘Charged because of my political beliefs’: Palmer represents himself in $12m court case Cloe Read September 7, 2026 — 4:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Billionaire businessman Clive Palmer has claimed criminal charges against him are politically motivated, as he represented himself in court in a long-running fraud case centred on a transfer of $12 million between his companies. Palmer was charged in 2020 following an Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) investigation into the transfers from his mining company, Mineralogy, to other companies, including the now-defunct Palmer United Party. The 72-year-old faces several charges, including fraud, over allegations he authorised the transactions while he was Mineralogy’s director. Billionaire businessman Clive Palmer outside Brisbane Magistrates Court on September 7. Cloe Read Palmer, who represented himself in the Brisbane Magistrates Court on Monday, argued for the case to be adjourned based on an appeal relating to infringement of his human rights.



The prosecution told the court the appeal had already been dismissed. Palmer said recently disclosed correspondence from current Solicitor-General Warren Day for the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions referred to significant ongoing media or political interest in his case. He said Day called the proposed prosecution of Palmer a “try-on”, firstly by the Australian Federal Police, then by ASIC and the Chinese-owned City Group. “I don’t think I should have been charged with something because of my ... political beliefs,” he said. “At that time, I was a leader of a federal party, which had the balance of power in the senate, and this charge reflected badly upon it.”



He argued the case should be adjourned until his other matter was heard, and submitted that if not, there would be a danger that court resources would be wasted. Palmer said he would also make an application to the United Nations about his human rights. He said multiple tranches of evidence had been disclosed to him since he was first charged, and he was still unable to properly assess whether the prosecution had disclosed all its evidence. Prosecutor Dane Marley, for the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions, asked for the case to be adjourned for a hearing to address the various applications Palmer had already made. The court heard there were four applications before the court, and Palmer foreshadowed there would be more from his defence.



Magistrate Cameron McKenzie adjourned the case to October 23. Outside court, Palmer referred to Day’s correspondence being written in 2015, when he was a leader of a political party that had “been successful in protecting the Australian people against the Abbott budget”. “The two documents that came up today was a letter from Warren Day, currently solicitor-general for the CDPP, where he said he thinks the prosecution against me is a try-on,” he said. Palmer said the letter was written during a time when there was a “lot of frustration” in government about him “rocking the boat”. “So it was good that these letters are finally released after nearly 10 years because it’s a serious thing for anyone to be charged with a criminal offence,” he said.



“And after all the final analysis, I’m charged with taking what is my own money and using it on my own endeavours.” He denied his legal strategy was focused on delay tactics, saying he was at the court in person to represent himself. “Well, I enjoy it, especially when you’re winning and you’re telling people the truth,” he said. World.title: Bringing internet feeds to heel is not suppressing free speech
World.content:
PoliticsFederalSocial media Editorial Bringing internet feeds to heel is not suppressing free speech The Herald's View Editorial September 7, 2026 — 4:20pm

September 7, 2026 — 4:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Albanese government’s proposed digital duty of care reforms aim to give Australians the right to use social media feeds free of algorithms, and to force platforms to stop harm before it occurs rather than respond to individual complaints about content. But the reforms are now running a gauntlet of spurious claims that the legislation will suppress freedom of speech. For under 18s, areas of “psychosocial harm” will be identified, including content about body image and bullying. iStock Social media companies will have to give users a choice to turn off their algorithm through pop-up messages. The government is also considering a Greens demand requiring internet users to opt in to algorithms to secure the legislation’s passage. The onus will be put on social media companies to identify and mitigate risks on their platforms and prevent the sharing of harmful content, including illegal pornography, being made available to adults. For under 18s, about half a dozen additional areas of “psychosocial harm” would be identified, including content about body image and bullying, and the companies face fines of $100 million-plus for breaching the law. Whether the legislation contains the ability to opt in or opt out, the reforms raise many questions and carry potential problems.



But free speech is not one of them. The reforms will not stymie free speech, but rather give people agency over their choices. The new legislation complements the Albanese government’s world-leading law to delay access to social media until the age of 16. It also follows the recent death of a 16-year-old girl in a suspected case of sexual choking that highlighted the ubiquity of violent pornography and misogynistic content on social media. It prompted Teach Us Consent chief executive and founder Chanel Contos’ #fixourfeeds campaign to renew her call for the introduction of an opt-in feature for social media algorithms, designed to prevent young men’s feeds from being flooded by default with misogynistic content. At such a febrile time, and with help seemingly on the way, politicians, technology companies, privacy advocates and free speech groups have joined the pile-on, attacking the reforms as censorship, ineffectual and bad for business. Liberal leader Angus Taylor dismissed the legislation as an attempt to censor social media, while Nationals leader Matt Canavan said he wanted “to protect my kids against radical transgender ideologies” but doubted whether that was the government’s main intent.



One Nation leader Pauline Hanson even evoked a Big Brother future, saying Australia should be moving away from government censorship, instead of building Orwellian machinery. Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership Hanson, Coalition ready to fight Labor’s plan to tame social media feeds The rise of One Nation, of course, has been inflated by the fact-free free-for-all that circulates in right-wing media circles, so Hanson predictably criticised the government’s existing social media legislation as a complete failure. Social media remains alive with 16-year-olds. It will be difficult to convince 17-year-olds to opt out. But we should persist, not least because we’re fed up with unwelcome guests. People once could close their doors on trespassers. But social media intruders, both wanted and unwanted, are already inside our home computers and mobiles. The tech companies have rarely been asked to wait outside. Until now. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Infini drill bit hunts 7.5% uranium source in Canada
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Infini drill bit hunts 7.5% uranium source in Canada Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward September 7, 2026 — 4:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Infini Resources has fired up the drill rig for a significant 5000-metre diamond drilling campaign at its Portland Creek uranium project in Newfoundland, Canada, marking the start of the most extensive exploration program ever undertaken at site. The current program, which has been expanded fivefold, will include the first-ever drill test of the demagnetised granite, believed to lie beneath the rock scree slope at the Falls Lake prospect. It is an enticing target, given previous soil sampling in the area returned a stunning peak result of 7.5 per cent uranium oxide. That work defined a high-grade surface anomaly stretching some 800m by 100m. Infini Resources has kicked off a phase three drilling program at its Portland Creek uranium project in Newfoundland, Canada. The phase three program represents a substantial test of what the company believes is a district-scale, underexplored hydrothermal uranium system. It follows a suite of modern exploration work, including airborne magnetic, electromagnetic and radiometric surveys, field mapping and a detailed reinterpretation of all available data. Infini’s exploration model at Portland Creek is centred on a structurally controlled, granite-hosted system. The company’s geologists have used high-resolution magnetic data to identify linear zones where the host granite has been altered by oxidising hydrothermal fluids, a process often conducive to the deposition of uranium.



‘The scale of what the geophysics has revealed is what drove us to expand this program so significantly.’ Infini Resources chief executive officer Rohan Bone Infini’s 5310m of phase two drilling has already confirmed the geological model, intersecting fracture-controlled uraninite mineralisation associated with chlorite and hematite alteration. The drill targets have been carefully selected to test areas where multiple datasets converge. Specifically, the company is targeting zones where interpreted structural intersections coincide with magnetic alteration footprints and known uranium anomalism from surface sampling and radiometric surveys. In parallel with the drilling, a 1000m trenching program continues to expose bedrock for structural mapping and radiometric assessment, which should help further sharpen drill targeting on the fly. Infini Resources chief executive officer Rohan Bone said: “Our 2026 airborne surveys, field program and reinterpretation of the project’s combined datasets have transformed Portland Creek from a scattering of uranium occurrences into a coherent, district-scale target set with defined geometry at depth and we are now drilling it.”



Infini’s 329-square-kilometre Portland Creek project covers a large regional uranium anomaly that was first identified by a government lake sediment sampling program in the 1970’s. Subsequent work has delineated a six-kilometre zone of anomalous uranium and radon gas in lake sediments, soils and airborne radiometric data. Meanwhile in Saskatchewan, the company has wrapped up the first-ever diamond drilling program at its Reynolds Lake and Reitenbach Lake uranium projects along the margin of the world-class Athabasca Basin. The maiden 16-hole campaign totalled 3314m and was designed to provide the first subsurface test of the project’s uranium potential,with assays pending. The Canadian push sits against a robust uranium backdrop supported by reactor life extensions, new nuclear builds and rising interest in reliable power as electricity demand grows. Western energy-security concerns are also focusing attention on politically aligned nuclear-fuel supplies, adding strategic weight to successful Canadian exploration. With the drill bit now turning on its most ambitious program to date, Infini is looking to see if the compelling surface evidence translates into a significant discovery lurking at depth. Given the spectacular grades unearthed at surface and a systematic approach to targeting, punters will likely be laser-focused on the first batch of assays from the lab. World.title: Two people killed in light plane crash south of Brisbane
World.content:
Updated NationalQueenslandAviation Two people killed in light plane crash south of Brisbane Julius Dennis and William Davis Updated September 7, 2026 — 4:12pm ,first published 11:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two people were killed when a light plane crashed into a paddock on a private property south of Brisbane on Monday morning. The Beech A36 Bonanza aircraft took off from Archerfield Airport shortly after 11am. It crashed 18 minutes later into a field along Musch Road in the Logan suburb of Stockleigh, sparking a grass fire. Emergency services at the crash site. William Davis “All I can tell you is the aircraft departed Archfield Airport ... as to what happened whilst that aircraft was in the air, we have no information at this time,” Logan district officer Chief Superintendent Mel Adams told reporters on Monday afternoon.



It took firefighters about an hour to gain control of the blaze, but a tree stump continued smouldering for hours. Adams said police were in the process of contacting the families of the pilot and passenger, and appealed for anyone who saw the plane in the air, or witnessed the crash to come forward. “The fire was quickly put out. It was a very confronting scene, as you can imagine,” she said. The scene of the light plane crash that killed two people. Nine News “What I would ask is for anybody who heard the aircraft, saw the aircraft in the air before it crashed in the Stockleigh area ... [or] for anybody that may have witnessed the aircraft hit the ground – it was close to a roadway, perhaps there is vehicle dashcam or something of that nature – please, as a matter of priority, contact police.”



Adams said the plane crashed in the vicinity of rural, residential homes. “But no [other] person was hurt, and there was no damage to other property,” she said. About a dozen emergency vehicles remained at the scene in the early afternoon, but fire teams and ambulances began leaving before 2pm. A smouldering tree stump that caught fire after the crash. William Davis The Australian Transport Safety Bureau has deployed a team of three investigators to the scene.



“Once on site from Monday afternoon they will commence evidence-gathering activities including site and wreckage examination, and the recovery of any aircraft components of interest for further examination,” a spokesperson said. “Investigators will also interview any witnesses and involved parties, and collect relevant recorded information including flight tracking data, as well as pilot and aircraft maintenance records, and weather information.” The ATSB asks anyone with video footage of the plane or the crash to send it to investigators via its website: atsb.gov.au/witness. World.title: Manhattan bites into high-grade gold at Canadian Jaws target
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Manhattan bites into high-grade gold at Canadian Jaws target Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward September 7, 2026 — 4:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Manhattan Gold Corporation has kicked another goal at the company’s Hook Lake project in Canada, with its maiden drilling campaign continuing to deliver high-grade gold and significantly expanding the footprint of its flagship Jaws prospect. The company’s latest results include a shallow, high-grade hit of 15.24 metres grading an impressive 5.35 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from just 35.05m downhole, contained within a broader 74.67 metre zone running 1.61g/t gold. A reverse circulation drill rig at the Jaws prospect targeting historic gold mineralisation at Manhattan Gold Corporation’s Hook Lake project in Nunavut, Canada. A second hole returned 7.62m at a hefty 7.05g/t gold from 82.3m within a wider 51.82-metre section at 1.88g/t gold. The hole also confirmed mineralisation at depth with 24.38m grading 1.15g/t gold from 204.22m. The drilling has materially expanded the footprint of the gold-bearing system at Jaws, materially extending it by more than 290m to the northeast and taking the total drill-tested strike length to 588m. Notably, the system has also been confirmed to a vertical depth of 223m, well below the extent of any historic drilling.



‘These results materially strengthen the case for both scale and grade at Jaws.’ Manhattan Gold Corporation technical; advisor Eric Sondergaard The results are the latest in a string of successes from Manhattan’s first-ever drill program at the project, which sits in the tier-one mining jurisdiction of Nunavut. Last month, the company’s first assays from Jaws returned an impressive intercept of 41.15 metres at 4.66g/t gold. Manhattan Gold Corporation technical advisor Eric Sondergaard said: “These results materially strengthen the case for both scale and grade at Jaws.We are now seeing grade, width and scale come together across a system that remains open at depth and along strike. Jaws is developing into a substantially larger and more compelling gold system than the historic work suggested.” Manhattan bought the Hook Lake project in mid-2025, picking up ground that hosted a historical, non-JORC “foreign” estimate from the late 1980’s of 3.4 million tonnes grading 2.38g/t gold for 285,000 ounces at Jaws. The 665-square-kilometre Hook Lake project runs along the underexplored Rankin-Ennadai greenstone belt, a geological feature that houses mining giant Agnico Eagle’s 6.7-million-ounce Meliadine operation, 225 kilometres to the northeast and one of Canada’s largest gold mines. Peers such as B2Gold and BG Gold are also advancing programs, underscoring the district-scale appetite for new ounces.



The company’s thesis was that modern exploration could build substantially on the old data, and its maiden drill program appears to be proving the point, consistently delivering thicker and higher-grade intercepts than the historic work. With Jaws now shaping up as a significantly larger and higher-grade gold system than historic work suggested, Manhattan is pushing ahead with metallurgical test work to lay the groundwork for future technical studies. And the news flow looks set to continue, with a further 14 drill holes from the current campaign still at the laboratory pending assay. The pending assays also include the first-ever drill tests of the company’s Spectre and Lotus prospects. Spectre is a high-grade volcanogenic massive sulphide target where historic drilling in 1974 returned impressive polymetallic hits including 10.51 metres at 2.91 per cent copper, 6.70 per cent zinc, 95.67g/t silver and 1.04g/t gold. The Lotus prospect, described as a “Jaws-style” gold target, has never been drilled despite rock chip sampling in 2025 returning high-grade results of 8.01g/t gold and 2660g/t silver. It’s one thing to pick up a project with a historical resource; however, it’s another to consistently punch out intercepts that are thicker and higher in grade than the old drilling. With a rapidly expanding mineralised footprint at Jaws and a conga line of assays still in the lab, the odds on Manhattan’s Canadian gold punt appear to be shortening fast. Skipper Callum Mills also succumbed to a serious knee injury, but Sydney rallied to triumph by 53-points. Black admits he “wasn’t overly confident at half-past-five on Saturday afternoon” that the Lions would have the mettle to conduct the same fightback as last season, given the nature in which their defensive pressure completely left them at the SCG. Loading However, the three-time premiership hero believed his former club had the know-how to rectify those misgivings again, having already demonstrated that this year.



After their last loss – a 76-point drubbing against Carlton – they went on a three-game winning streak with victorious margins of 67 (Hawks), 42 (Suns) and 63 (Magpies), while before that, they won seven-straight following three successive fadeouts. Black empathised with the physical and mental toll Brisbane’s run of deep finals campaigns has taken on the group – having himself felt that burden after four-straight grand final appearances for the Lions from 2001 to 2004. “It does become a little more fatiguing, but that’s the sport right? This is why you make the sacrifices and build resilience mentally and physically,” Black said. Michael Voss and Simon Black celebrate another of the three premierships wins in the 2000s. Vince Caligiuri But Black felt the “lethargic” group which rocked up to Sydney would not be seen again against Adelaide at the Gabba, as they chase a triple-title dynasty to rival that of his all-conquering outfits.



“We know the scoring power they have, so I just feel if they can find their defensive pressure they’ll kick a score close enough to winning. Defensive will in finals is so important, it wasn’t there Saturday,” Black said. “We’ve seen the Lions have an ordinary game throughout the season and bounce back. I’ll be surprised if they don’t do that this Saturday night.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Charged because of my political beliefs’: Palmer represents himself in $12m court case
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts ‘Charged because of my political beliefs’: Palmer represents himself in $12m court case Cloe Read September 7, 2026 — 4:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Billionaire businessman Clive Palmer has claimed criminal charges against him are politically motivated, as he represented himself in court in a long-running fraud case centred on a transfer of $12 million between his companies. Palmer was charged in 2020 following an Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) investigation into the transfers from his mining company, Mineralogy, to other companies, including the now-defunct Palmer United Party. The 72-year-old faces several charges, including fraud, over allegations he authorised the transactions while he was Mineralogy’s director. Billionaire businessman Clive Palmer outside Brisbane Magistrates Court on September 7. Cloe Read Palmer, who represented himself in the Brisbane Magistrates Court on Monday, argued for the case to be adjourned based on an appeal relating to infringement of his human rights.



The prosecution told the court the appeal had already been dismissed. Palmer said recently disclosed correspondence from current Solicitor-General Warren Day for the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions referred to significant ongoing media or political interest in his case. He said Day called the proposed prosecution of Palmer a “try-on”, firstly by the Australian Federal Police, then by ASIC and the Chinese-owned City Group. “I don’t think I should have been charged with something because of my ... political beliefs,” he said. “At that time, I was a leader of a federal party, which had the balance of power in the senate, and this charge reflected badly upon it.”



He argued the case should be adjourned until his other matter was heard, and submitted that if not, there would be a danger that court resources would be wasted. Palmer said he would also make an application to the United Nations about his human rights. He said multiple tranches of evidence had been disclosed to him since he was first charged, and he was still unable to properly assess whether the prosecution had disclosed all its evidence. Prosecutor Dane Marley, for the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions, asked for the case to be adjourned for a hearing to address the various applications Palmer had already made. The court heard there were four applications before the court, and Palmer foreshadowed there would be more from his defence.



Magistrate Cameron McKenzie adjourned the case to October 23. Outside court, Palmer referred to Day’s correspondence being written in 2015, when he was a leader of a political party that had “been successful in protecting the Australian people against the Abbott budget”. “The two documents that came up today was a letter from Warren Day, currently solicitor-general for the CDPP, where he said he thinks the prosecution against me is a try-on,” he said. Palmer said the letter was written during a time when there was a “lot of frustration” in government about him “rocking the boat”. “So it was good that these letters are finally released after nearly 10 years because it’s a serious thing for anyone to be charged with a criminal offence,” he said.



“And after all the final analysis, I’m charged with taking what is my own money and using it on my own endeavours.” He denied his legal strategy was focused on delay tactics, saying he was at the court in person to represent himself. “Well, I enjoy it, especially when you’re winning and you’re telling people the truth,” he said. World.title: Infini drill bit hunts 7.5% uranium source in Canada
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Infini drill bit hunts 7.5% uranium source in Canada Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward September 7, 2026 — 4:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Infini Resources has fired up the drill rig for a significant 5000-metre diamond drilling campaign at its Portland Creek uranium project in Newfoundland, Canada, marking the start of the most extensive exploration program ever undertaken at site. The current program, which has been expanded fivefold, will include the first-ever drill test of the demagnetised granite, believed to lie beneath the rock scree slope at the Falls Lake prospect. It is an enticing target, given previous soil sampling in the area returned a stunning peak result of 7.5 per cent uranium oxide. That work defined a high-grade surface anomaly stretching some 800m by 100m. Infini Resources has kicked off a phase three drilling program at its Portland Creek uranium project in Newfoundland, Canada. The phase three program represents a substantial test of what the company believes is a district-scale, underexplored hydrothermal uranium system. It follows a suite of modern exploration work, including airborne magnetic, electromagnetic and radiometric surveys, field mapping and a detailed reinterpretation of all available data. Infini’s exploration model at Portland Creek is centred on a structurally controlled, granite-hosted system. The company’s geologists have used high-resolution magnetic data to identify linear zones where the host granite has been altered by oxidising hydrothermal fluids, a process often conducive to the deposition of uranium.



‘The scale of what the geophysics has revealed is what drove us to expand this program so significantly.’ Infini Resources chief executive officer Rohan Bone Infini’s 5310m of phase two drilling has already confirmed the geological model, intersecting fracture-controlled uraninite mineralisation associated with chlorite and hematite alteration. The drill targets have been carefully selected to test areas where multiple datasets converge. Specifically, the company is targeting zones where interpreted structural intersections coincide with magnetic alteration footprints and known uranium anomalism from surface sampling and radiometric surveys. In parallel with the drilling, a 1000m trenching program continues to expose bedrock for structural mapping and radiometric assessment, which should help further sharpen drill targeting on the fly. Infini Resources chief executive officer Rohan Bone said: “Our 2026 airborne surveys, field program and reinterpretation of the project’s combined datasets have transformed Portland Creek from a scattering of uranium occurrences into a coherent, district-scale target set with defined geometry at depth and we are now drilling it.”



Infini’s 329-square-kilometre Portland Creek project covers a large regional uranium anomaly that was first identified by a government lake sediment sampling program in the 1970’s. Subsequent work has delineated a six-kilometre zone of anomalous uranium and radon gas in lake sediments, soils and airborne radiometric data. Meanwhile in Saskatchewan, the company has wrapped up the first-ever diamond drilling program at its Reynolds Lake and Reitenbach Lake uranium projects along the margin of the world-class Athabasca Basin. The maiden 16-hole campaign totalled 3314m and was designed to provide the first subsurface test of the project’s uranium potential,with assays pending. The Canadian push sits against a robust uranium backdrop supported by reactor life extensions, new nuclear builds and rising interest in reliable power as electricity demand grows. Western energy-security concerns are also focusing attention on politically aligned nuclear-fuel supplies, adding strategic weight to successful Canadian exploration. With the drill bit now turning on its most ambitious program to date, Infini is looking to see if the compelling surface evidence translates into a significant discovery lurking at depth. Given the spectacular grades unearthed at surface and a systematic approach to targeting, punters will likely be laser-focused on the first batch of assays from the lab. World.title: Two people killed in light plane crash south of Brisbane
World.content:
Updated NationalQueenslandAviation Two people killed in light plane crash south of Brisbane Julius Dennis and William Davis Updated September 7, 2026 — 4:12pm ,first published 11:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two people were killed when a light plane crashed into a paddock on a private property south of Brisbane on Monday morning. The Beech A36 Bonanza aircraft took off from Archerfield Airport shortly after 11am. It crashed 18 minutes later into a field along Musch Road in the Logan suburb of Stockleigh, sparking a grass fire. Emergency services at the crash site. William Davis “All I can tell you is the aircraft departed Archfield Airport ... as to what happened whilst that aircraft was in the air, we have no information at this time,” Logan district officer Chief Superintendent Mel Adams told reporters on Monday afternoon.



It took firefighters about an hour to gain control of the blaze, but a tree stump continued smouldering for hours. Adams said police were in the process of contacting the families of the pilot and passenger, and appealed for anyone who saw the plane in the air, or witnessed the crash to come forward. “The fire was quickly put out. It was a very confronting scene, as you can imagine,” she said. The scene of the light plane crash that killed two people. Nine News “What I would ask is for anybody who heard the aircraft, saw the aircraft in the air before it crashed in the Stockleigh area ... [or] for anybody that may have witnessed the aircraft hit the ground – it was close to a roadway, perhaps there is vehicle dashcam or something of that nature – please, as a matter of priority, contact police.”



Adams said the plane crashed in the vicinity of rural, residential homes. “But no [other] person was hurt, and there was no damage to other property,” she said. About a dozen emergency vehicles remained at the scene in the early afternoon, but fire teams and ambulances began leaving before 2pm. A smouldering tree stump that caught fire after the crash. William Davis The Australian Transport Safety Bureau has deployed a team of three investigators to the scene.



“Once on site from Monday afternoon they will commence evidence-gathering activities including site and wreckage examination, and the recovery of any aircraft components of interest for further examination,” a spokesperson said. “Investigators will also interview any witnesses and involved parties, and collect relevant recorded information including flight tracking data, as well as pilot and aircraft maintenance records, and weather information.” The ATSB asks anyone with video footage of the plane or the crash to send it to investigators via its website: atsb.gov.au/witness.
